Option C is doubly detective: the log never saw the tailgater, and end-of-shift review adds hours of delay to a record of an event it cannot contain. Match the control to the exploited mechanism. Tailgating is a throughput problem at the doorway, and only single-person interlocks close it.

questions.question: Regulators reviewing the bank's new fingerprint-enabled ATMs demand that a breach of the biometric database must not hand attackers images of customers' fingerprints. Which property of a well-designed biometric system should the design team cite in response?

options.A: Raw scans are retained, but encrypted under keys lodged with an independent escrow agent.
options.B: Only mathematical templates are stored, from which the original fingerprint image cannot be rebuilt.
options.C: Fingerprint images are hashed with SHA-256 at enrollment and compared by digest thereafter.
options.D: Scans are held solely at the central host as opposed to on the individual ATM units.

questions.explanation: Well-designed biometric systems never keep the picture: enrollment extracts a template, a mathematical summary of minutiae features, and matching compares fresh templates against it, so a stolen database yields feature vectors instead of reproducible fingerprint images, which is exactly the assurance the regulator asked for (B). A keeps the dangerous artifact and bets everything on key custody. Escrowed keys can be compelled, leaked, or stolen, and the moment they are, full images spill; escrow answers a lawful-recovery requirement, not a data-minimization one. C misapplies a password technique to fuzzy data: two scans of the same finger never match bit-for-bit, so cryptographic digests of images can never be compared successfully; the scheme simply does not function. D changes where the images sit, not whether they exist, and centralization may even raise the stakes by pooling every customer's biometric in one breachable place. Biometric privacy comes from storing derived, non-reversible templates; controls that merely encrypt or relocate raw images leave the irrevocable secret intact.

questions.question: A vendor pitches a proprietary cipher whose strength, it argues, comes from keeping the algorithm itself secret; a competitor offers standard AES with disciplined key management. On which principle should the security architect ground the recommendation between them?

options.A: Defense in depth: deploy both ciphers in layers so each covers the other's weaknesses.
options.B: Security through obscurity: an unpublished algorithm denies attackers the starting point that any practical cryptanalysis requires.
options.C: Kerckhoffs's principle: assume the algorithm is known and let security rest on the key alone.
options.D: Crypto-agility: select whichever cipher will be easiest to swap out in later years.

questions.explanation: Cryptography's foundational design rule is that a system must remain secure even when everything about it except the key is public. That is Kerckhoffs's principle, and it decides this vendor choice cleanly: AES has survived decades of open, worldwide analysis, while the proprietary cipher's secrecy is both its only defense and a guarantee it was never seriously reviewed (C). Option B is the pitch itself restated, and the reason it fails is practical: algorithms leak through reverse engineering, departing staff, and binary analysis, restoring the 'denied' starting point in full, and unlike a key, a leaked algorithm cannot be rotated. A misuses a sound principle as a tiebreaker dodge. Layering a weak cipher adds complexity and a false sense of margin, and depth was never meant to launder unvetted components into a design. Option D is a genuine engineering virtue that presupposes the question already answered: agility governs how easily you replace an algorithm, not which algorithm deserves trust today, and it would in fact argue for the standard, widely supported option. Trust ciphers that survive publication, not ciphers that depend on it never happening; secrecy belongs in keys, because keys can be changed.

stimuli.title: Nexus: the platform split
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank is replacing the fleet-management platform that administers its SlimLine terminals. Today it is one Windows server in the bank's own data center. The target design splits it four ways: a browser console for branch staff, an application tier of Linux containers on a shared cluster, event-driven functions at a cloud provider that reconcile cash balances overnight, and the legacy dispenser-control service, which nobody will rewrite and which will run as a guest on the bank's hypervisor. The migration board has ten weeks and no budget for a second cluster. Security must sign off on each tier separately, and the board meets once a month.

profile.organization: Nexus Bank · SlimLine subway ATM fleet
profile.environment: Browser console · shared container cluster · cloud functions · one hypervisor
profile.state: Ten weeks to migrate, four tiers to sign off separately

stimuli.title: Nexus: the SlimLine II program
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank has funded a replacement for its SlimLine subway terminal, the SlimLine II, after an interposer device fitted inside the original captured PINs at dozens of sites. The program board meets monthly and has just approved the architecture. Three decisions are still open: how the security requirements become a concrete control set, how the new dispenser interface will be joined to the existing transaction switch, and how 900 SlimLine units leave service. The bank's examiner has asked for evidence at each gate. Finance wants the retired units sold to a secondary-market refurbisher, which pays considerably more than a recycler does and collects from the branch loading dock.

profile.organization: Nexus Bank · SlimLine II replacement program
profile.environment: 900 SlimLine units in service · new dispenser interface · existing transaction switch
profile.state: Architecture approved, control set not yet chosen

stimuli.title: A device between the pad and the core
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank has recovered small interposer devices from dozens of its SlimLine subway terminals. Each sat on the internal USB bus between the encrypting PIN pad and the Windows core, reading keystrokes and injecting its own traffic. The cash dispenser accepted dispense commands from that unauthenticated device without question. The pad shipped with a compatibility mode enabled that sent the first keystrokes of each PIN in clear text unless an installer opted out. The bank assumes its communication keys will eventually be stolen and wants recorded past sessions to stay unreadable when that happens.

profile.environment: Encrypting pad on an internal USB bus to a Windows core · units in unattended public space
profile.state: Interposer devices recovered from dozens of machines

stimuli.title: What integrity measurement does not reach
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank's board wants to know why the controls it already paid for missed an interposer fitted inside its terminals. Every unit has a trusted platform module and measured boot. The network intrusion detection system watches all terminal traffic. Panel locks were the only barrier between passers-by and the internal bus, and the units stand in public subway space around the clock. Forensic examiners have since recovered a later device that never touched the data lines at all: it inferred PINs from tiny fluctuations in the pad's power draw as each digit was processed.

profile.environment: Trusted platform modules across the fleet · panel locks · network intrusion detection
profile.state: Board asking why existing controls missed it

stimuli.title: Designing the terminal that replaces it
stimuli.text: Calderwood Payments is designing the terminal that will replace its current self-service estate. The proposal treats the large general-purpose core as untrusted and runs all PIN handling inside a small sealed module. Engineers want a fleet in which even a fully compromised core would have no independent ability to dispense cash. They also want architectural assurance that when a customer types a PIN, the keystrokes reach the trusted hardware over a route software on the core cannot intercept or imitate, and that the link between the two carries nothing readable if another device is ever installed on it.

profile.environment: Thin-client design proposed · all PIN handling in a sealed module · untrusted general-purpose core
profile.state: Architecture under review, ten weeks to sign-off

stimuli.title: Buying cryptography that will still be acceptable
stimuli.text: Calderwood Payments is replacing the PIN-block encryption across its estate as part of a payment-industry compliance program, and wants a choice that will remain acceptable as the standards evolve. Procurement is drafting the requirements for replacement pads and wants independent, third-party assurance that the modules physically resist intrusion and erase their keys when the enclosure is breached. It will only buy software whose security functionality has been independently evaluated against a published protection profile. One vendor's pads ship with their protective configuration switched off unless the installer turns it on.

profile.environment: Triple-DES being phased out · replacement pads on tender · protection profile required
profile.state: Tender responses under evaluation

stimuli.title: Getting keys into thousands of machines
stimuli.text: Vessel Bank must load initial symmetric keys into thousands of new terminals across untrusted carrier networks, and each terminal has to verify that key-loading messages genuinely come from the bank's host. Once loaded, those keys protect PIN blocks in transit. Thieves have already captured a batch of encrypted PIN blocks and are attempting offline recovery by trying every possible key. A settlement dispute is separately running with a card processor over a batch file each side says the other sent. Thieves also pried a pad out of one machine and carried it off.

profile.environment: Thousands of new terminals · untrusted carrier networks · offline attacks on captured blocks
profile.state: Key bootstrapping design being approved

stimuli.title: Who really sent the instruction
stimuli.text: During a fraud investigation at Vessel Bank an administrator claims a disputed transfer order did not originate from her. The bank can show the order's signature could only have been produced by the private key on her personal smart card, and must explain to the regulator what that demonstrates. Two of the bank's host gateways separately need to agree a fresh session key across an untrusted carrier network with no pre-shared secret, and the key itself must never cross the wire. A data warehouse must let lower-clearance staff query a table that also holds covert investigation records.

profile.organization: Vessel Bank · fraud investigation and data services
profile.environment: Smart cards issued to administrators · warehouse serving cleared and uncleared staff
profile.state: Disputed transfer under investigation

stimuli.title: Stored passwords and the arithmetic against them
stimuli.text: An auditor at Linden Systems finds the fleet-management console stores administrator passwords as unsalted SHA-256 hashes, and notices two administrators who chose the same password have identical stored values. A cryptanalyst evaluating a vendor's proprietary cipher separately reports that flipping a single bit of plaintext changes only the corresponding byte of ciphertext. A code review of the console's log-encryption routine finds every record encrypted in CBC mode under the same fixed initialization vector, so identical entries produce identical ciphertext. Exploit developers have shown shellcode placed in a driver's data buffer and then executed.

profile.environment: Console passwords stored as unsalted digests · proprietary cipher under evaluation
profile.state: Audit findings open

stimuli.title: Conflicts of interest in a shared consultancy
stimuli.text: Harrow Advisory audits two banks that compete directly with each other, and management wants access enforcement in which a consultant who opens one bank's engagement files becomes dynamically barred from the other's, based on that access history. The same platform must offer kiosk users a guaranteed way to summon the genuine login screen that no application-level malware can imitate or suppress, after phishing simulations showed staff typing credentials into full-screen fakes. A new battery-powered device program needs asymmetric cryptography on a tight processor budget, with certificates small enough for a slow link.

profile.organization: Harrow Advisory · consultancy to competing banks
profile.environment: Engagement files for competing clients on one platform · constrained device program
profile.state: Access model being specified

stimuli.title: Managing rights, tenancy and identity
stimuli.text: Harrow Advisory's platform team is settling three designs at once. The console needs formal rules for how administrator subjects and device objects are created and deleted, and how access rights are granted, transferred and revoked between them. The firm subscribes to a vendor-hosted fleet application in which the vendor operates the servers, operating systems and application code while the firm's staff simply log in. A redesigned field unit will authorize transactions locally during connectivity outages and reconcile later. Regulators reviewing planned fingerprint enrollment want assurance about what a database breach would expose.

profile.regime: Client confidentiality agreements · cloud provider terms
profile.environment: Vendor-hosted fleet application · stand-in authorization at the edge · fingerprint enrollment planned
profile.state: Design decisions open across three areas

stimuli.title: Everything through one gate
stimuli.text: An engineer at Linden Systems proposes that every request from any process to reach the dispenser interface pass through a single small enforcement component that is tamper-proof, impossible to bypass, and small enough to be fully verified. On the same platform an engineer must encrypt high-volume transaction logs on hardware with a constrained processor, where symmetric keys can be provisioned to each unit securely in advance. A disgruntled developer at the software supplier has embedded a routine that will corrupt a driver on the first business day after his contract ends, and a data-loss investigation is running.

profile.environment: Single enforcement component proposed for the dispenser API · departing contractor with commit access
profile.state: Design and personnel risks under review

stimuli.title: Signals leaving by unintended routes
stimuli.text: An assessment of Stonebridge Rail's station payment machines has found malware signaling captured card numbers to a nearby receiver by modulating the fascia status LED, a component never intended to carry data. City planners are separately asking the operator where to site new walk-up machines so as to discourage both skimmer installation and robbery, without paying for guards. Fuzz testing has shown that a machine's USB driver crashes whenever a peripheral sends a malformed descriptor longer than 64 bytes, overwriting adjacent memory. A vendor is pitching a cipher whose strength rests on keeping the algorithm secret.

profile.environment: Machines in unattended concourses · fascia status LEDs · siting decisions with city planners
profile.state: Assessment findings under discussion

stimuli.title: One key for the whole estate
stimuli.text: Attackers opened the service panels of dozens of Stonebridge Rail's machines using a single stolen vendor key that fitted the entire estate. The operator wants to make sure one lost key can never again expose everything. Its assurance team is separately shortlisting two independently evaluated payment-pad products, one certified at a higher assurance level than the other, and the finance director wants to know what the higher number actually buys before approving the premium. A consultant is also modeling the payment platform formally, with account balances as constrained data and raw customer input arriving unconstrained.

profile.environment: One service-panel key fits every unit · two evaluated products shortlisted
profile.state: Control decisions pending

stimuli.title: Fitting out a data hall on the third floor
stimuli.text: Bramwell Mutual is fitting out a 380 square meter data hall on the third floor of a converted office building to run its claims platform. Twenty-two racks will draw 190 kW. The landlord's wet sprinkler risers cross the ceiling void above the hall and cannot be rerouted. One utility feed enters the building, and a 750 kVA generator in the car park has a fuel contract but has not been transfer-tested since it was installed. Badge readers on the two hall doors run from a controller mounted inside the hall itself. The fit-out design goes to the risk committee in three weeks.

profile.organization: Bramwell Mutual · claims platform data hall
profile.environment: 380 m² data hall · 22 racks · 190 kW · converted office building
profile.state: Fit-out design before the risk committee

stimuli.title: One forest, one local administrator password
stimuli.text: Wexford Pathology runs one Active Directory forest for 4,200 workstations across eleven laboratories. A March penetration test reached domain administrator from a single phlebotomy workstation in under two hours. The testers found the same local administrator password on every clinical workstation, sixty service accounts carrying service principal names with passwords last set in 2019, and a krbtgt account that has not been reset since the forest was built in 2014. Help desk staff sign in to user workstations with domain administrator credentials to clear print queues. The board has asked for a remediation sequence, in order, before the payer audit in October.

profile.environment: Single AD forest · 4,200 workstations · 60 service accounts with SPNs
profile.state: Sequencing remediation for the board

questionsV2.question: The browser console hides the cash-limit field from any user whose role is not permitted to change it. Which finding about that console design is MOST serious?

options.A: Authorization is enforced in console code the user controls, not on the server.
options.B: The console is served over TLS 1.2 and not TLS 1.3, which weakens the transport.
options.C: The console hides the field with client script instead of a server-rendered template.
options.D: The console does not write cash-limit changes to the bank's central audit repository.

questionsV2.explanation:
The console hides the field with script that runs on the user's machine. The user owns that machine, the script and the request. A hidden field can be restored from a developer console, or the request replayed with the field set, and Nexus has no server-side objection ready (A).
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-3 Access Enforcement puts the obligation on the system to enforce approved authorizations. OWASP Top 10:2025 files client-only enforcement under A01 Broken Access Control.
Decide where enforcement runs before deciding how the interface looks.
questionsV2.recallLine: A browser console hides a privileged field by role. What is the most serious design finding?

optionsShort.A: Client-side authorization, no server recheck
optionsShort.B: TLS 1.2 and not TLS 1.3
optionsShort.C: Script hiding, not server template
optionsShort.D: Changes not centrally logged

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: A real transport finding aimed at a different party. TLS protects the request from a third party on the wire, not from the sender.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: The symptom. A server-rendered page hides the field more tidily and the server still accepts whatever arrives.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Detective where the question asks for preventive. The log names whoever raised a limit, after the cash left.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 Access Enforcement
OWASP Top 10:2025 | A01 Broken Access Control

questionsV2.question: The migration will lift the existing server image into the new environment unchanged, including services nobody has used in three years. Which action BEST reduces the attack surface it carries across?

options.A: Run an authenticated vulnerability scan against the image and remediate the findings it reports.
options.B: Place the server behind a firewall that inspects traffic to each of its listening ports.
options.C: Rebuild the image from a documented baseline limited to the services the platform needs.
options.D: Deploy host-based intrusion detection so an unused service raises an alert when it is touched.

questionsV2.explanation:
Those unused services are capability the platform does not need. Rebuilding the image from a documented baseline limited to what the platform uses (C) takes them away.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-7 Least Functionality requires the system to provide only mission-essential capabilities, with defined functions, ports, protocols and services prohibited or restricted. CM-2 Baseline Configuration is where that configuration gets written down and held.
Remove capability first, then defend what is left.
questionsV2.recallLine: A legacy server image moves unchanged into a new environment. What best reduces the surface it carries?

optionsShort.A: Scan the image and remediate findings
optionsShort.B: Firewall in front of listening ports
optionsShort.C: Rebuild from a minimal documented baseline
optionsShort.D: Host intrusion detection on unused services

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: A correct action in the wrong order. A scan tells Nexus what is listening and removes none of it.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Governs who reaches a port. The question is whether the port should exist, and a shared cluster puts plenty of traffic inside the boundary.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Treats the service as permanent and waits for someone to touch it. That is detection where the stem asks for prevention.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 Least Functionality
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-2 Baseline Configuration

questionsV2.question: The application tier will pull its base images from a public registry at build time. Which control MOST directly addresses the risk that introduces?

options.A: Network policy restricting which pods in the cluster may open connections to each other.
options.B: Verification of a digital signature on every image before the cluster is allowed to run it.
options.C: Scanning each built image for known-vulnerable packages before it is promoted to production.
options.D: An immutable root filesystem in each container, so a compromised process gets no writes to disk.

questionsV2.explanation:
Pull an image by name and tag and the cluster runs whatever answers to that name. Both are attacker-controllable in a way a version number is not. Signature verification before the cluster may run the image (B) closes it.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-14 Signed Components requires the organization to prevent installation of defined components without verification that the component was signed with a certificate the organization recognizes and approves. SR-4 Provenance and SR-11 Component Authenticity carry the supply-chain half of the same obligation. NIST's dedicated container publication is SP 800-190, though the control obligation above stands on its own.
Decide what is allowed to run before deciding how it may behave.
questionsV2.recallLine: Base images come from a public registry at build time. Which control most directly addresses that risk?

optionsShort.A: Network policy between pods
optionsShort.B: Verify image signatures before running
optionsShort.C: Scan built images for known CVEs
optionsShort.D: Immutable root filesystem per container

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Network policy addresses lateral movement once a pod is already compromised. It says nothing about what was allowed to run.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Finds known-bad packages inside an image whose origin is still unverified. A malicious image with current packages sails through.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Limits what a running container may do, after an unverified image has already been admitted.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-14 Signed Components
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SR-4 Provenance; SR-11 Component Authenticity
NIST SP 800-190 (Application Container Security Guide), named as the dedicated source

questionsV2.question: The architects note that the provider patches the function runtime and isolates tenants. Given that division, which control should the bank's own review focus on MOST?

options.A: Hardening the guest operating system image the reconciliation functions run inside.
options.B: Agreeing an availability service level for the overnight reconciliation window.
options.C: Scheduling a quarterly vulnerability scan of the provider's platform endpoints.
options.D: Scoping each function's execution role to the permissions it actually needs.

questionsV2.explanation:
The provider owns the host, the runtime and the tenant boundary. What is left for Nexus to get wrong is the identity each function runs as and what that identity may reach (D). A function with a broad role is a standing credential that fires on a schedule with nobody watching.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 Least Privilege holds access authorizations to no more than necessary for assigned tasks. SA-9 External System Services requires the organization to define and document the roles and responsibilities of an external provider, which turns the division in the stem into a contractual fact the bank can hold someone to.
Ask what the provider has not taken away.
questionsV2.recallLine: A provider patches the runtime and isolates tenants. Where should the bank's own review concentrate?

optionsShort.A: Harden the guest operating system
optionsShort.B: Agree an availability service level
optionsShort.C: Quarterly scan of provider endpoints
optionsShort.D: Least-privilege execution role per function

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: The provider owns the runtime. There is no guest operating system image the bank controls to harden.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: An availability commitment. Useful, and a different surface from what the functions are permitted to reach.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Tests someone else's platform, where the bank holds neither authorization nor residual risk.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 Least Privilege
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-9 External System Services

questionsV2.question: The dispenser-control service will run as a hypervisor guest and the team plans to keep a snapshot of every release. Which practice MOST reduces the risk that arrangement creates?

options.A: Encrypting the guest's virtual disk so its contents are unreadable if the file is copied.
options.B: Restricting access to the hypervisor management console to a named administrator group.
options.C: Enrolling every guest and retained snapshot in the same inventory and patching program as physical hosts.
options.D: Taking a fresh snapshot before every change so the service can be rolled back quickly.

questionsV2.explanation:
A guest is created by an API call and a snapshot by a menu item. Virtual estates grow faster than the processes meant to govern them, and every retained snapshot is a complete machine holding whatever data it held on the day it was taken. Enrolling guests and snapshots in the same inventory and patching program as physical hosts (C) keeps them counted.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-8 System Component Inventory requires an inventory that accurately reflects the system and is updated as components are installed or removed. CM-2 Baseline Configuration governs what each of those components should look like. SA-22 Unsupported System Components is what a forgotten legacy guest eventually becomes. The catalog carries no hypervisor-specific control; the obligation rides on these general ones.
Count the machines before hardening them.
questionsV2.recallLine: A legacy service runs as a hypervisor guest and every release is snapshotted. What most reduces the risk?

optionsShort.A: Encrypt the guest's virtual disk
optionsShort.B: Limit hypervisor console access
optionsShort.C: Inventory and patch guests and snapshots
optionsShort.D: Snapshot before every change

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Protects a disk file at rest. It does not stop guests and snapshots accumulating outside the inventory.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Governs who administers the platform. Guests accumulate under any administrator.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Makes the problem bigger. A rollback measure that manufactures more of the artifacts the stem is worried about.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-8 System Component Inventory
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-2 Baseline Configuration; SA-22 Unsupported System Components

questionsV2.question: The program board asks how the SlimLine II's control set should be arrived at. Which sequence BEST describes a defensible selection?

options.A: Adopt the control set the previous SlimLine program used, then add controls for the new interface.
options.B: Categorize the system by impact, take the matching baseline, then tailor it with documented justification.
options.C: Take the highest baseline available and remove the controls the examiner agrees are not applicable.
options.D: Ask the examiner which controls it expects to see and build the set from that answer.

questionsV2.explanation:
Selection is a chain, and each link supplies the reason for the next (B). FIPS 199 Section 3 categorizes the system by the impact a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability would have. FIPS 200 Section 3 turns that category into an obligation to apply the corresponding minimum controls. NIST SP 800-53B Chapters 2 and 3 supply the Low, Moderate and High baselines and the tailoring guidance. SP 800-53 Rev 5 made both steps auditable in their own right with PL-10 Baseline Selection and PL-11 Baseline Tailoring, and SP 800-37 Rev 2 Section 3.3 walks the same ground as RMF tasks S-1 through S-6.
Categorize first, and the argument writes itself.
questionsV2.recallLine: How should a new terminal's control set be arrived at so the choice can be defended?

optionsShort.A: Reuse the previous program's control set
optionsShort.B: Categorize, take baseline, tailor with justification
optionsShort.C: Start highest and subtract by agreement
optionsShort.D: Build from what the examiner names

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Reuses a set chosen against the old terminal's categorization. The SlimLine II has a different interface and a different impact.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Starts at the top and subtracts. Tailoring stands in for selection, so nothing ever states what the system needs.

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Asks the examiner to do the system owner's job. The owner categorizes and selects; the examiner assesses what was done.

sources: FIPS 199 | Section 3, Security Objectives and categorization
FIPS 200 | Section 3, Minimum Security Requirements
NIST SP 800-53B | Chapters 2 and 3, baselines and tailoring
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PL-10 Baseline Selection; PL-11 Baseline Tailoring
NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 | Section 3.3 SELECT, tasks S-1 to S-6

questionsV2.question: The new dispenser interface and the existing transaction switch were built by different teams against the same written specification. Which activity is MOST likely to expose a defect neither team's own testing found?

options.A: A static analysis run over each team's source code against the bank's coding standard.
options.B: A penetration test of the assembled terminal conducted after it has entered production.
options.C: A design review comparing each team's architecture document with the approved specification.
options.D: Integration testing of the assembled interfaces against cases where the two readings disagree.

questionsV2.explanation:
Two teams reading one specification produce two specifications. The gap between them is invisible to any test that examines one side alone, which is why integration testing against cases where the readings disagree (D) is the activity most likely to find it.
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 Appendix H.8 Integration is the lifecycle process that synthesizes system elements into a realized system. It is the first activity that exercises the seam, so interface and composition weaknesses surface there. SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-3 Information Exchange governs the resulting connection; Rev 5 renamed it from the Rev 4 title System Interconnections, so material still using the older name is dated.
Test the joint.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two teams built either side of one interface from one specification. What best exposes a seam defect?

optionsShort.A: Static analysis per team
optionsShort.B: Penetration test after production
optionsShort.C: Design review against the specification
optionsShort.D: Integration testing where readings disagree

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Tests each element on the terms each team already passed. The gap between two readings of one specification stays invisible.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Arrives after the terminal is live, once the cheapest moment to fix a seam has gone.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Compares a document with a document. The defect lives in behavior.

sources: NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.8 Integration
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-3 Information Exchange (renamed from Rev 4 System Interconnections)

questionsV2.question: Fifty SlimLine II units are ready and the board wants them in service this quarter. Which condition should the security lead insist on BEFORE the first unit is cut over?

options.A: A documented back-out procedure and the retained configuration the units would be restored to.
options.B: A signed statement from the vendor that the units meet the approved specification.
options.C: A penetration test report covering the units in their final production configuration.
options.D: An updated asset inventory listing each unit's serial number and installation site.

questionsV2.explanation:
Cutover turns a design into an operating system, and reversibility is the property that makes it survivable. Insist on a documented back-out procedure and the retained configuration to restore to (A).
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-2(3) Baseline Configuration | Retention of Previous Configurations exists for exactly this. It requires a defined number of previous baseline versions to be retained to support rollback, and its discussion counts hardware, software, firmware, configuration files and records among them. NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 Appendix H.10 Transition frames the wider obligation: preserve the system's verified security characteristics through an orderly, planned move into the operational environment.
Never move something you cannot move back.
questionsV2.recallLine: Fifty new terminals are ready to cut over. What condition should the security lead insist on first?

optionsShort.A: Back-out procedure and retained configuration
optionsShort.B: Vendor statement of conformance
optionsShort.C: Penetration test of production build
optionsShort.D: Updated asset inventory

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: Evidence the bank weighs. It remains the vendor's word, and the bank owns the gate.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Belongs earlier in the lifecycle, at the verification gate. A report is also no way back.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Needed to operate the fleet. It does nothing to make the first fifty units reversible.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-2(3) Retention of Previous Configurations
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.10 Transition
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 Configuration Change Control

questionsV2.question: Finance wants the 900 retired SlimLine units sold to a refurbisher. Which step MOST directly addresses the disposal risk the security lead must sign off?

options.A: A contract clause making the refurbisher liable for any data recovered from the units.
options.B: Removing each unit from the asset inventory once the refurbisher confirms collection.
options.C: Sanitizing every storage component to a level matched to the data it held, with verification recorded.
options.D: Physically destroying the encrypting PIN pad in each unit before the units leave the site.

questionsV2.explanation:
A retired terminal is a filing cabinet on wheels: card data, logs, keys, configuration and whatever a technician once copied to it locally. Sanitize every storage component to a level matched to the data it held, and record the verification (C).
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 MP-6 Media Sanitization requires media to be sanitized before disposal, release out of organizational control or release for reuse, using defined techniques and procedures. SR-12 Component Disposal, new in Rev 5, extends that to the component itself. SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 Appendix H.14 Disposal is the lifecycle process, and it includes removing information and deactivating accesses and dependencies. NIST SP 800-88 decides between clear, purge and destroy; cite it without pinning a revision, because Revision 1 was withdrawn on 26 September 2025 and superseded by Revision 2.
Sanitize to the data, not to the device.
questionsV2.recallLine: Retired terminals are being sold to a refurbisher. What most directly addresses the disposal risk?

optionsShort.A: Contractual liability on the refurbisher
optionsShort.B: Retire units from the asset inventory
optionsShort.C: Sanitize storage to the data's level, verified
optionsShort.D: Destroy each encrypting PIN pad

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Moves liability to the refurbisher. The data still leaves the building.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: A records step that follows sanitization. Do it first and the bank erases its own account of what left.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Treats one component while customer data sits on the terminal's other storage.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | MP-6 Media Sanitization; SR-12 Component Disposal; SI-12(3) Information Disposal
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.14 Disposal
NIST SP 800-88 (revision not pinned: Rev 1 withdrawn 2025-09-26, superseded by Rev 2)

questionsV2.question: Which design change would MOST directly address the dispenser accepting commands from an unauthenticated device?

options.A: Require the dispenser and the PC core to establish a mutually authenticated, encrypted session before commands are accepted.
options.B: Deploy application allow-listing on the Windows core so unauthorized executables are unable to run.
options.C: Install a firewall between the ATM and the bank host to filter suspicious dispense traffic.
options.D: Fit tamper-evident seals to every service panel so that any future shim installation is discovered during scheduled servicing.

questionsV2.explanation:
The dispenser obeyed any device on the bus because nothing required the sender to prove its identity. The fix has to make the dispenser verify its controller. With a mutually authenticated, encrypted session (A), a future interposer can neither read PIN traffic nor issue commands the dispenser will accept.
Physical presence on a bus is not authorization. Peripherals should authenticate their controller.
questionsV2.recallLine: A shim on the ATM's internal USB bus made the cash dispenser obey its commands. Which design change MOST directly removes that weakness?

optionsShort.A: Mutually authenticated encrypted session before commands
optionsShort.B: Application allow-listing on the Windows core
optionsShort.C: Firewall between the ATM and bank host
optionsShort.D: Tamper-evident seals on every service panel

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Real hardening aimed at a different threat. The shim never executed code on Windows, so allow-listing would never engage.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Guards the wrong boundary. The attack lived on the internal USB link and never crossed the external network a firewall inspects.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Detective where the question asks for preventive. Seals reveal the intrusion at the next inspection, after the cash is gone.

questionsV2.question: Given the device read keystrokes and injected its own traffic, which classification is MOST appropriate in the threat taxonomy?

options.A: A replay attack, because previously captured valid messages were retransmitted to the host.
options.B: A race condition, because the shim won a timing window during the EPP's startup handshake.
options.C: A denial of service, because the legitimate encrypted channel was ultimately disrupted.
options.D: An on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack, because an interposed device read and injected traffic.

questionsV2.explanation:
A third device sat inside a two-party communication path, eavesdropping and originating traffic. That is the definition of an on-path or man-in-the-middle attack (D). The 50-millisecond plaintext window at startup is how it got in; the classification comes from where it sat.
Name attacks by their mechanism. Interception plus injection on a path means an on-path attacker.
questionsV2.recallLine: A device seated on the PIN pad's USB link both read keystrokes and injected its own. Which threat classification MOST accurately names that mechanism?

optionsShort.A: Replay of previously captured valid messages
optionsShort.B: Race condition during the startup handshake
optionsShort.C: Denial of service disrupting the channel
optionsShort.D: On-path interception and injection by interposed device

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: A narrower technique the shim did not need. Replay is re-sending captured legitimate messages to trick a receiver.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: A race condition is a concurrency flaw where two processes contend for shared state. The shim listened during a window the protocol created.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Mistakes a side effect for the goal. Service continued normally, which is what let the theft run undetected.

questionsV2.question: Which placement of PIN encryption BEST ensures an attacker with full control of the Windows core never sees a key or a cleartext PIN?

options.A: Store the keys inside a TPM on the motherboard and let the operating system perform the PIN encryption.
options.B: Encrypt PINs with a software library on the core, keeping the keys obfuscated inside the application binary.
options.C: Perform encryption inside the PIN pad's dedicated hardware security module, so keys and cleartext stay out of the core.
options.D: Hold the keys on a self-encrypting drive that unlocks automatically once the ATM boots successfully.

questionsV2.explanation:
The requirement assumes the core is already compromised. Encryption therefore has to happen before data touches the core, inside a tamper-resistant boundary that performs the cryptography and refuses to export its keys. An HSM-class PIN pad (C) is that boundary.
If the host is untrusted, the cryptography must live in hardware the host cannot see into.
questionsV2.recallLine: An attacker owns the ATM's Windows core completely. Which placement of PIN encryption BEST keeps every key and cleartext PIN out of that attacker's reach?

optionsShort.A: Keys in the TPM, encryption in the OS
optionsShort.B: Software library with keys obfuscated in the binary
optionsShort.C: Encrypt inside the PIN pad's hardware security module
optionsShort.D: Self-encrypting drive unlocking automatically at boot

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: A TPM protects keys at rest. The encryption still runs in the operating system, exposing the cleartext PIN and working key in host memory.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Security through obscurity. Obfuscated keys in a binary come out easily for anyone who owns the operating system.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Protects stored data on the drive, and its automatic unlock at boot means a running, compromised system reads everything.

questionsV2.question: A low-integrity unauthorized device wrote commands to the high-integrity dispenser. Which formal model MOST directly describes the rule that was violated?

options.A: Bell-LaPadula, whose simple security property forbids reading data at a higher classification.
options.B: Biba, whose star integrity axiom forbids a subject writing up to higher-integrity objects.
options.C: Brewer-Nash, which partitions access to prevent conflicts of interest between clients.
options.D: Clark-Wilson, which channels every change through certified well-formed transactions enforcing separation of duties.

questionsV2.explanation:
A low-integrity subject wrote to a high-integrity object. Biba's star integrity axiom, 'no write up', prohibits exactly that (B).
Untrusted wrote to trusted: name Biba. Changes bypassed certified procedures: name Clark-Wilson.
questionsV2.recallLine: An unauthorized low-integrity device wrote commands to the high-integrity cash dispenser. Which formal model MOST directly states the rule that violation broke?

optionsShort.A: Bell-LaPadula: no reading above your classification
optionsShort.B: Biba: no writing up to higher integrity
optionsShort.C: Brewer-Nash: partition to prevent conflicts of interest
optionsShort.D: Clark-Wilson: certified transactions with separation of duties

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Bell-LaPadula governs confidentiality. Its rules say who may read secrets, and nothing was read up here.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Brewer-Nash solves a different problem: walling off datasets dynamically so one consultant cannot serve competing clients.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: An integrity model too, but Clark-Wilson works through certified transformation procedures and duty separation, with no rule on writes.

questionsV2.question: Which cryptographic property should the engineer specify so recorded past sessions stay unreadable after a key theft?

options.A: Perfect forward secrecy, deriving each session key from an independent ephemeral exchange.
options.B: Key stretching, increasing the computational cost of deriving keys from short secrets.
options.C: Key escrow, lodging recoverable copies of the master key with a trusted third party.
options.D: Zero-knowledge authentication, proving possession of a key without transmitting it.

questionsV2.explanation:
Compromise of a long-term key must leave earlier captured traffic unreadable. That is perfect forward secrecy (A). Each session key comes from an ephemeral agreement such as ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, so no stored master secret decrypts old recordings.
Forward secrecy is about the past. It decouples yesterday's traffic from tomorrow's key compromise.
questionsV2.recallLine: The bank expects its long-term communication keys to be stolen eventually. Which cryptographic property keeps sessions recorded before that theft unreadable afterwards?

optionsShort.A: Perfect forward secrecy from ephemeral session keys
optionsShort.B: Key stretching to slow derivation from short secrets
optionsShort.C: Key escrow with a trusted third party
optionsShort.D: Zero-knowledge proof of key possession

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Key stretching makes low-entropy secrets like PINs and passphrases slower to brute-force. It says nothing about recorded sessions.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Works against the requirement. Escrow creates another copy of key material, enlarging the set of secrets whose theft exposes traffic.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Keeps the authentication exchange itself from disclosure and says nothing about how session traffic keys are derived.

questionsV2.question: What is the MOST accurate assessment of whether measured boot would have stopped a bus interposer?

options.A: Secure boot would have detected the shim, because the TPM measures every USB peripheral attached at power-on.
options.B: Secure boot would have stopped the dispenser from accepting commands lacking a valid digital signature.
options.C: Secure boot protects bootloader and firmware integrity, but a bus interposer sits outside what it measures.
options.D: Secure boot becomes effective against hardware implants once it is combined with full-disk encryption.

questionsV2.explanation:
Measured and secure boot validate signatures over firmware, bootloader and OS components, so they defeat persistent software and firmware tampering. A passive electrical device inserted on a cable never enters that chain of measurements (C).
Secure boot answers whether the software stack is authentic. It never answers whether the wiring is trustworthy.
questionsV2.recallLine: Every terminal has a TPM and measured boot, yet a bus interposer went unnoticed. What is the MOST accurate assessment of what boot verification covers?

optionsShort.A: TPM measures every USB peripheral at power-on
optionsShort.B: Boot verification would reject unsigned dispense commands
optionsShort.C: Boot measurement covers firmware, not a bus device
optionsShort.D: Secure boot needs full-disk encryption alongside

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Overstates the TPM's reach. Platform configuration registers record boot-time software measurements, not attached USB hardware.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Confuses two mechanisms. Authenticating dispense commands is a job for mutual authentication on the peripheral link.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Bolts on an unrelated control. Full-disk encryption protects data at rest on the drive and does nothing about a live interposer.

questionsV2.question: An engineer argues network intrusion detection should have caught it. What is the MOST accurate response?

options.A: Physical-layer tampering inside the chassis is invisible to network monitoring; detection requires hardware integrity controls at the device.
options.B: The network IDS would have seen the shim with its sensor placed inline to the bank host.
options.C: Enabling deep-packet inspection on the existing sensors would have revealed the injected dispense commands.
options.D: Correlating the carrier's NetFlow records against transaction logs would have exposed the additional device.

questionsV2.explanation:
Monitoring sees only traffic that reaches its sensor. PIN capture and command injection both happened on an internal peripheral bus that never touches the network stack, so no network tool at any placement had visibility. The detectable evidence lives in hardware integrity checks, peripheral authentication failures and tamper alarms at the device (A).
Trace where the malicious traffic actually flows before crediting a monitoring control. A sensor on the wrong bus detects nothing, however deeply it inspects.
questionsV2.recallLine: An engineer insists the network IDS should have caught the interposer inside the terminal chassis. What is the MOST accurate response to that claim?

optionsShort.A: Chassis-internal tampering is invisible to network monitoring
optionsShort.B: Inline sensor placement would have seen it
optionsShort.C: Deep-packet inspection would reveal the injected commands
optionsShort.D: NetFlow correlated against transaction logs exposes the device

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Moves the sensor and keeps the blind spot. Inline placement sees ATM-to-host traffic, and the dispenses were injected downstream of it.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Deepens inspection of the same wrong stream. Deep-packet inspection parses payloads crossing the network; these commands crossed USB.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Correlating NetFlow with transaction logs flags the theft's accounting shadow at reconciliation. The device itself stays invisible.

questionsV2.question: Which attack category should the forensic report record for the later device?

options.A: A covert channel exploiting an unauthorized signaling path between cooperating processes.
options.B: A brute-force attack enumerating the PIN space until a matching value was found.
options.C: A fault-injection attack inducing computational errors to make the device expose key material.
options.D: A side-channel attack recovering secrets from the physical emanations of the device.

questionsV2.explanation:
The attacker learned secrets by observing unintended physical byproducts of computation: power consumption, timing, electromagnetic emission. That is side-channel analysis (D). The device leaked; nobody inside it was transmitting.
Passive observation of emissions is a side channel. Deliberate signaling over a forbidden path is a covert channel. The discriminator is whether a cooperating sender exists.
questionsV2.recallLine: A recovered device inferred PINs from fluctuations in the pad's power draw without touching the data lines. Which attack category should the forensic report record?

optionsShort.A: Covert channel between cooperating processes
optionsShort.B: Brute-force enumeration of the PIN space
optionsShort.C: Fault injection forcing errors that expose keys
optionsShort.D: Side-channel recovery from physical emanations

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: A covert channel needs a cooperating sender, such as an implant modulating an LED. Here there is only an observer.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Describes exhaustive guessing against the credential itself, which the attacker specifically avoided by measuring.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Means actively disturbing the device with voltage glitches or clock manipulation to force faulty outputs. This shim was purely passive.

questionsV2.question: In the defense-in-depth review, which weakness should the assessor flag as the PRIMARY enabler of the installation?

options.A: Transaction traffic to the host traversed shared cellular carrier infrastructure.
options.B: The modular design connected security-critical internal components with cheap, widely available industry-standard cables.
options.C: Maintenance staff shared one common login for the fleet-management console.
options.D: A single, quickly defeated physical lock guarded direct access to the internal bus.

questionsV2.explanation:
Every step of the attack depended on reaching the bus, and one commodity lock in an unattended public space was the whole barrier. A single physical layer where depth was needed most: that is the enabling failure (D).
Rank findings by their position on the actual kill chain. The primary enabler is the control whose failure unlocked everything downstream.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which weakness should the assessor flag as the PRIMARY enabler of an interposer being fitted inside terminals standing unattended in public subway space?

optionsShort.A: Traffic crossed shared cellular carrier infrastructure
optionsShort.B: Security-critical parts joined by commodity standard cables
optionsShort.C: Maintenance staff shared one console login
optionsShort.D: A single easily defeated lock guarded the bus

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Describes a real exposure this attack never used. The shim worked entirely inside the chassis.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Deserves a finding of its own. Commodity USB made the shim cheap to build, but standard interfaces bite only once an attacker is inside.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: A genuine identity-management weakness with no causal link to this incident.

questionsV2.question: Replacement locks must resist picks and bump keys and identify who opened each panel and when. Which choice BEST meets both?

options.A: High-security pin-tumbler locks with restricted keyways and patent-protected key blanks.
options.B: Warded locks re-keyed uniquely per ATM so that one key opens only a single unit.
options.C: Electronic locks with per-technician credentials and centrally logged opening events.
options.D: Paired wafer locks installed so the panel opens only with two keys turned together.

questionsV2.explanation:
The requirement has two halves and one option carries both. An electronic lock removes the mechanical keyway, which defeats picking and bumping outright, and per-technician credentials produce the attributable log the bank asked for (C).
Read compound requirements as an AND. A control that excels at one clause and silently drops the other is a wrong answer.
questionsV2.recallLine: Replacement panel locks must resist picks and bump keys and record who opened each panel and when. Which lock choice BEST meets both requirements?

optionsShort.A: High-security pin-tumbler locks with restricted keyways
optionsShort.B: Warded locks re-keyed uniquely per machine
optionsShort.C: Electronic locks with per-technician credentials and logging
optionsShort.D: Paired wafer locks needing two keys together

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: The strong runner-up on covert entry. A mechanical key leaves no record of who used it, so the audit half of the requirement fails.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Improves key management and worsens attack resistance. Warded locks are among the easiest designs to defeat, one machine at a time.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Adds dual control, valuable for cash loading. Wafer mechanisms are readily picked, and two anonymous keys write no audit trail.

questionsV2.question: Which architecture BEST ensures a fully compromised core cannot dispense cash on its own?

options.A: Client-side validation, with the core checking each withdrawal against locally stored business rules.
options.B: A peer-to-peer design in which nearby ATMs cryptographically cross-check and vouch for each other's transactions.
options.C: A thin-client design in which dispensing requires a cryptographically signed authorization from the bank host.
options.D: A distributed ledger recording every dispense event across the fleet for later reconciliation.

questionsV2.explanation:
Assume the machine in the field is hostile and the authority to move money has to live somewhere else. A thin-client dispenser acts only on instructions signed by the bank host, so a compromised core can request cash and can no longer conjure an approval (C).
Put authorization authority on the most trustworthy tier and make the exposed tier an executor of signed instructions.
questionsV2.recallLine: Engineers want a terminal fleet in which even a fully compromised core cannot dispense cash on its own. Which architecture BEST delivers that guarantee?

optionsShort.A: Core checks withdrawals against locally stored rules
optionsShort.B: Neighboring ATMs cryptographically vouch for each other
optionsShort.C: Thin client; host signs every dispense authorization
optionsShort.D: Distributed ledger recording dispenses for later reconciliation

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Puts the decision inside the component being distrusted. Local rules are the attacker's rules once the core falls.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Relocates trust sideways. Peer ATMs share the same hardware, software and exposure, so a fleet-wide flaw compromises the voters too.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Detective by construction. An immutable record proves afterwards that cash left, and by then the money is gone.

questionsV2.question: Which architectural concept does concentrating PIN handling in a small sealed module BEST illustrate?

options.A: Concentrating security functions in a minimal trusted computing base, isolated from untrusted components.
options.B: Sandboxing, which confines a single untrusted application inside a restricted, monitored runtime environment.
options.C: Virtualization, which runs the sensitive workload inside a hypervisor-managed guest machine.
options.D: Network segmentation, which divides the system into zones separated by filtering devices.

questionsV2.explanation:
Sealing PIN handling into one small, verifiable, physically hardened element shrinks the set of components that must be trusted. That is the trusted computing base argument, and a small TCB is easier to protect and evaluate than a sprawling one (A).
Minimizing and isolating the TCB is the architectural move. Sandboxes, hypervisors and network zones are tools that can implement it.
questionsV2.recallLine: Calderwood's design runs all PIN handling inside one small sealed module. Which architectural concept does that concentration BEST illustrate?

optionsShort.A: Minimal trusted computing base, isolated from untrusted parts
optionsShort.B: Sandboxing: untrusted code confined in a restricted runtime
optionsShort.C: Virtualization: sensitive workload inside a hypervisor guest
optionsShort.D: Network segmentation into zones separated by filters

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Inverts the relationship. Sandboxing contains something untrusted inside restrictions; here the trusted element is what gets isolated.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Names a technology and skips the principle. Nothing here requires virtual machines, and a guest leans on the hypervisor's trustworthiness.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: The right instinct at the wrong layer. Zones and filtering describe network topology; this boundary sits inside one device.

questionsV2.question: Which concept should the requirements document cite for the protected route from the keypad to the trusted hardware?

options.A: An air gap, physically disconnecting the security hardware from all other system components.
options.B: A trusted path, a protected channel linking the user directly to the trusted computing base.
options.C: Covert channel analysis, verifying that no unauthorized signaling routes exist in the design.
options.D: An out-of-band channel, carrying the authentication data across a separate network dedicated to management traffic.

questionsV2.explanation:
A channel between the human and the TCB that untrusted software can neither eavesdrop on nor spoof is a trusted path (B). It is the same idea as the secure attention key on a workstation login.
When the threat is the user's own machine lying between them and the TCB, the requirement is a trusted path. A separate or encrypted route is a different promise.
questionsV2.recallLine: Keystrokes must reach the sealed module by a route software on the core cannot intercept or imitate. Which concept should the requirements document cite?

optionsShort.A: Air gap disconnecting the security hardware entirely
optionsShort.B: Trusted path from the user to the TCB
optionsShort.C: Covert channel analysis of the design
optionsShort.D: Out-of-band channel on a separate management network

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Proves too much. A fully disconnected EPP could never deliver the encrypted PIN block for the transaction at all.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: An assurance activity. Covert channel analysis hunts a design for unintended leakage paths and protects no PIN entry by itself.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Moves the traffic to a different network and still runs it through ordinary software stacks, leaving the compromised host at the endpoint.

questionsV2.question: Which proposal MOST effectively protects PIN data even if another interposer is physically installed later?

options.A: Shorten the internal cable run and route it through a locked metal conduit inside the chassis.
options.B: Replace the standard USB connectors with a proprietary keyed plug that commodity shim hardware does not fit.
options.C: Disable all of the core's unused USB ports through centrally managed operating-system group policy objects.
options.D: Encrypt and authenticate all traffic on the link, end to end from the EPP to the host.

questionsV2.explanation:
The question stipulates that an interposer gets installed anyway. The winning control therefore has to make interception worthless. End-to-end encryption with authentication does that: the shim sees ciphertext and its injected commands fail authentication (D).
Assume the adversary reaches the wire and protect the data on the wire. Controls that only gate access lose to the stipulated breach.
questionsV2.recallLine: Assume another interposer is fitted on the internal link later. Which proposal MOST effectively protects the PIN data despite that installation?

optionsShort.A: Shorter cable inside a locked metal conduit
optionsShort.B: Proprietary keyed plug commodity shims do not fit
optionsShort.C: Group policy disabling the core's unused ports
optionsShort.D: Encrypt and authenticate the link end to end

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Raises the physical effort and leaves the payoff intact. Defeat the conduit and the same plaintext flows. A delay control, not a fix.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Security through obscurity in hardware form. A gang that already manufactures custom shims will tool a proprietary connector.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Misses the topology. The shim splices into an in-use cable between two authorized devices, so disabling unused ports never touches it.

questionsV2.question: A partner program must confine information flow so material moves only upward or laterally within compartments, each user bounded by labels. Which approach is the MOST natural fit?

options.A: Role-based access control, mapping users to permissions through defined job functions.
options.B: Discretionary access control, letting document owners share their files as they judge best.
options.C: Lattice-based access control, assigning each subject upper and lower bounds over labels.
options.D: Rule-based access control, evaluating each request against an ordered list of conditions.

questionsV2.explanation:
Bounded flow between ordered labels and compartments is the lattice structure itself (C). Every subject and object sits at a point in a partially ordered set, each pair of labels has a least upper and greatest lower bound, and models like Bell-LaPadula and Biba are enforced over that scaffolding. The stem's 'highest and lowest labels' is the lattice's defining feature.
Label dominance, compartments and bounded flow point to a lattice. The named models are policies riding on it.
questionsV2.recallLine: A partner program must confine information flow upward or laterally within compartments, each user bounded by a highest and lowest label. Which approach fits MOST naturally?

optionsShort.A: Role-based: permissions mapped to job functions
optionsShort.B: Discretionary: owners share files at their judgment
optionsShort.C: Lattice: subjects bounded between upper and lower labels
optionsShort.D: Rule-based: an ordered list of conditions

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Organizes permissions around job function. A role grants what it grants, with no notion of dominance or of forcing information upward.

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: The opposite philosophy. Owner discretion is what mandatory flow control exists to remove, and an owner could share downward at will.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Generic machinery. Firewall-style condition lists carry no inherent ordering, so the flow guarantees would live in hand-maintained rules.

questionsV2.question: Which selection BEST aligns with where the payment standards are heading as legacy algorithms are retired?

options.A: RC4, because a fast stream cipher minimizes latency on the slow serial links.
options.B: AES, which the standards bodies are adopting as legacy triple-DES is phased out.
options.C: SHA-256, providing a stronger one-way transformation of each PIN block.
options.D: Single DES with unique per-transaction keys derived under the DUKPT scheme.

questionsV2.explanation:
PIN blocks need a strong, standards-approved block cipher that host security modules can translate, and the industry direction is explicit. PCI PIN requirements and the ISO 9564 format-4 PIN block move the ecosystem from triple-DES to AES (B).
Check the algorithm and its key management against the current standard. A strong scheme cannot rescue a retired cipher.
questionsV2.recallLine: Calderwood is replacing PIN-block encryption across the estate. Which choice BEST aligns with where payment standards are heading as legacy algorithms retire?

optionsShort.A: RC4 stream cipher chosen for low latency
optionsShort.B: AES, as triple-DES is phased out
optionsShort.C: SHA-256 hashing of each PIN block
optionsShort.D: Single DES with DUKPT per-transaction keys

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Fails twice over. RC4 has well-known keystream biases and has been withdrawn from security protocols, and no payment standard permits it.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: The wrong primitive. A hash is one-way, and the acquiring host has to translate and verify the PIN block, which needs reversible encryption.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Wraps a good key-management scheme around a dead cipher. A 56-bit DES key is brute-forceable however often DUKPT changes it.

questionsV2.question: Which contractual requirement BEST captures physical intrusion resistance and key erasure on tamper?

options.A: Common Criteria evaluation of the vendor's product at assurance level EAL1.
options.B: Validation of the cryptographic module at FIPS 140-3 Level 3 or higher.
options.C: Vendor attestation of an ISO/IEC 27001-certified information security management system.
options.D: FIPS 140-3 Level 1 validation of the module's approved cryptographic algorithm implementations.

questionsV2.explanation:
Physical tamper resistance and zeroization of keys on enclosure breach are what FIPS 140-3 introduces at Level 3, with Level 4 adding environmental attack protection. Accredited independent laboratories perform the validation (B).
Match the certification to the object being assured, product or organization. Then check that the level actually mandates the property you need.
questionsV2.recallLine: Procurement wants independent assurance that replacement pads physically resist intrusion and erase their keys when the enclosure is breached. Which contractual requirement BEST captures both?

optionsShort.A: Common Criteria evaluation at assurance level EAL1
optionsShort.B: FIPS 140-3 Level 3 module validation or higher
optionsShort.C: Vendor attestation of an ISO 27001 management system
optionsShort.D: FIPS 140-3 Level 1 algorithm implementation validation

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Independent evaluation at the wrong depth. EAL1 is functional testing, and Common Criteria wants tamper response only if the profile does.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Certifies the vendor's management system. An organization with a fine ISO/IEC 27001 program can still ship a probeable PIN pad.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: The correct standard at the wrong level. FIPS 140-3 Level 1 imposes essentially no physical security beyond production-grade components.

questionsV2.question: Which framework should the procurement team reference for independently evaluated, comparable assurance ratings?

options.A: FIPS 140-3, which validates cryptographic modules against tiered government security requirements through accredited laboratories.
options.B: ISO/IEC 27002, which catalogs organizational security controls with detailed implementation guidance for practitioners.
options.C: Common Criteria, ISO/IEC 15408, which evaluates product security claims to graded assurance levels.
options.D: PCI DSS, which sets baseline requirements for any entity handling cardholder data.

questionsV2.explanation:
Independent laboratories, published protection profiles, graded EAL ratings, a mutual recognition arrangement spanning national schemes: every element the stem lists is Common Criteria, ISO/IEC 15408 (C).
Independently evaluated product, comparable assurance level, recognized internationally: that is Common Criteria. Standards for organizations or single components solve different problems.
questionsV2.recallLine: Calderwood will only buy software independently evaluated against a published protection profile. Which framework should procurement reference for comparable, internationally recognized ratings?

optionsShort.A: FIPS 140-3 validation of cryptographic modules
optionsShort.B: ISO 27002 catalog of organizational control guidance
optionsShort.C: Common Criteria graded product assurance levels
optionsShort.D: PCI DSS baseline for cardholder data handlers

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Narrower than the need. FIPS 140-3 validates one class of component, cryptographic modules, not a whole product's security functionality.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Addresses the organization. ISO/IEC 27002 is a catalog of controls to implement, with no evaluation, rating or product certificate attached.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Compliance where the stem wants comparative assurance. PCI DSS sets a baseline for entities handling cardholder data and grades no products.

questionsV2.question: Which design principle, applied at manufacture, would have removed the shipped-insecure exposure?

options.A: Least privilege, limiting every component to the minimum permissions its function requires.
options.B: Separation of duties, dividing sensitive operations between two independent parties.
options.C: Defense in depth, layering independent, overlapping controls along every stage of the attack path.
options.D: Secure defaults, shipping the device with its protective configuration active from the start.

questionsV2.explanation:
Encryption existed. The exposure was that the insecure state was the out-of-box state, and safety took deliberate action. Reversing that is secure defaults (D): ship encrypted-only and make legacy mode the explicit, documented exception.
When the unsafe option is what you get unless someone intervenes, the missing principle is secure defaults.
questionsV2.recallLine: One vendor's pads ship with their protective configuration switched off unless the installer turns it on. Which design principle, applied at manufacture, removes that exposure?

optionsShort.A: Least privilege: minimum permissions for each component
optionsShort.B: Separation of duties across two independent parties
optionsShort.C: Defense in depth: layered overlapping controls
optionsShort.D: Secure defaults, with protection enabled at shipment

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Governs what a subject is permitted to do. The pad's rights were never the problem; the configuration it shipped with was.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Applies to human processes such as key ceremonies, where one person should not complete a sensitive act alone.

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: The near-winner. More layers would have limited the damage, and layering on top of an insecure default leaves the root cause where it is.

questionsV2.question: Which cryptographic approach BEST satisfies both key transport and proof of origin over untrusted networks?

options.A: AES key wrap protected by a single fleet-wide pre-shared transport key.
options.B: HMAC values appended to each key block to demonstrate its authenticity.
options.C: Asymmetric cryptography, using public keys for transport and signatures for origin.
options.D: Independent password-derived keys generated locally at each individual terminal.

questionsV2.explanation:
Bootstrapping is the giveaway. Before any shared secret exists, only public-key techniques can move a secret across a hostile network and prove who sent it. Encrypt the key under the terminal's public key, sign the load under the host's private key: the pattern of remote key loading schemes (C).
Symmetric methods maintain trust that already exists. Establishing trust from nothing over an untrusted channel is asymmetric cryptography's defining job.
questionsV2.recallLine: Vessel Bank must load initial keys into thousands of terminals over carrier networks, each terminal verifying the host sent them. Which cryptographic approach BEST satisfies both?

optionsShort.A: AES key wrap under one fleet-wide transport key
optionsShort.B: HMAC appended to each key block
optionsShort.C: Public keys for transport, signatures for origin
optionsShort.D: Password-derived keys generated locally at each terminal

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Presupposes the problem solved. The fleet-wide transport key has to be distributed first, and it recreates the shared-master-key weakness.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Circular in the same way. An HMAC verifies origin only for parties that already share the MAC key, so it establishes no first contact.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Produces keys and no relationship. Independently derived local keys are unknown to the host, so terminal and host could never transact.

questionsV2.question: Which mechanism BEST gives every future batch file proof of origin the sender cannot disavow, plus evidence of tampering?

options.A: Encrypt each file with AES under a key shared between the two organizations.
options.B: Digitally sign each file with the sender's private key under a managed PKI.
options.C: Attach an HMAC computed with a secret key that both organizations hold.
options.D: Record a SHA-256 checksum of every transmitted file in the operations log.

questionsV2.explanation:
Settling a he-said-she-said takes evidence a neutral third party can verify against exactly one possible originator. A digital signature does that. Only the holder of the private key could have produced it, and any alteration breaks verification, so integrity and non-repudiation arrive together (B).
Non-repudiation demands an asymmetric secret. Any mechanism built on a shared key collapses the moment the two key-holders point at each other.
questionsV2.recallLine: Vessel Bank and a card processor each blame the other for the disputed batch file. Which mechanism BEST proves origin undeniably and detects tampering?

optionsShort.A: AES encryption under a shared organizational key
optionsShort.B: Digitally sign with the sender's private key
optionsShort.C: HMAC computed with a key both hold
optionsShort.D: SHA-256 checksum recorded in the operations log

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Addresses none of the requirement. Shared-key encryption hides content and leaves origin unprovable; either side can decrypt and dispute.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: The classic trap. An HMAC proves integrity and origin between the two parties, and because both hold the key, either could have made it.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Detects accidental corruption at best. Anyone can recompute an unkeyed SHA-256 over a modified file and update the log.

questionsV2.question: The stolen module erased its key material before extraction completed. Which capability acted, and which risk did it MOST directly reduce?

options.A: Zeroization on tamper, denying the thieves any use of the bank's cryptographic keys.
options.B: Full-disk encryption, keeping the stored transaction records unreadable after the theft.
