optionsShort.D: Cloud edge enforcing identity and device posture

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Genuinely fixes the latency complaint and can be driven from one console. Enforcement still keys on the segment a device sits in.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Buys capacity. The concentrators stop being the bottleneck and the trust model is untouched.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Inserts another hop into the datacenter the traffic was already crossing, which is the opposite of what a latency complaint asks for.

sources: NIST SP 800-207 | Zero Trust Architecture, policy decision and enforcement points
NIST SP 800-215 | Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.1.11 Secure access service edge

questionsV2.question: Wren Valley Water treats 38 million liters a day. Its plant network carries 60 programmable logic controllers and four operator stations still running Windows 7, all on one flat VLAN reachable from the corporate network through a routed firewall rule opened years ago for the historian. During the last assessment an authenticated vulnerability scan crashed a chlorine dosing controller and the plant ran on manual dosing for six hours. The controller vendor withdraws support if operating system patches are applied outside its validated bundles, which arrive once a year. Which measure BEST reduces risk under those constraints?

options.A: Divide the plant network into zones joined by conduits that pass historian data outbound to a broker
options.B: Run the authenticated vulnerability scan monthly instead of annually, inside the maintenance window
options.C: Install endpoint detection agents on the four operator stations and on the historian server
options.D: Apply the operating system patches within thirty days and accept the loss of vendor support

questionsV2.explanation:
Three facts in the stem are the ordinary conditions of an operational technology environment: a vendor bundle that arrives annually, controllers that fall over when actively probed, and a treatment process that cannot be stopped. Between them they rule out the controls an enterprise IT team reaches for first. What is left is to change what can reach the controllers at all (A). IEC 62443-3-3 builds its entire system requirement set on zones and conduits. NIST SP 800-82 Rev 3 gives the same advice for control systems that cannot be patched on an IT cadence: compensate with segmentation and one tightly specified data path.
In operational technology the first question is how to shrink what may speak to the endpoint.
questionsV2.recallLine: A water plant runs unpatchable controllers on one flat VLAN, and a scan has already crashed one. Which measure BEST reduces risk?

optionsShort.A: Zones and conduits passing historian data outbound
optionsShort.B: Scan monthly inside the maintenance window
optionsShort.C: Endpoint detection agents on the operator stations
optionsShort.D: Patch within thirty days, lose vendor support

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: The activity that produced the six-hour manual run. Twelve times a year multiplies an outage risk and touches no exposure.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: A sound control on a Windows host the vendor lets you instrument, and a support-voiding change on a validated operator station.

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Trades a certain loss of vendor validation, a real problem for the safety case, against a patch cadence the plant cannot consume.

sources: IEC 62443-3-3 | System security requirements and security levels, zones and conduits
NIST SP 800-82 Rev 3 | Guide to Operational Technology Security, network segmentation
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.5.5 Operational Technology/ICS

questionsV2.question: Ravensmoor Legal has moved matter files for 4,000 active cases onto a multi-tenant software-as-a-service platform. Under the contract the firm may not deploy an agent, may not scan the application and has no access to the underlying hosts, and the provider encrypts everything at rest under keys the provider generates and holds. A partner asks what would happen if the provider were served a subpoena for the firm's files, or if one of the provider's administrators were bribed. Which control gives the firm the GREATEST technical ability to keep provider staff from reading matter files?

options.A: Route every user session through a cloud access security broker running in reverse-proxy mode
options.B: Negotiate an annual right to audit the provider's access controls and administrator activity
options.C: Encrypt matter files under keys the firm generates and holds in its own hardware security module
options.D: Enable the provider's at-rest encryption on every tenant volume and rotate those keys quarterly

questionsV2.explanation:
A subpoena served on the provider and a bribed provider administrator are one technical problem: somebody inside the provider can turn stored ciphertext into readable files with the firm taking no part. The location of the key is what changes that.
Generate the key at Ravensmoor and keep it in a module the firm operates (C). Every decryption then becomes a call to a service the firm can log, delay and refuse, and a silent disclosure becomes an event the firm witnesses. The partner should also hear the limit: the platform still handles plaintext while a user has a file open, so what this removes is the provider's unilateral ability to produce readable data at rest.
In this service model the customer's remaining leverage is the key, the identity and the log. Everything else has been handed over.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which control gives a law firm the GREATEST technical ability to stop a provider's own administrators reading its matter files?

optionsShort.A: Access broker in reverse-proxy mode
optionsShort.B: Annual right to audit provider access
optionsShort.C: Firm-held keys in its own hardware module
optionsShort.D: Provider-held keys rotated every quarter

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Governs which users and devices reach the tenant and what they may download. It sees nothing of what an administrator does inside.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: The right instrument for assurance about the provider's controls, and it would surface a weak process. An audit right is a promise.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Leaves the key with the party the partner is asking about. Rotating it changes nobody's ability to read the files.

sources: NIST SP 800-144 | Guidelines on Security and Privacy in Public Cloud Computing, key management
NIST SP 800-145 | The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, service models
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.5.6 Cloud-based systems

questionsV2.question: Thornbury Metering is specifying 40,000 gas meters with a twelve-year field life, mounted inside customer premises and reachable over a low-power wide-area network. The draft specification already mandates AES-128 on the radio link and a tamper switch on the enclosure. The security architect has room for one more mandatory clause before the tender closes, and the finance director has ruled out funding any mid-life hardware refresh. Which requirement MOST reduces the fleet's security exposure across the whole twelve years?

options.A: A unique credential and device certificate provisioned to each meter during manufacture
options.B: A signed firmware update path the meter authenticates, refusing rollback to earlier images
options.C: A hardware secure element holding the radio key outside the microcontroller's readable flash
options.D: A daily heartbeat to the head end so a removed or silent meter is noticed

questionsV2.explanation:
Twelve years outlasts every cryptographic and software assumption in the draft, and the finance director has just removed the option of replacing the hardware. The ability to change the software in the field is therefore the clause everything else depends on (B). A fleet that can be updated can be given a new algorithm, a new certificate chain and a fix for a defect nobody has found yet. A fleet that cannot is frozen at the security of its tender document.
Refusing older images belongs in the same clause. An update path that accepts a previously signed build lets an attacker reinstate a vulnerability the vendor already closed. NISTIR 8259A lists device software update as a core baseline capability for that reason.
For any device you will struggle to reach again, ask first what you would do if a flaw were published next year.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which specification clause MOST reduces exposure across twelve years for 40,000 field meters that will never be refreshed?

optionsShort.A: Unique credential and certificate per meter
optionsShort.B: Authenticated firmware updates with rollback protection
optionsShort.C: Secure element holding the radio key
optionsShort.D: Daily heartbeat to the head end

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Strong, and it belongs in the specification too. It acts once at manufacture, and a 2026 certificate expires inside the field life.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Defends one secret against one attack: flash extraction from a meter somebody has unscrewed. The software stays exactly as shipped.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Tells the head end that a meter has gone quiet. Useful detection, arriving after whatever happened to the meter has happened.

sources: NISTIR 8259A | IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline, software update
ETSI EN 303 645 | Provision 5.3, keep software updated
NIST SP 800-193 | Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines, rollback protection

questionsV2.question: Calderhall Aerospace operates an internal certificate authority whose root is trusted by every workstation, server and build agent in the company. A supplier that manufactures a flight-control subassembly has asked Calderhall to issue it a subordinate certificate authority, so the supplier can sign its own device certificates without anyone installing a second trust anchor on Calderhall machines. The security architect is willing in principle but wants to bound what a compromise of the supplier's authority key could do. Which measure MOST limits the damage such a compromise would cause?

options.A: Require the supplier to hold the subordinate authority key inside a validated hardware security module
options.B: Require the supplier to publish a revocation list every twenty-four hours for certificates it issues
options.C: Issue the subordinate with a twelve-month validity period, renewed after each supplier audit
options.D: Issue the subordinate with critical name constraints that permit the supplier's own namespaces alone

questionsV2.explanation:
A subordinate authority inherits the reach of the root that signed it. Write no restriction into the certificate and a key stolen from the supplier can mint a certificate for any name Calderhall's estate trusts: the payroll system, the code-signing service, the identity provider. Every workstation accepts it, because the chain validates.
RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.10 defines the name constraints extension for this exact case (D). Marked critical, with permitted subtrees covering the supplier's domains, a conforming relying party rejects anything issued outside them whoever holds the key, and a pathLenConstraint of zero stops the supplier delegating further.
Likelihood, duration and blast radius are three different answers. Only one of them is enforced by the relying party.
questionsV2.recallLine: A company will issue a supplier a subordinate certificate authority. Which measure MOST limits what a compromise of that key reaches?

optionsShort.A: Supplier key held in a validated module
optionsShort.B: Supplier publishes a revocation list daily
optionsShort.C: Twelve-month validity renewed after each audit
optionsShort.D: Name constraints binding it to supplier namespaces

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: A real and standard requirement that makes theft less likely. The question is what the theft would reach, and a module says nothing.

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: How the two parties would react afterwards. A client that cannot fetch the revocation list, or soft-fails, trusts the forged certificate.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Shortens the window and leaves the width alone. A twelve-month subordinate compromised in month two is wide open for the remaining ten.

sources: RFC 5280 | Section 4.2.1.10, Name Constraints
RFC 5280 | Section 4.2.1.9, Basic Constraints and pathLenConstraint
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 | Recommendation for Key Management, trust anchors

questionsV2.question: Meridian Clearing leases a dark-fiber pair between two datacenters and protects it with a layer-2 encryptor at each end. During a cable inspection an engineer finds an optical splitter spliced into the run inside a third-party manhole, feeding a recorder that has been sitting there for roughly fourteen months. The recorder captured traffic and did nothing else: it could not inject frames, it never reached a host, and the encryptors' management ports sit on a separate out-of-band network. Which weakness MOST determines what fourteen months of recording is worth to whoever collected it?

options.A: The encryptors return a distinguishable error frame when a received frame fails its integrity check
options.B: The encryptors derive every session key from one pre-shared secret configured at install
options.C: The encryptors will negotiate down to a legacy cipher suite whenever a peer advertises it
options.D: The certificate each encryptor presents carries no revocation distribution point for a relying peer

questionsV2.explanation:
Start from what the collector can do. A splitter in a manhole yields recorded ciphertext: no frame submitted, no host touched, no negotiation influenced. That is a ciphertext-only position, and it rules out three of the four items in front of the engineer.
What matters to a passive collector is whether the recording stays worthless. Fourteen months of frames whose session keys all descend from one installation-time secret have no forward secrecy (B). Obtain that secret later, from a decommissioned chassis, a configuration backup or a departing engineer, and the whole archive opens at once. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 sets cryptoperiods for this reason, and MACsec key agreement rekeys a live association for the same one.
Intercepted ciphertext is worth whatever the chance of recovering its key is worth. How strong the cipher looked on the day it was chosen decides nothing.
questionsV2.recallLine: A passive optical tap recorded fourteen months of encrypted link traffic. Which weakness MOST determines the value of that recording?

optionsShort.A: Distinguishable error frame on integrity failure
optionsShort.B: One install-time secret behind every session key
optionsShort.C: Negotiates down to a legacy cipher suite
optionsShort.D: Certificates carry no revocation distribution point

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: An oracle, and an oracle needs a questioner. A recorder in a manhole cannot ask.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: A downgrade takes an attacker present in the negotiation in real time. This one is reading a tape afterwards.

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Concerns a peer deciding whether to trust a certificate. The collector is no peer.

sources: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 | Cryptoperiods and the consequences of key compromise
IEEE 802.1X-2020 | MACsec Key Agreement, session key derivation and rekeying
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.2 Ciphertext only

questionsV2.question: Aldergate Logistics exchanges shipment files with 60 carriers. Each carrier is given a static 256-bit key at onboarding, and files are protected with a stream cipher whose keystream is generated from that key and nothing else. Every file opens with the same 106-byte interchange header, whose layout is published in the trading standard. One carrier's archive, several thousand files under a single carrier key, has appeared for sale on a criminal forum. Which change BEST reduces what an analyst can recover from that archive and from future exchanges?

options.A: Compress each file before encrypting it, so that the repeated header structure largely disappears
options.B: Move each carrier from a 256-bit key to a 512-bit key issued on the same cadence
options.C: Derive the keystream from the key and a random value chosen afresh for every file
options.D: Add a keyed message authentication code over each file so a modified one is rejected

questionsV2.explanation:
One key and no per-file variation means the cipher has produced the same keystream for every file it ever protected for that carrier. Exclusive-or any two of the several thousand ciphertexts and the keystream cancels. What remains is the combination of two plaintexts, and 106 bytes of published header at the front of each gives an analyst the crib to unwind them.
Known plaintext alone is not the defect; a fixed header is public in almost every format. The defect is that header plus keystream reuse, and one change attacks the reuse. Feed a fresh random value into the generator for every file (C) and no two files share a keystream. That is why every modern stream construction takes a nonce as an argument and why NIST SP 800-38A insists an initialization vector be unpredictable and unrepeated.
Wherever a stream cipher appears, ask first whether any keystream has been used twice.
questionsV2.recallLine: Thousands of shipment files share one stream-cipher key and a published 106-byte header. Which change BEST limits what an analyst recovers?

optionsShort.A: Compress each file before encrypting it
optionsShort.B: Move each carrier to a 512-bit key
optionsShort.C: Fresh random value in each file's keystream
optionsShort.D: Authentication code detecting a modified file

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Sound advice that does reduce redundancy. Two files under one repeated keystream still cancel to the combination of two plaintexts.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Answers a brute-force problem this archive does not pose. Nobody searches a key space when the keystream repeats.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Supplies integrity, worth having, and no help at all to a reader of files that have already been stolen.

sources: NIST SP 800-38A | Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation, initialization vectors
RFC 8439 | ChaCha20 and Poly1305, nonce uniqueness requirement
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.3 Known plaintext

questionsV2.question: Meridian Health Analytics warehouses 4.1 million claim rows. So that business intelligence users can group and join on it, the diagnosis group column is encrypted deterministically: identical plaintext always yields identical ciphertext under the column key. The column carries nine distinct values across the whole table, and one of them, the behavioral health group, is the value the privacy office cares about most. Analysts hold read access to the encrypted table and no access to the key. Which exposure should the architect raise as the GREATEST?

options.A: An analyst can rank the nine ciphertexts by row count and match them against published prevalence
options.B: An analyst can infer the ordering of the nine values and reconstruct the ranges between them
options.C: An analyst can submit a known ciphertext in a predicate and confirm one patient's group
options.D: Backups written before the column key was last rotated stay readable under the retired key

questionsV2.explanation:
Determinism is what makes the join work and what makes the column countable. Nine distinct ciphertexts over 4.1 million rows is a distribution, and a distribution over a small published domain is a solved problem. One grouping query, sort the counts, line them up against national prevalence figures for the nine groups (A). No key is needed, no cryptography is broken, and the table is deanonymized in a single statement. Deterministic encryption is documented as leaking equality and frequency, and NIST SP 800-38A rejects the electronic codebook mode that carries the same property at block level.
Where a column must be deterministic, the control is a keyed index over a high-entropy value. Hoping nobody counts the rows is not a control.
questionsV2.recallLine: A warehouse encrypts a nine-value diagnosis column deterministically so analysts can join on it. Which exposure is GREATEST?

optionsShort.A: Rank ciphertext counts against published prevalence
optionsShort.B: Infer ordering and reconstruct ranges between values
optionsShort.C: Confirm one patient's group by predicate
optionsShort.D: Old backups readable under the retired key

B.label: true of a different thing
B.wouldAnswer: Describes order-preserving encryption, a different scheme with a different leak. Deterministic ciphertexts sort in no meaningful order.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Real, since equality testing is what deterministic encryption offers. It discloses one row at a time to somebody who already has a target.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: A genuine key management gap that would appear in the same review. It needs an attacker holding both the retired key and the old media.

sources: NIST SP 800-38A | Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation, electronic codebook
NIST SP 800-175B Rev 1 | Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards, mode selection
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.4 Frequency analysis

questionsV2.question: Brightwater Payments runs a tokenization service. A client submits an encrypted card blob, the service decrypts it with AES in cipher block chaining mode and returns a token. Where the padding is malformed the service answers HTTP 400 with the body bad_padding, and where the padding is well formed but the record fails its checksum it answers HTTP 422 with bad_record. A tester recovered a full card number in about four thousand requests without ever holding the key. Which change MOST directly removes the technique the tester used?

options.A: Return the same HTTP 400 and generic body for the padding and the checksum failures
options.B: Alert the fraud team when one client produces more than fifty decryption failures a minute
options.C: Rotate the tokenization key every twenty-four hours instead of on the current quarterly schedule
options.D: Authenticate the blob with a code verified before any decryption, discarding it on failure

questionsV2.explanation:
The tester never needed the key, because the service answered a question it should not have been willing to answer: is the padding on this blob well formed? Four thousand of those answers is a byte-by-byte plaintext recovery.
Verify a message authentication code over the ciphertext before anything is decrypted (D) and the question disappears. A blob the tester has modified fails that check, one response comes back, and the decryption routine whose behavior differed is never reached. RFC 7366 defines encrypt-then-MAC for TLS on this reasoning, and authenticated modes such as AES-GCM, specified in NIST SP 800-38D, refuse to release plaintext until the tag verifies.
When a service leaks a yes-or-no answer about a ciphertext handed to it, stop processing the ciphertext.
questionsV2.recallLine: A tokenization service answers differently for bad padding and a bad checksum, and a tester recovered a card number. Which change MOST directly stops it?

optionsShort.A: One generic error for both failures
optionsShort.B: Alert on fifty decryption failures a minute
optionsShort.C: Rotate the tokenization key every day
optionsShort.D: Verify authentication before anything is decrypted

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Closes the channel the tester was reading and leaves the mechanism running. Different work on the two paths moves the attacker to timing.

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: Notices the four thousand requests while they happen. An attacker who paces requests under the threshold is invisible to it.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Shortens the life of a key the tester was never attacking.

sources: RFC 7366 | Encrypt-then-MAC for Transport Layer Security
NIST SP 800-38D | Recommendation for Galois/Counter Mode, authenticated encryption
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.5 Chosen ciphertext

questionsV2.question: Halloway Systems ships an electricity meter whose cryptographic core is a validated AES-128 software library running on a general-purpose microcontroller. An independent laboratory recovered the full device key in forty minutes by measuring the microcontroller's power draw across 20,000 encryptions with an oscilloscope and a shunt resistor. The engineering director proposes moving the product to AES-256. The security architect has to tell the board what the finding actually shows and what the next hardware specification must require. Which requirement is the PRIMARY response to the laboratory's result?

options.A: A module tested against non-invasive attack mitigation, with masked and randomized execution
options.B: A move from AES-128 to AES-256 with the same library on the same microcontroller
options.C: A tamper-evident enclosure whose seal shows that a returned meter's case has been opened
options.D: A move from AES to a different symmetric algorithm with a published constant-time design

questionsV2.explanation:
Nothing in the laboratory's result says anything is wrong with AES. The key came out of the power trace. Current draw varies with the data the microcontroller is handling, and differential power analysis across twenty thousand traces separates the key hypothesis that fits from the ones that do not.
That is an implementation attack: the target is how the algorithm was built in silicon and code. So the countermeasure has to live at the same layer (A). Masking splits every intermediate value into random shares, so instantaneous power draw stops correlating with the secret. FIPS 140-3, with the non-invasive attack mitigation metrics of NIST SP 800-140F, is where a purchaser can require that this be tested.
When an attack reads a physical property of a device, look at what the device is doing.
questionsV2.recallLine: A laboratory pulled a meter's AES key out of its power traces in forty minutes. Which requirement is the PRIMARY response?

optionsShort.A: Module tested for non-invasive attack mitigation
optionsShort.B: Move the same library to AES-256
optionsShort.C: Tamper-evident seal on the meter case
optionsShort.D: A different constant-time symmetric algorithm

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Doubles the key length of a cipher whose key space was never searched. The laboratory repeats the measurement and needs a little longer.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Tells an investigator afterwards that a meter was opened. No obstacle to a laboratory that opens one meter on a bench and never returns it.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Changes the algorithm on the same leaking hardware. A constant-time design addresses execution time, a different channel from power.

sources: FIPS 140-3 | Non-invasive security requirements for cryptographic modules
NIST SP 800-140F | CMVP Approved Non-Invasive Attack Mitigation Test Metrics
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.6 Implementation attacks

questionsV2.question: Farrow Silicon builds a hardware security module that signs firmware for a car maker. Its RSA-2048 signing routine uses the Chinese remainder theorem for speed, computing the signature modulo each prime and recombining the two halves. A laboratory clamped the module's supply rail for two microseconds during one recombination, obtained a single faulty signature, and factored the modulus from it with a greatest common divisor. The module already signs 90 images an hour and the car maker's pipeline will not absorb a fourfold increase in signing time. Which change MOST directly removes the recovery path the laboratory used?

options.A: Compute the signature without the Chinese remainder theorem, accepting the slower modular exponentiation
options.B: Add a supply-rail monitor that zeroizes the key store when voltage leaves its tolerance band
options.C: Verify each signature with the public exponent inside the module and suppress it if verification fails
options.D: Add random delays and dummy operations so that the moment of recombination is unpredictable

questionsV2.explanation:
The recombination is what makes the attack work. A signature correct modulo one prime and wrong modulo the other differs from the true signature by a multiple of one prime, so a greatest common divisor against the modulus hands the laboratory a factor.
Two of these four genuinely close that path, and the stem supplies the tiebreaker. Verifying with the public exponent before the signature leaves the module (C) costs one exponentiation with e = 65537, a few hundred multiplications against the thousands the signature itself consumed. It catches a fault injected anywhere in the routine, because any corrupted signature fails verification. Boneh, DeMillo and Lipton proposed exactly this alongside the attack, and FIPS 140-3 conditional self-testing expects it of a signing module.
Where two answers both work, argue for the one that costs least and covers most of the attack surface.
questionsV2.recallLine: One injected fault during RSA-CRT signing gave a laboratory the private key. Which change MOST directly removes that recovery path?

optionsShort.A: Sign without the Chinese remainder theorem
optionsShort.B: Zeroize the key store on voltage excursions
optionsShort.C: Verify every signature before it leaves the module
optionsShort.D: Random delays and dummy operations while signing

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Also closes the path, and loses on cost. Abandoning the Chinese remainder theorem is roughly the fourfold slowdown the pipeline has refused.

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: Catches a crude glitch and misses a well-shaped one. A module that wipes its key store on supply noise is an availability problem.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Raises the number of attempts the laboratory needs. What one successful attempt yields is unchanged.

sources: Boneh, DeMillo and Lipton (1997) | On the Importance of Checking Cryptographic Protocols for Faults
FIPS 140-3 | Conditional self-tests, pairwise consistency for signature generation
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.8 Fault injection

questionsV2.question: Cobalt Ledger receives webhooks from a payment processor, each carrying an HMAC-SHA256 signature in a header. The verifier compares the received signature against the computed one using the language's default string equality, which returns as soon as two bytes differ. A penetration tester calling from a virtual machine in the same cloud region forged a valid signature for a payload of their own choosing after roughly half a million requests, without ever holding the shared secret. Which change MOST directly closes the technique the tester used?

options.A: Throttle each source address to ten webhook deliveries a minute at the network edge
options.B: Compare the two signatures with a routine that examines every byte before returning
options.C: Require a timestamp header and reject any delivery whose timestamp is over five minutes old
options.D: Move the signature from HMAC-SHA256 to HMAC-SHA512 and widen the shared secret

questionsV2.explanation:
The secret never leaked. The comparison did. An equality routine that stops at the first differing byte finishes fractionally sooner when the first byte is wrong than when the first four are right, and across enough samples that difference is measurable. From a virtual machine in the same region the network noise that would normally bury it is at its smallest, and the tester recovers the correct signature a byte at a time.
Compare every byte before returning (B). Every cryptographic library ships a comparison that runs for the same duration whatever it finds, and CWE-208 records the observable timing discrepancy as the defect.
Any leak in how you check a secret is a leak of the secret.
questionsV2.recallLine: A webhook verifier compares signatures with early-exit string equality, and a tester forged one. Which change MOST directly closes the technique?

optionsShort.A: Throttle each source to ten deliveries a minute
optionsShort.B: Compare every byte before returning a result
optionsShort.C: Reject deliveries older than five minutes
optionsShort.D: Move to HMAC-SHA512 with a longer secret

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: The strongest alternative. Half a million requests at ten a minute is over a month, and an attacker can spread them across addresses.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Stops a captured delivery being replayed tomorrow. It has nothing to say about a signature the attacker has just constructed.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Makes the digest longer. The comparison over it exits early in exactly the same way, so the tester needs more requests and no new insight.

sources: CWE-208 | Observable Timing Discrepancy
FIPS 198-1 | The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code, MAC verification
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.9 Timing

questionsV2.question: Ashgrove Manufacturing lost 340 file servers to ransomware across one weekend. The intruder had held domain administrator credentials for eleven days beforehand and used them to delete the storage array's snapshots and to encrypt the backup repository, which was domain-joined and permanently mounted by the backup service account. Recovery took nineteen days from tapes shipped offsite in 2024. The board has funded one architectural change to the recovery estate. Which change MOST reduces the chance that a repeat event also destroys the recovery copies?

options.A: Increase storage array snapshot frequency from daily to hourly across all file server volumes
options.B: Deploy application allow-listing on the file servers so that unsigned binaries are refused execution
options.C: Replicate the backup repository to a second site across the existing domain-joined management network
options.D: Hold one repository copy under retention lock, released by credentials outside the Windows domain

questionsV2.explanation:
Every copy Ashgrove lost was reachable with one credential. The snapshots, the repository and the mount all authenticated against the directory the intruder had owned for eleven days. There was never more than one thing to compromise.
A retention-locked copy released by an identity that directory does not control breaks the shared dependency (D). The write is immutable for its retention period, and no domain administrator can shorten it. NIST SP 1800-11 and NIST SP 800-209 both put an offline, immutable or otherwise logically separated copy at the center of a recovery design for this reason.
Ransomware needs no cryptographic weakness to beat you. It needs your backups to share an identity with your production estate.
questionsV2.recallLine: Ransomware deleted array snapshots and encrypted a domain-joined backup repository. Which change MOST reduces the chance recovery copies die again?

optionsShort.A: Hourly as opposed to daily array snapshots
optionsShort.B: Application allow-listing on the file servers
optionsShort.C: Replicate the repository to a second site
optionsShort.D: Retention-locked copy held outside the domain

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Multiplies copies on the array whose snapshots were deleted. Hourly and daily snapshots are equally reachable to that same account.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: The strongest preventive control on the list. It aims at the encryption event, and a domain administrator can change the policy too.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Gives a second site and a second copy inside the same trust boundary. Replication faithfully copies encrypted files over good ones.

sources: NIST SP 1800-11 | Data Integrity: Recovering from Ransomware and Other Destructive Events
NIST SP 800-209 | Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 3.7.13 Ransomware

questionsV2.question: Ferngate Analytics leases floors nine and ten of a multi-tenant tower. Its access switches and patch panels sit in the building's telecommunications room on each floor, a space the landlord owns and shares with two other tenants. Building engineers, a cabling contractor and the cleaning crew all hold keys to that room, and the landlord will not fit a tenant-controlled lock or release the master. Ferngate's equipment is mounted in an open two-post rack with the console ports facing the door. Which control MOST directly reduces the risk this arrangement creates?

options.A: Enclose the rack in a locked, alarmed cabinet whose openings are logged to Ferngate.
options.B: Encrypt the links between the access switches and the core so captured frames are unreadable.
options.C: Negotiate a lease clause obliging the landlord to escort and log every entry.
options.D: Disable unused ports and require certificate-based 802.1X on every port in that room.

questionsV2.explanation:
The exposure is physical possession. Anyone holding a key to that room can reach a console port, reset a switch, splice a tap or walk out with the hardware, and nothing in Ferngate's records would show it happened.
A locked, alarmed cabinet inside the shared room re-establishes a boundary Ferngate controls (A), and the alarm contact turns an undetectable event into a recorded one.
Where you cannot own the room, own the enclosure inside it.
questionsV2.recallLine: A tenant's switches sit in a landlord-keyed telecom room shared with two other tenants. Which control MOST directly reduces the risk?

optionsShort.A: Locked alarmed cabinet, openings logged
optionsShort.B: Encrypt switch-to-core links against capture
optionsShort.C: Lease clause requiring landlord escort
optionsShort.D: Disable unused ports, require 802.1X

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Protects data in transit and is worth doing. An unenclosed switch can still be consoled into, powered off or carried out of the room.

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: The right instrument where a landlord will change building procedure. This one has refused, so it buys a promise.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Stops an unauthorized device on a live port and leaves the equipment itself reachable.

sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | Annex A 7.12 Cabling security
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PE-4 Access Control for Transmission

questionsV2.question: Bellweather Actuarial is converting an interior office suite into a twelve-rack server room. The partition walls stop at the suspended ceiling grid, and the plenum above runs on without interruption into a neighboring suite let to a recruitment agency. The architect's drawings show a card reader on the door, a camera in the corridor, and a locking cabinet for each row of racks. Construction goes out to tender in three weeks. Which change should the security lead insist on FIRST?

options.A: Fit a second card reader inside the door so exits are recorded as well.
options.B: Add a motion detector above the ceiling grid that alarms to the corridor camera.
options.C: Extend the partition walls slab to slab and seal every penetration through them.
options.D: Replace the cabinet locks with electronic locks that log each cabinet opening.

questionsV2.explanation:
Every control on those drawings guards the door, and the room does not stop at the door. The plenum is a continuous void into a suite Bellweather does not control, so an intruder need never pass the card reader.
Closing that void (C) is also the one change that becomes expensive once the walls are built and the tender is let. That is what makes it first.
A perimeter is only as high as its lowest continuous barrier, and drop ceilings are where that gets forgotten.
questionsV2.recallLine: A server room's partition walls stop at a suspended ceiling shared with a neighboring tenant. Which change should the security lead insist on FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Second card reader recording exits
optionsShort.B: Motion detector above the ceiling grid
optionsShort.C: Walls extended slab to slab, penetrations sealed
optionsShort.D: Electronic cabinet locks logging each opening

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Records who leaves and helps against tailgating. It does nothing about a route that bypasses the doorway entirely.

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: Would tell the security team afterwards that somebody had been in the ceiling. The ask is to stop them.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Hardens a cabinet inside a room whose perimeter is still open.

sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | Annex A 7.1 Physical security perimeters
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PE-3 Physical Access Control

questionsV2.question: Thackray Health keeps fourteen months of encrypted backup cartridges in a media library on its own site: a windowless room with a card reader, a fire-rated safe and racking for 900 cartridges. Cartridges leave the room for restore rehearsals and for a quarterly courier run to a second site. Staff sign a paper sheet on the way out and, in principle, on the way back. An internal audit counts the shelves and finds 23 cartridges the catalog says are held there and which are not present. Which control BEST closes the weakness the audit exposed?

options.A: Upgrade the room's card reader so entry needs a second factor as well.
options.B: Bar-code every cartridge and reconcile a scanned shelf count against the backup catalog monthly.
options.C: Shorten the retention period so fewer cartridges are held on the shelves at once.
options.D: Move the quarterly courier run to a bonded carrier that signs transfer receipts.

questionsV2.explanation:
Twenty-three cartridges are gone and nobody noticed. That is an accountability failure: the shelf and the catalog are allowed to disagree indefinitely.
Scan the shelf against the catalog on a fixed cycle (B) and the disagreement surfaces within a month. Bar-coding is what makes the count cheap enough to actually happen.
Encryption limits what a lost cartridge discloses. Inventory is what tells you it is lost.
questionsV2.recallLine: A media library's paper sign-out sheet failed: 23 cartridges are cataloged but missing. Which control BEST closes that weakness?

optionsShort.A: Second factor on the room's card reader
optionsShort.B: Bar-code cartridges, reconcile shelf count monthly
optionsShort.C: Shorten retention so fewer cartridges are held
optionsShort.D: Bonded courier signing transfer receipts

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Raises the bar on who may enter. The people who removed these cartridges were almost certainly entitled to enter.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Reduces how much there is to lose and changes nothing about whether a loss is seen. The same paper sheet would fail on a smaller library.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Tightens the leg of the journey that already carries a receipt, and leaves the restore rehearsals, the likelier route out, untouched.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | MP-4 Media Storage
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | MP-5 Media Transport
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | Annex A 7.10 Storage media

questionsV2.question: Elverton Insurance suspects a claims handler of altering settlement records. A forensic contractor images two laptops and a server volume and hands the drives and its working notes to Elverton's in-house investigator. She puts them in a stationery cupboard in the security team's office, which four analysts open with a shared key, and emails the contractor's report to the legal team. Counsel warns that the handler's union will contest every artifact if the matter reaches a tribunal. Which arrangement gives the GREATEST protection to what has already been collected?

options.A: Ask the forensic contractor to re-image both laptops so a clean copy exists.
options.B: Require two analysts to be present whenever the cupboard is opened for anything.
options.C: Restrict the contractor's report to counsel so the work stays under legal privilege.
options.D: Hold the drives in a safe under one named custodian, logging every transfer.

questionsV2.explanation:
A tribunal will test whether anybody could have altered the material and whether Elverton can show that nobody did. A shared cupboard answers neither: four people had equal access and no record exists of who took what, or when.
Name a single custodian, hold the drives in a safe and sign each handover (D). That produces the continuous account that survives cross-examination.
Custody is a written chain. A strong lock is a different thing.
questionsV2.recallLine: Forensic images sit in a cupboard four analysts share, and a tribunal is likely. Which arrangement gives the GREATEST protection to the material collected?

optionsShort.A: Re-image both laptops for a clean copy
optionsShort.B: Two analysts present whenever the cupboard opens
optionsShort.C: Keep the report under legal privilege
optionsShort.D: Named custodian, safe, every transfer signed

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Re-acquires material that has already sat in an uncontrolled space, so the second image inherits the doubt attaching to the first.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Narrows access at one container and leaves the handovers between contractor, investigator and counsel undocumented.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Protects the report from disclosure and says nothing about whether the drives are what they are claimed to be.

sources: NIST SP 800-86 | Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
ISO/IEC 27037:2012 | Preservation of digital evidence and chain of custody

questionsV2.question: Ledbury Trust runs a 320-kilowatt data hall cooled by two chillers in an N+1 arrangement. During a heat advisory the second chiller trips on high head pressure and will not restart; the vendor quotes six hours to attend. The surviving chiller can reject about sixty percent of the hall's present heat load, and supply temperature is climbing two degrees every ten minutes. The operations manager holds a load-shed schedule agreed with each service owner last year and never yet used. Which action should the operations manager take FIRST?

options.A: Raise the supply-air setpoint to the top of the hall's allowable envelope.
options.B: Run the agreed load-shed schedule, powering down the services it lists as sheddable.
options.C: Prop the hall doors open to the office floor and bring in fans.
options.D: Escalate to the chiller vendor for an engineer sooner than the six-hour quote.

questionsV2.explanation:
Forty percent of the heat going into that hall has nowhere to go. No adjustment to how the surviving plant runs changes that arithmetic. The one lever that closes a capacity gap is to stop producing the heat, and the load-shed schedule (B) is that lever. It exists so the decision is not improvised while temperature is rising, and it already carries each service owner's agreement, which makes it executable in minutes.
In a thermal event, shed load first and negotiate afterwards.
questionsV2.recallLine: One of two chillers fails and the survivor carries sixty percent of the load. Which action should the operations manager take FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Raise supply-air setpoint to the allowable limit
optionsShort.B: Run the agreed load-shed schedule
optionsShort.C: Open hall doors and bring fans
optionsShort.D: Escalate the vendor for a faster engineer

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Widens the temperature difference the coil works across and buys a few minutes. The missing forty percent still has nowhere to go.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Pushes warm air into occupied space, defeats the hall's access control and breaches its fire compartmentation.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Necessary, and it will matter in hours. The next twenty minutes are the problem.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PE-14 Environmental Controls
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | Annex A 7.11 Supporting utilities
ASHRAE TC 9.9 | Thermal Guidelines for Data Processing Environments

questionsV2.question: Padstow Mutual is renewing a ten-year lease on the building that houses its policy platform. The data hall sits on a raised podium, its finished floor 1.4 meters above the street. The generator, the 4,000-liter fuel tank and the main switchgear are in the basement, reached by a ramp from the car park. Since the last renewal the county has redrawn its flood mapping and the site now falls inside the revised 100-year floodplain, at a modeled depth of 1.2 meters. The hall carries twenty minutes of battery runtime. Which finding presents the PRIMARY risk to the platform?

options.A: Twenty minutes of battery runtime leaves no margin if the generator starts slowly.
options.B: The hall's finished floor clears the modeled flood depth by twenty centimeters.
options.C: Generator, fuel tank and switchgear all sit below the modeled flood depth.
options.D: The lease commits the insurer to this site for another ten years.

questionsV2.explanation:
Rank these by certainty and by what each one costs. In the event as modeled the basement floods. Generator, fuel tank and switchgear all sit beneath the water line (C), so the platform loses utility power and its replacement in the same hour.
Site risk is settled by where the standby plant sits.
questionsV2.recallLine: A podium data hall now falls inside a revised 100-year floodplain modeled at 1.2 meters. Which site finding presents the PRIMARY risk to the platform?

optionsShort.A: Twenty minutes of battery runtime
optionsShort.B: Hall floor clears the flood level narrowly
optionsShort.C: Standby plant sits below the modeled depth
optionsShort.D: Lease binds the insurer for ten years

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Describes a gap that bites when a generator exists to start. Here the generator is the thing being lost.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Comes closest. Twenty centimeters of freeboard is a thin margin, and the hall itself stays dry at the modeled depth.

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Constrains what the property committee can do about any of this. By itself it threatens nothing.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PE-18 Location of System Components
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PE-11 Emergency Power
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | Annex A 7.5 Protecting against physical and environmental threats

questionsV2.question: Kettleby Payments authorizes card transactions from four regions, each with its own application nodes and its own database replica. Every node stamps events with its local clock, and a review finds the regions drift up to ninety seconds apart, with two of them synchronizing over unauthenticated NTP to a public pool. Session tokens carry an absolute expiry and are honored by whichever region receives them. Investigating a disputed transaction, the fraud team cannot establish which of two events logged forty seconds apart happened first. Which change would MOST directly correct the underlying defect?

options.A: Synchronize every node to a common authenticated time source and alert on drift.
options.B: Shorten token lifetimes to five minutes so a skewed expiry check matters less.
options.C: Have the log pipeline restamp each event with the collector's clock on arrival.
options.D: Sign each token with a per-region key so its issuing region is identifiable.

questionsV2.explanation:
Two symptoms come from one cause. Tokens outliving their expiry in a neighboring region, and an event order nobody can reconstruct. The four regions do not agree what time it is, and two of them take their answer from a source that can be spoofed.
An authenticated common reference removes the disagreement, and alerting on drift keeps it removed (A).
In a distributed system time is a shared dependency, and an unauthenticated one is an attack surface.
questionsV2.recallLine: Four regions of an authorization service drift ninety seconds apart, two using unauthenticated NTP. Which change would MOST directly correct the underlying defect?

optionsShort.A: Common authenticated time source, drift alerted
optionsShort.B: Shorten token lifetimes to five minutes
optionsShort.C: Log pipeline restamps events on arrival
optionsShort.D: Per-region signing key identifies the issuer

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Narrows the window in which a skewed check can be wrong. Regions ninety seconds apart still accept dead tokens, and ordering is untouched.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Makes the log internally consistent by discarding the timestamp of when the event happened, while the authorization path keeps drifting.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Tells you which region issued a token. It says nothing about when.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-8 Time Stamps
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-45 System Time Synchronization

questionsV2.question: Ainsdale Genomics runs a 400-node cluster under a batch scheduler that packs two or three tenants' jobs onto each node. Every node mounts a parallel filesystem and carries a local NVMe scratch volume that jobs use for working files. A regulated cohort of 60,000 patient genomes is analyzed on the cluster twice a month. A researcher from an unrelated group reports finding readable working files from somebody else's job in the scratch directory of a node she had just been allocated. Which control MOST directly addresses the exposure?

options.A: Encrypt the parallel filesystem at rest with keys held in the cluster key manager.
options.B: Allocate regulated jobs whole nodes and purge local scratch in the job epilogue.
options.C: Enable full-disk encryption on the local NVMe scratch volume of every compute node.
options.D: Tighten the default umask so working files are written without group read permission.

questionsV2.explanation:
Scratch is a shared system resource that outlives the job which wrote to it, and the scheduler hands the same node to the next tenant with the data still on the disk.
Allocate regulated jobs whole nodes and purge local scratch in the job epilogue (B). That removes the sharing and the residue together.
Encryption at rest answers theft. Co-tenancy is a different question.
questionsV2.recallLine: A shared HPC node's local scratch still held another tenant's readable working files. Which control MOST directly addresses the exposure?

optionsShort.A: Encrypt the parallel filesystem at rest
optionsShort.B: Exclusive nodes plus scratch purge at job end
optionsShort.C: Full-disk encryption on node scratch volumes
optionsShort.D: Tighten the default umask on new files

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Defends the wrong storage tier. The leak was on node-local disk, and the parallel filesystem is not where the researcher found anything.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Defends a disk that has left the building. To a process on a running node with the volume mounted, full-disk encryption is transparent.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Changes the mode bits on new files and leaves the data resident for whoever the scheduler seats there next.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | MP-6 Media Sanitization

questionsV2.question: Garrowby Instruments is finalizing a utility telemetry unit with a fifteen-year field life. Ten thousand units will be sealed in kerbside cabinets, powered from the meter, and reachable over a narrowband radio link carrying a few kilobytes a day. The firmware team must fix the transport's cipher suite before the board layout is frozen next month, and the units cannot be visited economically once installed. Which property of the design BEST limits what a withdrawal of the chosen algorithm in year eight would cost?

options.A: Selecting the largest key size the microcontroller sustains inside the unit's power budget.
options.B: Choosing a suite from a national standard whose approval horizon is published beyond year fifteen.
options.C: Commissioning an independent review of the transport design before the first units ship.
options.D: Negotiating the suite at session setup, with an identifier the field can update remotely.

questionsV2.explanation:
The cost being asked about is the cost of change, and it is dominated by whether a fielded unit can be told to use something different without a visit. Negotiate the suite at session setup, behind an identifier the field can update remotely (D), and the algorithm becomes a value the device can be given. Weld it into a frozen board and it becomes a constant.
Design for the algorithm you will have to replace.
questionsV2.recallLine: A sealed telemetry unit has a fifteen-year life and no economic site visits. Which design property BEST limits the cost of an algorithm withdrawal?

optionsShort.A: Largest key size the microcontroller sustains
optionsShort.B: Standard suite with a long published horizon
optionsShort.C: Independent design review before first shipment
optionsShort.D: Negotiated suite with a remotely updatable identifier

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Answers a different threat, the steady growth in what brute force can reach. A longer key inside a broken algorithm is still broken.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Lowers the probability that a withdrawal happens at all, which is worth doing. The bill, if it happens anyway, is unchanged.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: An activity that belongs before shipment and cannot reach a decision taken in year eight.

sources: RFC 7696 (BCP 201) | Guidelines for Cryptographic Algorithm Agility
NIST SP 800-131A Rev 2 | Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 | Recommendation for Key Management

questionsV2.question: Rothersay Council is procuring a case-management system for adult social care. The program board is the service director, two team managers, the IT delivery lead and the supplier's account manager. Requirements came from six workshops with case workers and the finance team. Three weeks before the requirements baseline is signed, the council's information governance officer finds the design makes no provision for the statutory seventy-five-year retention of care records, nor for the redaction workflow the council must run when a resident asks to see their file. What is the PRIMARY failure this reveals?

options.A: Elicitation captured what users wanted instead of testing it against the service's obligations.
options.B: Requirements were not traced forward into acceptance tests the supplier can be held to.
options.C: The council relied on the supplier's standard product instead of specifying its own needs.
options.D: Stakeholder identification omitted the parties whose statutory duties constrain how records are handled.

questionsV2.explanation:
Nobody in the room owned the obligation. Case workers know how they work and finance knows what it costs. Neither can say that these records must survive seventy-five years and be redactable on request. The information governance officer is that party, and she was not a stakeholder until she stumbled across the design (D).
Requirements you never hear about were gathered from the wrong people.
questionsV2.recallLine: A council's case-management design lacks the retention and redaction the law requires, three weeks before baseline. What is the PRIMARY failure this reveals?

optionsShort.A: Elicitation captured wants, not obligations
optionsShort.B: Requirements not traced into acceptance tests
optionsShort.C: Reliance on the supplier's standard product
optionsShort.D: Stakeholders with statutory duties were never identified

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: A real failure mode, and the workshops did their job. The fault is in who was invited.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Describes an activity that follows the existence of a requirement. There is nothing here to trace.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Names the visible result, a product-shaped design. The mechanism that let it through was the missing duty-holder.

sources: ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 | Stakeholder Needs and Requirements Definition process
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems

questionsV2.question: Winsford Freight has approved a business case for a driver-facing mobile application. The security requirements handed to the development team read, in full: the application shall be secure; strong encryption shall be used; and the application shall comply with relevant regulation. The delivery manager wants sprinting to start next week and argues that a penetration test before go-live will catch whatever the wording missed. The security architect has been given one week inside requirements analysis and no more. What is the BEST use of that week?

options.A: Rewrite each statement as a testable requirement with acceptance criteria and a control reference.
options.B: Choose the cipher suite, key lengths and certificate profile the application will use.
options.C: Book the penetration test early so a slot exists before the go-live date.
options.D: Map the application against the regulator's guidance and list every clause that applies.

questionsV2.explanation:
None of the three statements can fail a test, so none of them can be delivered or refused. Secure has no threshold. Strong has no definition. Relevant regulation has no list.
Turn each into a requirement with an acceptance criterion and a control reference (A). That gives the team something to build to and the tester something to check, and it is the artifact this project is short of.
A requirement you cannot test is a wish with a paragraph number.
questionsV2.recallLine: Security requirements read 'the application shall be secure' and 'strong encryption shall be used'. What is the BEST use of one week of requirements analysis?

optionsShort.A: Rewrite as testable requirements with acceptance criteria
optionsShort.B: Choose cipher suite, key lengths, certificate profile
optionsShort.C: Book the penetration test slot early
optionsShort.D: List every regulatory clause that applies

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Settles how, and how is a design decision a requirement should constrain. Fixing the suite now freezes it before any threat model exists.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Accepts the delivery manager's premise, that a test at the end substitutes for a specification at the start.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Produces the input to one of the three statements and leaves the other two unwritten.

sources: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 | Characteristics of individual requirements, including verifiability
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems

questionsV2.question: Calverton Life is at architecture review for a replacement annuity platform. In the proposed design the policy service writes each transaction's audit record into a table in its own database, using the same credential it uses for policy data, and holds update and delete rights on that table. The architects say a nightly export to the log platform gives auditors the assurance they want. The board sets the design baseline at the end of this meeting, after which structural change goes through a change board. Which change should the review board require BEFORE it approves the design?

options.A: Move audit writes to a separate append-only service outside the policy service's control.
options.B: Restrict the policy service's database credential to insert-only on the audit table.
options.C: Increase the nightly export to hourly so less audit data waits in place.
options.D: Alert the log platform's operators when a nightly export arrives late or short.

questionsV2.explanation:
Whoever can rewrite the record is not audited by it. This design leaves the audit trail inside the trust boundary of the very service it is meant to hold to account.
The remedy is structural: a writer that can append, and a store it does not administer (A). It also has to be settled at this meeting, because after the baseline it becomes a change board item competing with delivery dates. Everything else on the list can be added later.
Separate the writer from the store, then argue about privileges.
questionsV2.recallLine: An annuity platform's policy service writes and may delete its own audit records. Which change should the review board require BEFORE approving the design?

optionsShort.A: Separate append-only audit service outside the writer
optionsShort.B: Restrict the service's grant to insert-only
optionsShort.C: Export to the log platform hourly
optionsShort.D: Alert when the nightly export misses

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: The strongest rival, and worth doing. A grant is configuration, changed by the same team, and it survives no compromise of the service.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Shortens the window in which records can be altered and leaves the ability intact.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Notices afterwards that an export went wrong. That is a different thing from the records being trustworthy.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 Protection of Audit Information
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9(4) Access by Subset of Privileged Users

questionsV2.question: Harlowe Grocery builds its checkout service in a container pipeline. The production database password is passed to the image build as a build argument so a schema migration can run during the build, and the finished image is pushed to a registry every engineer can pull. A developer in her first week finds the password in clear text in one of the image layers on her laptop. The team has rotated the password and closed the ticket. Which practice BEST prevents this recurring?

options.A: Scan every image for embedded credentials in the pipeline and fail on a hit.
options.B: Restrict registry pull rights to the service accounts that deploy the checkout service.
options.C: Issue a migration credential that expires twenty-four hours after the build completes.
options.D: Supply the credential at run time from a secrets manager instead of at build.

questionsV2.explanation:
A container image is a distributable artifact. Whatever is present when a layer is committed travels with it to every machine that pulls it, and rotation removes one password while the mechanism that published it stays in the pipeline.
Fetch the credential from a secrets manager when the container starts (D) and no layer ever holds one.
Secrets belong to the runtime.
questionsV2.recallLine: A production database password reached an image layer as a build argument. Which practice BEST prevents that recurring?

optionsShort.A: Scan images for embedded credentials in CI
optionsShort.B: Restrict registry pulls to deployment accounts
optionsShort.C: Short-lived migration credential expiring after build
optionsShort.D: Runtime injection from a secrets manager

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: Finds the mistake after it has been made, and is worth having as a backstop. A scanner that misses a novel format ships the image anyway.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Narrows the audience for the artifact and does nothing about the secret inside it, which travels when the artifact is copied.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Shortens the useful life of the leaked value while values go on being baked into layers.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5(7) No Embedded Unencrypted Static Authenticators
NIST SP 800-190 | Application Container Security Guide

questionsV2.question: Culverdale Diagnostics has built the cryptographic module for a blood-analyzer platform. The three engineers who wrote the module also wrote its test harness, ran the tests and produced the ninety-page evidence pack now sitting with the assurance lead. Every requirement in the baseline traces to at least one passing test. The platform ships to hospitals in eleven weeks and the program has no budget line for outside work. Which condition should the assurance lead insist on FIRST?

options.A: A penetration test of the assembled analyzer once it runs in a pilot hospital.
options.B: Verification of the module against the requirement baseline by testers outside the team.
options.C: Peer review of the module's source by a fourth engineer on the team.
options.D: A doubling of the test cases so each requirement traces to three tests.

questionsV2.explanation:
The evidence pack has one weakness, and coverage is not it. Every claim rests on the judgment of the people whose work is being judged, so a requirement they misread was tested against the same misreading.
Independence is what the pack lacks (B), and it is also the cheapest thing to add. A second set of eyes running the existing tests against the baseline costs weeks, not budget.
Independence is a property of who tested.
questionsV2.recallLine: A cryptographic module's developers wrote, ran and evidenced its own tests. Which condition should the assurance lead insist on FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Penetration test of the assembled analyzer later
optionsShort.B: Testers outside the team verify the baseline
optionsShort.C: Peer review by another engineer inside
optionsShort.D: Double the test cases per requirement

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Examines something else, later, and after the acceptance decision this question turns on.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Keeps the review inside the group whose shared assumptions are the problem. A fourth engineer read the same specification.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Multiplies tests written from one interpretation. The count rises and the assurance does not.

sources: ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 | Verification process
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-11 Developer Testing and Evaluation

questionsV2.question: Netherfield Utilities has run its outage-management system for nine years. Change control was tight at go-live; today two thirds of changes are raised as emergencies, approved verbally by the duty manager and written up afterwards if at all. The configuration baseline in the CMDB was last refreshed four years ago. A change to a reporting view last month silently dropped the filter that kept customers' medical-dependency flags out of a report sent to a contractor. The report has been recalled and the filter restored. Which change to how the system is run should the sustainment manager make NEXT?

options.A: Re-baseline the CMDB so the recorded configuration matches what is actually running.
options.B: Review quarterly who holds the rights to raise a change on the system.
options.C: Require a security impact analysis on each change before it is approved.
options.D: Have the contractor sign a data-processing agreement covering medical-dependency flags.

questionsV2.explanation:
The filter came out because nobody was required to ask what the change would expose, and an emergency route approved verbally has no point at which that question could be put.
Put a security impact analysis in front of approval (C) and every future change has to answer it, emergencies included.
Sustainment fails quietly. The controls do not break; the discipline around them does.
questionsV2.recallLine: Nine years into sustainment, an emergency change silently exposed medical-dependency data. Which change should the sustainment manager make NEXT?

optionsShort.A: Re-baseline the CMDB against what runs
optionsShort.B: Quarterly review of who may raise changes
optionsShort.C: Security impact analysis before each approval
optionsShort.D: Data-processing agreement with the contractor

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Genuinely needed, and also perishable. A baseline refreshed today is stale within a quarter unless changes are assessed as they arrive.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Governs who may raise a change. It would not have stopped an authorized engineer editing a reporting view.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Constrains what a contractor may do with data it should never have received, and leaves the disclosure route open.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-4 Impact Analyzes
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 Configuration Change Control

questionsV2.question: Peverell Group has bought a plot for an operations center that will hold its recovery data hall. The plot fronts a public road on one side; the other three sides adjoin an unfenced supermarket car park. The concept drawings place the building at the pavement edge, put staff parking and the goods loading bay hard against the wall of the hall itself, and run glazing the length of the ground floor. The drawings can still be changed at no cost. Which change to the concept does MOST to apply sound site design principles?

options.A: Replace the ground-floor glazing with laminated glass rated to resist forced entry.
options.B: Fence the three boundaries adjoining the car park and gate the pedestrian routes.
options.C: Set the building back from the road, with parking and deliveries away from the hall.
options.D: Light the perimeter to an even level and cover the approaches with cameras.

questionsV2.explanation:
Everything that could hurt this building has been invited to touch it. Vehicles at the road edge, vehicles in the car park, deliveries at the hall wall.
Standoff cannot be retrofitted once a footprint is poured. Set the building back and move parking and deliveries away from the hall (C), and the volume that matters is separated from the routes that reach it.
Distance is the cheapest control on a drawing and the most expensive one after construction.
questionsV2.recallLine: Concept drawings put a recovery data hall at the pavement edge with deliveries at its wall. Which change does MOST to apply site design principles?

optionsShort.A: Laminated glass on the ground floor
optionsShort.B: Fence and gate the car-park boundaries
optionsShort.C: Set back, with parking and deliveries moved
optionsShort.D: Even perimeter lighting and camera coverage

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Hardens one surface of a building a vehicle can still park against.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Draws a boundary the site badly needs, and one that can be added later. The hall would still sit at the pavement with a loading bay.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Would tell the guard force that somebody is approaching a building they can already reach.

sources: UFC 4-010-01 | DoD Minimum Antiterrorism Standards for Buildings, standoff distance
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | Annex A 7.1 Physical security perimeters

domains.title: Communication and Network Security
domains.caseStudy:
Domain 4 covers the design and protection of networks: the OSI and TCP/IP layers, secure protocols, VPNs, wireless and cellular links, and the components that carry data between systems that do not trust each other.

Case Study: The "AirLink" Cellular Intercept (IMSI Catcher Attack)

### Context

CityBank deployed portable "AirLink" ATMs to a major music festival. The machines reached the bank's processing center over 4G/LTE modems on a private APN. The network engineers judged the carrier's link encryption and the private APN sufficient, and did not configure an IPsec tunnel or application-layer TLS. The transaction messages travelled in clear text above the cellular layer.

### What went wrong

Criminals parked a rogue base station, an IMSI catcher, near the festival grounds and broadcast a stronger signal than the legitimate towers. The modems attached to it. The rogue station forced a downgrade from 4G, where the network and the device authenticate each other, to 2G GSM, where only the device authenticates. Now the attackers were the tower. They decrypted the 2G A5/1 stream, which has been practically broken for years, and read the application traffic underneath: customer track data and PIN blocks, captured in real time.

The white paper's section on network attacks covers this family: interception by a rogue device on the line, eavesdropping when the payload is not independently encrypted, and, one step further, modifying a host's "declined" into "approved" or impersonating the host outright, which is jackpotting by another route. It makes the same point the AirLink engineers missed: the value of sniffing depends entirely on whether TLS and a VPN are in place above the transport.

### What a practitioner does differently

Assume the carrier is hostile. Encrypt at the layer you control: an IPsec tunnel from modem to bank, and TLS 1.2 or later between the ATM application and the host with mutual certificate validation, so a spoofed host fails the handshake. Add a message authentication code to each transaction message; a forged approval then fails verification even if the tunnel is somehow breached. The white paper lists all three, TLS with mutual validation, VPN, and MACing, among its network controls.

Configure the modems for LTE only and disable 2G and 3G fallback. The default "stay connected at any cost" chose availability over integrity; for a cash dispenser, dropping the link is the safe failure. Monitor the modems for downgrade events and the host for response anomalies, and segment the festival fleet from the rest of the ATM network so a compromised unit is not a path inward, a risk the white paper calls out for any ATM connection.

### Outcome

The captured track data went to fraud. CityBank pulled the AirLink units, reissued the cards, and rebuilt the mobile ATM design with a tunnel, application TLS and LTE-only modems before the next event.

### What the exam tests

Expect questions on where encryption sits in the stack and why link encryption is not end-to-end encryption, on downgrade attacks and mutual authentication, on IPsec modes versus TLS, on wireless and cellular authentication, and on defense in depth as a network design principle instead of a slogan.

### Related reading

The bank in this scenario is a composite. The attack and the controls are documented in:

- [Technical Risks and Attack Vectors Targeting ATMs](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-technical-risks-white-paper.pdf), the sections on network attacks and on network security controls.
- [ATM Security Capability Maturity Worksheet](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-capability-maturity-worksheet.pdf), Domain 2, logical and network controls.
- [The four-part ATM security series on the ATM Availability blog](https://atmavailability.com/blog/).

questions.question: During the post-incident review of the AirLink intercept, CityBank's monitoring team reports that the TLS-inspection and firewall infrastructure at the processing centre observed nothing unusual while the rogue base station forced the ATM modems from 4G down to 2G. Which statement BEST explains why controls operating higher in the stack had no visibility of the downgrade?

options.A: The radio negotiation happens at the data link and network layers of the cellular stack, below anything the centre's application-layer controls can observe.
