options.B: The downgrade messages were encrypted with the 2G A5/1 stream cipher, which the centre's inspection devices could not decrypt quickly enough to raise an alarm.
options.C: The rogue base station silently discarded the ATMs' logging traffic before it could ever reach the processing centre's collectors.
options.D: The modems' TLS sessions renegotiated automatically as the bearer changed, and the monitoring stack treated the renegotiation as a routine handshake instead of an alarm.

questions.explanation: Visibility follows the layer at which a control operates: the forced fallback was negotiated between modem and tower in the lower layers of the cellular stack, and nothing about it is ever presented to equipment inspecting application traffic at the far end. A explains the blindness structurally and would hold for any similar radio-layer attack. (B) misplaces the mechanism: A5/1 encrypts user traffic after the downgrade, and radio signaling between modem and tower never transits the centre's inspection path at all; it would be a fair answer if the question were why over-the-air captures were unreadable to bystanders. (C) invents an action the attacker did not need; a relay that quietly forwards traffic is precisely why MITM interception is hard to spot. (D) fails on the facts of the case: the fleet had no TLS configured, which is what made the cleartext capture possible. An attack at layer N is invisible to controls that only see layer N+1's payloads, so monitoring must exist at the layer where the trust decision is made.

questions.question: An engineer on the AirLink review board claims that an IPsec tunnel from each ATM to the processing centre would have prevented the incident entirely. Which assessment of that claim is MOST accurate?

options.A: The tunnel would have stopped the rogue base station from forcing the modems down to 2G in the first place.
options.B: The interception would still have occurred, but the captured traffic would have been unreadable ciphertext instead of cardholder data.
options.C: IPsec's added overhead would have made transactions over a 2G link time out, so the ATMs would simply have gone offline.
options.D: The tunnel would have alerted the SOC as soon as the peer's identity could no longer be cryptographically verified.

questions.explanation: Encryption at a layer the bank controls changes what the attacker obtains, not whether the attacker can sit on the path: the rogue tower would still relay traffic, but every intercepted packet would be ESP ciphertext, so the loss event (cardholder data exposure) is averted even though the attack itself proceeds. That distinction is why Option B is the accurate assessment and why 'prevented entirely' overstates. (A) puts IPsec at the wrong layer: the downgrade is negotiated in the radio stack beneath the tunnel, which IPsec neither sees nor influences; refusing 2G fallback is a modem configuration, not a VPN feature. (C) is a performance guess, not a security property: IPsec's overhead is modest and 2G, while slow, carries small transaction messages. (D) misunderstands a relay MITM. The attacker forwards the IKE exchange untouched between the true endpoints, so peer authentication succeeds and no alarm exists to raise.

questions.question: CityBank is redesigning the AirLink fleet and must choose where to protect cardholder data in transit. The carrier offers a hardened private APN, the modem vendor offers stronger link-layer encryption, and a consultant instead recommends TLS 1.3 between the ATM application and the processing centre. Which property of the consultant's option BEST justifies the recommendation?

options.A: The protection travels with the data end to end, so compromise of any intermediate network still yields only ciphertext.
options.B: It operates at a lower layer than the carrier's controls, so it protects the radio negotiation as well as the payload.
options.C: It removes the need to pay for the private APN, releasing recurring carrier costs to fund other controls.
options.D: It authenticates the cellular towers to the modems, closing the downgrade path the attackers used before.

questions.explanation: What failed in the original design was transitive trust: security ended wherever the carrier's link ended, and the data itself crossed the compromise point naked. End-to-end TLS binds confidentiality and integrity to the data instead of to any segment of the path, which is exactly the property that survives a hostile or downgraded underlay, hence A. (B) inverts the stack: TLS rides above the transport, so radio negotiation happens beneath it and is untouched; it would be the right description of a control built into the cellular layer itself. (C) may even be true financially, but cost release is not a security justification, and defence in depth argues for keeping the APN's segregation anyway. (D) attributes a cellular-layer property to an application-layer protocol; TLS authenticates the processing centre's endpoint, not towers. Tower authentication is what 4G mutual authentication provides. Place mandatory protection at a layer whose endpoints you own; everything below it is then merely transport.

questions.question: Analysts reconstructing the AirLink attack note that the ATMs' modems accepted the rogue tower immediately once forced onto 2G GSM, while in 4G mode the same impersonation attempt failed. Which weakness of 2G MOST directly enabled the tower impersonation?

options.A: Its A5/1 stream cipher can be broken in near real time with commodity hardware.
options.B: The handset authenticates itself to the network, but the network never proves its identity to the handset.
options.C: Its signaling messages carry no integrity protection, so their contents can be forged or altered by an interceptor.
options.D: Its short session keys are reused across successive calls and data sessions on the same device, easing later cryptanalysis.

questions.explanation: Impersonation succeeds when one party has no way to test the other's identity: 2G's authentication is one-way, so a modem on 2G will accept any sufficiently strong transmitter claiming to be the network. The rogue tower did not have to break anything to be believed, which is why the same trick failed against 4G's mutual authentication. That direct causal link makes B the answer to 'MOST directly enabled'. (A) is a genuine 2G weakness, but it explains the later decryption of captured traffic, not the acceptance of the fake tower; it would be the right answer to how the attackers read the intercepted stream. (C) describes a real gap that supports related bidding-down tricks, yet the impersonation here needed no forged signaling, only an unauthenticated identity claim. (D) points at key hygiene, which affects cryptanalysis, not attachment decisions. Verifying the network's identity matters as much as the network verifying yours; one-way authentication is an open invitation to rogue infrastructure.

questions.question: Privacy counsel asks the AirLink incident team what the festival attackers could have learned from IMSI captures alone, before any traffic was decrypted. Which answer is MOST accurate?

options.A: The cardholder PIN blocks queued up for onward transmission by each of the affected festival ATMs.
options.B: The contents of calls and data sessions that passed through the rogue base station while it operated.
options.C: The unique subscriber identity of each nearby SIM, letting individual devices be identified and tracked.
options.D: The street-level home addresses registered by the carrier against each captured subscriber account in its own records.

questions.explanation: An IMSI is the identifier a SIM presents to the network, and an IMSI catcher harvests exactly that: which subscriber identities are present, when, and where. That alone supports identification and movement tracking of everyone near the rogue tower, a privacy harm independent of any decryption, which is what counsel needs stated, so C. (A) confuses the identifier layer with the payload: PIN blocks are application data, obtainable only after the traffic itself was captured and read. It describes the later data-capture stage of this incident, not the IMSI harvest. (B) likewise requires interception and decryption of session content; capturing identities does not open the sessions. (D) reaches into the carrier's subscriber database, which the radio interface never transmits; an attacker would need a separate compromise of carrier records to get it. Identifiers leak presence and movement; metadata is a privacy breach in its own right, even when every payload stays sealed.

questions.question: CityBank's incident commander must classify the AirLink event for the regulator. During the attack the rogue station relayed every transaction between the ATMs and the carrier network while silently recording cardholder data, and ATM service was never interrupted. Which classification BEST fits?

options.A: A denial-of-service attack, because the ATMs were forced away from the legitimate 4G network they should have used.
options.B: A replay attack, because the transactions captured by the rogue station could be resubmitted at a later time.
options.C: An on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack, because the adversary sat between the endpoints and observed live traffic in transit.
options.D: An injection attack, because the rogue station inserted itself into the carrier's trusted infrastructure.

questions.explanation: Classification should follow the mechanism that caused the loss: an adversary interposed between two communicating parties, relaying their traffic while reading it, is the definition of an on-path/MITM attack, and the stem's details (full relay, silent recording, uninterrupted service) match it exactly, so C. (A) fixes on the forced network change but draws the wrong conclusion: availability was preserved throughout (deliberately, to keep victims transacting), so denial of service misstates the impact; it would fit if the rogue tower had attached the ATMs and then black-holed them. (B) names a real follow-on risk of holding captured transactions, but nothing was resubmitted during the event — replay is what the regulator would be told if duplicate withdrawals had been executed. (D) stretches 'injection', which denotes inserting crafted data into an application or protocol stream, not positioning a device in a path. A MITM's hallmark is service that keeps working while confidentiality quietly fails.

questions.question: After migrating the AirLink fleet to TLS, CityBank's architects worry that a compromised public certificate authority could issue attackers a valid certificate for the processing centre's hostname, letting a future rogue network impersonate the centre. Which control MOST directly addresses this specific risk?

options.A: Purchasing extended-validation certificates for the processing centre's public hostname from one of the largest and best-known public certificate authorities.
options.B: Increasing the public key length on the processing centre's certificate to strengthen its cryptography against attack.
options.C: Checking each certificate's revocation status through OCSP before the session is established, so known mis-issued certificates are rejected.
options.D: Embedding the expected certificate or public key in the ATM software so any other certificate is rejected.

questions.explanation: The threat is mis-issuance: some other trusted CA signing a certificate the bank never requested. Pinning removes that CA ecosystem from the trust decision entirely: the ATM accepts only the specific certificate or key it was built to expect, so even a technically valid rogue certificate fails, which is as direct as a countermeasure gets; hence D, and a closed fleet of bank-owned clients is the ideal place for it. (A) changes the vetting tier of the bank's own certificate but constrains no other CA; a compromised authority can still issue for the hostname. EV answers a question about phishing look-alike sites, not mis-issuance. (B) hardens against cryptanalysis of a key nobody is attacking; the rogue certificate carries its own perfectly good key. (C) helps only after the bad certificate is discovered and revoked, and an on-path attacker can often suppress the check; it is the right hygiene for retiring known-bad certificates. When the CA ecosystem itself is the threat, pin the identity you expect instead of trusting the ecosystem to police itself.

questions.question: CityBank's portable AirLink ATMs reach the processing centre over 4G modems. The network team relied on the carrier's link encryption and a private APN, and configured neither IPsec nor TLS. An attacker's rogue base station forced the modems down to 2G, broke the A5/1 link encryption, and read cardholder track data in cleartext. Which change would MOST reduce the impact of an attack of this kind?

options.A: Configure the fleet's modems to refuse any 2G/GSM fallback so a forced downgrade cannot occur.
options.B: Terminate an IPsec tunnel from each ATM to the processing centre, encrypting the payload.
options.C: Require mutual authentication at the cellular radio layer so the ATM verifies the tower it joins.
options.D: Deploy a wireless IDS on site to detect the rogue base station and alert the SOC.

questions.explanation: The root failure is implicit trust in a layer CityBank does not own. Moving confidentiality and integrity up to a layer they do control means any compromise of the carrier link, this downgrade or any later one, yields ciphertext instead of track data; the discriminator is impact of an attack 'of this kind', and Option B is the only option whose protection does not depend on predicting the attacker's method. (A) is real, recommended hardening; the case study lists 'Disconnect on 2G' as a missing configuration. But it closes only this one downgrade path while leaving the payload cleartext against any other link-layer compromise; it answers 'which change would have prevented the downgrade step?'. (C) is the correct diagnosis of what 2G lacks, but CityBank cannot impose mutual authentication on a carrier's radio network; it is a property of the network generation, not a control the bank can deploy. (D) is detective where the question asks preventive: by the time the SOC is alerted, the track data is captured; it answers 'how would CityBank detect a rogue base station?'. When a lower layer is untrusted, protect at a layer you control; detection and attack-specific hardening are complements, not substitutes.

questions.question: A network engineer at the festival site notices that two AirLink support laptops on the same switch exchange file transfers that never appear in the site router's flow logs, while the same laptops' sessions to the processing centre always do. Which statement BEST explains the difference?

options.A: The laptops negotiate a direct transport-layer session with each other that bypasses the lower network layers entirely.
options.B: The switch routes the local traffic itself using private internal IP addresses that the site's flow-logging router is configured to silently ignore.
options.C: An access list on the router discards the laptops' local traffic before the flow exporter can record it, while permitting their processing-centre sessions.
options.D: Frames between hosts on one segment are switched by MAC address and reach the router only when traffic leaves the network.

questions.explanation: The router simply never sees the local traffic: within a segment, delivery is a data link function (the switch forwards frames by learned MAC address), and the network-layer device participates only when a packet's destination lies in another network. Sessions to the processing centre cross that boundary and are logged; laptop-to-laptop transfers do not, which D states, and it is the structural explanation requiring no additional assumptions. (A) is impossible as described: transport sessions are carried inside network and data link layers, not around them; layers encapsulate, they cannot be skipped. (B) misassigns roles: a Layer 2 switch forwards frames and consults no routing logic, and 'ignoring' private addresses is not standard router behaviour on an internal network. (C) is conceivable in some other network, but it presumes an ACL nobody mentioned, and dropped traffic would still typically be countable; the layered explanation accounts for the evidence without inventing configuration. Knowing which device touches traffic at which layer tells you where visibility exists, and where a monitoring blind spot is architectural, not a fault.

questions.question: CityBank's developers are designing two AirLink data flows: transaction messages, where every message must arrive intact and in order, and once-per-second status telemetry, where an occasional lost sample is acceptable but freshness matters. Which transport-layer design is MOST appropriate?

options.A: UDP for both flows, because its lower overhead maximises battery life and bandwidth on cellular links.
options.B: TCP for the transaction messages and UDP for the telemetry, matching each flow's delivery requirements.
options.C: TCP for both flows, because a connection-oriented protocol is required before traffic can be encrypted.
options.D: UDP for the transactions and TCP for the telemetry, keeping time-critical payments off the slower protocol.

questions.explanation: Transport selection is requirements matching. Transactions need what TCP's connection, sequencing, acknowledgment and retransmission machinery provides: guaranteed, ordered delivery. Telemetry inverts the trade: a retransmitted stale sample is worth less than the next fresh one, so connectionless UDP's fire-and-forget model fits, and B assigns each flow accordingly. (A) optimises the wrong variable. The efficiency gain is real, but applying it to transactions means a dropped withdrawal message simply vanishes, an unacceptable integrity-of-delivery failure for financial traffic; UDP-everywhere is the right answer only when every flow tolerates loss. (C) rests on a false premise: encryption does not require a connection-oriented transport — DTLS and IPsec protect datagram traffic routinely. (D) reverses the analysis, treating TCP's reliability as mere slowness; payments are exactly the traffic that must not be 'fast but maybe lost'.

questions.question: A SOC analyst investigating a flood against CityBank's public web presence finds it consists of large UDP responses arriving from thousands of legitimate DNS and NTP servers that the bank never queried. Which property of UDP MOST directly makes this reflection technique possible?

options.A: It performs no handshake, so a request carrying a forged source address is answered as though the victim had sent it.
options.B: It provides no delivery guarantee, so attack packets lost in transit are simply gone instead of retransmitted.
options.C: It has lower per-packet header overhead than TCP, so each response consumes less of the attacker's own bandwidth.
options.D: It supports broadcast and multicast delivery, letting a single request reach many amplifying servers at once.

questions.explanation: Reflection depends on servers answering someone who never asked, and that requires the victim's address to be forgeable: because UDP exchanges datagrams with no connection establishment, a server has no handshake in which the claimed source must prove it can respond, so it obligingly sends its large reply to the spoofed address. That is the enabling property named in A. TCP's three-way handshake is precisely what defeats this, since a spoofed SYN never completes. (B) is a true UDP property but irrelevant to the mechanism; unreliable delivery describes what happens to lost packets, not why reflectors answer forged ones. (C) is also true and does improve the attacker's amplification economics, but it is a secondary efficiency, of no use without spoofability. (D) misdescribes the technique: reflectors are queried unicast, one request per server; multicast is how the attacker might reach local segments, and answers a different question about one-to-many delivery. Connectionless protocols accept unverified source addresses, and every reflection/amplification attack is built on that single fact.

questions.question: An analyst is tuning an IDS rule for a payment gateway to distinguish completed inbound TCP connections from mere connection attempts. Which observed packet sequence confirms that a connection was fully established?

options.A: A SYN from the client, a RST from the server, then a fresh SYN from the client.
options.B: A SYN from the client followed by a SYN-ACK from the server, with nothing further exchanged.
options.C: A SYN from the client, a SYN-ACK from the server, then an ACK from the client.
options.D: An ACK from the client answered by a FIN from the server shortly afterwards.

questions.explanation: Establishment is the three-way handshake completing: the client proposes (SYN), the server agrees and proposes back (SYN-ACK), and the client's final ACK confirms both directions are synchronized. Only after that third packet does either side hold an established connection, so Option C is the sequence the rule should match. (A) shows the opposite outcome: a RST is the server refusing or aborting the attempt, and the client simply trying again; it is what the analyst would match to detect rejected connections, such as scans of closed ports. (B) is a half-open connection: the server has committed state and is waiting for an ACK that never comes; matching this pattern at volume is how the analyst would detect a SYN flood, not a success. (D) belongs to the wrong phase entirely: FIN initiates orderly teardown of a session, so it presupposes an existing connection; it cannot confirm one being built. SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK is the signature of establishment, and its missing final ACK is the signature of the attack that abuses it.

questions.question: During a festival sales surge, CityBank's online banking tier stops accepting new connections; the SOC finds tens of thousands of half-open TCP sessions from spoofed addresses consuming the servers' connection backlog. When recording impact for the incident report, which security property should the team list as MOST directly affected?

options.A: Confidentiality, because the spoofed half-open sessions can read responses cached for other customers.
options.B: Integrity, because sessions abandoned in mid-handshake leave affected customer transactions only partially committed.
options.C: Authenticity, because the source addresses presented on each of the incoming connections are deliberately forged.
options.D: Availability, because legitimate customers can no longer establish sessions with the service.

questions.explanation: Impact classification follows the harm actually realized: the backlog exhaustion means real customers cannot connect, which is a loss of availability, the defining outcome of a SYN flood, so D belongs in the report. (A) has no mechanism behind it: a half-open session is unacknowledged handshake state, not an authenticated channel; the attacker receives nothing through it, and no data is disclosed. (B) confuses connection state with application state: a handshake that never completes never reaches the application, so no transaction exists to be left half-done; integrity would be the finding if an attacker were altering data in flight. (C) is the most tempting wrong answer because the addresses genuinely are forged, but spoofing is the attack's technique, not its impact: authenticity would matter if the forged identity were being trusted for access decisions, whereas here it merely hides the attacker. Report attacks by the property they degrade for users, not by the trick used to mount them; SYN floods spend spoofing to buy denial of service.

questions.question: CityBank is building a site-to-site VPN between a festival operations trailer and the processing centre. Compliance requires that internal host addresses never appear on the carrier network, and the gateway at each end will terminate the cryptography for the hosts behind it. Which IPsec configuration BEST meets these requirements?

options.A: Transport mode using AH, authenticating each packet's origin while leaving its payload readable in transit.
options.B: Tunnel mode using ESP, encrypting each original packet whole inside a new outer header between the gateways.
options.C: Transport mode using ESP, encrypting the payload while the original addresses stay visible for routing.
options.D: Tunnel mode using AH alone, protecting header integrity without concealing the packet contents.

questions.explanation: Two requirements decide this: hiding internal addressing, and gateway-terminated crypto. Tunnel mode encapsulates the entire original IP packet, internal source and destination included, inside a new packet addressed gateway-to-gateway, and ESP encrypts that inner packet, so the carrier sees only the gateways talking; B satisfies both conditions, which is why tunnel-mode ESP is the standard site-to-site construction. (A) fails on both axes: transport mode leaves the original header exposed for routing, and AH provides authentication and integrity with no confidentiality at all; it suits host-to-host traffic that must be genuine but may be public. (C) does encrypt the data, but transport mode by definition preserves the original header, so the internal addresses ride the carrier network in the clear, violating the compliance term; it is the right choice when the communicating hosts themselves are the crypto endpoints. (D) wraps the packet but never encrypts it. AH-only tunnels prove origin, not secrecy. Tunnel mode hides the original packet, transport mode hides only its payload; pick by whether topology itself is sensitive.

questions.question: Two application servers inside CityBank's data centre must exchange settlement files confidentially, the servers themselves are to terminate the cryptography, and the team wants the least added packet overhead. The data centre network routes between the two hosts directly. Which IPsec configuration is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Transport mode using ESP, encrypting the payload end to end while the original IP headers route the packets.
options.B: Tunnel mode using ESP terminated on the data centre's perimeter firewalls and not on the two servers themselves.
options.C: Tunnel mode using ESP running directly between the two servers, wrapping every packet inside a second, outer IP header.
options.D: Transport mode using AH, signing each packet so any modification in transit is detected on receipt.

questions.explanation: When the communicating hosts are the security endpoints and the path between them is routable as-is, transport mode is the natural fit: ESP encrypts the payload, the original headers keep doing the routing, and no second IP header is added. That meets the confidentiality requirement at minimum overhead, so A. (B) moves the crypto boundary to devices the requirement excluded: firewall-terminated tunnels leave the server-to-firewall legs unprotected inside the very network the files traverse, and the requirement was host-terminated protection. (C) works and protects the data, but it fails the stated tiebreaker: encapsulating host-to-host traffic adds a redundant outer header carrying the same addresses; tunnel mode earns its overhead when gateways speak for hidden networks, which is the previous question's scenario, not this one. (D) chooses the wrong service: AH detects tampering but transmits the settlement data readable, so confidentiality, the actual requirement, is unmet. Mode follows the endpoints (hosts: transport; gateways: tunnel), and protocol follows the property needed (secrecy: ESP; origin integrity alone: AH).

questions.question: After a failed gateway router at the festival site was replaced with a spare using the same IP address, several ticketing kiosks could reach it only after some minutes, and a capture taken during the gap shows the kiosks still addressing frames to the failed device's hardware address. Which mechanism BEST explains the delay?

options.A: The kiosks' DNS caches kept resolving the gateway's hostname to the address of the old device.
options.B: The kiosks' ARP caches still mapped the gateway's IP address to the old MAC address until those entries expired.
options.C: Spanning tree kept the replacement's switch port in a blocking state until the topology reconverged.
options.D: The kiosks' DHCP leases still named the failed device as default gateway until each lease renewed.

questions.explanation: The capture is the tell: frames addressed to a hardware address that no longer exists on the wire mean the IP-to-MAC mapping is stale, and that mapping is ARP's. Each kiosk cached the old resolution and kept using it until the entry timed out or was refreshed, exactly producing a minutes-long outage that heals by itself, so B. (A) works at the wrong translation: DNS maps names to IP addresses, and the gateway's IP never changed, so no DNS record was invalidated; DNS staleness answers a scenario where a service moved to a new IP. (C) is a real convergence delay when new switch links come up, but it would block the replacement's traffic wholesale, not cause kiosks to address the wrong MAC; the capture contradicts it. (D) fails the same way as A: the lease hands out a gateway IP, and that IP is unchanged, so renewal alters nothing. Layer-2 reachability lives in ARP caches: when a device is swapped behind a retained IP, stale ARP entries (until cleared or gratuitously updated) are the first suspect.

questions.question: A penetration test of CityBank's branch LAN showed that a laptop plugged into a meeting-room port could announce itself as the default gateway and silently proxy other hosts' traffic to the real one. Which switch capability MOST directly defeats this specific technique?

options.A: Dynamic ARP inspection, validating ARP replies against trusted address bindings before forwarding them.
options.B: Port security, limiting each access port to a single learned hardware address at a time.
options.C: Storm control, rate-limiting the volume of broadcast and multicast traffic accepted on access ports.
options.D: 802.1X authentication, requiring devices to authenticate successfully before their switch port forwards any traffic.

questions.explanation: The technique is ARP spoofing: unsolicited or false ARP messages claim the gateway's IP maps to the attacker's MAC. Dynamic ARP inspection attacks it at the root: the switch checks every ARP reply against known-good IP-to-MAC bindings (typically from DHCP snooping) and drops the forgeries, so the poisoning never reaches victim caches, regardless of who sent it; that is A, and note it works even against an authorized, already-admitted device. (B) sounds apt but misses: the attacking laptop uses one MAC of its own, so a one-address limit is satisfied while the poisoning proceeds; port security answers the rogue-hub and MAC-flooding problems. (C) governs traffic volume, and gratuitous ARP is a trickle, nowhere near storm thresholds. (D) is the strongest-sounding distractor: it would have kept this unauthorized laptop off entirely, but it authenticates admission, not behaviour. A compromised authenticated host could run the identical attack, so it does not defeat the technique itself. Admission control and protocol validation are different layers of defence; ARP spoofing is stopped by validating ARP, not by authenticating ports.

questions.question: Customers report certificate warnings when visiting CityBank's online portal, and an analyst finds their queries for the portal's hostname returning an address in an attacker's netblock, while the records on the bank's authoritative name servers are verified unchanged and the registrar's delegation is intact. Which point in the resolution chain was MOST likely compromised?

options.A: The bank's authoritative name servers, altered to serve the attacker's address for the portal's name.
options.B: The registrar account, with the domain's delegation quietly repointed at attacker-controlled name servers.
options.C: The recursive resolvers' caches, poisoned to return the attacker's address for the portal hostname.
options.D: The customers' local hosts files, each overwritten by malware to pin the portal to the attacker's address.

questions.explanation: Work the chain against the evidence: answers are wrong at the clients, yet the zone's source of truth is clean and the delegation still points at it, so the corruption sits between authority and client, which is the recursive resolver layer, where forged answers can be cached and then served to every user of that resolver; C fits all three facts at once and explains many customers being hit through a shared point. (A) is directly contradicted: the stem verifies the authoritative records unchanged; it would be the finding in a zone-tampering incident. (B) is likewise excluded by the intact delegation, and a registrar hijack typically redirects the whole domain, visible in WHOIS and NS records; it answers a scenario where delegation data changed. (D) could produce identical symptoms on one machine, but requires separate malware on every affected customer, a far larger assumption than one poisoned shared cache, and mass reports across ISPs point upstream. DNS trouble localizes by comparing answers at each tier (client, resolver, authority), and cache poisoning lives in the middle tier that everyone shares.

questions.question: Following the cache-poisoning incident, CityBank's architect must recommend a control that lets resolvers verify that answers for the bank's zone are genuine and unmodified, wherever those answers were obtained. Which control MOST directly provides that assurance?

options.A: DNS over HTTPS between customers' machines and their resolvers, encrypting every query and response in transit.
options.B: Shorter TTL values on the bank's records, so poisoned cache entries expire and are replaced more quickly.
options.C: Restricting zone transfers so that only the bank's own secondary name servers can copy the zone.
options.D: DNSSEC on the bank's zone, publishing signed records that resolvers validate for origin and integrity.

questions.explanation: The requirement is data authenticity, proof that an answer is what the zone owner published, and that is DNSSEC's exact function: records are cryptographically signed in a chain anchored at the root, so a validating resolver detects any forged or altered answer no matter which cache or path supplied it; D matches the requirement verbatim. (A) protects a different property on a different segment: DoH encrypts the client-resolver channel against eavesdropping and tampering en route, but the resolver's answer is trusted as received: a poisoned resolver serves its forgery over beautifully encrypted transport; DoH answers a query-privacy question. (B) shrinks the damage window without adding any verification; poison simply expires sooner and can be re-inserted; a mitigation, not an assurance. (C) guards bulk zone disclosure and copy integrity between the bank's own servers, a hygiene control unrelated to what resolvers can verify. Encryption of the channel and signing of the data are different guarantees, and only signatures survive whatever path the data took.

questions.question: Reopening the AirLink design file, an auditor finds the original justification: the carrier's private APN 'keeps the traffic private', so no further transit protection was configured. Which evaluation of the private APN is MOST accurate?

options.A: It separates the fleet's traffic from other subscribers, but by itself encrypts nothing end to end.
options.B: It encrypts each modem's traffic all the way through to the processing centre using keys the carrier manages.
options.C: It makes the cellular towers authenticate themselves to the modems, closing the rogue-base-station attachment path at the radio layer.
options.D: It places a carrier-managed stateful firewall between the fleet and the internet, making any further transit protection redundant.

questions.explanation: A private APN is a segregation construct: the carrier gives the fleet its own access point and routing context, keeping its traffic logically apart from other subscribers and often off the public internet. That is valuable containment, but the data still crosses radio and carrier infrastructure protected only by whatever the link layer offers, which the incident proved breakable; 'separate' was mistaken for 'encrypted', and A names the distinction. (B) asserts a service the APN does not provide: there is no APN-level end-to-end cryptography; believing this is precisely the design error being audited. (C) confuses the APN, which lives in the carrier's core, with radio-layer authentication, which is a property of the cellular generation. The APN was present throughout the downgrade attack and stopped nothing. (D) overstates a side effect: private APNs commonly restrict inbound reachability, but access restriction at the edge does nothing for confidentiality of data in transit, so 'redundant' does not follow. Segmentation controls who shares your path; only encryption controls who can read it, and every 'private network' claim should be tested against that pair.

questions.question: The festival operations team is standing up Wi-Fi for staff handhelds. A prior assessment showed attackers in the crowd capturing WPA2-PSK four-way handshakes and running offline dictionary attacks against the passphrase at their leisure. Which wireless configuration MOST directly removes the offline-guessing exposure?

options.A: WPA2-Personal with a forty-character random passphrase that is rotated every week.
options.B: WPA3-Personal, whose SAE exchange gives a captured handshake no material for offline password guessing.
options.C: Hiding the staff SSID from broadcast and filtering client hardware addresses at each access point.
options.D: WPA2 with TKIP disabled, so every access point requires AES-CCMP for the data frames.

questions.explanation: The exposure is structural to WPA2-PSK: its four-way handshake lets anyone who captures it test passphrase guesses offline, off the air, at hardware speed. SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) redesigns the exchange so each guess requires a live interaction with the network; a capture yields nothing to grind on. That removes the offline attack as a class outright, which is B, and 'MOST directly removes' is the discriminator. (A) is respectable hardening and a truly random forty-character secret resists dictionaries well, but the captured handshake remains attackable offline; the exposure is shrunk, not removed, and weekly rotation of a shared secret across a fleet invites operational leakage. It is the right answer where WPA3 hardware is unavailable. (C) is visibility theatre: SSIDs appear in probe and association frames anyway, and MAC filters fall to trivial spoofing; neither touches the handshake. (D) hardens the data cipher, but the dictionary attack targets the key derivation, not TKIP-vs-CCMP. When an attack is inherent to a protocol's design, the fix is the successor protocol that redesigned the exchange; configuration tuning around it only adjusts the attacker's effort.

questions.question: An audit of CityBank's headquarters finds that a visitor can plug a laptop into any lobby network jack and receive an address on the corporate LAN. The security manager wants every device authenticated against corporate identity infrastructure before its traffic is admitted at all. Which control BEST meets the requirement?

options.A: 802.1X port-based access control, with a RADIUS server validating each device's credentials or certificate.
options.B: Static MAC-address filtering, maintained by hand by the network team for every access port in the building.
options.C: Assignment of all the lobby wall jacks to a segregated guest VLAN restricted to internet access only.
options.D: DHCP reservations for known machines, so unrecognized devices receive no usable address.

questions.explanation: The requirement has two parts, authentication against corporate identity and enforcement before any traffic passes, and 802.1X is the mechanism built for exactly that pairing: the switch port stays closed to everything except the authentication exchange until the RADIUS server accepts the device's credentials or certificate, so admission is an identity decision, not a wiring decision; hence A. (B) is identity by hardware address, which is no identity at all: MACs are observed on the wire and spoofed in seconds, and a hand-maintained list across a headquarters decays immediately; it approximates the goal only on tiny, static networks. (C) is worthwhile containment and pairs well with 802.1X as the destination for failed authentications, but by itself it authenticates nobody; it answers 'how do we serve visitors safely', not 'how do we admit only authenticated devices'. (D) merely declines to hand out configuration: a visitor who statically assigns an address bypasses it entirely, since the port itself forwards freely. Enforcement must sit at the point of connection and be keyed to identity. Anything that filters after admission, or keys on spoofable attributes, is a courtesy as opposed to a control.

questions.question: CityBank's administrators need to manage servers inside the card-processing enclave from the corporate network. The security architect requires that every administrative session pass through a single hardened, fully logged entry point protected by multi-factor authentication. Which design BEST implements the requirement?

options.A: Firewall rules permitting SSH and RDP from each administrator's registered workstation to the enclave hosts.
options.B: A bastion (jump) host in a controlled segment, the only source permitted to reach enclave management interfaces.
options.C: Individual VPN profiles on administrator laptops, each terminating inside the enclave's server network.
options.D: A dedicated management VLAN trunked from the administrators' desk switches into the enclave switches.

questions.explanation: The architecture asked for is a choke point: one hardened system that every management session must traverse, where MFA is enforced once and session logging is complete. That is the definition of a bastion or jump host, made effective by firewall policy that admits management traffic from it alone; B implements the requirement instead of approximating it. (A) creates as many entry points as there are administrators: each workstation becomes an attack path into the enclave, MFA and logging must be replicated everywhere, and one compromised desktop reaches the servers directly. It is the pattern the requirement exists to eliminate. (C) also multiplies entry points, just tunnelled: per-laptop VPNs terminate inside the enclave, so a stolen laptop carries the enclave with it, and sessions bypass any central recording. It suits remote access to a general network, not privileged access to an enclave. (D) extends Layer 2 adjacency across the boundary: a trunked VLAN is connectivity, not control, and offers no authentication or session capture at all. Privileged access wants concentration, one heavily instrumented door, because every additional path into a sensitive zone is a full copy of the risk.

questions.question: A firewall review at a CityBank branch finds a packet-filtering rule set that permits all inbound TCP on ports above 1023, kept so that replies to outbound sessions can return. The reviewer wants return traffic admitted only when it belongs to a connection a branch host actually initiated. Which firewall capability MOST directly meets this?

options.A: An application-layer proxy gateway terminating each session and re-originating it toward the destination on the client's behalf.
options.B: Restricting the inbound high-port rules to source addresses inside the ISP's own network space.
options.C: Stateful inspection, tracking outbound connections and admitting only packets that match an existing session.
options.D: Network address translation, hiding branch addressing behind a single public address at the perimeter.

questions.explanation: The gap is memory: a static packet filter judges each packet in isolation, so 'replies must get back in' degenerates into 'leave the high ports open'. A stateful firewall records each outbound connection in a state table and admits inbound packets only when they correspond to a tracked session, which is word-for-word the reviewer's requirement; C closes the hole without breaking return traffic. (A) would also achieve it, and more besides: a proxy fully mediates the protocol. But it is the heavier instrument, with per-application support and termination overhead, bought for content inspection; as the direct fix for connection-tracking it exceeds the question. It wins when payload-level policy is required. (B) narrows who can exploit the standing hole yet the hole remains: any host in that ISP space can reach branch high ports unsolicited, and source addresses can be spoofed besides. (D) does incidentally drop unsolicited inbound flows for lack of a translation entry, but it is an addressing mechanism whose 'filtering' is a side effect with no policy control. The next question a reviewer asks is what happens when a mapping exists.

questions.question: CityBank must block uploads of files to personal cloud-storage sites and strip risky HTTP methods from branch web traffic, while continuing to allow ordinary browsing of those same sites. Which control is BEST suited to enforce decisions at that level of detail?

options.A: A stateful inspection firewall filtering each connection by source address, destination address and destination port.
options.B: An access control list applied directly to the router at each branch office's internet uplink.
options.C: A circuit-level gateway that relays outbound TCP sessions to the internet after validating each connection handshake.
options.D: An application-layer proxy gateway that terminates sessions and applies policy to methods and content.

questions.explanation: The policy is written in the vocabulary of the application protocol (this HTTP method but not that one, this action on a site while permitting the site itself), so enforcement requires a device that reads that vocabulary. An application-layer proxy terminates the client's session, sees full requests and payloads, and can strip a method or block an upload while passing the page view: only D operates where the policy's distinctions exist. (A) is an excellent connection gatekeeper, but its decision space is addresses, ports and connection state; an upload and a page view to the same site are identical at that resolution, so it can only allow or forbid the site wholesale. (B) is the same limitation with less: stateless address-and-port matching at the uplink, right for coarse boundary hygiene and blind to content. (C) sits one layer higher than a packet filter yet still below the need: a circuit-level gateway vets and relays sessions without interpreting the data inside them, so it too cannot tell method from method.

questions.question: CityBank is deploying a customer web portal that must be reachable from the internet and must query an internal database. The architect wants the design itself to limit what an attacker who compromises the web tier can reach next. Where should the web server be placed?

options.A: On the internal LAN beside the database server, keeping their connection short and simple.
options.B: In a screened subnet (DMZ), with only its specific database port permitted through the inner firewall.
options.C: With an external hosting provider, keeping the exposed service outside the bank's perimeter entirely.
options.D: On the firewall's outside interface, relying on the server's own hardening as its protection.

questions.explanation: Anything internet-reachable must be assumed compromisable, so the design question is what that compromise is adjacent to. A screened subnet puts the portal in a buffer zone with filtering on both sides: the internet reaches only the portal, and the portal reaches the internal network only on the one database port it needs. An attacker who wins the web tier inherits a nearly empty room, which is the containment the architect asked for; hence B. (A) is the worst adjacency: from a compromised portal on the internal LAN, the database, directory and everything else are one hop away with no screen between, so the design contributes nothing once the first host falls. (C) sounds like risk transfer but breaks on the requirement: the portal still needs its database query path into the bank, so the exposure returns as a tunnel from infrastructure the bank neither controls nor monitors. It suits static content with no internal dependencies. (D) leaves a single host's hardening as the entire defence, with no filtered zone around it; hardening is necessary and is not architecture. Place exposed services so that their compromise is the end of a corridor, not the middle of the building; segmentation is designed for the day the host falls.

questions.question: Two reports reach the festival SOC together: one staff handheld received an unsolicited anonymous message over Bluetooth, and a second handheld shows evidence that its contact list was retrieved over Bluetooth by an unknown device. In prioritising the response, which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: The second event is the more serious: unauthorized retrieval of data (bluesnarfing) breaches confidentiality, while unsolicited messages (bluejacking) are a nuisance.
options.B: The first event is the more serious, because successful message delivery proves the attacker has already completed a pairing relationship with the handheld.
options.C: The two events deserve equal priority, since each one demonstrates the same unauthorized radio-layer reach to devices carried by festival staff.
options.D: Neither event warrants a response, because Bluetooth's short operating range means the attacker will already have moved on and left the venue.

questions.explanation: Triage ranks by impact: pushing an unwanted message at a device (bluejacking) alters nothing and takes nothing (an annoyance and a warning sign), while pulling data off a device (bluesnarfing) is a completed confidentiality breach of whatever was reachable, here a contact list and possibly more; A states the ranking and the reason. (B) rests on a false technical premise: bluejacking abuses the object-push mechanism precisely because it works on discoverable devices without pairing, so delivery proves proximity, not trust; had the stem shown an attacker-initiated pairing, escalation would be right. (C) flattens the distinction triage exists to draw: shared attack surface does not equal shared impact, and treating spam and data theft alike misallocates the SOC's attention. (D) turns a targeting constraint into a dismissal. Short range means the attacker was on-site and close, which at a multi-day festival argues for response (sweeps and a staff notice), not for shrugging. Prioritise by what the attacker achieved against CIA, not by which technology carried the attack. Same radio, very different losses.

questions.question: Following the incidents, the mobile team must cut the risk of further Bluetooth data theft from the staff handheld fleet, which still needs Bluetooth to drive its payment card sleds. Which set of measures is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Disable Bluetooth across the whole handheld fleet by written policy until the current festival season has completely ended.
options.B: Rely on Bluetooth's frequency-hopping physical layer, whose channel changes defeat attempts to intercept the pairing and data traffic.
options.C: Instruct staff to keep handhelds within arm's reach and to decline any pairing prompt they were not expecting.
options.D: Make the handhelds non-discoverable, require authenticated pairing, and remove the Bluetooth profiles the sleds do not use.

questions.explanation: The constraint rules out amputation, so the risk has to be engineered down while the radio stays up: non-discoverable mode removes the fleet from casual scanning, authenticated pairing stops unknown devices from establishing the relationship bluesnarfing rides on, and deleting unused profiles removes the very services (object exchange, file transfer) that data-theft attacks call. D layers three cuts into the actual attack path and keeps the sleds working. (A) meets the security goal by failing the business one: the stem says the payment sleds depend on Bluetooth, so a blanket disable trades an incident for an outage; it is the right answer only where no business function needs the radio. (B) mistakes a coexistence mechanism for a security control: frequency hopping fights interference, and every Bluetooth chipset follows the hop sequence as a matter of protocol. (C) is worth issuing and worthless alone: purely procedural, dependent on busy staff noticing prompts, and no barrier to attacks on discoverable services that never prompt. When a risky capability must stay enabled, shrink it: visibility, authentication, and surface (unused services) are the three dials that turn.

questions.question: A wireless assessment of CityBank's branch offices finds consumer-grade access points with WPS enabled 'to make onboarding easier'. The assessor must state the WPS risk accurately so the finding survives challenge and drives remediation. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: It weakens the encryption in use, forcing access points to fall back from AES to TKIP for all clients.
options.B: It broadcasts the network passphrase in cleartext during every new client association handshake, so anyone capturing the exchange can read it directly.
options.C: Its PIN can be brute-forced in hours because each half is validated separately, after which the passphrase is recoverable.
options.D: It lets joining clients bypass captive-portal authentication on nearby guest wireless networks that gate access through a web page.

questions.explanation: Findings survive challenge only when the mechanism is stated correctly: WPS's external-PIN design confirms the two halves of its eight-digit PIN independently, collapsing the search space to a few thousand tries per half, so an online brute force completes in hours and the protocol then hands over the network passphrase. Option C is the defensible statement and the reason 'disable WPS' is standard remediation. (A) invents a cipher interaction: WPS automates enrolment and has no effect on the AES/TKIP suite the AP negotiates; a reviewer who knows this discards the finding, the credibility failure the stem warns about. (B) also misstates the mechanism: the passphrase is delivered inside the WPS protocol exchange after PIN authentication, not broadcast in cleartext at each association; close enough to sound right, wrong enough to be challenged. (D) connects WPS to captive portals, which are unrelated web-layer gating on open networks.

questions.question: Festival staff report that their handhelds briefly dropped off the staff Wi-Fi, reconnected by themselves, and then began showing certificate warnings in the timekeeping app; a spectrum survey finds a second network broadcasting the staff SSID at higher power from the crowd area. Which attack sequence BEST explains all of these observations?

options.A: A deauthentication flood pushed clients off the legitimate network so they would re-associate to an evil twin carrying the same SSID.
options.B: A WPS PIN attack recovered the staff passphrase overnight, after which the attacker quietly joined the staff network as one more ordinary client.
options.C: Wideband jamming across the festival Wi-Fi channels overwhelmed the access points and temporarily forced the staff handhelds onto their cellular fallback connectivity.
options.D: DHCP pool exhaustion on the staff network denied new leases until the access points were power-cycled by staff.

questions.explanation: A good explanation covers every observation: forged deauthentication frames account for the sudden drop; auto-rejoin plus a stronger same-SSID signal accounts for clients landing on the impostor; and traffic now traversing an attacker's network accounts for the TLS certificate warnings. A strings all three into the classic deauth-then-evil-twin sequence, corroborated by the survey. (B) explains at most a quiet attacker presence on the real network: a joined client causes no mass disconnects, no reconnection anomalies, and no certificate errors; it answers a scenario about passphrase compromise, and WPS is an AP-side feature besides. (C) fails on the reconnect: jammed handhelds falling back to cellular would not re-associate to Wi-Fi, and jamming cannot explain a second network advertising the staff SSID. (D) is an availability fault with the wrong footprint: no drop of already-associated clients, no rogue SSID, no TLS warnings. Certificate warnings after an unexplained Wi-Fi bounce are the signature of traffic re-homed through an impostor.

questions.question: CityBank must give external auditors access to three internal web applications. The auditors work from their own firms' locked-down laptops, on which no VPN client software may be installed, and from office networks that commonly allow only web ports outbound. Which remote-access approach BEST fits these constraints?

options.A: An IPsec VPN, with a preconfigured client software profile distributed to each visiting auditor before the engagement begins.
options.B: PPTP, selected because every major desktop operating system already supports it natively with no additional client software required.
options.C: A clientless TLS (SSL) VPN portal, published on TCP port 443 and reached through a standard browser.
options.D: L2TP over IPsec, relying on the operating system's built-in virtual private network client support.

questions.explanation: Both constraints point the same way: no installable software means the access method must live in what the laptops already have, a browser, and restrictive egress means it must ride the one port those networks reliably pass, 443. A clientless TLS VPN portal satisfies both, brokering the three web applications through an authenticated gateway without touching the endpoint; Option C is the fit, and web apps are exactly the workload such portals serve. (A) fails the first constraint outright, since a client profile is precisely the software installation the auditors' firms forbid, and IPsec's protocols are commonly dropped by strict egress filtering; it is the right answer for managed corporate laptops needing full network access. (B) clears the install hurdle and fails the security one: PPTP's authentication and cipher (MSCHAPv2, MPPE/RC4) are broken, and it is deprecated; native support does not rehabilitate it. (D) still needs per-laptop VPN configuration and the same firewall-unfriendly IPsec transport underneath. Remote-access selection is constraint-driven: who controls the endpoint and what the intervening networks pass decide the technology before security preferences do.

questions.question: Remote work has saturated CityBank's VPN concentrators, and engineering proposes split tunneling so that only traffic for corporate address ranges uses the tunnel. Before approving, the CISO asks for the MOST accurate statement of the security trade-off involved. Which is it?

options.A: The tunnel's cryptography is weakened, because the concentrator must maintain two separate policies for every connected client.
options.B: There is no meaningful change, because traffic to the corporate ranges remains encrypted exactly as it was before the split tunnel was introduced.
options.C: Exposure is doubled, because corporate traffic now traverses both the tunnel and the public internet on every request.
options.D: Corporate traffic stays protected, but the endpoint's internet traffic bypasses corporate inspection while the device holds a path into the internal network.

questions.explanation: A trade-off statement has to name what is gained and what is genuinely given up. Split tunneling leaves the corporate flow encrypted and relieves the concentrators (the gain) while sending the endpoint's general internet traffic outside the corporate security stack (web filtering, DLP, monitoring), on a device that simultaneously holds an authenticated route into the LAN: a browser compromise now sits one hop from the internal network with the defences unsighted. D captures exactly that, which is what a CISO must weigh. (A) invents a cryptographic cost: policy routing decides which packets enter the tunnel and leaves the cipher untouched. (B) is the engineer's half-truth: the encryption claim is correct, but 'no meaningful change' ignores the inspection bypass, which is the entire trade-off. (C) reverses the mechanism: corporate traffic still travels only the tunnel; nothing is sent twice. Evaluate tunneling changes by where the traffic stops being watched, more than where it stays encrypted. Protection and visibility are separate properties.

questions.question: CityBank operates 200 branches over a mixture of MPLS, broadband and LTE links, each branch configured locally; successive audits keep finding branches whose firewall and routing policies have drifted from the corporate standard. Which capability of SD-WAN MOST directly addresses this audit finding?

options.A: It replaces the branches' broadband and LTE circuits with uniformly provisioned MPLS.
options.B: It raises each branch's usable bandwidth by bonding whatever links the site has available.
options.C: It applies centrally defined policy to every branch edge device, independent of each site's underlying transport.
options.D: It encrypts traffic between branches using keys that each site's edge device manages for itself.

questions.explanation: The finding is configuration drift, 200 hand-tended devices diverging from standard, and the SD-WAN property that answers it is the separation of control plane from transport: policy is authored once in the orchestrator and pushed to every edge, so the architecture itself enforces the standard, with no reliance on 200 acts of local discipline, and an audit compares sites against one source of truth; that is C, and 'independent of transport' is what lets one policy span MPLS, broadband and LTE alike. (A) reverses SD-WAN's economics: the technology exists to use cheap heterogeneous links safely, not to standardize on the expensive one, and uniform circuits would not stop local config drift anyway. (B) is a genuine SD-WAN benefit aimed at a different complaint; more bandwidth fixes congestion findings, not policy findings. (D) undercuts itself in the second clause: SD-WAN does encrypt its overlay, but per-site self-managed keying is the decentralization the finding indicts; the value lies in central orchestration of the crypto too. Recurring drift across many sites is a management-plane problem; buy centralization of control, not more capacity or faster links.

questions.question: After CityBank moved branch telephony onto the same WAN links as nightly data replication, users report choppy, garbled calls every evening while the file transfers themselves complete without error. Which change would MOST directly restore call quality?

options.A: Increasing the TCP window size on the replication servers so the nightly transfers complete sooner each evening.
options.B: Re-encoding the branch calls with a noticeably higher-bitrate audio codec to improve their perceived sound fidelity.
options.C: Enabling compression on the WAN links to reduce the total volume of traffic they must carry.
options.D: Applying quality-of-service policies so voice packets are queued and forwarded ahead of bulk transfer traffic.

questions.explanation: The symptom pair is diagnostic: bulk TCP transfers ride out congestion by retransmitting and reordering, so they 'complete without error', while real-time voice cannot wait for retransmission; every delayed or jittered packet is a gap the listener hears. The fix is therefore not more capacity arithmetic but scheduling: QoS classifies voice into a priority queue so it crosses the congested link with bounded delay and jitter while the replication absorbs the slack it tolerates so well; that is D. (A) does the opposite of helping: a larger window lets the transfers fill the path more aggressively, deepening the queues that voice is stuck behind; window tuning answers a throughput problem. (B) raises fidelity per packet while making the stream heavier and just as delayed: garbling here is loss and jitter, not codec quality. (C) buys some headroom at the cost of processing delay, and an already-compressed replication stream yields little, and nothing about compression protects voice at the moment of contention. Real-time traffic fails on latency and jitter, elastic traffic on throughput; when they share a link, priority queueing reconciles them.

questions.question: A red-team capture from a branch LAN shows CityBank's telephony call-setup traffic readable in cleartext: dialled numbers, internal extensions, and the negotiated session parameters for upcoming calls were all recovered. Which control MOST directly protects this signaling traffic?

options.A: Transporting SIP over TLS, so call setup and teardown exchanges are encrypted between the endpoints and call servers.
options.B: Enabling SRTP, so the media streams carrying the audio between endpoints are encrypted and authenticated.
options.C: Moving the handsets onto a dedicated voice VLAN, separated from the workstation segments of the LAN.
options.D: Enforcing 802.1X on handset ports, so only authorized telephones can join the branch network.

questions.explanation: What leaked is signaling, the SIP conversation that sets calls up and tears them down, and the direct control is to encrypt that channel itself: SIP over TLS wraps the setup exchange, hiding numbers, extensions and, critically, the session keys that the endpoints negotiate for the media; A protects precisely the traffic that was captured. (B) guards the other half of a call: SRTP encrypts the audio stream, but the capture here was of signaling, which SRTP does not touch. Unprotected signaling can expose the very keys SRTP depends on, which is why the two controls are deployed together; B answers the next question, about recorded audio. (C) reduces who can easily reach the packets by separating segments, but a VLAN is a containment measure, and this capture happened on the LAN; traffic within the voice VLAN remains cleartext to anyone who gets there. (D) governs which devices may join, not what their traffic reveals: an authorized-but-compromised host still reads cleartext signaling. Telephony has two channels with two protections, TLS for the signaling and SRTP for the media, and encrypting either one leaves the other exposed.

questions.question: The same red-team exercise showed that packet streams recorded from a mirrored switch port could be reassembled into playable audio of customer-service calls. Which control MOST directly prevents an eavesdropper from recovering conversation content this way?

options.A: SIP over TLS, encrypting the call-setup channel between the handsets and the call servers.
options.B: SRTP, encrypting and authenticating the media streams that actually carry the audio.
options.C: Disabling port mirroring on branch switches except during approved troubleshooting windows.
options.D: Transcoding calls with a proprietary audio codec so captured streams resist casual decoding.

questions.explanation: The recovered artefact is audio, and audio travels in the media stream (RTP), separate from signaling; the control that makes a captured stream unplayable is SRTP, which encrypts and integrity-protects the media packets themselves, so a mirrored copy yields ciphertext wherever it was collected. B addresses the exact loss demonstrated. (A) is the complement, not the fix: TLS on SIP hides call metadata and protects key negotiation, but the audio packets it sets up still travel unencrypted if SRTP is off; it is the right answer to the previous finding, about readable signaling. (C) attacks one collection method as opposed to the exposure: mirroring is merely how this red team listened; taps, compromised switches, or any on-path position hear the same cleartext, and the control evaporates the moment an attacker can configure a switch. (D) is obscurity with a shelf life: codecs are identified from RTP headers and decoders are public or reversible; 'harder to decode' is not a confidentiality property. Protect the data, not the vantage point: if content is cleartext on the wire, somewhere to stand and listen will always exist.

questions.question: CityBank's internet gateway is saturated by ICMP echo replies arriving from hundreds of hosts inside a university network, though the bank sent no echo requests; the university reports that its hosts each received requests appearing to come from the bank's address. Which technique BEST explains this traffic pattern?

options.A: A SYN flood launched against the bank's internet gateway with the university's address space forged as the source of every packet.
options.B: A teardrop attack sending overlapping packet fragments through many separate hosts inside the university network.
options.C: A smurf attack, in which echo requests forged with the bank's address reached a broadcast address and every host replied.
options.D: A ping sweep of the bank's public address range conducted from a set of compromised university hosts.

questions.explanation: Every detail is the smurf signature: the victim receives echo replies it never solicited (so its address was forged on someone else's requests), the repliers are ordinary legitimate hosts (so they were used as amplifiers), and they all sit in one network (so one broadcast-addressed request reached them all at once). C reconstructs the mechanism that generates precisely this evidence, one spoofed request multiplied into hundreds of replies. (A) has the spoofing backwards and the protocol wrong: a SYN flood would show TCP SYNs arriving at the bank, and forging the university's addresses would send the backscatter to the university, not replies to the bank. (B) is a malformed-fragment crash attack against a single target's reassembly code; nothing about it recruits hundreds of repliers or involves echo traffic. (D) would produce echo requests arriving at the bank and replies flowing back out; the observed direction is inverted, which is exactly how an analyst distinguishes being scanned from being reflected at. Read amplification attacks from the victim's inbox: unsolicited replies from many honest hosts in one network mean your address was borrowed and a broadcast did the multiplying.

questions.question: During a penetration test of CityBank's legacy ATM controllers, a single crafted ICMP packet whose fragments reassemble to more than 65,535 bytes reliably crashes a controller's network stack. Which attack class does this MOST precisely demonstrate, and why does it work?

options.A: Teardrop: the fragments' offsets deliberately overlap, and the reassembly logic corrupts adjacent memory when it tries to combine them.
options.B: Smurf: amplified echo traffic from many distant sources exhausts the controller's inbound network bandwidth.
options.C: SYN flood: half-open connection state accumulates until the controller's session table is exhausted.
options.D: Ping of death: the reassembled datagram exceeds the maximum legal IP size, overflowing the buffer that receives it.

questions.explanation: The two facts that classify it are 'single packet' and 'reassembles beyond 65,535 bytes': IP's length field cannot describe a larger datagram, so old stacks allocated buffers assuming that ceiling, and fragments summing past it overflow the buffer on reassembly: a crash from one malformed packet, which is the ping of death; D names both the class and the mechanism the test demonstrated. (A) is the near cousin and the trap: teardrop is also a fragmentation-reassembly exploit, but its lever is overlapping offsets confusing the reassembly logic, not total size exceeding the legal maximum. The stem specifies size, not overlap. (B) and (C) are volume attacks and fail the arithmetic of the evidence: a smurf needs many amplified senders saturating bandwidth, and a SYN flood needs a stream of TCP connection attempts building state; neither can be demonstrated by one ICMP packet, and both degrade service instead of crash a stack. One-packet kills point to malformed-input bugs. Classify fragmentation exploits by their lever, oversize (ping of death) versus overlap (teardrop), and remember such flaws live on in unpatched embedded stacks.

questions.question: An acquisition adds a partner campus whose farthest segment sits 18 router hops from CityBank's core, and the merged network must route around a failed link within seconds. The partner proposes keeping RIP everywhere because it is simple to operate. Which limitation of RIP is MOST relevant to rejecting the proposal?

options.A: RIP carries its routing updates in cleartext, so route advertisements can be captured and read off the wire by listeners.
options.B: RIP treats 16 hops as unreachable and converges slowly, so both the 18-hop path and the recovery target fail.
options.C: RIP requires a backbone-area hierarchy to scale, which a merged campus network cannot easily support.
options.D: RIP floods complete topology maps on every change, consuming bandwidth on the WAN links between the merged sites.

questions.explanation: Relevance means the limitation that breaks the stated requirements, and RIP breaks both at once: its metric counts to 15, with 16 meaning unreachable, so an 18-hop destination is administratively nonexistent; and its periodic-update, distance-vector convergence takes minutes (with hold-downs), not the seconds required. Option B is the direct, two-count rejection. (A) is a real hygiene concern (RIPv2 supports authentication, and updates are observable), but confidentiality of advertisements is not among the requirements the proposal must meet, so it cannot carry the rejection. (C) belongs to the wrong protocol: the backbone-area design (area 0) is OSPF's architecture; RIP has no areas at all, and citing this hands the partner an easy rebuttal. (D) also describes the other family: flooding link-state advertisements to build topology maps is OSPF/IS-IS behaviour, whereas RIP sends distance vectors, not maps. Reject a protocol on the requirements it measurably fails, for RIP its diameter (15 hops) and convergence time, and keep the failings of one protocol family from being pinned on the other.

questions.question: CityBank is redesigning interior routing for a 60-site network in which link failures must be routed around within seconds, and the addressing plan aggregates by region. Which routing protocol choice BEST fits these requirements, and for the right reason?

options.A: RIP, because a simple hop-count metric stays easy to reason about across all 60 sites.
options.B: Static routes pushed to every site by configuration management, avoiding dynamic routing protocols and their failure modes entirely.
options.C: BGP, because a protocol that scales to the entire global internet will comfortably handle routing for a 60-site network.
options.D: OSPF, because routers recompute from a full topology map for fast reconvergence, and its areas match regional aggregation.

questions.explanation: Both requirements select link-state: OSPF routers share a synchronized topology map and recompute paths locally the moment a failure is flooded, delivering the seconds-scale reconvergence asked for, and its area hierarchy exists precisely to summarize regions into a backbone, and the addressing plan maps onto it directly; Option D is right for reasons that match the requirements point for point. (A) fails the speed requirement: distance-vector convergence with hold-down timers is measured in minutes, and hop count ignores link capacity; simplicity was nobody's stated requirement. (B) removes reconvergence altogether: static routes do not react to failures, so 'within seconds' becomes 'when an operator intervenes'. That is right only for stub sites with a single path. (C) is capable but mis-reasoned and mis-fit: BGP is a path-vector policy protocol for routing between autonomous systems, tuned for stability over speed; 'scales to the internet' is the classic bigger-is-better fallacy, and interior fast convergence is the one thing it is not designed for. Interior networks needing fast failover want link-state protocols, and a design whose areas mirror the address hierarchy is choosing the protocol for what it was built to do.

questions.question: A festival equipment workshop still connects its five diagnostic PCs through an old Ethernet hub. Technicians complain that transfers slow sharply whenever several PCs are busy, and a consultant demonstrated that a sniffer on any hub port captures every station's traffic. Which upgrade MOST directly addresses both observations, and why?

options.A: Replace the hub with a switch, giving each port its own collision domain and forwarding unicast frames only to the destination port.
options.B: Replace the hub with a small router, so that every PC is placed into a separate IP subnet of its own.
options.C: Cascade a second hub off the first and split the PCs between the two devices, halving the shared load.
options.D: Upgrade to a faster hub, so the shared medium offers more headroom to every attached station.

questions.explanation: Both complaints have one cause: a hub is a shared medium that repeats every bit out of every port, so contention throttles throughput and every NIC in promiscuous mode hears everything. A switch fixes both with one change: per-port collision domains end the contention, and MAC-learned forwarding delivers unicast frames only where they belong, so a sniffer on another port sees broadcasts and its own traffic, no more; A resolves the cause itself. (B) would also isolate traffic, but at the wrong layer and cost: per-PC subnets add addressing and gateway complexity a five-PC workshop does not need. It is the right shape of answer when policy boundaries between segments are required, not connectivity. (C) misunderstands cascading; hubs joined to hubs still form one collision domain and one listening zone, so both problems survive intact. (D) buys speed for a medium that stays shared: contention scales down but persists, and the confidentiality exposure is untouched at any speed. Shared-medium problems, collisions and universal sniffing alike, are solved by switching to per-port forwarding, not by making the shared medium faster or more numerous.

questions.question: During an internal assessment at a branch, a tester on an access port captures only broadcast frames and the tester's own sessions, where the same technique through the site's old hub once captured everything. The tester's report must explain the change accurately. Which explanation is MOST accurate?

options.A: The switch encrypts frames travelling between its ports, so other stations' traffic is still present in the capture but cryptographically unreadable.
options.B: The switch forwards unicast frames only to the learned destination port, so other conversations no longer reach the tester's port.
options.C: The switch's VLAN configuration has isolated every access port into its own separate per-port broadcast domain.
