options.D: The switch performs routing between its ports, so frames cross from one port to another only when a gateway forwards them.

questions.explanation: A switch learns which MAC address lives on which port from source addresses, then forwards each unicast frame only toward its destination; traffic between two other stations therefore has no reason to appear at the tester's port, while broadcasts still flood to all ports of the VLAN, which matches the capture contents exactly, so B. It also frames the honest caveat for the report: this is a forwarding behaviour, not a security guarantee, and techniques like MAC flooding or ARP spoofing exist precisely to defeat it. (A) invents a service switches do not provide: frames between ports are unmodified, and an 'unreadable' theory is contradicted by a capture where other traffic is simply absent, not garbled. (C) is refuted by the tester's own evidence: broadcasts were captured, so the port shares a broadcast domain with their senders; one-port-per-VLAN would have silenced those too. (D) moves the device up a layer. A Layer 2 switch forwards frames by MAC with no gateway involved; inter-VLAN routing exists but is not why unicasts go quiet on an access port. Report the mechanism itself, learned per-port forwarding, because knowing why the sniffer went quiet is exactly knowing which attacks make it loud again.

questions.question: A flat network of 500 devices at CityBank's operations centre suffers periodic slowdowns, and captures attribute them to high volumes of legitimate broadcast traffic (ARP, discovery protocols) reaching every host. The team wants to shrink how far broadcasts propagate while keeping the existing switch hardware. Which change MOST directly accomplishes this?

options.A: Enable port security, so each switch port accepts frames from only one learned hardware address.
options.B: Enable spanning tree on the switches, removing the redundant paths that broadcasts can loop across.
options.C: Define VLANs on the switches, dividing the flat network into several smaller broadcast domains.
options.D: Replace the busiest access switches with faster models that can process broadcasts with less delay.

questions.explanation: Broadcast reach is defined by the broadcast domain, and a flat network is one giant domain: every ARP request touches all 500 hosts. VLANs partition the same physical switches into multiple logical domains, so each broadcast now floods only its own segment. Propagation shrinks by design, on existing hardware, exactly as asked; Option C is the mechanism that maps to the requirement. (A) polices who may send on a port; it neither reduces the number of hosts a legitimate broadcast reaches nor addresses volume at all; port security answers an unauthorized-device question. (B) is the closest miss: spanning tree prevents pathological broadcast storms by blocking forwarding loops, but the stem describes legitimate broadcast load in a loop-free network, and STP leaves the single 500-host domain fully intact. It is the right answer when the capture shows the same frames circulating endlessly. (D) treats propagation as a performance problem: faster switches forward the same broadcasts to the same 500 hosts, merely sooner, and every host still spends cycles processing them. To limit how far broadcasts travel, cut the domain into pieces; VLANs resize broadcast domains without new hardware or new cabling.

questions.question: CityBank centralizes DHCP at headquarters. When a newly routed branch segment comes online, its clients receive no addresses, though the same laptops obtain leases immediately on the headquarters LAN, and the WAN link between the sites tests clean in both directions. Which explanation BEST fits the evidence, and points to the standard fix?

options.A: The DHCP scope is exhausted, so the server has no addresses left to offer the branch clients; extend the pool.
options.B: The WAN provider is filtering the lease traffic somewhere in transit; request an exception for those flows.
options.C: The branch clients' requests carry addressing the server cannot recognize; renumber the branch to match the server's scopes.
options.D: DHCP discovery is broadcast, and routers do not forward broadcasts; configure a relay agent on the branch router.

questions.explanation: The evidence isolates the variable: same clients, same server, success on the local LAN, failure across a routed boundary, healthy link. What changes across that boundary is broadcast reach: a client's DHCPDISCOVER is broadcast because the client has no address yet, and routers terminate broadcasts at the segment edge, so the plea for an address dies on the branch wire. The standard cure is a relay agent (IP helper) on the branch router, which converts the broadcast to a unicast aimed at the headquarters server; D explains the failure and names the fix, which is why relays exist in every centralized-DHCP design. (A) cannot survive the control case. An exhausted scope would refuse the same laptops at headquarters too, and exhaustion is a fault that appears under load, not precisely at a new segment's turn-up. (B) contradicts the clean bidirectional link test and, more basically, the traffic pattern: without a relay, no lease traffic enters the WAN to be filtered. (C) reverses DHCP's premise: clients request precisely because they have no addressing, and scope selection is driven by the relay's tagged source information. Protocols that begin from nothing must broadcast, and broadcasts stop at routers, so centralized services for such protocols work only through per-segment relays.

questions.question: A technician 'improving redundancy' patches a second uplink between two access switches through a third distribution switch, creating a physical ring. Within seconds the operations-centre network is unusable: switch CPUs are pinned, and captures show the same broadcast frames circulating endlessly. Which mechanism, correctly deployed, would have kept the redundant path without the outage?

options.A: Spanning Tree Protocol, which detects the loop and blocks one segment of it until a working path fails.
options.B: Storm control, which caps the incoming rate of broadcast and multicast traffic accepted on each individual switch port.
options.C: Link aggregation, which bundles parallel cables between two switches into one logical link.
options.D: Port security, which limits which hardware addresses may be learned on the new uplink port.

questions.explanation: Ethernet frames carry no hop count, so a physical loop recirculates broadcasts forever, amplifying them each lap; that is the storm in the captures. The requirement is to keep the redundant path yet forward over a loop-free topology, and that is spanning tree's whole function: elect a topology, place the loop-forming port in a blocking state, and unblock it automatically when the primary path dies; A delivers redundancy and stability together, which is what the technician actually wanted. (B) is a damage limiter, not a topology manager: rate caps would blunt the storm's peak while the loop keeps regenerating traffic, and legitimate broadcasts get throttled along with the noise. It is right as a second line of defence, wrong as the mechanism. (C) fails on topology: aggregation bundles parallel links between the same two devices; this ring runs through a third switch, which is exactly the case bundling cannot express and spanning tree exists for. (D) filters which MACs may speak on a port; nothing about it detects or breaks forwarding loops. Layer 2 redundancy is safe only under a loop-management protocol; without spanning tree (or a modern equivalent), every backup cable is a scheduled outage.

questions.question: At a small branch with no RADIUS or certificate infrastructure, an auditor finds staff attaching unmanaged mini-switches under desks, fanning single wall jacks out to several personal devices. As an interim measure using only the existing access switches, which control MOST directly curbs the practice?

options.A: Reassign the affected wall jacks into an isolated guest VLAN with internet-only access.
options.B: Configure port security, limiting each access port to a small fixed number of learned hardware addresses.
options.C: Deploy 802.1X authentication on every access port, with each connecting device's credentials checked against the corporate directory service.
options.D: Enable DHCP snooping, blocking lease offers that originate from any port not designated as a server port.

questions.explanation: The observable signature of a desk mini-switch is several source MAC addresses appearing on one access port, and port security acts on exactly that signal: cap the learned addresses at one or two, violate into shutdown or restrict, and the fan-out stops working the moment a second device speaks, configured entirely on the switches already in place, which honours both stated constraints; Option B is the direct interim fit. (A) changes what the extra devices can reach, while leaving them free to connect: the mini-switch keeps working inside the guest VLAN, so the practice is accommodated, not curbed. It is the right move for jacks meant for visitors. (C) is the better end-state and the wrong answer today: 802.1X needs the RADIUS infrastructure the stem rules out; it answers the follow-up question of what the branch should build toward. (D) watches a different protocol: snooping polices rogue DHCP servers and builds binding tables; personal laptops taking leases through a mini-switch never trip it. Pick controls whose trigger condition matches the behaviour you want to stop; multiple MACs on one port is the fingerprint here, and port security is the control that reads it.

questions.question: A SOC analyst reviewing perimeter IPS alerts finds a stream of fragmented packets, addressed to a legacy branch controller, whose fragment offsets overlap so the pieces can never reassemble consistently; the controller has crashed twice during the alert windows. Which attack does the evidence MOST specifically indicate?

options.A: Ping of death: fragments that reassemble into a datagram beyond the maximum legal size.
options.B: Smurf: amplified echo replies converging on the controller from a broadcast network.
options.C: Teardrop: overlapping fragment offsets that crash vulnerable reassembly implementations.
options.D: SYN flood: connection requests that exhaust the controller's half-open session table.

questions.explanation: The IPS has already isolated the discriminating feature: offsets that overlap. Teardrop-class attacks craft fragment sequences whose offset arithmetic is self-contradictory, and reassembly code that fails to handle the overlap corrupts memory and crashes. Malformed input plus a crashing legacy stack is this evidence exactly, so C. (A) is the sibling fragmentation attack and the intended confusion: ping of death's lever is total reassembled size exceeding 65,535 bytes, not overlap. An analyst who names the wrong lever will chase the wrong patch, since the two bugs live in different checks of the reassembly path. (B) fails on both traffic type and mechanism: a smurf is a flood of well-formed echo replies that saturates capacity; it involves no fragmentation trickery and kills by volume, not by crash. (D) is TCP state exhaustion: a rising tide of SYNs and half-open sessions, degrading service progressively, nothing like a malformed-fragment signature followed by outright crashes. Fragmentation attacks are told apart by their lever, oversize versus overlap, and naming the lever correctly is what turns an alert into the right remediation for the vulnerable stack.

questions.question: CityBank plans to stream a live all-hands video to 2,000 desktops. A trial that sent each desktop its own unicast copy saturated the campus core, so the network team will use multicast delivery instead. Which protocol should the team also run so that the stream is delivered only where there are viewers?

options.A: IGMP, letting hosts join and leave multicast groups so the network forwards the stream only to segments with subscribers.
options.B: ICMP, reporting delivery errors and diagnostic information about the stream's path back to its source.
options.C: SNMP, letting the operations team watch link utilization on each distribution switch in real time while the broadcast is running.
options.D: BGP, advertising the multicast group's addresses outward to each of the campus routers ahead of the event.

questions.explanation: Multicast saves the core only if the network knows where the viewers are: IGMP is the membership protocol in which hosts announce joining or leaving a group, and routers (with switches snooping the exchanges) use that state to replicate the stream solely onto segments holding subscribers: one copy in the core, fan-out at the edges, silence on portless segments. Option A is the missing piece that makes 'only where there are viewers' true. (B) trades on the one-letter similarity: ICMP carries error and diagnostic messages (unreachables, time-exceeded) and manages no group membership; it is the answer to how routers report delivery problems. (C) is how the team would watch the rollout succeed, not how the rollout works; it is management-plane telemetry with no role in forwarding decisions. (D) routes between autonomous systems on the internet's scale; an interior campus stream neither needs nor uses exterior route advertisement, and BGP carries no membership semantics. Efficient one-to-many delivery is two problems, replication (multicast forwarding) and audience discovery (IGMP membership), and the design fails without the second.

questions.question: CityBank leases dark fiber between its two data centres, and the WAN team argues that because the bank lights and operates the fiber itself, the replication traffic crossing it can run unencrypted. Which evaluation of this argument is MOST accurate?

options.A: It holds: traffic on a point-to-point fiber that the bank alone lights cannot realistically be observed anywhere in transit.
options.B: It holds, provided the fiber's full physical route is inspected on a regular schedule for evidence of splices or taps.
options.C: It fails: dark fiber carries other tenants' wavelengths on the same strand, so their equipment can observe the bank's frames.
options.D: It fails: fiber can be tapped with minimal signal loss along uncontrolled ground, so traffic in transit still requires encryption.

questions.explanation: Leasing dark fiber buys exclusivity of the strand, not custody of the path: the glass runs through ducts, vaults and rights-of-way the bank neither owns nor watches, and optical taps (a bend coupler leaking a fraction of the light) extract traffic with losses small enough to hide in normal attenuation. Exclusive use therefore does not equal confidentiality, and encryption of data in transit remains required; D states why the argument fails. (A) mistakes a commercial arrangement for a physical guarantee: 'we light it' says who transmits, not who can listen along kilometres of accessible cable. (B) converts a preventive requirement into detective comfort: route inspections are periodic and taps are built to be unobtrusive, so the exposure window between visits is exactly what an attacker uses; inspection supplements encryption, it cannot substitute. (C) reaches the right verdict through the wrong facts. Sharing one strand via multiple wavelengths describes a lit/wavelength service; dark fiber is precisely the product where the strand is yours alone, so the stated reason is refutable and would sink the finding. Control of the endpoints is not control of the ground between them. Data crossing territory you cannot secure gets encrypted, whatever the contract says about the medium.

questions.question: A carrier's proposal assures CityBank that its MPLS service is 'a private network' on which encryption 'is unnecessary'. Before signing, the bank's architect must characterize what MPLS actually provides. Which characterization is MOST accurate?

options.A: MPLS encrypts each labelled packet between the provider's edge routers using carrier-managed keys.
options.B: MPLS separates customers' traffic using labels but applies no encryption, so confidentiality rests on trust in the provider.
options.C: MPLS wraps traffic in IPsec automatically whenever a label-switched path crosses the provider's shared core.
options.D: MPLS varies each packet's path through the core unpredictably, which makes interception impractical in the first place.

questions.explanation: MPLS is a forwarding technology: labels steer each customer's packets down its own label-switched paths and keep tenants' traffic logically separated across a shared core, but the payload rides exactly as submitted, cleartext in and cleartext through. 'Private' therefore means separated, and confidentiality reduces to trusting the provider's staff, equipment and interconnects; B gives the architect the accurate characterization, and the standard consequence follows: run IPsec or TLS over the MPLS service for data that matters. (A) asserts a cryptographic service that plain MPLS has no mechanism to perform; label operations are header manipulation, and no carrier keys touch the payload. (C) imagines a default that does not exist; IPsec over MPLS is precisely the customer-side overlay the accurate characterization leads to, never an automatic property of the carrier's LSPs. (D) inverts MPLS's behaviour to manufacture comfort: traffic engineering makes paths deterministic along established LSPs, and in any case an observer at one traversed point reads everything regardless of route variety. Like the private APN before it, a carrier's 'private network' is a separation claim. Test it by asking who could read the payload, and encrypt at a layer you control when the answer includes anyone but you.

questions.question: CityBank is adding tap-to-pay NFC readers to the AirLink ATMs, and a risk workshop must decide how much protection NFC's short operating range actually provides against payment interception. Which risk statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The range is a hard physical ceiling, so capturing a transaction requires physically tampering with the reader itself.
options.B: The NFC standard already encrypts each session on its own, so the operating range question is largely irrelevant to the workshop's risk analysis.
options.C: Short range raises attacker difficulty, but relay and skimming equipment can still extend or capture transactions, so transaction-layer cryptographic protection remains necessary.
options.D: Interception is a practical concern only in crowded environments, so readers installed in well-supervised branch locations need no additional protective controls beyond supervision.

questions.explanation: Range is an attacker-cost parameter, not a security boundary: purpose-built antennas read NFC from further than the nominal few centimetres, skimming hardware can sit at the reader, and relay attacks defeat proximity entirely by piping the exchange between a victim's card and a distant terminal in real time. So the workshop should treat short range as difficulty, and place the real protection in the payment protocol's cryptography (dynamic per-transaction cryptograms), which is what C says. (A) converts a nominal figure into a physics guarantee; eavesdropping and relay both work without touching the reader, so 'tampering required' understates the surface. (B) misattributes the protection: baseline NFC communication is not encrypted; the confidentiality and anti-replay strength lives in the payment application above it, not in the radio standard. (D) turns risk into a seating chart: a festival ATM is the crowded case, and supervision does not perceive radio-layer relay or a skimmer inside the housing. Proximity limits are attack-cost assumptions, not controls. Price them as difficulty, and put the actual defence in cryptography that does not care where the attacker stands.

questions.question: In a lab reconstruction of the AirLink incident, testers capture a valid, fully encrypted withdrawal authorization and retransmit it an hour later; the processing centre accepts it a second time and dispenses cash again. Which protocol change MOST directly prevents this?

options.A: Upgrading to a stronger cipher, so captured authorization messages take far longer to decrypt.
options.B: Rotating the encryption keys used by each ATM on a daily schedule instead of monthly.
options.C: Hashing each message body, so any modification made to it in transit is detected on receipt.
options.D: Adding timestamps and sequence numbers that the processing centre validates, so a repeated message is recognized and refused.

questions.explanation: The demonstration is a replay attack, and its defining lesson is that the attacker needed to read nothing: a captured ciphertext, re-sent intact, is decrypted and honoured by the legitimate recipient like the original. The missing property is freshness: the receiver cannot tell a first presentation from a repeat. It is supplied by validated timestamps, sequence numbers or nonces, which make the duplicate detectably stale; D adds exactly the property whose absence the testers proved. (A) strengthens a lock the attacker never picks: replay works on unread ciphertext, so cipher strength is orthogonal; it is the right investment when the finding is cryptanalysis, not repetition. (B) narrows the replay window to the key's lifetime, and an hour-old message sails through a daily rotation; a mitigation of degree where the question demands one of kind. (C) protects integrity, but the replayed message is unmodified, so a hash over it verifies perfectly and endorses the fraud; integrity checks answer tampering findings. Confidentiality, integrity and freshness are separate guarantees; a protocol can encrypt and authenticate flawlessly and still pay twice, until something in each message proves it is new.

questions.question: After a hypervisor migration, several CityBank branch servers drift about twenty minutes from the domain controllers, and users on those servers begin failing Kerberos authentication until time synchronization is restored. Which explanation BEST connects the clock drift to the failures?

options.A: Kerberos rejects authenticators whose timestamps fall outside the permitted clock skew, a freshness check that keeps captured tickets from being replayed.
options.B: Kerberos derives its session keys from the current clock value, so drifted machines compute mismatched keys.
options.C: Ticket lifetimes are measured by the client alone, so a drifted client discards its own still-valid tickets before they have truly expired.
options.D: The domain controllers sign tickets with time-based one-time codes that drifted servers can no longer generate.

questions.explanation: Kerberos builds replay resistance out of time: each request carries an encrypted authenticator whose timestamp the verifier checks against its own clock, and anything outside the allowed skew (five minutes by convention) is refused as possibly re-sent. Twenty minutes of drift puts every honest authenticator outside that window, so authentication fails wholesale until the clocks agree. A ties the symptom to the mechanism and names the security purpose the check serves. (B) misplaces time in the cryptography: session keys come from the KDC's key distribution, encrypted under principal and service keys; the clock gates validity decisions, it is not key material. (C) has the arbiter wrong: lifetimes are stamped into the ticket by the KDC and enforced at validation; clients do not adjudicate their own tickets, and early self-discard would not produce server-side rejections. (D) imports TOTP, a different authentication family, into a protocol that uses plain timestamps within encrypted structures, not generated one-time codes. When authentication breaks in step with clock drift, you are watching an anti-replay freshness check do its job, which is why time synchronization is a security dependency, not an operational nicety.

questions.question: Mall security reports a person parked outside a CityBank branch for several hours with a laptop and a roof-mounted antenna; the branch wireless logs show no association attempts during the period. The SOC must classify the activity and choose a proportionate first response. Which assessment is BEST?

options.A: An active intrusion is underway; disable the branch wireless network until law enforcement arrives on site.
options.B: Probable wireless reconnaissance (war driving); review how far the branch SSIDs propagate and confirm the strength of the authentication they require.
options.C: Harmless behaviour; passively observing radio signals from a parking lot yields nothing of value to an attacker.
options.D: An evil twin attack is already in progress; direct branch staff to move every handheld onto its cellular fallback connectivity at once.

questions.explanation: The evidence supports collection, not contact: hours of dwell with a high-gain antenna and zero association attempts is the profile of war driving: passively mapping SSIDs, security modes and signal reach. The proportionate response treats it as a warning about exposure: measure how far the branch networks bleed past the walls, trim transmit power where warranted, and verify that what is reachable from a parking lot demands strong authentication; B matches classification to evidence and response to classification. (A) declares an intrusion the logs refute and answers it by inflicting an availability loss on the branch — self-imposed denial of service as a precaution against observation. (C) waves away the collection phase: SSIDs, hardware vendors, security modes and coverage maps are targeting data, and reconnaissance is how attacks are scoped; 'passive' does not mean 'valueless'. (D) names an attack whose evidence (duplicate SSIDs, client disruptions, certificate warnings) is entirely absent, and triggers an operational upheaval on none of it. Reconnaissance observed is your prompt to shrink what an observer can learn and harden what an observer can reach.

questions.question: A wireless survey inside CityBank headquarters finds an unlabelled consumer access point plugged into a wall jack behind a printer, broadcasting an open network bridged onto the corporate LAN; a facilities employee explains that a contractor added it 'for convenience'. Which statement BEST captures the primary risk?

options.A: The open network lets passers-by consume the corporate internet connection's bandwidth without any usage accounting.
options.B: The device's radio may interfere with the sanctioned access points operating on nearby channels in the same band.
options.C: It creates an unauthenticated radio bridge into the wired LAN that bypasses the perimeter and network access controls.
options.D: Its consumer firmware will fall behind on security patches, since no one in the organization owns its ongoing maintenance.

questions.explanation: Rank the harms and one dwarfs the rest: an open AP bridged to the corporate wired network extends that network, unauthenticated, into radio range. Anyone in the parking lot obtains what amounts to an inside jack, entering behind the firewall, behind admission control, invisible to perimeter monitoring. That nullification of the boundary architecture is the primary risk, and it is why rogue access points are treated as incidents as opposed to tidiness problems; C. (A) is real and trivial by comparison, a bandwidth and acceptable-use nuisance that would top the list only for an AP isolated from corporate assets. (B) is an airtime-management concern for the wireless team; interference degrades performance and confers no access. (D) is a genuine secondary finding (unowned devices do rot), but patch latency matters on this device mostly because of the exposure C already describes; unmanaged lifecycle is the chronic issue, the open bridge is the acute one. Severity ranking asks what the finding gives an attacker. A rogue AP gives interior network access from outside the walls, which outranks every operational side effect it also causes.

questions.question: Festival staff handhelds automatically join any network broadcasting the staff SSID, and last season's incident showed an attacker exploiting exactly that with a stronger transmitter. Which measure gives the handhelds the MOST reliable way to distinguish the legitimate network from an impostor?

options.A: Rename the staff SSID to an obscure value and suppress it from the access points' beacon broadcasts.
options.B: Brief staff to join manually and only when the displayed signal strength is high and steady.
options.C: Lock the handhelds to 5 GHz channels, which inexpensive rogue equipment less commonly serves.
options.D: Deploy WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X), with client profiles that validate the authentication server's certificate before connecting.

questions.explanation: An SSID is a self-declared name that any radio can claim, so telling twin from truth requires the network to prove an identity that cannot be copied. Under 802.1X the handheld's supplicant validates the authentication server's certificate before it will complete the join: an evil twin can echo the SSID but cannot present the certificate's private key, so a properly pinned client simply refuses it. That is cryptographic distinction, enforced by configuration as opposed to vigilance; D. (A) is concealment, and thin: clients probe for hidden SSIDs, advertising the name in every probe, and the twin answers with whatever name it hears; renaming resets the attacker's knowledge for a day. (B) delegates authentication to a bar graph, when the incident's premise is an attacker who transmits stronger; signal strength favours the twin by design. (C) raises the equipment bill trivially (dual-band hardware is commodity), and a band is a venue, not an identity. Names and signal properties are claimable; only a key-backed identity check lets a client refuse a perfect imitation, so make the network authenticate itself to the device.

questions.question: An inventory review finds warehouse barcode scanners that support only WEP still attached to a CityBank network that also carries settlement traffic. To justify an urgent replacement budget, the security team must state the WEP risk accurately. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: WEP's short initialization vectors force keystream reuse, letting an attacker who captures traffic recover the key within minutes and join the network.
options.B: WEP's weakness is chiefly short passphrases, so configuring the longest supported key makes it acceptable for scanner traffic.
options.C: WEP's flaw is primarily its one-way authentication, so adding MAC-address filtering restores adequate protection for the warehouse fleet.
options.D: WEP is breakable only with prolonged physical access to an access point, so the risk stays confined to the warehouse floor and its equipment.

questions.explanation: The budget case must survive technical challenge, and Option A is the statement that does: WEP's 24-bit initialization vector space is so small that busy traffic repeats IVs quickly, RC4 keystream reuse plus related-key weaknesses then yield the shared key to passive capture in minutes with public tooling, and the recovered key is the network key, so the attacker joins the same LAN the settlement traffic crosses. Mechanism, feasibility and consequence, each correct. (B) misdiagnoses: the attacks recover whatever key is configured (104-bit keys fall the same way), so 'use a longer key' is the fix for guessable secrets, a different disease. (C) pairs a real observation with a useless remedy: authentication is not the broken part that matters, and MAC filters fall to address spoofing in seconds; a reviewer refutes this in one sentence, taking the budget with it. (D) inverts the exposure: the attack is passive radio capture from anywhere in range, parking lot included. Legacy-crypto findings are argued from the mechanism of the break (small IV space, keystream reuse, passive recovery), because an accurate one-paragraph mechanism is what makes 'replace it now' unanswerable.

questions.question: While hardening branch wireless, an engineer finds access points running WPA2 in mixed mode, accepting both TKIP and AES-CCMP 'so older devices keep working', yet the device inventory shows nothing that still requires TKIP. What should the engineer do, and why?

options.A: Keep mixed mode, because each client negotiates the strongest cipher it supports, so capable devices already use CCMP.
options.B: Require CCMP only: TKIP is a deprecated RC4-based fallback with known attacks, and permitting it lets devices negotiate downward.
options.C: Retire wireless encryption at the access points and rely on TLS from each application instead, simplifying the radio estate.
options.D: Require CCMP and also suppress SSID broadcast, since network visibility matters more than the cipher choice.

questions.explanation: Every cipher a network will accept is attack surface: TKIP was a transitional wrapper around RC4, deprecated with practical attacks against it, and offering it means the network's floor, not its ceiling, defines the exposure, including for downgrade tricks against the negotiation. With the inventory showing no TKIP-dependent devices, the compatibility rationale is empty, so the fallback is pure liability; the AirLink incident already taught what negotiable fallbacks cost. B removes it. (A) is the seductive half-truth: capable clients do negotiate CCMP for themselves, but the network's security is judged by what it will accept, and mixed mode also drags group (broadcast) traffic down to the weakest common cipher for all clients. (C) misapplies a sound principle: application-layer encryption is defence in depth, not a license to open the radio layer, which alone protects the LAN from unauthenticated joining and local attacks TLS never sees. (D) spends effort on concealment that probing clients defeat, bundled with the correct move to look reasonable. When nothing needs the legacy option, its only remaining function is to weaken you. Disable fallbacks affirmatively; do not trust negotiation to avoid them.

questions.question: Reviewing a wireless design document that reads 'the WLAN will be secured by EAP', a CityBank security architect returns it and asks the author to specify which EAP method will be deployed. Which statement BEST justifies the architect's objection?

options.A: EAP is a proprietary protocol controlled by a single wireless vendor, and it has since been superseded by newer open standard alternatives.
options.B: EAP mandates RC4 for its inner encryption, which current corporate cryptographic policy no longer permits anywhere in the bank.
options.C: EAP is only an authentication framework; its security depends on the method carried inside it, which may be strong or weak.
options.D: EAP applies only to wired 802.1X deployments and therefore offers no real protection on wireless networks.

questions.explanation: 'Secured by EAP' specifies nothing yet: EAP is a carrier framework, an envelope in which some concrete method performs the actual authentication, and the methods span mutual certificate authentication with strong key derivation (EAP-TLS) down to legacy exchanges with no server authentication or usable keying (EAP-MD5). Until the method is named, the design's security properties are indeterminate, which is precisely a reviewable defect; Option C is the architect's justification. (A) confuses the framework with LEAP, a vendor's lightweight method that genuinely was proprietary and broken. EAP itself is an open IETF standard, and an objection argued this way gets corrected, not actioned. (B) invents a mandate: EAP specifies no cipher at all, and that indifference is the very reason the method choice carries all the weight, making this backwards in an instructive way. (D) is simply false: carrying EAP over the air (802.1X on WLANs, historically 'EAP over LAN' extended to wireless) is the flagship enterprise Wi-Fi architecture. A framework named in a design is a decision deferred. Review the concrete method, because 'uses EAP' constrains security exactly as much as 'uses encryption' does.

questions.question: CityBank will deploy 802.1X on its branch WLANs. No client-certificate PKI exists and none is budgeted, so users will authenticate with their directory passwords, and the design must keep those credentials protected in transit over the air. Which EAP method BEST fits the constraints?

options.A: EAP-TLS, mutually authenticating the client and the server with X.509 certificates issued to each side.
options.B: EAP-MD5, hashing the password exchange so the credential itself is not transmitted over the air.
options.C: LEAP, using a lightweight proprietary vendor challenge-response protocol designed specifically for early wireless deployments.
options.D: PEAP, opening a server-authenticated TLS tunnel and passing the password exchange inside it.

questions.explanation: The constraints are explicit (password authentication, no client PKI, credentials protected over the air), and PEAP is the method shaped to them: the client first validates the server's certificate and builds a TLS tunnel (one server-side certificate is the entire PKI bill), then runs the password exchange inside that encrypted, server-authenticated channel, so credentials neither travel exposed nor get offered to an impostor AP; D satisfies every stated condition. (A) is the stronger method and the wrong fit: mutual certificate authentication presupposes issuing and lifecycle-managing a certificate per client, exactly the PKI the stem rules out; it is the right answer the day that budget exists. (B) fails the transit requirement it pretends to meet: an unprotected challenge-response hash invites offline guessing, the method authenticates no server, and it yields no keying material for the wireless session. (C) is a broken legacy proprietary method whose challenge-response fell to practical cracking tools years ago, and choosing it re-imports the problem. When passwords must cross wireless, wrap them in a server-authenticated tunnel. Read constraints as hard requirements: the technically strongest method is wrong when it needs infrastructure the design cannot have.

questions.question: After a WAN circuit fails at a partner site still running a distance-vector protocol, an engineer watches two of its routers re-advertise the dead network to each other for several minutes, the route's metric climbing step by step until it reaches the protocol's maximum and the route is finally purged. Which underlying behaviour of distance-vector routing BEST explains the episode?

options.A: Each router floods a complete topology map after every change, so a failure generates duplicated route advertisements.
options.B: The two routers' update timers fell out of synchronization, so each advertised stale route information on a different periodic refresh cycle.
options.C: Routers learn only their neighbours' summarized distances, so two of them can keep re-advertising a failed path to each other.
options.D: The failed circuit kept flapping between up and down states, and every transition triggered a fresh advertisement.

questions.explanation: The stair-step metric is the fingerprint: in distance-vector routing no router sees the topology, each believing whatever distances its neighbours summarize, so when the network died, each router took the other's stale advertisement as evidence of an alternate path, re-advertised it back one hop worse, and the pair inflated the metric in lockstep until the protocol's 'infinity' ceiling declared the route unreachable. That mutual rumour loop is count-to-infinity, and it is why split horizon, poison reverse and a small maximum metric exist; C names the mechanism that generates exactly this trace. (A) describes the other protocol family: link-state routers flood topology advertisements and would each compute the loss locally in seconds, never bidding a metric upward. (B) blames scheduling for a structural problem: timer alignment changes when stale routes are spoken, not why each router believes the other's. (D) predicts a different trace: flapping yields alternating up/down advertisements tracking the circuit, not a monotonic climb to a fixed maximum on a link that stayed dead. Routing-by-rumour fails by believing your own echo; read a steadily inflating metric as count-to-infinity, the signature pathology of distance-vector convergence.

questions.question: CityBank's customer portal web server was compromised through a vulnerable plugin, yet forensics shows the attacker spent a week probing from that server without reaching the card database or the directory service. The portal sits in a screened subnet between external and internal firewall interfaces. Which design property MOST directly accounts for the containment?

options.A: The inner screen permitted the web server only one database port inward, so every other probe from it was dropped.
options.B: Address translation at the perimeter hid the internal numbering plan, leaving the attacker unable to identify any internal targets worth probing.
options.C: The portal host's hardening baseline had already removed the scanning and enumeration tooling an intruder would need to probe internal ranges.
options.D: The outer firewall's alerting brought the SOC in early, and its containment actions cut the probing short.

questions.explanation: The screened subnet earned its keep on the inward side: the architecture's premise is that exposed hosts will eventually fall, so the inner screen restricts what a fallen host may initiate (here, one database port to one destination), and a week of probing becomes a week of drops at a policy boundary the attacker cannot alter from the web server. That least-privilege egress from the DMZ is the property doing the containing; A. (B) overrates obscurity: translation hides numbering from the outside, but the attacker was inside the DMZ, learning real reachable addresses from the server's own configuration and its permitted database path. Concealment, unlike filtering, ends at first compromise. (C) is worthwhile friction that cannot carry the outcome: attackers bring or fetch tooling, and hardening the host does not constrain where its packets may go; the firewall does. (D) is contradicted by the timeline: a week of unimpeded probing is the opposite of early detection, and the stem credits design, not response. Measure a DMZ by its inner rules; the design succeeds when a compromised exposed host discovers that almost nothing inward will answer it.

questions.question: CityBank's marketing launch is expected to drive a fifty-fold traffic spike, plus probable volumetric DDoS attention, to a promotional site currently served from one origin data centre. The infrastructure team must keep the site available without re-platforming the origin. Which measure BEST achieves this?

options.A: Double the origin's web servers behind the existing load balancer ahead of the launch window.
options.B: Add a second internet circuit at the origin data centre, roughly doubling the total ingress bandwidth available for the launch.
options.C: Set aggressive browser-caching headers, so returning visitors render the promotional pages from their own local caches.
options.D: Front the site with a content delivery network, serving cached content from edge locations near the traffic's sources.

questions.explanation: Fifty-fold plus a flood is a scale problem that a single origin cannot meet at the origin: a CDN answers it by moving the serving edge outward: promotional content is cached across many distributed points, each visitor is served nearby, and both the legitimate spike and volumetric attack traffic are spread across the provider's aggregate capacity instead of converging on one building. The origin keeps its architecture and sees a trickle of cache fills; D meets the availability goal within the no-re-platforming constraint, and static promotional content is the ideal cacheable workload. (A) buys 2x against 50x, and compute was never the choke point a volumetric flood aims at; the pipe is. (B) widens that pipe finitely while leaving every packet converging on one location; volumetric attacks are sized in multiples of any circuit pair. (C) helps only visitors who have already been served once, and launch traffic is first visits by definition, and attackers' tools ignore cache headers entirely. Availability at internet scale comes from distributing where demand is absorbed; capacity added at a single point is spent the moment the internet aims at it.

questions.question: A configuration audit finds CityBank's branch routers and switches managed over Telnet, with TACACS+ giving each administrator an individual account. The network team argues the per-admin accounts make Telnet acceptable. Which response to that argument is MOST accurate?

options.A: The team is right: per-administrator accountability addresses the principal risk, which is untraceable shared access to devices.
options.B: The team is right if management traffic is confined to a dedicated VLAN, since that separation is functionally equivalent to encryption.
options.C: The team is wrong: Telnet carries those individual credentials and every session in cleartext, so interception yields working administrator access; replace it with SSH.
options.D: The team is wrong about switches but right about routers, which sit behind the perimeter and face less interception risk.

questions.explanation: The argument defends the wrong property: TACACS+ gives attribution (who logged in, what they typed), but Telnet transmits the login and the session as cleartext on the wire, so anyone positioned to capture branch traffic collects the very credentials the accounting system so carefully individualizes, plus every configuration detail that scrolls by. Accountability and confidentiality are independent, and the fix is the encrypted equivalent, SSH, which preserves the TACACS+ model intact; C. (A) names a real risk Telnet-with-TACACS+ does solve, then stops one property short: attribution of sessions an attacker can read and hijack is cold comfort. (B) is the segmentation-equals-encryption fallacy this domain keeps refuting: a management VLAN narrows who is positioned to listen, and whoever gets there, by one compromised host or one misconfigured trunk, reads everything; separation bounds exposure, encryption removes it. (D) invents a perimeter distinction with no basis: both device classes carry credentials in the clear, interception risk is about path, not device type, and cleartext administrative access is unacceptable anywhere. Evaluate a protocol against each property separately. Telnet plus perfect AAA still fails confidentiality, and 'we know who logged in' does not answer 'who else was reading'.

questions.question: An external scan of CityBank's public address space, reviewed by a new analyst, shows TCP port 22 open on forty hosts, and the firewall permits that port inbound from any source 'so engineers can work remotely'. Which risk assessment of this finding is MOST accurate?

options.A: The exposure is minor, because the service listening on that port encrypts every session between client and server.
options.B: Forty hosts are offering remote administrative shells to the entire internet; that access should instead be concentrated through one hardened, MFA-protected entry point.
options.C: The finding is a false positive in effect: an open TCP port carries no real risk until a vulnerability is published for the listening service.
options.D: The principal risk is information disclosure through service banners, which changing the daemon's banner text will resolve.

questions.explanation: Port 22 is SSH, remote administrative shell access, so the finding reads: forty separately maintained doors to command-line control, reachable by every address on the internet, each accepting credential-guessing at line rate and each exposed to the next pre-auth vulnerability in its daemon. The assessment that captures both the severity and the fix is B: collapse the surface to a single bastion with MFA, logging, and firewall rules admitting enclave SSH from it alone. Forty exposures become one instrumented chokepoint. (A) mistakes the session's property for the exposure's: encryption protects traffic from observers, and does nothing about who may connect, guess, or exploit; the risk here is reachability, not readability. (C) inverts the discipline: brute force works against weak credentials with no CVE required, and 'wait for the advisory' concedes the race to whoever scans first. Attack surface is managed before vulnerabilities are announced. (D) trims the leaf and leaves the tree: banners ease reconnaissance slightly, and rewording them changes no attacker's ability to connect. Assess an open port by the capability behind it and the audience in front of it. Administrative capability plus a global audience is a critical finding whatever the protocol's cryptography.

questions.question: CityBank's egress firewall permits outbound TCP only on port 443, and the SOC had assumed this made bulk data theft impractical. A red team nonetheless exfiltrates a large test dataset in a single afternoon session without raising any alert. Which explanation of the result is MOST accurate?

options.A: The red team tunnelled the data out inside TLS on the permitted port, indistinguishable at the firewall from ordinary encrypted web traffic.
options.B: The rule set must also have been permitting a second port, since one allowed port cannot carry both browsing and the exfiltration.
options.C: The red team split the dataset into small transfers spaced across many days, staying beneath volume-based alerting thresholds.
options.D: The red team routed the data out through the firewall's own management interface, which egress policy does not evaluate.

questions.explanation: A port-only egress policy asks one question, 'is this TCP to 443?', and an attacker's TLS tunnel answers it identically to a browser: the red team wrapped its exfiltration in encrypted traffic to a server it controlled, and at the firewall's level of inspection there is nothing to distinguish stolen gigabytes from a long video call; no rule was broken, which is why no alert fired. A explains the result and exposes the assumption: port filtering was treated as data-loss control, a job that needs TLS-inspecting proxies, egress destination reputation, or DLP with visibility into the tunnel. (B) misunderstands multiplexing: one permitted port carries unlimited concurrent sessions to unlimited destinations, and that generosity is exactly what the tunnel exploits. (C) proposes a real evasion technique that the stem's facts exclude: a single afternoon session is the opposite of low-and-slow, and no volume thresholds existed to duck. (D) invents a bypass with the wrong direction of risk: management interfaces are an attack surface for reaching the firewall, not a side channel exempting traffic through it. An allowed encrypted port is a tunnel anyone may use. Egress control by port number decides where traffic may go, and says nothing about what leaves inside it.

questions.question: Ransomware at a CityBank subsidiary is traced to an internet-exposed server: initial access was a brute-forced login on TCP port 3389, opened 'temporarily' for a vendor and then forgotten. For the post-incident report, which pairing of lesson and remediation is MOST appropriate?

options.A: The password policy failed; require substantially longer and more complex vendor-account passwords, rotated regularly, while keeping the existing access path unchanged.
options.B: Vendor management failed; terminate the vendor's contract and permanently disable the account that was brute-forced.
options.C: External visibility failed; raise the frequency of the bank's perimeter vulnerability scanning so that temporary firewall openings are discovered and closed sooner.
options.D: Remote desktop was internet-reachable; move it behind an MFA-protected gateway and give every firewall exception an owner and expiry.

questions.explanation: Port 3389 is RDP, interactive desktop control, and the causal chain has two links a report must break: the service was exposed to the whole internet, and the exposure was created ad hoc with no expiry, so it outlived its purpose silently. D fixes both: remote desktop reachable only through an authenticated, MFA-protected gateway ends internet-facing password guessing as an access route, and exceptions carrying owners and expiry dates end the 'temporary and forgotten' pattern that created the target. Lesson is matched to root cause, remediation to lesson. (A) hardens the credential while preserving the exposure: longer, regularly rotated passwords slow guessing against a service that should not be guessable from the internet at all; symptom, not cause. (B) punishes a party the analysis does not blame (the vendor needed access; the bank chose the mechanism), and the pattern survives for the next vendor. (C) buys faster discovery of mistakes the process will keep making: detection of standing exposures is worthwhile, and it is the compensating control, not the fix. Incident lessons should name the decision that created the exposure. Administrative interfaces belong behind authenticated gateways, and every 'temporary' rule needs a mechanism that ends it.

questions.question: During an architecture review, a CityBank branch design justifies its lack of inbound filtering with a note reading 'the site is behind NAT, which hides it from the internet'. Which evaluation of NAT's security value is MOST accurate?

options.A: NAT is equivalent to a stateful firewall, since both maintain per-connection state tables that gate what may enter the network.
options.B: NAT obscures internal addressing and incidentally drops unsolicited inbound traffic, but enforcing security policy still requires a firewall.
options.C: NAT reduces security overall, because rewriting packet headers strips the very fields that inspection devices depend on.
options.D: NAT gives translated sessions confidentiality, since outside observers see only the rewritten public addresses on the wire.

questions.explanation: NAT was built to stretch IPv4 addresses: it rewrites headers and keeps translation state so replies find their way back. Two side effects look like security: internal numbering is not visible outside, and unsolicited inbound packets die for lack of a mapping. But side effects have no policy: no rule language, no logging designed for security decisions, and the protection evaporates wherever mappings exist (port forwards, hairpins, protocol helpers) or wherever traffic is solicited, which is how phishing-delivered malware connects out and NAT obligingly sustains the session. B credits the incidental benefit and names the missing thing: enforced, auditable policy, which is a firewall's job. (A) is the equivalence the design note depends on, and it fails at the definition: both keep state, but only one consults policy; a translation table answers 'how do I rewrite this', not 'should this pass'. (C) manufactures a downside from a real nuisance. NAT complicates some inspection and end-to-end protocols, but 'reduces security overall' does not follow. (D) confuses hiding an address with protecting a payload: translated traffic is as readable in transit as any other cleartext. Classify controls by what they were designed to decide. NAT decides address rewriting; only a control whose purpose is admission policy should be cited as your inbound defence.

questions.question: During a change-window mistake, two of CityBank's core routers briefly pointed default routes at each other. Captures from the window show the same packets shuttling between the two devices, a header field decrementing at every pass, until each packet is discarded and an ICMP 'time exceeded' error goes back to its source. Which mechanism was limiting the damage, and what is it for?

options.A: The TCP retransmission timer, which bounds how long any unacknowledged segment stays in flight before the sending host finally gives up.
options.B: The fragmentation offset field, which forces malformed or oversized packets to be discarded at each hop along the forwarding path they traverse.
options.C: The IP time-to-live field, decremented at each router so that packets caught in forwarding loops are eventually discarded.
options.D: The Ethernet frame check sequence, which discards any frame whose contents were corrupted somewhere in transit between two directly adjacent devices.

questions.explanation: The capture narrates the mechanism: a field decreasing at each router, a discard when it runs out, and 'time exceeded' notifications. That is the IP TTL (hop limit in IPv6), a per-packet self-destruct decremented by every forwarding hop precisely so that a routing loop degrades into discarded packets and error messages instead of a link-saturating storm of immortal traffic. The mutual default routes made the loop; TTL made it survivable, and the same expiry mechanism is what traceroute exploits deliberately. C identifies both mechanism and purpose. (A) lives in the endpoints, not the path: retransmission timers govern when a sender tries again and cannot expire a packet already circling between routers; arguably they add traffic while the loop persists. (B) is a reassembly bookkeeping field; nothing about fragmentation offsets counts hops or expires looping datagrams. (D) checks integrity per link: the shuttling packets were perfectly intact, and corruption detection has no opinion about forwarding sanity. Networks assume routing will sometimes be wrong, so packets carry a hop budget. Recognize TTL expiry and 'time exceeded' backscatter as the visible signature of a loop being safely bled off.

questions.question: CityBank's public web tier is under a SYN flood from constantly shifting spoofed addresses: connection tables fill with half-open sessions and real customers time out. The team needs a mitigation that keeps accepting legitimate connections while the flood continues. Which approach MOST directly addresses the exhaustion mechanism?

options.A: Block the flood's source addresses at the perimeter firewall as the SOC identifies them.
options.B: Raise the servers' connection-table limits so that more half-open sessions can be held at once.
options.C: Shorten the servers' keep-alive timers so established HTTP sessions are released sooner.
options.D: Enable SYN cookies, so the servers commit no connection state until a client's final handshake acknowledgment arrives.

questions.explanation: The flood's lever is asymmetry: each spoofed SYN costs the attacker one packet but costs the server a table entry held open for a timeout. SYN cookies remove the lever: the server answers with a SYN-ACK whose sequence number cryptographically encodes the pending connection and stores nothing; only when a real client returns the final ACK does state get created. Spoofed SYNs, whose ACKs will come from nowhere, now cost the server nothing, while legitimate handshakes complete normally, exactly 'keep serving customers during the flood'. D dismantles the exhaustion mechanism itself. (A) chases addresses that are forged and rotating: each block lags the flood by design, legitimate users behind reused addresses become collateral, and the firewall rule base becomes its own exhaustion problem. (B) enlarges the bucket under an open tap; the flood fills any finite table, minutes later; sizing answers organic growth, not adversarial load. (C) tunes the wrong lifecycle phase: keep-alive governs established sessions after the handshake, and the flood never gets that far — its damage is entirely pre-establishment. Durable DoS mitigations attack the attacker's asymmetry: make the unverified party carry the cost of state, and a flood of fakes loses its purchase.

stimuli.title: A tower that was not the carrier's
stimuli.text: CityBank deploys portable cash machines that reach its processing center over 4G modems. The network team relied on the carrier's link encryption and a private access point name, and configured neither IPsec nor TLS. At a music festival an attacker's rogue base station forced the modems down to 2G, broke the older link encryption and read cardholder track data in clear. The TLS-inspection and firewall infrastructure at the processing center observed nothing unusual throughout. Voice traffic on the same site links has separately become choppy every evening while bulk transfers run.

profile.environment: Machines on 4G modems · carrier link encryption only · no IPsec, no TLS
profile.state: Cardholder track data read in clear at a festival

stimuli.title: What the interception actually yielded
stimuli.text: CityBank's incident commander must classify an event for the regulator. During it a rogue base station relayed every transaction between the machines and the carrier network while silently recording cardholder data, and machine service was never interrupted. Privacy counsel wants to know what the attackers could have learned from subscriber identity captures alone, before any traffic was decrypted. An engineer on the review board claims an IPsec tunnel to the processing center would have prevented the incident entirely. Staff handhelds at the same site were separately found to have had contact lists retrieved over Bluetooth.

profile.environment: Rogue base station relaying live transactions · service never interrupted
profile.state: Event being classified for the regulator

stimuli.title: Reading the design file afterwards
stimuli.text: An auditor reopening CityBank's design file finds the original justification: the carrier's private access point name 'keeps the traffic private', so no further transit protection was configured. The bank also leases dark fiber between its two data centers, and the wide-area team argues that because the bank lights and operates that fiber itself, replication traffic across it can run unencrypted. A separate proposal would terminate an IPsec tunnel from each machine to the processing center. The mobile team must also cut the risk of further Bluetooth data theft from handhelds that still need Bluetooth for card sleds.

profile.environment: Private access point name relied on for confidentiality · dark fiber between data centers
profile.state: Original design justification under audit

stimuli.title: Naming the attack, and the ones like it
stimuli.text: Meridian Transit Authority is agreeing a threat taxonomy for its fare payment network before it reports to the board. In one event an interposed device sat between two endpoints, read live traffic and injected its own. Architects separately worry that a compromised public certificate authority could issue attackers a valid certificate for the processing center's hostname, letting a future rogue network impersonate it. A flat operations network of 500 devices suffers periodic slowdowns from legitimate broadcast traffic reaching every host. Mall security has reported someone parked outside a station for hours with a laptop and a roof antenna.

profile.organization: Meridian Transit Authority · fare payment network
profile.environment: Public concourse machines · certificate authorities outside the authority's control
profile.state: Threat taxonomy being agreed with the board

stimuli.title: What a switch changed
stimuli.text: A workshop at Meridian Transit Authority still connects its five diagnostic machines through an old Ethernet hub. Technicians complain transfers slow sharply when several are busy, and a consultant has shown that a sniffer on any hub port captures every station's traffic. When a technician patched a second uplink through a third switch to give the workshop a backup path, the same broadcast frames began circulating endlessly and the segment slowed to a crawl. Tap-to-pay readers are being added to the fare machines, and a risk workshop is weighing how much protection the short operating range gives.

profile.organization: Meridian Transit Authority · station equipment workshop
profile.environment: Old Ethernet hub still in service · access ports in meeting rooms · tap-to-pay readers planned
profile.state: Workshop upgrade being justified

stimuli.title: Loops, leases and broadcast
stimuli.text: A technician at Northfield Health patched a second uplink between two access switches through a third, creating a physical ring, and within seconds the campus network was unusable: switch processors pinned, the same broadcast frames circulating endlessly. The hospital centralizes its address assignment at headquarters, and when a newly routed ward segment came online its machines received no addresses at all, though the same laptops obtain leases immediately at headquarters and the link between the sites tests clean. Warehouse barcode scanners supporting only an obsolete wireless standard are still attached to a network that also carries clinical traffic.

profile.environment: Flat operations segment · DHCP centralized at headquarters · redundant uplinks patched by hand
profile.state: Outage during a change window

stimuli.title: Keeping the front door open under load
stimuli.text: Northfield Health's public web tier is under a flood of connection attempts from constantly shifting spoofed addresses: connection tables fill with half-open sessions and real patients time out. The team needs a mitigation that keeps accepting legitimate connections while the flood continues. An audit has separately found that a visitor can plug a laptop into any lobby network jack and receive an address on the corporate network, and a penetration test showed a laptop in a meeting room announcing itself as the default gateway and silently proxying other hosts' traffic. Access points in branches run a deprecated cipher for compatibility.

profile.environment: Public portal behind a perimeter firewall · access ports in public waiting areas
profile.state: SYN flood in progress

stimuli.title: Two ends of a tunnel
stimuli.text: Redcliff Bank is specifying two encrypted paths at once. The first joins a temporary operations trailer to the processing center: compliance requires that internal host addresses never appear on the carrier network, and a gateway at each end will terminate the cryptography for the hosts behind it. The second joins two application servers inside one data center that must exchange settlement files confidentially, terminate the cryptography themselves, and add as little packet overhead as possible. Branch wireless is moving to 802.1X with no client certificate infrastructure and none budgeted.

profile.environment: Festival operations trailer · data center application servers · branch wireless on 802.1X
profile.state: Two tunnels being specified at once

stimuli.title: Letting outsiders in, carefully
stimuli.text: Redcliff Bank must give external auditors access to three internal web applications. The auditors work from their own firms' locked-down laptops, on which no client software may be installed, and from office networks that commonly allow only web ports outbound. Separately, the bank's own administrators need to manage servers inside the card-processing enclave from the corporate network, and the architect requires every administrative session to pass through a single hardened, fully logged entry point protected by a second authentication factor. Two application servers must also exchange settlement files with minimal added overhead.

profile.environment: Auditors on their own locked-down laptops · card enclave management interfaces
profile.state: Access designs being approved

stimuli.title: Answers that were not the bank's
stimuli.text: Customers of Colville Savings are reporting certificate warnings on the online portal, and an analyst finds their queries for the portal's hostname returning an address in an attacker's netblock. The records on the bank's own authoritative name servers are verified unchanged and the registrar's delegation is intact. Elsewhere, the bank's internet gateway is being saturated by echo replies from hundreds of hosts inside a university network the bank never contacted, and the university reports its hosts each received requests appearing to come from the bank. A lobby audit found unauthenticated devices receiving corporate addresses.

profile.environment: Authoritative name servers verified unchanged · registrar delegation intact
profile.state: Customers seeing certificate warnings

stimuli.title: Proving an answer is genuine
stimuli.text: Colville Savings' architect must recommend a control that lets resolvers verify answers for the bank's zone are genuine and unmodified, wherever those answers were obtained. A marketing launch is separately expected to drive a fiftyfold traffic spike, plus probable volumetric attack attention, to a promotional site currently served from one origin data center, and the infrastructure team must keep it available without re-platforming that origin. At a small branch with no certificate infrastructure, staff have been attaching unmanaged mini-switches under desks to fan single wall jacks out to personal devices.

profile.environment: Zone signing under consideration · promotional site on one origin · unmanaged switches under desks
profile.state: Controls being recommended after the poisoning incident

stimuli.title: Handshakes worth capturing
stimuli.text: Fenwick Events is specifying the wireless build for its festival season. A prior assessment showed attackers in the crowd capturing the four-way handshakes of its shared-passphrase network and running offline dictionary attacks against the passphrase at leisure. In a lab reconstruction of a separate incident, testers captured a valid, fully encrypted withdrawal authorization and retransmitted it an hour later; the processing center accepted it and dispensed cash again. Administrators manage the site's routers and switches over an unencrypted protocol, with individual accounts on a central server.

profile.environment: Staff handhelds on a shared passphrase · crowd within radio range · replayed authorizations tested
profile.state: Wireless build being specified for the season

stimuli.title: Convenience features with a cost
stimuli.text: A wireless assessment of Fenwick Events' permanent offices finds consumer-grade access points with push-button setup enabled to make onboarding easier, and the assessor must state the risk accurately so the finding survives challenge. A configuration audit separately finds the routers and switches managed over an unencrypted terminal protocol, with a central server giving each administrator an individual account; the network team argues the per-administrator accounts make that acceptable. A red-team capture from one site showed telephony call-setup traffic readable in clear: dialed numbers, extensions and negotiated session parameters.

profile.organization: Fenwick Events · branch and site equipment
profile.environment: Consumer access points with push-button setup · voice on the site network · administrators on Telnet
profile.state: Assessment findings being written up

stimuli.title: A stronger transmitter in the crowd
stimuli.text: Fenwick Events' staff handhelds automatically join any network broadcasting the staff network name, and last season an attacker exploited exactly that with a stronger transmitter. Staff reported handhelds briefly dropping off, reconnecting by themselves, then showing certificate warnings, while a spectrum survey found a second network broadcasting the same name at higher power from the crowd area. A survey inside headquarters separately found an unlabeled consumer access point plugged into a wall jack behind a printer, broadcasting an open network bridged onto the corporate network. Recorded call audio was reassembled from a mirrored port.

profile.environment: Handhelds auto-joining any network with the staff name · unlabeled access point found on a jack
profile.state: Post-season review of wireless incidents

stimuli.title: Carrier promises and what they cover
stimuli.text: A carrier has assured Ravensworth Group that its label-switched service is 'a private network' on which encryption 'is unnecessary', and the group's architect must characterize what the service actually provides before anyone signs. The group runs 200 branches over a mixture of transports, each configured locally, and successive audits keep finding branch firewall and routing policies that have drifted from the corporate standard. A customer portal compromised through a plugin was contained by the design around it. Auditors need read access to firewall configurations for six weeks.

profile.environment: Label-switched carrier service on offer · voice and data sharing links · branch policies drifting
profile.state: Contract under review before signature

stimuli.title: Getting data out through the one open port
stimuli.text: Ravensworth Group's egress firewall permits outbound traffic only on the standard encrypted web port, and the security operations team had assumed this made bulk data theft impractical. A red team nonetheless exfiltrated a large test dataset in a single afternoon without raising any alert, and the team must explain the result. A wireless design document has separately come back from the architect with a note asking the author to specify which authentication method will actually be deployed instead of naming the framework. Domain machines have also begun failing authentication after a hypervisor migration left clocks drifting.

profile.environment: Egress firewall permitting outbound web only · directory-integrated wireless planned
profile.state: Red-team result under discussion

stimuli.title: One security group, 180 workloads
stimuli.text: Meridian Claims Exchange settles motor claims for 42 carriers and has moved 180 workloads into one cloud virtual private cloud with three subnets: public, application and data. Every workload sits in a single security group that permits all traffic between its members, because the migration team could not enumerate the dependencies in time. A peering connection joins the analytics account, which also holds the payroll instances. Flow logs are enabled and written to a bucket nobody reads. A penetration test finds that a compromised image-resizing container in the application subnet reached the claims database, the analytics account's payroll instances and the cloud metadata service, none of which it needs. The internet edge, by contrast, permits only 443 to the load balancer.

profile.organization: Meridian Claims Exchange · motor claims settlement
profile.regime: NAIC Insurance Data Security Model Law
profile.environment: single-region public cloud, one VPC, three subnets
profile.state: post-migration, penetration test just reported

stimuli.title: A dairy plant on one switching fabric
stimuli.text: Ferrand Dairy Cooperative processes milk from 340 member farms at a single plant outside Rochester. Its office and process networks share one campus switching fabric: pasteurizer controllers, a historian and 90 IP telephones all ride the same 48-port access switches, installed in 2013 and separated by VLANs. One switch of the core pair lost vendor support in March, and the cooperative holds no spare. A filling line commissioned in June arrived with a cellular modem the machine builder uses for remote diagnostics, reaching the equipment without touching the plant firewall. The board has approved one quarter of engineering time and wants the plant's network risks addressed before the autumn production peak.

profile.organization: Ferrand Dairy Cooperative · member-owned milk processing
profile.environment: single plant, one campus switching fabric
profile.state: aging core, one engineering quarter approved

questionsV2.question: Which weakness of 2G MOST directly enabled the tower impersonation?

options.A: Its A5/1 stream cipher can be broken in near real time with commodity hardware.
options.B: The handset authenticates itself to the network, but the network provides no proof of its own identity.
options.C: Its signaling messages carry no integrity protection, so their contents can be forged or altered by an interceptor.
options.D: Its short session keys are reused across successive calls and data sessions on the same device, easing later cryptanalysis.

questionsV2.explanation:
2G authenticates one way. The handset proves itself to the network and the network proves nothing back, so a modem on 2G accepts any sufficiently strong transmitter claiming to be the network (B). The rogue tower broke nothing to be believed, which is why the same trick failed against 4G's mutual authentication.
Verifying the network's identity matters as much as the network verifying yours. One-way authentication is an open invitation to rogue infrastructure.
questionsV2.recallLine: A rogue base station forced CityBank's ATM modems from 4G down to 2G. Which weakness of 2G MOST directly enabled the tower impersonation?

optionsShort.A: A5/1 breaks with commodity hardware
optionsShort.B: Network provides no proof of its identity
optionsShort.C: Signaling messages carry no integrity protection
optionsShort.D: Short session keys reused across sessions

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: A genuine 2G weakness that explains the later decryption of captured traffic. It says nothing about why the tower was believed.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Describes a real gap behind related bidding-down tricks. This impersonation needed only an unauthenticated identity claim.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Points at key hygiene, which affects cryptanalysis and not attachment decisions.

questionsV2.question: Which statement BEST explains why controls higher in the stack had no visibility of the downgrade?

options.A: The radio negotiation happens at the data link and network layers of the cellular stack, below anything the center's application-layer controls can observe.
options.B: The downgrade messages were encrypted with the 2G A5/1 stream cipher, which the center's inspection devices could not decrypt quickly enough to raise an alarm.
options.C: The rogue base station silently discarded the ATMs' logging traffic before it could ever reach the processing center's collectors.
options.D: The modems' TLS sessions renegotiated automatically as the bearer changed, and the monitoring stack treated the renegotiation as a routine handshake instead of an alarm.

questionsV2.explanation:
Visibility follows the layer at which a control operates. The forced fallback was negotiated between modem and tower in the lower layers of the cellular stack, and none of it is ever presented to equipment inspecting application traffic at the far end (A). That explanation holds for any similar radio-layer attack.
An attack at layer N is invisible to controls that only see layer N+1's payloads. Monitor at the layer where the trust decision is made.
questionsV2.recallLine: CityBank's TLS-inspection and firewall gear at the processing center saw nothing while the modems were forced onto 2G. Which statement BEST explains that blindness?

optionsShort.A: Radio negotiation sits below application-layer controls
optionsShort.B: A5/1 ciphertext outran the inspection devices
optionsShort.C: Rogue tower discarded the machines' logging traffic
optionsShort.D: Monitoring read TLS renegotiation as routine

B.label: wrong phase
