C.wouldAnswer: Also true here. Excessive rights widened what the insider could do, which goes to impact and not to attribution.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Misreads the evidence. Sessions were logged; the record said 'SuperAdmin logged in', so the logging itself worked.

questionsV2.question: A fingerprint reader elsewhere rejects staff in cold weather, so an administrator lowers the match-confidence threshold. What is the MOST significant consequence?

options.A: The false acceptance rate rises, so impostors will match more easily
options.B: The crossover error rate improves, making the sensor more accurate
options.C: The failure-to-enroll rate increases for users with worn fingerprints
options.D: The false rejection rate rises further, locking even more legitimate users out

questionsV2.explanation:
Lower the match-confidence threshold and the sensor begins accepting weaker matches. Some of those weaker matches are impostors, so the false acceptance rate rises (A). At an unattended cash machine that is the expensive direction of the trade.
FAR and FRR sit at opposite ends of one tuning curve. Relaxing the threshold to admit poorly captured legitimate prints necessarily admits poorer impostor prints too, trading Type I errors for Type II errors. Pick the operating point by the error that costs more where the sensor sits.
questionsV2.recallLine: An administrator lowers a fingerprint reader's match-confidence threshold so cold-weather rejections stop. What is the MOST significant consequence?

optionsShort.A: False acceptance rate rises; impostors match more easily
optionsShort.B: Crossover error rate improves; sensor more accurate
optionsShort.C: Failure-to-enroll rises for worn fingerprints
optionsShort.D: False rejection rate rises further, locking users out

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Misunderstands CER, a fixed property measured where FAR equals FRR. Moving the operating threshold does not change it.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Confuses verification with registration. Failure to enroll happens at enrollment, out of the matching threshold's reach.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Inverts the change. Rejections were the pre-change complaint, and a lower threshold reduces them.

questionsV2.question: Which additional control would have been MOST effective at stopping remote use of a credential the attacker already knew?

options.A: A stricter complexity policy applied to every administrative password
options.B: Quarterly security-awareness training on credential handling for technicians
options.C: A second authentication factor, such as a hardware token, for remote sessions
options.D: An intrusion detection sensor alerting the SOC whenever administrative logins originate from residential networks

questionsV2.explanation:
The attacker already knew the password. Only a control demanding evidence he does not have will stop the session at the point of entry, and that is possession of an enrolled hardware token (C).
Against a credential the attacker already holds, prevention has to come from a second, different factor.
questionsV2.recallLine: The insider already knew the shared console password. Which additional control would MOST effectively stop him using it from home?

optionsShort.A: Stricter complexity policy on administrative passwords
optionsShort.B: Quarterly awareness training for the technicians
optionsShort.C: Hardware token as a second factor
optionsShort.D: IDS alerts on residential-network administrative logins

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Hardens the secret and leaves a single factor already shared among five technicians.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Targets negligence. No amount of training restrains an insider acting deliberately.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Detective. It fires while the abuse is under way or after it, never at the point of entry.

questionsV2.question: Which change should the security manager recommend FIRST with the budget available?

options.A: Enforce a 16-character password on the shared account and rotate it monthly
options.B: Issue each technician a uniquely named account and disable the shared account
options.C: Require multi-factor authentication for all remote logins to the console
options.D: Reduce the technicians' rights from SuperAdmin to a scoped field-service role

questionsV2.explanation:
Identification precedes authentication, authorization and accountability. Until each person has a distinct identity, nothing downstream can produce an attributable log entry. So the first move is a uniquely named account for each technician and the shared account disabled (B).
The word FIRST decides it. The other three are all correct controls, and all three become fully effective only once unique identities exist. That dependency orders them, not managerial preference.
questionsV2.recallLine: One shared SuperAdmin account serves five technicians, and one quarter's budget is available. Which change should the security manager recommend FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Longer password on the shared account, rotated
optionsShort.B: Unique named accounts; disable the shared one
optionsShort.C: Require MFA for remote console logins
optionsShort.D: Scope technicians down to a field-service role

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Strengthens the secret without changing whom it identifies. Five people would still share the longer password.

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Serious, and five technicians on one account share the MFA enrollment too, so attribution stays broken.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Limits blast radius. A scoped field-service role shared by five people is still shared.

questionsV2.question: Which answer BEST captures the architectural flaw in that design, before anyone misused it?

options.A: The account's password was subject to no scheduled rotation, expiry, or complexity requirement
options.B: Too few administrators were available to cover shifts across 300 sites
options.C: The account's name openly advertised its privilege level to attackers
options.D: Concentrating unrestricted shared privilege in one credential made a single point of compromise

questionsV2.explanation:
The danger was designed in, before anyone touched it. One credential that could do everything, known to five people, reduced the whole ATM estate's security to a single secret (D). That is a single point of failure and a maximally attractive target, and it holds whether the eventual abuser turned out to be an insider or an outsider.
Concentration is the flaw. Password hygiene, headcount and naming all sit on top of it and leave it exactly where it is.
questionsV2.recallLine: Five technicians shared one credential that could do anything on 300 machines. Which statement BEST captures the design flaw before any misuse?

optionsShort.A: No rotation, expiry or complexity requirement
optionsShort.B: Too few administrators for 300 sites
optionsShort.C: Account name advertised its privilege level
optionsShort.D: One credential concentrating unrestricted shared privilege

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Names a genuine contributing weakness. A stronger, regularly rotated master key is still a master key.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Reframes a security flaw as a staffing shortage. The design would be equally dangerous with fifty administrators sharing it.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Cosmetic. Renaming the account hides nothing from an attacker enumerating privileged group membership.

questionsV2.question: A team must set biometric thresholds for an unattended vault door and a staffed entrance where a guard also checks badges. How should it bias them?

options.A: Apply one uniform threshold at both doors so error rates remain consistent
options.B: Bias the vault door toward acceptance to avoid delaying cash-handling operations
options.C: Bias the vault door toward false rejections and the guarded entrance toward false acceptances
options.D: Bias both doors toward acceptance because badge checks already provide a compensating control everywhere

questionsV2.explanation:
What surrounds each door decides which error you can afford there. At the unattended vault a false acceptance is unrecoverable, so the threshold should be strict even though staff get rejected more often. At the guarded entrance the guard catches the occasional false acceptance, so a looser threshold that cuts queue-building rejections is the better trade. That pairing is (C).
Tune to the consequence, not to a house standard. Whatever human control stands behind a door is part of the setting.
questionsV2.recallLine: An unattended vault door and a guarded entrance both use biometrics. How should the team bias each door's threshold?

optionsShort.A: One uniform threshold at both doors
optionsShort.B: Vault biased toward acceptance for speed
optionsShort.C: Vault strict, guarded entrance permissive
optionsShort.D: Both permissive; badge checks compensate everywhere

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Treats tuning as a consistency exercise. Uniformity fits doors that protect equivalent assets, and these two do not.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Optimizes convenience exactly where an admitted impostor does the greatest damage.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Half right. Badge checks do compensate at the staffed entrance, and no human control waits at the unattended vault.

questionsV2.question: Which attack technique is MOST likely to still succeed against the upgraded webmail login?

options.A: Credential stuffing that replays username and password pairs harvested from breaches of unrelated services
options.B: Offline cracking of stolen password hashes using precomputed tables
options.C: A scripted brute-force loop guessing all possible six-digit codes against the login endpoint
options.D: A proxy page that captures and instantly relays both the password and current code

questionsV2.explanation:
A TOTP code is bound to a clock and to nothing about the site the user typed it into. A proxy page can therefore capture the password and the current code and relay both to the real service inside the validity window (D). The upgrade does not touch that flow.
OTP-based MFA raises the bar and stays phishable in real time. Closing that gap takes an origin-bound, phishing-resistant method such as FIDO2/WebAuthn.
questionsV2.recallLine: Webmail now requires an app-generated time-based code after employees were phished. Which attack technique is MOST likely to still succeed?

optionsShort.A: Credential stuffing with pairs from other breaches
optionsShort.B: Offline hash cracking with precomputed tables
optionsShort.C: Brute-forcing every six-digit code
optionsShort.D: Proxy page relaying password and live code

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Credential stuffing now fails, because a stolen password alone no longer completes a login.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Yields passwords and then meets the same second-factor wall.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Dies on the 30-second code lifetime combined with ordinary attempt throttling.

questionsV2.question: Which control would MOST reliably have surfaced that accumulation of entitlements earlier?

options.A: SIEM alerting tuned to anomalous use of the finance applications
options.B: Periodic recertification of each user's entitlements by their manager
options.C: A stronger multi-factor policy on all finance system logins
options.D: Automated birthright provisioning for employees joining the firm

questionsV2.explanation:
Privilege creep is a condition of the account. The excess rights sit there whether or not anyone exercises them, so the control that finds them has to compare periodically what a person holds against what their current role needs. Manager-driven recertification (B) does exactly that, which is why it catches accumulation from transfers.
Reviews audit entitlement state; monitoring audits behavior. Creep hides in the first, so schedule recertification around transfers.
questionsV2.recallLine: An employee who transferred three times can approve invoices, edit vendor records and view payroll. Which control would MOST reliably surface that accumulation earlier?

optionsShort.A: SIEM alerts on anomalous finance-application use
optionsShort.B: Managers periodically recertify each user's entitlements
optionsShort.C: Stronger MFA on finance system logins
optionsShort.D: Automated birthright provisioning for new joiners

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Watches usage. Dormant excess rights fire no events to alert on.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Makes it more certain the right person is behind the login. Whether that login should hold those rights goes unasked.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Governs the joiner moment. This risk was created by moves, the lifecycle phase birthright provisioning never revisits.

questionsV2.question: Which figure gives the fairest single basis for comparing the three products?

options.A: The lowest false acceptance rate that each vendor quotes in its datasheet
options.B: The false rejection rate each vendor measured during its own pilot
options.C: The failure-to-enroll rate observed across the user population
options.D: The crossover error rate, where false accepts and false rejects are equal

questionsV2.explanation:
FAR and FRR both move with the threshold, so a vendor can make either number look excellent by choosing where to measure. The crossover error rate (D) removes that freedom. It fixes the comparison at the setting where the two rates meet, so a lower CER means a genuinely more accurate sensor.
Compare products at a fixed point on the curve. Tune to the site's risk bias afterward, once the product is chosen.
questionsV2.recallLine: Three fingerprint vendors quote error rates measured at thresholds each chose. Which figure gives the fairest single basis for comparing the products?

optionsShort.A: Lowest false acceptance rate each vendor quotes
optionsShort.B: False rejection rate from each vendor's pilot
optionsShort.C: Failure-to-enroll rate across the user population
optionsShort.D: Crossover error rate, where both rates meet

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: One end of a tunable trade. Quoted alone it is a marketing figure, useful again only when tuning the sensor you picked.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: The other end of the same trade, measured on the vendor's own pilot, at whatever threshold flattered the product.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Measures how many users can register at all. It says nothing about matching accuracy once a user is enrolled.

questionsV2.question: Which combination should the auditor accept as meeting the multi-factor requirement?

options.A: A smart card inserted at the console together with a memorized PIN
options.B: A primary password backed by answers to personal challenge questions
options.C: A fingerprint scan confirmed by an iris scan at the same panel
options.D: A console password plus a second passphrase held by the same technician

questionsV2.explanation:
Multi-factor means evidence from two different categories: something you know, something you have, something you are. Credentials drawn from one category tend to fall to the same attack. A smart card plus a memorized PIN (A) pairs possession with knowledge, and each half is useless alone - a shoulder-surfed PIN without the card, a stolen card without the PIN.
Count the factor categories, not the number of prompts.
questionsV2.recallLine: The bank's standard requires genuine multi-factor authentication at the console. Which of the offered credential combinations should the auditor accept?

optionsShort.A: Smart card inserted plus memorized PIN
optionsShort.B: Password backed by personal challenge questions
optionsShort.C: Fingerprint confirmed by iris at one panel
optionsShort.D: Console password plus a second passphrase

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Stacks knowledge on knowledge. Challenge answers are memorized facts, often researchable, and one phishing call harvests both.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Stacks inherence on inherence. Two strong biometrics, one category, still single-factor. The second scan buys accuracy.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Two knowledge secrets in one head. A single keylogger session captures both.

questionsV2.question: Which change to the reset process would MOST reduce the help-desk exposure?

options.A: Add several further personal questions about employment history to the verification script
options.B: Require reset callers to also state their employee ID number and department
options.C: Rotate the personal verification questions on a monthly schedule across the whole team
options.D: Confirm each request via a push prompt to the employee's enrolled device

questionsV2.explanation:
Every check in the current script is knowledge that lives outside the company's control, so an attacker who researches the target walks straight through it. The flaw is structural. A push prompt to the employee's enrolled device (D) moves verification onto a possession factor that research cannot fake.
Identity proofing has to rest on something the caller must hold. Anything a stranger can look up will eventually be looked up.
questionsV2.recallLine: The help desk resets a password for any caller who states a birthday and a manager's name. Which change would MOST reduce that exposure?

optionsShort.A: More personal questions about employment history
optionsShort.B: Also require employee ID and department
optionsShort.C: Rotate the verification questions every month
optionsShort.D: Push prompt to the employee's enrolled device

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: More of the same failed category. Employment history is exactly what professional networking profiles publish.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Fails the same way. Employee IDs leak through email signatures and directory exports, so they stay harvestable knowledge.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Changes which facts are asked while facts remain the medium. Rotation suits shared secrets, not identity proofing.

questionsV2.question: Now that one login unlocks everything, which recommendation about protecting the portal credential is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Rotate the retired downstream application passwords on a shorter schedule
options.B: Keep separate standalone passwords for the three most sensitive applications
options.C: Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication at the portal login
options.D: Extend the portal session lifetime so users authenticate less often

questionsV2.explanation:
Single sign-on concentrates authentication risk on purpose. Convenience rises, and the portal credential becomes the key to the kingdom, so that one credential has to be hardened to a level none of the forty passwords ever needed. Phishing-resistant MFA at the portal (C) is that level.
When one login opens everything, spend the protection where the concentration is.
questionsV2.recallLine: Forty applications now sit behind one sign-on portal. Which recommendation about protecting the portal credential is MOST appropriate?

optionsShort.A: Rotate retired downstream application passwords faster
optionsShort.B: Keep standalone passwords for three sensitive applications
optionsShort.C: Require phishing-resistant multi-factor at the portal
optionsShort.D: Extend session lifetime so users authenticate less

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Polishes credentials that single sign-on has taken off the attack path.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Quietly abandons single sign-on for the crown jewels, and multiplies user friction to do it.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Moves the wrong way, lengthening the window a hijacked session stays valid.

questionsV2.question: Which component must the red team have compromised to forge tickets for any principal?

options.A: The certificate authority that signs the realm's TLS certificates
options.B: The key distribution center holding the realm's long-term secret keys
options.C: The RADIUS server brokering the site's network access requests
options.D: The LDAP directory replica storing user attributes and group membership information

questionsV2.explanation:
Forging a valid TGT requires the long-term key that TGTs are encrypted under: the krbtgt secret, held by the key distribution center (B). Realm-wide impersonation - the classic golden ticket - can start nowhere else. The KDC is the trusted third party whose keys underwrite every ticket in the realm.
In Kerberos, whoever holds the KDC's keys is the realm. Protect it above every other identity component.
questionsV2.recallLine: A red team can forge ticket-granting tickets for any principal in the Kerberos realm. Which component must it have compromised?

optionsShort.A: Certificate authority signing the realm's TLS certificates
optionsShort.B: Key distribution center holding long-term keys
optionsShort.C: RADIUS server brokering network access requests
optionsShort.D: LDAP replica storing attributes and group membership

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Anchors a different trust system. Certificates secure TLS sessions, and controlling the CA buys server impersonation at that layer.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Belongs to a separate AAA protocol for network devices and remote access, and it holds no Kerberos keys.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Exposes attribute data and group membership, which is valuable reconnaissance. It cannot mint a ticket.

questionsV2.question: Which second factor is MOST appropriate for the field workforce given the coverage and policy constraints?

options.A: One-time codes delivered to each technician by SMS text message
options.B: Push-notification approvals sent to a corporate smartphone application
options.C: A dedicated hardware token displaying time-based one-time codes
options.D: One-time codes emailed to each technician's corporate mailbox

questionsV2.explanation:
A hardware TOTP token computes its codes locally, from a synchronized clock and a stored seed. No signal, no phone, no mailbox (C), which is the only option compatible with both stated constraints.
Offline sites need possession factors that compute their codes on the spot.
questionsV2.recallLine: Field technicians work where mobile coverage fails, and policy bars personal phones. Which second factor is MOST appropriate for them?

optionsShort.A: One-time codes sent by SMS
optionsShort.B: Push approvals to a corporate smartphone app
optionsShort.C: Hardware token displaying time-based codes
optionsShort.D: One-time codes emailed to corporate mailboxes

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Depends on cellular coverage at exactly the sites where coverage is unreliable, and NIST SP 800-63B classes SMS as restricted.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Needs a data connection plus a smartphone, and collides with both constraints.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Requires network reachability at the site. If the mailbox is guarded by the password under attack, both factors are one channel.

questionsV2.question: The stolen table held unsalted MD5 digests. Which property MOST enabled such rapid recovery?

options.A: MD5 digests can be mathematically reversed once the algorithm is identified
options.B: The digests were stored in the same table as the account usernames
options.C: Identical passwords produced identical digests, enabling precomputed lookup tables
options.D: The database file itself was unencrypted at the storage layer

questionsV2.explanation:
With no salt, hashing is deterministic across the whole user base. 'Welcome123!' digests to the same value for every account that uses it, so an attacker looks each digest up in rainbow tables computed years ago and every repeated password falls at once (C). Hours, where the arithmetic alone should have taken centuries.
Salts exist to break precomputation. Without them, one rainbow table amortizes across every user and every breach.
questionsV2.recallLine: A stolen table of unsalted MD5 digests was ninety percent published within hours. Which property MOST enabled that rapid recovery?

optionsShort.A: Digests can be mathematically reversed
optionsShort.B: Digests stored beside the account usernames
optionsShort.C: Identical passwords hashed identically, enabling precomputed lookups
optionsShort.D: Database file unencrypted at the storage layer

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Misstates how hashes fail. MD5 is one-way even now; its weakness for password storage is speed and precomputability.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Changes nothing about cracking difficulty. Usernames help an attacker use the passwords once they are recovered.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Concerns how the data was stolen, which the stem has already granted. The question is how it was cracked afterward.

questionsV2.question: Which process change MOST directly ends a departing employee's access before the termination window opens?

options.A: Trigger automatic account suspension from HR termination workflow events
options.B: Add a quarterly manager recertification of every technician's access
options.C: Shorten the maximum password age on privileged accounts to thirty days
options.D: Collect badges, tokens and master keys during each exit interview

questionsV2.explanation:
The gap is timing. The organization knew the termination was coming before the employee did. Only an automated feed from the HR termination workflow (A) turns that knowledge into disabled access at the right moment, uniformly across every site.
Deprovisioning is an event. Wire identity systems to HR triggers so access dies the moment trust does.
questionsV2.recallLine: The bank knows a technician is being terminated before he does. Which process change MOST directly ends his access in that window?

optionsShort.A: Automatic suspension from HR termination workflow events
optionsShort.B: Quarterly manager recertification of technician access
optionsShort.C: Thirty-day maximum password age on privileged accounts
optionsShort.D: Collect badges and tokens at exit interview

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: The correct tool for finding quietly accumulated rights. A quarterly cadence can trail a termination by months.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Rotates a credential the departing insider legitimately holds until the rotation lands. It narrows stale secrets instead.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Recovers physical credentials at or after the exit conversation, inside the window the lead wants closed, and touches nothing logical.

questionsV2.question: Which biometric modality BEST satisfies contactless capture, very high accuracy and stable performance under controlled indoor lighting?

options.A: Fingerprint scanning using a ridge-pattern contact sensor
options.B: Iris recognition using near-infrared pattern imaging
options.C: Retina scanning of the eye's blood vessel pattern
options.D: Facial recognition using a standard visible-light camera

questionsV2.explanation:
Iris recognition captures a highly distinctive, stable pattern from a comfortable distance (B). Its accuracy sits in the same class as retinal scanning, it is genuinely contactless, and controlled indoor lighting is its ideal operating condition.
Read the stem's constraints as a filter. Accuracy alone chooses nothing once contactless capture and hygiene are also stated.
questionsV2.recallLine: The stores need a contactless biometric with very high accuracy under controlled indoor lighting. Which modality BEST satisfies all three?

optionsShort.A: Fingerprint ridge patterns from a contact sensor
optionsShort.B: Iris recognition by near-infrared imaging
optionsShort.C: Retina scan of the eye's blood vessels
optionsShort.D: Facial recognition using a visible-light camera

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Accurate and cheap, and users must touch the sensor, which fails the contactless requirement outright.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Matches or exceeds iris accuracy, and capture puts an eye against an optic. That defeats hygiene and raises medical-privacy concerns.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: The most convenient and fully contactless, and the weakest matcher of the four: sensitive to angle, appearance and presentation attacks.

questionsV2.question: Which attack MOST likely explains the login attempt pattern?

options.A: Credential stuffing exploiting password reuse across unrelated services
options.B: Password spraying of a few common passwords against many accounts
options.C: A brute-force attack iterating a password list against one account
options.D: A phishing campaign harvesting credentials through lookalike pages

questionsV2.explanation:
The telltale is where the guesses come from. Attempted pairs matching a third-party breach dump mean the attacker is replaying known-good credentials from elsewhere and betting on reuse (A). One or two tries per account is all stuffing needs, and the successes are the users who recycled.
That the attack works at all is the strongest argument there is against password reuse.
questionsV2.recallLine: Millions of logins hit thousands of usernames, one or two tries each, and many pairs match a breach dump. Which attack MOST likely explains it?

optionsShort.A: Credential stuffing exploiting reuse across unrelated services
optionsShort.B: Password spraying common passwords across many accounts
optionsShort.C: Brute force iterating a list against one account
optionsShort.D: Phishing campaign harvesting credentials via lookalike pages

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: The same wide, shallow shape, and the strong near miss. Without the breach-dump correlation it would be the better answer.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Inverts the observed pattern: depth against one target, where the log shows breadth across thousands.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: How credentials get stolen in the first place. No user in this evidence was lured anywhere.

questionsV2.question: Which password storage design BEST resists offline cracking the next time a table is stolen?

options.A: Unsalted SHA-512 digests, substituting a longer modern hash for MD5
options.B: Per-user salts fed into a slow, memory-hard function such as Argon2
options.C: AES-encrypted passwords with the key kept in the application's config file
options.D: Salted MD5 digests, retaining the fast algorithm but defeating rainbow tables

questionsV2.explanation:
Offline cracking is an economics problem, and per-user salts fed into a slow, memory-hard function such as Argon2 (B) attack both of its terms. Unique salts force the attacker to work one user at a time, with no precomputed tables. A deliberately slow, memory-hard function cuts guessing from billions per second to thousands. NIST SP 800-63B prescribes this approach for memorized secrets.
Break precomputation, then raise the price of every remaining guess.
questionsV2.recallLine: Brackley must redesign password storage so the next stolen table resists offline cracking. Which storage design BEST achieves that?

optionsShort.A: Unsalted SHA-512, a longer modern digest
optionsShort.B: Per-user salts into a slow memory-hard function
optionsShort.C: AES encryption, key in the application config
optionsShort.D: Salted MD5, fast but rainbow-table proof

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Swaps one fast, unsalted digest for another. SHA-512's extra bits do nothing against lookup tables or GPU throughput.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Makes passwords recoverable by design, and whoever stole the database plausibly holds the config file key too.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Half the fix. The salt kills precomputation; MD5's speed still permits enormous per-user guessing rates.

questionsV2.question: Which principle did giving every technician full administrative rights MOST directly violate?

options.A: Least privilege, because the accounts carried powers the job did not require
options.B: Separation of duties, because one team both requested and approved its access
options.C: Dual control, because sensitive operations could proceed without a second person
options.D: Need to know, because technicians could browse customer transaction records

questionsV2.explanation:
The stem describes a mismatch between duties and powers. The job needed service functions, the account granted everything, and that surplus of capability is exactly what least privilege forbids (A).
When powers exceed duties, cite least privilege. Reserve need to know for surplus access to information.
questionsV2.recallLine: Every technician on the old console held full administrative powers regardless of the job. Which principle did that MOST directly violate?

optionsShort.A: Least privilege: powers the job never required
optionsShort.B: Separation of duties: one team requested and approved
optionsShort.C: Dual control: no second person for sensitive acts
optionsShort.D: Need to know: technicians could browse customer records

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Real governance weakness here, and the direct answer only if one person could both initiate and authorize a payment.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Requires two people for a single sensitive act. The question asks which principle the rights assignment itself breaks.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: The data-access sibling of least privilege, arguably violated too. The stem's examples are capabilities, not records.

questionsV2.question: At which modality is the medical-disclosure objection MOST accurately aimed?

options.A: Iris recognition, which photographs the colored muscular ring that surrounds the pupil
options.B: Facial recognition, which maps the geometry of facial features
options.C: Fingerprint recognition, which reads surface ridge endings and minutiae patterns
options.D: Retina scanning, which images blood vessels at the back of the eye

questionsV2.explanation:
The retina is living vascular tissue, and its blood vessel pattern visibly changes with conditions like diabetes, hypertension and pregnancy. Retinal images therefore carry incidental health information (D), which is why this modality draws privacy objections that go beyond intrusiveness.
The two eye modalities split cleanly. Retina: internal and medically revealing. Iris: external and comparatively privacy-neutral.
questionsV2.recallLine: Employee representatives say the proposed eye scans could reveal medical conditions. At which modality is that objection MOST accurately aimed?

optionsShort.A: Iris recognition, the colored ring around the pupil
optionsShort.B: Facial recognition mapping feature geometry
optionsShort.C: Fingerprint ridge endings and minutiae
optionsShort.D: Retina scanning, vessels behind the eye

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: The conflation the question tests. The iris is an external muscle pattern, stable from childhood and revealing little about health.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Can hint at broad conditions the way any photograph can, and it images no internal physiology.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Captures surface skin patterns with no meaningful medical content.

questionsV2.question: Which protocol is the standard fit for the network access use case?

options.A: RADIUS, relaying access requests from VPN concentrators and wireless controllers
options.B: TACACS+, separating authentication from per-command authorization decisions
options.C: LDAP, exposing the directory for applications to query group memberships
options.D: Kerberos, issuing service tickets to hosts inside the Windows domain

questionsV2.explanation:
VPN concentrators and wireless controllers speak RADIUS natively (A). Each forwards a connection attempt to the AAA server, receives the accept or reject, and streams the session accounting records the chargeback requirement calls for.
RADIUS fronts network access, TACACS+ fronts device administration, and the directory sits behind both.
questionsV2.recallLine: An engineer must centralize wireless and remote-access authentication with per-session accounting for chargeback. Which protocol fits that use case?

optionsShort.A: RADIUS relaying VPN and wireless access requests
optionsShort.B: TACACS+ separating authentication from per-command authorization
optionsShort.C: LDAP exposing directory group memberships to applications
optionsShort.D: Kerberos issuing service tickets inside the domain

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: The stronger choice for administrator logins to routers and switches. Nobody here is administering the gear.

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Usually present, one layer back. The RADIUS server queries the directory; access hardware does not bind to LDAP itself.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Provides ticket-based single sign-on among domain members, and no part in a VPN concentrator's accept or reject.

questionsV2.question: Which measure would have MOST limited lateral movement using an extracted local administrator hash?

options.A: Enforcing longer and more complex local administrator passwords
options.B: Migrating stored credentials from NTLM to a slower hashing algorithm
options.C: Forcing password changes on local accounts every thirty days
options.D: Randomizing every workstation's local administrator password individually

questionsV2.explanation:
Pass-the-hash works because the hash itself is the authenticator. It reached two hundred machines because every machine shared one local admin credential. Randomize each workstation's local administrator password individually (D) - the LAPS pattern - and the stolen hash is valid on exactly one host.
Against hash replay, uniqueness beats strength. Once shared local credentials are gone, NTLM restrictions and credential isolation reinforce the fix.
questionsV2.recallLine: One extracted local administrator hash authenticated to two hundred workstations. Which measure would have MOST limited that lateral movement?

optionsShort.A: Longer, more complex local administrator passwords
optionsShort.B: Move stored credentials from NTLM to slower hashing
optionsShort.C: Force local password changes every thirty days
optionsShort.D: Randomize each workstation's local administrator password

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Aimed at cracking, and nothing here was cracked. Complexity is invisible to a replay attack.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Slows offline guessing the attacker never had to perform. The hash was used exactly as it stood.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Narrows how long the stolen value works and leaves it valid everywhere until the next rotation. A sweep takes minutes.

questionsV2.question: A scheduling app must read users' calendars at a third-party provider without ever seeing their passwords. Which framework should the team implement?

options.A: OAuth 2.0, so each user authorizes a scoped access token for the app
options.B: OpenID Connect, so the app receives a signed ID token identifying each authenticated user
options.C: SAML 2.0, so the provider asserts each user's authentication to the app
options.D: Kerberos delegation, so the app forwards each user's service tickets

questionsV2.explanation:
The requirement is delegated authorization: let this app read my calendar, nothing more, and never show it my password. That is OAuth 2.0's exact purpose (A). The user consents at the provider, and the app receives an access token limited to the calendar scope.
OAuth answers what may this app touch. OIDC and SAML answer who is this user.
questionsV2.recallLine: A scheduling app must read users' calendars at a third-party provider without ever seeing their passwords. Which framework should the team implement?

optionsShort.A: OAuth 2.0: user authorizes a scoped token
optionsShort.B: OpenID Connect: signed ID token naming the user
optionsShort.C: SAML 2.0: provider asserts the user's authentication
optionsShort.D: Kerberos delegation: app forwards the user's tickets

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Tells the app who the user is. Identity alone confers no right to read resource data.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Asserts authentication between organizations and carries no resource-scoped delegation for an API.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: An intra-domain mechanism for services acting on a user's behalf inside one Kerberos realm, not a pattern across providers.

questionsV2.question: Which cause should the engineer investigate FIRST for the rejected codes?

options.A: Clock drift on the migrated server breaking time-step agreement
options.B: Counter desynchronization between the apps and the server
options.C: Corrupted shared seeds requiring re-enrollment of every authenticator
options.D: An expired TLS certificate on the affected validation endpoint

questionsV2.explanation:
TOTP validation computes a code from the shared seed and the current 30-second time step, so both ends have to agree on the time. A virtual machine migration is a classic way for one guest's clock to drift while its peer stays true. Clock drift on the migrated server (A) matches the evidence exactly: same users, same seeds, one server rejecting.
When one validator rejects what another accepts, suspect whatever differs between them. For TOTP that is almost always the clock.
questionsV2.recallLine: After a hypervisor migration, one authentication server rejects every authenticator code its peer accepts. Which cause should the engineer investigate FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Clock drift breaking time-step agreement
optionsShort.B: Counter desynchronization between apps and server
optionsShort.C: Corrupted seeds requiring re-enrollment of every authenticator
optionsShort.D: Expired TLS certificate on the validation endpoint

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Describes HOTP, the counter-based variant. A counter problem would follow the user from one server to the other.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Cannot explain codes validating on the peer. Both servers verify against the same seeds, so corruption would fail everywhere.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Would stop clients connecting or raise certificate errors. The engineer is seeing a clean rejection of well-formed codes.

questionsV2.question: Which protocol BEST meets those device administration requirements for command authorization and encryption?

options.A: RADIUS, which combines authentication and authorization in a single accept-or-reject exchange
options.B: SNMPv3, which authenticates and encrypts management polling traffic
options.C: TACACS+, which separates the AAA functions and encrypts its entire payload
options.D: SSH, which encrypts each interactive session to the network device

questionsV2.explanation:
Both stem requirements map onto TACACS+ design decisions (C). It separates authentication from authorization, so the server can rule on every command an operator types. It encrypts the full packet body over TCP 49, so a capture shows nothing of the session content.
Separate the AAA functions when the authorization decision has to be taken command by command.
questionsV2.recallLine: The platform team wants every typed command authorized against the operator's profile, with the whole exchange encrypted. Which protocol BEST meets that?

optionsShort.A: RADIUS combining authentication and authorization in one exchange
optionsShort.B: SNMPv3 authenticating and encrypting management polling
optionsShort.C: TACACS+ separates AAA, encrypting the full packet
optionsShort.D: SSH encrypting each interactive session to the device

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Merges authentication and authorization into one accept, and encrypts only the password attribute. It fits VPN and wireless access.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Secures a management station's polling and configuration retrieval. It is no kind of login AAA protocol.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Encrypts the transport superbly and is purely point-to-point. No central profile decides which commands an operator may run.

questionsV2.question: A caller claiming to be a regional manager pressures an agent for an immediate privileged password reset. Which control MOST reduces the risk?

options.A: Filtering inbound email and attachments for credential-harvesting malware payloads
options.B: Publishing stronger password composition and rotation rules for all privileged accounts
options.C: Recurring social-engineering awareness training that rehearses helpdesk staff against pressure tactics
options.D: A mandatory callback to the requester's directory-listed number before privileged resets

questionsV2.explanation:
Vishing manufactures urgency to override judgment, so the defense that holds is one that takes judgment out of the moment. A mandatory callback to the requester's directory-listed number (D) makes the agent's sympathy or stress irrelevant: the reset waits until a number the attacker does not control answers.
Procedure beats instinct under pressure, because the procedure does not get flustered.
questionsV2.recallLine: A caller claiming to be a regional manager pressures a help-desk agent into an immediate privileged password reset. Which control MOST reduces the risk?

optionsShort.A: Filter inbound email for credential-harvesting payloads
optionsShort.B: Stronger composition and rotation rules for privileged accounts
optionsShort.C: Recurring social-engineering awareness training for agents
optionsShort.D: Mandatory callback to the directory-listed number

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Defends a different channel. This attack arrives by phone and touches no attachment.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Inert here. Nobody is guessing the password; the attacker is persuading someone to replace it.

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Genuinely helps and should exist. A skilled pretext is built to beat exactly the reflexes training builds.

questionsV2.question: Which change BEST corrects treating a bare access token as proof of identity?

options.A: Wrap every token exchange in mutually authenticated TLS so tokens are not intercepted
options.B: Shorten the access token lifetime so a stolen token expires quickly
options.C: Use refresh tokens and not access tokens for the login decision
options.D: Adopt OpenID Connect and base login on its signed, audience-bound ID token

questionsV2.explanation:
An access token proves that some client was authorized for some scope. It says nothing reliable about who is present, and a token issued to a different, malicious app can be replayed to log in as its victim. That is token substitution.
OpenID Connect exists to close the gap (D). Its ID token is a signed assertion of authentication, bound to a specific audience and nonce, so the app can verify both the user and that the token was minted for it.
OAuth authorizes; OIDC authenticates.
questionsV2.recallLine: A consumer web application logs any bearer in as the user on a bare access token. Which change BEST corrects that?

optionsShort.A: Wrap token exchanges in mutually authenticated TLS
optionsShort.B: Shorten token lifetime so stolen tokens expire
optionsShort.C: Use refresh tokens for the login decision
optionsShort.D: Adopt OpenID Connect's signed, audience-bound identity assertion

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Protects tokens in transit and leaves the semantic confusion untouched. The replayed token just arrives over a clean channel.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Narrows the abuse window. The flaw survives it.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Makes matters worse. Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials for getting new access tokens, further still from an identity proof.

questionsV2.question: Which property MOST supports choosing time-based over counter-based tokens for that goal?

options.A: Time-based codes contain more digits than counter-based codes and are harder to guess
options.B: Unused HOTP codes stay valid until redeemed, while TOTP codes lapse within seconds
options.C: Time-based tokens operate without any shared secret at the server
options.D: Counter-based tokens transmit their counter value openly with each code

questionsV2.explanation:
What invalidates a code is where the two schemes part. An HOTP code from a button press stays redeemable until the server-side counter moves past it, potentially hours or days if the user does not log in. A TOTP code dies with its 30-to-60-second time step (B), so a captured code is worthless almost at once.
Ask what retires a one-time code. That rule, and not the code's length, decides how long a capture is worth anything.
questionsV2.recallLine: A shoulder-surfing worry asks which token leaves a glimpsed code useful for the shortest time. Which property MOST supports choosing the time-based kind?

optionsShort.A: More digits than counter-based codes, harder to guess
optionsShort.B: Unused HOTP codes remain valid until redeemed
optionsShort.C: No shared secret is held at the server
optionsShort.D: Counter-based tokens transmit the counter openly

A.label: true of a different thing
A.wouldAnswer: False as a differentiator. Both standards typically emit six-to-eight digit codes of identical guessing difficulty.

C.label: true of a different thing
C.wouldAnswer: Misdescribes both schemes. Each is symmetric, with the server holding the same seed as the token.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Invents a weakness. The counter is synchronized state and never crosses the wire.

questionsV2.question: Which statement of the risk the lockout policy itself introduces is MOST accurate?

options.A: Attackers may adapt by spraying passwords at a rate below the lockout threshold
options.B: Anyone holding a list of valid usernames can deliberately lock out the workforce
options.C: Helpdesk workload will rise as legitimate users trip the threshold accidentally
options.D: Locked accounts will bury genuine intrusion attempts within the event logs

questionsV2.explanation:
A hard lockout turns failed logins into a weapon. Usernames are cheap to enumerate, and a script submitting three junk passwords per account can deny the whole workforce access for a day, then do it again tomorrow (B). The policy hands attackers an availability lever, which is why throttling with progressive backoff and monitoring is usually preferred at this exposure.
Any proposed control deserves a look at the attack surface it adds. This one trades a confidentiality defense for an availability vulnerability.
questionsV2.recallLine: A portal locks accounts after three failed logins. Which statement of the risk that lockout policy itself introduces is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Attackers spray below the lockout threshold
optionsShort.B: A username list can lock everyone out
optionsShort.C: Helpdesk workload rises from accidental lockouts
optionsShort.D: Lockouts bury genuine intrusion attempts in logs

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: True, and what it describes is an evasion the policy fails to stop. That belongs in a detection-coverage discussion.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Real, predictable, and an operational cost. The board asked for the security risk.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Backwards. Lockouts emit loud, countable events that make an attack wave more visible.

questionsV2.question: Which access control model fits the requirement that no file owner may override or reclassify?

options.A: Role-based access control driven by job assignments
options.B: Discretionary access control administered by resource owners
options.C: Mandatory access control enforced through security labels
options.D: Attribute-based access control evaluating contextual rules

questionsV2.explanation:
Two phrases in the stem decide it: classification markings, and decisions imposed by the system beyond any owner's authority. That pair defines mandatory access control (C), where subjects hold clearances, objects hold labels, and policy is centrally enforced.
Read the stem for who decides. Labels the system imposes, with no owner override, name one model only.
questionsV2.recallLine: A document system must enforce government classification markings so that no file owner can reclassify. Which access control model fits that requirement?

optionsShort.A: Role-based, driven by job assignments
optionsShort.B: Discretionary, administered by resource owners
optionsShort.C: Mandatory, enforced through security labels
optionsShort.D: Attribute-based, evaluating contextual rules

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Grants by job function, and an administrator can still adjust assignments, which the requirement excludes.

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: The direct opposite of the requirement. Owner discretion is exactly what has to be removed.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Could emulate labels among its attributes. Its purpose is dynamic, condition-based decisions, which is a different shape.

questionsV2.question: Which access control model BEST supports that automatic provisioning from HR job codes?

options.A: Discretionary access control, letting each store manager grant what is needed
options.B: Mandatory access control, labeling every resource by sensitivity level
options.C: Attribute-based access control, evaluating dynamic conditions at request time
options.D: Role-based access control, mapping permission bundles to defined job functions

questionsV2.explanation:
Standardized bundles keyed to a job code, with join-move-leave automation, is role-based access control's home ground (D). HR assigns the role, the role carries the pre-approved permissions, and revocation is one membership change.
When the permission set is the same for everyone doing a job, the job is the natural unit of administration.
questionsV2.recallLine: Brackley wants store associates' access created and removed automatically from HR job codes. Which access control model BEST supports that provisioning?

optionsShort.A: Discretionary: each store manager grants what's needed
optionsShort.B: Mandatory: label every resource by sensitivity
optionsShort.C: Attribute-based: dynamic conditions evaluated per request
optionsShort.D: Role-based: permission bundles mapped to job functions

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Would have hundreds of managers hand-crafting grants, which produces inconsistency and an orphaned right at every departure.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Solves a different problem, protecting classified material through clearance labels, and adds weight with no retail benefit.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Can express role-like logic through attributes. For identical static bundles it is added complexity.

questionsV2.question: Which mechanism should the agency deploy for smart-card initial authentication?

options.A: NTLM pass-through authentication to the domain controller
options.B: PKINIT, the Kerberos extension for public-key initial authentication
options.C: SESAME, the European ticket-based system built on public keys
options.D: Constrained delegation of the user's ticket-granting ticket

questionsV2.explanation:
Standard Kerberos derives the user's initial key from a password, which is the thing the agency wants gone. PKINIT (RFC 4556) replaces that first exchange with certificate-based proof using the private key on the smart card (B), and it is the mechanism underneath Active Directory smart card logon.
Smart card logon in a Kerberos world means PKINIT at the AS exchange, keeping everything password-derived out of the initial handshake.
questionsV2.recallLine: The agency is moving domain logons to smart cards so initial authentication uses certificates and not a password-derived key. Which mechanism should it deploy?

optionsShort.A: NTLM pass-through to the domain controller
optionsShort.B: PKINIT, Kerberos public-key initial authentication
optionsShort.C: SESAME, a European ticket-based public-key system
optionsShort.D: Constrained delegation of the ticket-granting ticket

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: The legacy Windows challenge-response fallback: password-hash based, certificate-blind, and the thing hardening tries to disable.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Correctly described and historical: a 1990s European research design layering public-key concepts onto Kerberos-like tickets.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Operates after authentication, letting designated services obtain tickets on a user's behalf. It is a delegation tool.

questionsV2.question: Which additional control MOST directly reduces the automated traffic?

options.A: Raising the minimum password length across all customer accounts
options.B: Locking each targeted account after several failed login attempts
options.C: Challenging suspicious login attempts with CAPTCHA or proof-of-work puzzles
options.D: Blocking authentication requests that originate from foreign address ranges

questionsV2.explanation:
The stated problem is volume from bots, so the control has to tell an automated client from a human one at the front door. CAPTCHA and proof-of-work challenges (C) do that, making each scripted attempt expensive enough that mass stuffing stops paying.
Match the control to what actually separates the bad traffic from the good. Here that is machine against human.
questionsV2.recallLine: Millions of automated stuffing attempts from residential proxies are degrading genuine login latency. Which additional control MOST directly reduces that traffic?

optionsShort.A: Raise minimum password length for all customers
optionsShort.B: Lock each targeted account after several failures
optionsShort.C: Challenge suspicious attempts with CAPTCHA or proof-of-work
optionsShort.D: Block authentication requests from foreign address ranges

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Changes nothing about traffic. Stuffing replays breached credentials, and the load arrives whatever the length rule says.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Misses the attack shape. Stuffing tries each account once or twice, and a tripped lockout punishes the legitimate owner.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Fails on the given facts. Residential proxies make the traffic look domestic, so geo-blocking sheds real customers.

questionsV2.question: Which characteristic of the file share environment made the company-wide readability possible?

options.A: Rule-based control applies one uniform policy to every subject
options.B: Discretionary control leaves grant decisions with each resource owner
options.C: Mandatory control ties every access decision to clearance levels
options.D: Role-based control links permissions to defined job functions

questionsV2.explanation:
Windows NTFS permissions follow the discretionary model (B). Whoever owns a file may share it at will, so a well-meaning creator can quietly grant the world access to regulated data. That owner discretion is the mechanism the auditor observed.
DAC's convenience is its risk. Owner-controlled sharing scales into sprawl unless it is monitored, or replaced for sensitive data.
questionsV2.recallLine: Cardholder spreadsheets on a Windows share were readable company-wide. Which characteristic of that file share environment made that possible?

optionsShort.A: Rule-based: one uniform policy for every subject
optionsShort.B: Discretionary: owners decide their own grants
optionsShort.C: Mandatory: decisions tied to clearance levels
optionsShort.D: Role-based: permissions linked to job functions

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Describes system-wide rules such as firewall-style conditions. Under one uniform policy the creator could not have loosened it.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Would have made the oversharing impossible, since labels and clearances remove the owner's choice. A different environment.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Would bound access by job function. The finding shows access following individual grant decisions.

questionsV2.question: Which access control model is BEST suited to evaluating all of those conditions together?

options.A: Attribute-based access control combining subject, environment and device attributes
options.B: Role-based access control assigning rights by technician job function
options.C: Mandatory access control comparing clearance labels against resource labels
options.D: Discretionary access control letting the console's owner assign permissions

questionsV2.explanation:
Network location, time window and device posture are environmental and device attributes. A policy has to weigh them per request: permit if role is technician AND network is corporate AND time is in window AND laptop is compliant. That is the definition of attribute-based access control (A).
Count the conditions the requirement names. Four of them, weighed at each request, is one model's whole purpose.
questionsV2.recallLine: Console sessions are permitted only from the corporate network, inside a maintenance window, on a patched managed laptop. Which model BEST evaluates those together?

optionsShort.A: Attribute-based: subject, environment and device attributes
optionsShort.B: Role-based: rights by technician job function
optionsShort.C: Mandatory: clearance labels against resource labels
optionsShort.D: Discretionary: the console's owner assigns permissions

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Answers who may act, by job, and has no vocabulary for when, from where, or from what device.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Decides by comparing sensitivity labels to clearances and cannot see clocks or patch levels.

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Hands the decision to a resource owner. That changes who decides and adds no vocabulary for conditions.

questionsV2.question: After a restore left clocks skewed, authentication failed outright. What does that strict time requirement protect against?

options.A: Expiration of stale service tickets held in the credential cache
options.B: Password-guessing attempts distributed across authentication servers
options.C: Replay of captured authenticators outside their short validity window
options.D: Negotiation of the session down to a weaker encryption type

questionsV2.explanation:
Every Kerberos request carries a timestamped authenticator, and a verifier rejects any timestamp outside a small tolerance, conventionally five minutes. An attacker who captures traffic therefore cannot usefully re-send it: by the time it is replayed, the timestamp has aged out (C). That is the protection the snapshot-skewed host is colliding with.
Kerberos treats accurate time as a security dependency. Replay resistance rests on synchronized clocks, so a time-infrastructure failure becomes an authentication outage by design.
questionsV2.recallLine: A restore left clocks skewed and Kerberos authentication failed outright. What does that strict time requirement protect against?

optionsShort.A: Expiry of stale tickets in the cache
optionsShort.B: Password guessing spread across authentication servers
optionsShort.C: Replay of captured authenticators after their window
optionsShort.D: Downgrade of the session to weaker encryption

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Confuses the skew check with ticket lifetime, a separate limit of hours governing how long a ticket stays valid.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Handled by throttling and lockout at the account layer. Timestamps do nothing to slow guessing.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Countered by the protocol's encryption-type negotiation and hardening settings. Clocks have no part in it.

questionsV2.question: Which replacement practice would BEST bring physical key handling into line with identity principles?

options.A: Issue keys individually from an audited cabinet with per-person sign-out records
options.B: Install a camera covering the key storage area so removals can be reviewed
options.C: Move the keys into a locked cabinet whose combination all technicians share
options.D: Remove the identifying label so the keys' purpose is hidden from a visitor

questionsV2.explanation:
Physical keys are credentials. The case study's core lesson - one identity per person, with attributable use - reaches them just as it reaches logins. An audited cabinet with per-person sign-out (A) restores identification and accountability for every key movement.
Treat a key the way you treat an account. Issue it to one person, and keep a record of who holds it.
questionsV2.recallLine: Safe master keys sit in an unlocked drawer any office visitor could reach. Which replacement practice BEST aligns key handling with identity principles?

optionsShort.A: Audited cabinet with per-person sign-out records
optionsShort.B: Camera covering the key storage area
optionsShort.C: Locked cabinet with a shared combination
optionsShort.D: Remove the label identifying what keys open

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: Purely detective. Footage may show who took a key after the cash has gone.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Upgrades the container and recreates the SuperAdmin defect in physical form. A shared combination is a shared credential.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Security through obscurity. An unlabeled unlocked drawer is still an uncontrolled credential store.

questionsV2.question: Which capability MOST directly restores individual accountability for a shared account's use?

options.A: Automatic rotation of the SuperAdmin password every twenty-four hours
options.B: Renaming the account so its privilege level is less conspicuous
options.C: Multi-factor authentication applied to the shared console login
options.D: Per-user credential checkout combined with full session recording

questionsV2.explanation:
Accountability requires a named person behind every privileged action, and per-user credential checkout with full session recording (D) supplies one. Each technician authenticates as themselves to withdraw the credential, the vault logs who held it and when, and the recording captures what they did with it. The shared account becomes attributable while it continues to exist.
Attribution is the requirement here. A control that still leaves five candidates has not met it.
questionsV2.recallLine: Nobody can tell which technician used the shared administrative account. Which privileged access capability MOST directly restores individual accountability?

optionsShort.A: Rotate the SuperAdmin password every twenty-four hours
optionsShort.B: Rename the account to hide its privilege
optionsShort.C: Multi-factor authentication on the shared console login
optionsShort.D: Per-user checkout with full session recording

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Retires the standing shared secret over time and says nothing about which of the five used it between rotations.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Security through obscurity. An attacker enumerating privileged groups finds the account whatever it is called.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Strengthens the proof that some technician logged in. Five people sharing one enrollment still leaves five suspects.

questionsV2.question: Which risk does provisioning by copying a colleague's account MOST directly create?

options.A: New hires' passwords will match those of the colleagues who were copied
options.B: Orphaned template accounts will linger after the copied employees depart
options.C: Colleagues will gain the ability to log in to the new hires' accounts
options.D: New accounts will inherit entitlements far beyond what the role requires

questionsV2.explanation:
Cloning a veteran's account clones their history. Every project share, exception grant and leftover group membership from years of transfers lands on someone whose job needs none of it (D). Privilege creep arrives at birth, and the least-privilege failure is built into the provisioning step itself.
Provision from role definitions. An account copied from a person inherits a person's clutter.
questionsV2.recallLine: The service desk provisions new hires by copying a long-serving colleague's account. Which risk does that practice MOST directly create?

optionsShort.A: New hires share the copied colleagues' passwords
optionsShort.B: Orphaned template accounts linger after those employees leave
optionsShort.C: Colleagues can log in to new hires' accounts
optionsShort.D: New accounts inherit entitlements the role never needs

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Misunderstands the mechanism. Directory copies duplicate group memberships and attributes; each account still gets its own credential.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Genuine hygiene issue in lifecycle management, and it concerns the template employee's own departure.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Confuses shared entitlements with shared authentication. Membership overlap does not let one person authenticate as another.

questionsV2.question: Which standard is designed for browser-based federation in which the partner never receives corporate passwords?

options.A: Kerberos, issuing service tickets from the corporate key distribution center
options.B: SAML 2.0, sending signed authentication assertions from the corporate identity provider
options.C: OAuth 2.0, issuing access tokens that delegate resource rights to the partner
options.D: TACACS+, centralizing authentication for devices at the network perimeter

questionsV2.explanation:
Cross-organization web single sign-on is the scenario SAML 2.0 was built for (B). The employee authenticates once to the corporate identity provider, the browser carries a signed XML assertion to the partner's service provider, and the partner trusts the assertion. No password ever reaches the partner.
Federation moves a signed claim about who signed in. The password stays with the party that issued it.
questionsV2.recallLine: A benefits portal is federated to a partner through the browser, and the partner must never receive corporate passwords. Which standard is designed for that?

optionsShort.A: Kerberos tickets from the corporate key distribution center
optionsShort.B: SAML 2.0: signed authentication assertions from the identity provider
optionsShort.C: OAuth 2.0: access tokens delegating resource rights
optionsShort.D: TACACS+: centralized authentication for network devices

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Kerberos excels inside a single realm or trusted domain. Its ticket exchange does not reach an external partner's website.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Answers what a client application may access on a user's behalf. An access token asserts nothing about who the user is.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Authenticates administrators to routers and switches, an infrastructure AAA role a long way from browser federation.

questionsV2.question: Which change should the team make FIRST to the directory authentication?

options.A: Require TLS on directory connections, using LDAPS or StartTLS
options.B: Move the portal to anonymous binds so credentials are no longer transmitted
options.C: Lengthen the directory account's password and rotate it quarterly
options.D: Restrict the portal's bind account to read access on the directory tree

questionsV2.explanation:
Simple bind sends the distinguished name and password essentially in cleartext, so every user login is harvestable by anyone positioned on the network path. Wrap the connection in TLS (A) - LDAPS on 636, or StartTLS upgrading 389 - and the exposure closes with the authentication model intact.
Fix the confidentiality of the channel before polishing the credentials that travel over it. A cleartext protocol undermines every secret it carries.
questionsV2.recallLine: A portal binds to the corporate directory over an unprotected port, sending every user password in clear. Which change should the team make FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Require TLS on directory connections
optionsShort.B: Switch to anonymous binds, transmitting no credentials
optionsShort.C: Lengthen and rotate the directory account password
optionsShort.D: Restrict the bind account to read access

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Stops transmitting credentials by abandoning authentication. An anonymous bind proves nothing about the user.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Hardens a secret that still crosses the wire readably. Stronger, rotated, and observable on every bind.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Worthwhile least-privilege hygiene for a different risk. Credentials in transit stay exposed either way.

questionsV2.question: Which arrangement should the redesign adopt to genuinely satisfy dual control?

options.A: One custodian carries both safe keys after signing a liability agreement
options.B: A supervisor approves each replenishment ticket before a technician opens the safe
options.C: Two authorized staff attend each opening, each turning a separately issued key
options.D: A monitored camera records the safe whenever a single keyholder opens it

questionsV2.explanation:
Dual control means the sensitive act is physically impossible for one person: two individuals, two credentials, both present at the moment the safe opens (C). That is what defeats a lone insider like the QuickCash technician.
Dual control is about presence at the moment of the act. A step before it or a record after it is a different control.
questionsV2.recallLine: The safes must open only under dual control, genuinely instead of in name. Which arrangement should the redesign adopt?

optionsShort.A: One custodian holds both keys, signing liability
optionsShort.B: Supervisor approves each ticket before the opening
optionsShort.C: Two staff attend, each turning a separate key
optionsShort.D: Camera records a single keyholder's openings

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Concentrates both credentials in one trusted person. The liability paper shifts blame afterwards and restrains nothing.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Adds a genuine authorization step, beforehand and away from the safe. Once the ticket exists a single actor still opens it.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Detective. The camera documents the theft it cannot interrupt.

questionsV2.question: Which risk does the split-knowledge arrangement MOST directly address?

options.A: A single trusted insider misusing the complete secret alone
options.B: Losing access to the vault when one officer resigns abruptly
options.C: Disclosure of the combination while it is first distributed
options.D: Systematic manipulation of the vault's mechanical dial

questionsV2.explanation:
Split the secret and no individual ever holds enough to act. Exploiting the vault now takes collusion between two trusted people (A), a far rarer event than one insider going bad - as the QuickCash case shows.
Splitting a secret buys collusion resistance and costs availability. Both belong in the recommendation.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two officers each memorize half a vault combination and neither may learn the other. Which risk does that split-knowledge arrangement MOST directly address?

optionsShort.A: A lone insider misusing the whole secret
optionsShort.B: Losing vault access when an officer resigns
optionsShort.C: Disclosure while the combination is first distributed
optionsShort.D: Manipulation of the vault's mechanical dial

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Gets the effect backwards. Split knowledge worsens availability, since a departed officer takes an irreplaceable half.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Untouched. Each half still has to reach its officer somehow, and a distribution channel can leak either one.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Concerns the lock's physical attack resistance, which no knowledge-management arrangement changes.

questionsV2.question: The board wants a detective measure it can enforce this quarter without restructuring anyone's job. Which control BEST fits?

options.A: Rotating the bookkeeper permanently into a different position at another branch
options.B: Requiring dual approval on all reconciliation entries going forward
options.C: Enforcing an uninterrupted two-week vacation with her duties reassigned meanwhile
options.D: Commissioning a penetration test of the accounting platform

questionsV2.explanation:
Concealed fraud of this kind survives on continuous personal control of the records. Force a genuine absence long enough that someone else has to perform the reconciliations (C) and the irregularities surface the moment fresh hands touch the books. It is the classic detective control, and it restructures nothing.
A detective control has to look backward. Ask what a measure would reveal about work already done.
questionsV2.recallLine: A bookkeeper has declined leave for four years. Which detective control can the board enforce this quarter without restructuring her job?

optionsShort.A: Move the bookkeeper permanently to another branch
optionsShort.B: Dual approval on all future reconciliation entries
optionsShort.C: Uninterrupted two-week absence, duties reassigned meanwhile
optionsShort.D: Penetration test of the accounting platform

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Would likely expose the fraud too, and it is the permanent restructuring the board excluded.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Preventive and prospective. It constrains future entries and leaves four years of manipulation unexamined.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Probes technical vulnerabilities in the platform. This scheme abuses authorized access and process.

questionsV2.question: Which Kerberos element makes it possible to open service after service all day without further credential prompts?

options.A: The session key cached from her first service connection
options.B: The NTLM hash of her password retained by the workstation
options.C: The ticket-granting ticket her workstation exchanges for service tickets
options.D: The plaintext password held in memory by the credential manager

questionsV2.explanation:
After the initial authentication the KDC issues a ticket-granting ticket. For every service after that, the workstation silently presents the TGT to the ticket-granting service and receives a service ticket (C). The password is needed once, which is exactly the all-day behavior observed.
One authentication, many tickets. That trade is what single sign-on buys, and the reason the TGT is worth guarding.
questionsV2.recallLine: After one morning logon a user opens service after service without further credential prompts. Which Kerberos element makes that possible?

optionsShort.A: Session key cached from the first service connection
optionsShort.B: NTLM hash of the password kept by the workstation
optionsShort.C: Ticket-granting ticket exchanged for service tickets
optionsShort.D: Plaintext password held by the credential manager

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Exists, and it secures traffic with one particular service. It cannot obtain access to print or mail.
