options.B: Tune the SIEM to suppress phishing alerts that score below a severity threshold.
options.C: Outsource the alert triage queue to a managed security service provider.
options.D: Implement SOAR playbooks automating the extraction, lookup, search, and quarantine steps.

questions.explanation: Work that is high-volume, well-understood, and identical every time is the defining use case for security orchestration: a playbook executes the extraction, intelligence lookup, mailbox search, and quarantine in seconds per alert, and analysts touch only the cases that need judgment. Option A is wrong because hiring scales cost linearly with a volume that will keep growing, and it spends scarce analysts on work that requires none of their skill - the right answer only when the workload genuinely demands human judgment. Option B is wrong because the stem says alert quality is good: suppression works by ignoring alerts, which converts a workload problem into missed phishing incidents. Option C is wrong because outsourcing relocates the manual toil without removing it, adds a coordination seam during incidents, and bills for exactly the repetitive steps automation would erase. Automate the repeatable; reserve people for decisions.

questions.question: An incident responder reaches a compromised, still-running ATM believed to hold the attacker's injected code in memory. Management wants the machine analyzed with as little evidence lost as possible. Following the order of volatility in NIST SP 800-86, which action should the responder take FIRST?

options.A: Power the machine down cleanly and create a forensic image of its hard drive.
options.B: Collect the ATM's transaction records from the central switch before they age out.
options.C: Capture the system's memory and other volatile state while the machine is still running.
options.D: Photograph the machine in place and interview branch staff about recent maintenance visits.

questions.explanation: The order of volatility dictates collecting the most perishable evidence first, and everything the stem cares about - the injected code, live network connections, running processes - exists only in memory and vanishes the moment power drops or the system reboots. Memory acquisition therefore leads. Option A is wrong because it is the classic volatility error: a clean shutdown preserves the disk perfectly while destroying the very RAM-resident evidence the case turns on; imaging the drive is correct as the following step. Option B is wrong because records on the central switch are among the most durable evidence available - stored remotely, subject to retention schedules measured in months - so deferring them costs nothing. Option D is wrong because photographs and interviews document context that is not decaying on a timescale of minutes; valuable, but nothing about a staff interview is volatile. Rank every collection task by how fast the evidence evaporates, then work down the list.

questions.question: Prosecutors reviewing Global ATM Corp's skimming case are weighing four items of evidence for trial. Which item is MOST likely to survive an admissibility challenge?

options.A: An analyst's recollection of a forum rumor naming the suspect as an ATM fraudster.
options.B: A hash-verified image of the ATM's drive, collected under a documented chain of custody.
options.C: A junior technician's personal opinion that the malware appeared to be foreign-made.
options.D: A screenshot of the attacker's marketplace listing, sent in by an anonymous tipster.

questions.explanation: Admissible evidence must be relevant to the case, material to its issues, and competent - lawfully obtained and reliable - and the drive image is the only item that can prove its own reliability: the hash values demonstrate the contents are unchanged, and the custody record accounts for every hand it passed through. The rumor A cites is hearsay layered on hearsay: the analyst cannot testify to facts heard third-hand, and no declarant is available to examine. Option C is wrong because opinion testimony carries weight only from a qualified expert, and a junior technician's impression about malware origin has no established expertise behind it. Option D is wrong because authenticity cannot be established: an anonymous source means no one can testify to when, where, or how the screenshot was made, or whether it was fabricated. Evidence wins by provenance, and provenance is built at collection time, not at trial.

questions.question: A flood disables Global ATM Corp's head office. The disaster recovery plan performs well: every IT system is restored at the recovery site within its RTO. Even so, the business stalls for days - the call centre has no workspace, the cash-in-transit contracts contain no fallback instructions, and no one holds authority to relocate staff. What does this outcome MOST clearly reveal?

options.A: The organization lacks a business continuity plan covering people, premises, and processes beyond IT.
options.B: The disaster recovery plan's recovery time objectives were set incorrectly for these systems.
options.C: The recovery site was under-provisioned for the workloads it was required to absorb.
options.D: The business impact analysis omitted the head office's IT systems when ranking critical functions.

questions.explanation: Everything that failed here sits outside IT: workspace for staff, supplier arrangements, and decision authority are continuity-of-business concerns, and the discipline that plans for them is business continuity management - the broader layer within which disaster recovery is only the IT component. Working systems with nowhere to sit and no one empowered to act is the signature of a DRP without a BCP. Option B is wrong because the RTOs were demonstrably achieved; sharpening targets that were met would change nothing about the days of stall. Option C is wrong for the same reason - the recovery site did its job, restoring every workload within objective; capacity was not the constraint. Option D is wrong on two counts: the IT systems plainly were covered, since they were restored on time, and a BIA gap in system ranking would have produced slow or missing systems, not homeless staff and silent suppliers. Restored servers are not a restored business.

questions.question: Following a ransomware detonation, Global ATM Corp's crisis team activates its continuity documentation. The recovery engineers ask specifically for the document containing the server rebuild sequences, the order in which systems must be restored, and the technical steps for failing over to the recovery site. Which document should the team hand them?

options.A: The business continuity plan maintained by the corporate resilience office.
options.B: The business impact analysis produced during last year's planning cycle.
options.C: The disaster recovery plan covering the affected systems.
options.D: The crisis communications plan held by corporate affairs.

questions.explanation: Rebuild sequences, restoration order, and failover procedures are the operational core of a disaster recovery plan - the tactical, IT-focused document written precisely so engineers in this moment have step-by-step instructions and not intentions. Option A is wrong because the business continuity plan operates a level above: it keeps business functions running through workarounds, alternate facilities, and staffing decisions, and delegates the technical system-restoration detail to the DRP. Handing engineers the BCP gives them strategy when they asked for procedure. Option B is wrong because the BIA is an analysis input, not an action document - it established which systems matter and how quickly they must return, information already baked into the DRP's priorities. Option D is wrong because the communications plan scripts messages to customers, regulators, and press; essential during a ransomware event, but not a word of it rebuilds a server. Match the document to the altitude of the question being asked.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp's BIA concludes that the settlement function can survive a maximum of 24 hours of downtime before the bank faces regulatory penalties and unrecoverable losses. The IT recovery proposal for the supporting systems specifies a 36-hour RTO, because faster options exceed this year's budget. How should the BCP coordinator respond?

options.A: Accept the proposal, since budget constraints legitimately override planning targets for a year.
options.B: Raise the documented MTD to 48 hours, since the recovery capability actually available should define the tolerance.
options.C: Accept it if the RPO remains within limits, since data loss outweighs downtime.
options.D: Reject the proposal, because the RTO must fit inside the MTD for the recovery to be viable.

questions.explanation: The maximum tolerable downtime is a statement of business fact - the point at which the organization suffers unrecoverable harm - and every recovery objective is derived beneath it. An RTO of 36 hours against a 24-hour MTD is a plan to recover the systems after the business they support has already been irreparably damaged, so the proposal fails on its face and the gap goes to management as a funding-or-risk decision. Budget pressure does not shrink the harm; A's silent acceptance is risk acceptance without the authority or visibility that decision requires. Option B is wrong because it reverses the derivation - the MTD comes from impact analysis of penalties and losses, and editing the number does not edit the regulator. Option C is wrong because the RPO governs data loss, an independent axis; flawless data recovered twelve hours too late still breaches the tolerance. Recovery targets cascade downward from business survival, never upward from this year's budget.

questions.question: The post-mortem examines why the automated rollback failed: the uninstall command never reached the ATMs because 4,000 crashing machines rebooting in a loop saturated the management network. Leadership accepts that despite better staging, some future change will eventually go wrong at scale. Which additional safeguard would BEST ensure a rollback can succeed under those conditions?

options.A: Requiring the CCB to record a named rollback owner for every change it approves.
options.B: A dedicated out-of-band management channel with reserved capacity for recovery commands.
options.C: Compressing rollback packages so they consume less bandwidth on the shared network.
options.D: Scheduling an automatic fleet-wide reboot to clear the check-in storm before rollback.

questions.explanation: The rollback failed for one reason: the recovery path shared the network that the failure itself destroyed. A management channel that is physically or logically separate, with capacity reserved for command traffic, keeps working precisely when the production network is drowning - which is the condition leadership has told the team to plan for. Option A is wrong because accountability is a governance improvement that changes nothing about deliverability; a named owner issuing commands into a saturated network fails identically. Option C is wrong because the bottleneck was the storm of 4,000 machines endlessly rebooting and checking in, not the rollback package size; shaving kilobytes off one command does not clear a saturated link. Option D is wrong because it prescribes more of the disease as the cure - a simultaneous fleet-wide reboot is a re-creation of the very storm that blocked the first rollback. Recovery mechanisms must not depend on the infrastructure whose failure they exist to fix.

stimuli.title: Global ATM: the Toledo prompt
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp operates 5,000 ATMs. Its service desk logs a report from a branch: an ATM in Toledo displayed a command prompt for a few seconds during a maintenance visit. The fleet runs a standard Windows build with anti-malware and a monthly patch cycle. Each machine writes its own event log locally and keeps thirty days of it. There is no rule about which programs may run. The maintenance vendor's technician says he ran a diagnostic tool he downloaded that morning. By the time an analyst calls back, the machine has been rebooted twice.

profile.environment: Standard Windows build · local event logs, 30 days · outsourced maintenance
profile.state: One reported command prompt, machine already rebooted twice

stimuli.title: Global ATM: two exercises
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp has a written disaster recovery plan for the transaction switch behind its 5,000 ATMs, and has run one tabletop against it. The plan names a recovery team of eleven people across three time zones, lists a call tree, and assumes the switch can be brought up at the Columbus site within four hours. Nobody has yet performed any of the steps. The board has approved two exercises this year and will not accept an outage of production. The operations director has asked what the two exercises should be and what evidence each will produce.

profile.regime: State banking examination · card brand availability requirements
profile.environment: Transaction switch · alternate site at Columbus · eleven-person recovery team, three time zones
profile.state: Plan written, one tabletop run, no procedure yet performed

stimuli.title: A patch that took the fleet down
stimuli.text: A security patch put every one of Global ATM Corp's 5,000 machines into a reboot loop, and customers could not withdraw cash for eighteen hours. No card data was exposed and no transaction record was altered. The test lab cannot replicate every dispenser hardware variant in the field, and the vendor certifies patches only against a reference build. Business impact analysis sets a four-hour recovery time objective and a twenty-four-hour maximum tolerable downtime for the fleet. An engineer has found a registry fix that would stop the loop, but the change board does not meet for three days.

profile.environment: Test lab cannot replicate every dispenser variant · vendor certifies against a reference build
profile.state: 18-hour outage, no data exposed

stimuli.title: Who may change what, and who checks
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp's change board is reviewing four backout plans submitted with a proposed dispenser firmware change, and only one of them is a plan at all. An outage review has separately noted that the lead engineer who wrote a deployment change request also approved it in the tracking system and then executed the deployment. A fleet audit found machines running inconsistent settings: some hardened, others with services re-enabled by field technicians, and no record of what any machine is supposed to look like. Operations also want to compare the reliability of two dispenser models over the coming year.

profile.organization: Global ATM Corp · change and configuration management
profile.environment: Firmware changes submitted with backout plans · machines running inconsistent settings
profile.state: Change process being rebuilt after an outage

stimuli.title: Objectives, and whether they were met
stimuli.text: Trentham Payments restored its transaction switch to working order three hours into a recovery test, after which data validation and reconciliation took another three hours before the business could resume processing. The recovery objective is four hours and the maximum tolerable downtime is eight. The business has separately determined the switch database can lose at most fifteen minutes of committed transactions in a disaster, and the architect must pick a data-protection design that meets that without overspending. A monitoring server was down for a day when its single disk failed.

profile.environment: Four-hour recovery objective, eight-hour maximum tolerable downtime · reconciliation after restore
profile.state: Recovery test results being assessed

stimuli.title: Copies, mirrors and what each protects
stimuli.text: An administrator at Trentham Payments proposes mirrored disks after a monitoring server was lost to a single disk failure, and asks whether nightly backups can then be retired. The same review found that an operator had accidentally deleted a week of alert history months earlier. An engineer is separately configuring local storage for a log-collection server with four drive bays, needing to tolerate any single drive failing while keeping as much usable capacity as possible. An archived-records system consulted a few times a month carries a two-week recovery objective on a tight budget, and leased machines are being returned.

profile.environment: Four drive bays in the log collector · nightly backups and a proposed mirror · archived records rarely consulted
profile.state: Backup design being revisited

stimuli.title: Full, differential, incremental
stimuli.text: An administrator at Ashcombe Mutual runs a full backup of the log server every Sunday night and a differential every other night, and the server's disk has failed on a Thursday morning. The nightly jobs have separately begun overrunning their window near the end of each week, because every night re-copies all changes since Sunday; the administrator must shorten them and accepts that restores may take longer. When a midday incremental was added to the existing scheme, the nightly differentials were afterwards found to be missing files changed during the mornings.

profile.environment: Sunday full backups · nightly differentials overrunning · a midday incremental added
profile.state: Restore and window problems together

stimuli.title: Rehearsing a plan nobody has run
stimuli.text: Ashcombe Mutual has just finished writing its first disaster recovery plan for the transaction switch. Nothing in it has been validated and management will accept no disruption to production while confidence remains low. A flood exercise at another firm is being studied as a warning: every system was restored within its objective, yet the business stalled for days because the call center had no workspace, cash-in-transit contracts held no fallback instructions and nobody held authority to relocate staff. The mutual's own analysis concludes settlement can survive at most twenty-four hours of downtime.

profile.regime: State insurance regulation · board risk appetite
profile.environment: First disaster recovery plan written · nothing validated · flood exposure at head office
profile.state: Confidence low, no disruption acceptable

stimuli.title: An objective that does not fit inside the tolerance
stimuli.text: Ashcombe Mutual's analysis concludes that its settlement function can survive a maximum of twenty-four hours of downtime before regulatory penalties and unrecoverable losses begin. The information technology recovery proposal for the supporting systems specifies a thirty-six-hour recovery objective, because faster options exceed this year's budget, and the continuity coordinator must respond. The mutual is separately outsourcing overnight monitoring of its machine estate and wants the provider's response to outages to be enforceable with defined consequences. An earlier midday incremental broke the nightly differentials.

profile.environment: 24-hour maximum tolerable downtime · 36-hour recovery proposal · service level agreement being drafted
profile.state: Proposal awaiting the coordinator's response

stimuli.title: A command prompt on a machine in Toledo
stimuli.text: A branch has reported to Halloway Cash Systems that one of its machines displayed a command prompt for a few seconds during a maintenance visit. The fleet runs a standard build with anti-malware and a monthly patch cycle, each machine writes its own event log locally and keeps thirty days of it, and there is no rule about which programs may run. The maintenance technician says he ran a diagnostic tool he downloaded that morning. By the time an analyst called back the machine had been rebooted twice. A USB stick with an unknown executable was found in another machine's port.

profile.environment: Standard build with anti-malware · thirty days of local event log · no rule on which programs may run
profile.state: Machine rebooted twice before an analyst called back

stimuli.title: Evidence that will survive a challenge
stimuli.text: Prosecutors reviewing Halloway Cash Systems' skimming case are weighing four items of evidence for trial and must pick the one most likely to survive challenge. An incident responder has separately reached a compromised machine that is still running and believed to hold the attacker's injected code in memory, and management wants it analyzed with as little evidence lost as possible. The security operations center wants visibility into attacks against the transaction network, but the network team refuses any inline device that could delay or drop legitimate transactions. Egress rules were written years ago.

profile.environment: Skimming case heading to trial · memory-resident code on a running machine
profile.state: Prosecutors weighing four items of evidence

stimuli.title: Blocking what has no patch yet
stimuli.text: A critical vulnerability in Halloway Cash Systems' transaction switch is being actively exploited across the industry, the exploit's network signature is well documented, and the vendor's corrected patch is three weeks away. After an earlier patching disaster the change board insists any patch must first complete full staging tests. The internet-facing gateway is separately being flooded with packets whose source addresses belong to the company's own internal ranges, arriving from outside. Peer firms have been breached by a group whose tooling evades signature detection, with dwell times of months.

profile.environment: Exploit signature published, vendor patch three weeks away · spoofed internal addresses at the border
profile.state: Change board insisting on full staging tests

stimuli.title: Too many alerts, too few people
stimuli.text: Cranfield Bank's security operations center receives hundreds of phishing-report alerts each week, and for every one analysts manually extract the indicators, check them against threat intelligence, search mailboxes for related messages and quarantine the hits: identical steps every time, consuming most of each shift. Alert quality is good; the volume is the problem. A fraud investigation separately needed four days to assemble a timeline because each machine keeps logs locally with inconsistent clocks and nothing can search across them. An audit found maintenance laptops trusted unconditionally once on the internal network.

profile.environment: Hundreds of phishing reports weekly · machine logs local with inconsistent clocks · maintenance laptops trusted once inside
profile.state: Analysts consumed by identical manual steps

stimuli.title: Least privilege, and the people problem
stimuli.text: A fraud investigator at Cranfield Bank assigned to a case involving twelve customer accounts turns out to be able to read the records of every customer in the bank, and his database account also carries administrative rights he has never used. Internal audit separately warns that only one engineer understands the settlement reconciliation jobs and could conceal an ongoing fraud indefinitely because nobody else touches the process. A further audit finds four operations staff sharing one domain administrator password, using it for routine work such as email and browsing, unchanged for two years.

profile.environment: Investigator able to read every customer record · one engineer owns settlement reconciliation · four staff sharing a domain administrator password
profile.state: Audit findings requiring response

stimuli.title: A transformer fire at the valve works
stimuli.text: Kestrel Valve Works machines industrial valves at a single plant in Sandusky, Ohio, and books ninety percent of its revenue through one ERP order-entry system. A transformer fire on a Saturday night cuts plant power and fills the ground-floor server room with suppression foam. All 340 staff are out of the building and accounted for by 23:40. The disaster recovery plan names the chief operating officer as the sole declaring authority, sets a four-hour recovery time objective for order entry, and holds a warm site in Toledo loaded nightly from a 22:00 backup. By 01:15 the plant manager, the DR coordinator and the property insurance broker are all on a bridge call, each pressing a different next move.

profile.organization: Kestrel Valve Works · industrial valve manufacturing
profile.environment: single plant, warm site ninety miles away
profile.state: disaster in progress, plan not yet declared

stimuli.title: Forty engineers, a storm zone and a two in the morning approval
stimuli.text: Halcyon Grid Partners is a 600-person power-transmission engineering firm whose only office sits four blocks from Tampa Bay, inside a mandatory storm evacuation zone. Forty of its engineers are about to spend twelve weeks on a substation joint venture in a country carrying a Level 3 travel advisory, taking the firm's proprietary relay-protection drawings with them. In March a night-shift engineer approved an authentication push at 02:10 after eleven consecutive prompts, and an attacker held VPN access for six hours. The firm runs an annual security-awareness course with a 98 percent completion rate and a fire drill every October that nobody has ever timed, and its emergency action plan was last revised in 2019.

profile.regime: client NERC CIP obligations; OSHA emergency action plan rules
profile.environment: single Tampa office; forty engineers deploying overseas
profile.state: pre-deployment, hurricane season, one MFA compromise on record

stimuli.title: A results portal starts shipping archives at 02:14
stimuli.text: Larkfield Diagnostics is a clinical laboratory whose results portal serves 340 physician practices and holds records for 2.1 million patients. At 02:14 the on-call analyst is paged: the portal's database server has written 40 GB of compressed archives into a staging folder, and a service account created eleven days ago is authenticating to it from a hosting provider in Frankfurt. No directory owner is listed for that account, and no change ticket matches its creation. The portal is still answering physician queries normally. Larkfield has a written incident response plan, a HIPAA breach-notification obligation, one forensic workstation, a 90-day log retention window, and an unused retainer with an outside response firm.

profile.regime: HIPAA Security Rule and Breach Notification Rule
profile.environment: on-premises results portal, hosted database tier
profile.state: live incident, first four hours

stimuli.title: A departing quant and 1.4 GB of models
stimuli.text: Aldergate Asset Management runs quantitative equity funds and keeps its pricing models on a repository share readable by its whole 240-person technology division. A developer resigned on Tuesday to join a competitor and works her notice until month end. Data loss prevention flagged 1.4 GB copied from that share into a personal cloud sync folder on her issued laptop at 21:40 on Sunday. Her line manager has already logged into the laptop with his administrator account and browsed the folder. The laptop sits powered on and unlocked at her desk; its disk encryption key is escrowed in the directory. Legal expects to seek an injunction. Aldergate keeps one trained examiner and a write blocker.

profile.organization: Aldergate Asset Management · quantitative fund manager
profile.regime: civil trade-secret litigation; SEC books-and-records retention
profile.environment: on-premises repository share, Windows laptops, cloud sync clients
profile.state: internal insider investigation, subject still employed

questionsV2.question: Management asks which change would have stopped the technician's downloaded tool from running at all. Which control BEST meets that description?

options.A: Anti-malware configured to submit unknown executables to the vendor for analysis.
options.B: A policy forbidding technicians from downloading software to fleet machines.
options.C: Blocking the fleet's outbound web access to sites known to host hacking tools.
options.D: A deny-by-default policy admitting software the organization has explicitly authorized to execute.

questionsV2.explanation:
A diagnostic tool downloaded that morning is on nobody's list of known-bad software. Any control that starts from an enumeration of what is forbidden will miss it.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-7(5) Least Functionality | Authorized Software - Allow-by-Exception is the precise control (D). Identify the software authorized to execute, employ a deny-all permit-by-exception policy to allow it, and review and update the list on a defined frequency. Its sibling CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software - Deny-by-Exception runs the weaker direction, and the catalog says so by structure. Watch the vocabulary too: Rev 5 uses allow-list and deny-list where older material says whitelisting and blacklisting.
Enumerate what is allowed to run.
questionsV2.recallLine: What would have stopped an unapproved downloaded tool from executing on a fleet machine?

optionsShort.A: Submit unknown executables to the vendor
optionsShort.B: Policy forbidding downloads
optionsShort.C: Block known hacking-tool sites
optionsShort.D: Deny all, permit authorized software

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: Detective when preventive is asked, and it acts on an executable that is unknown by definition.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Aims a rule at a person. The stem asks for a condition enforced on the machine.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Deny-by-exception on the network can never hold a complete list, and the tool arrived on a technician's laptop.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7(5) Authorized Software - Allow-by-Exception
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software - Deny-by-Exception; CM-10 Software Usage Restrictions

questionsV2.question: The analyst finds that the Toledo machine's local log now begins after the second reboot. Which change would MOST improve the company's ability to investigate the next report?

options.A: Extending local log retention on every machine from thirty days to one year.
options.B: Forwarding events to a separate repository as they are written, with synchronized time.
options.C: Requiring technicians to file a written report after every maintenance visit.
options.D: Configuring anti-malware to write its detections into the machine's Windows event log.

questionsV2.explanation:
Two reboots were enough to erase the record, because the record lived only on the machine it described.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9(2) Protection of Audit Information | Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components requires audit records to be stored on a system or component physically different from the one being audited. That is the whole answer to this failure (B). Around it, AU-4 Audit Log Storage Capacity, AU-11 Audit Record Retention, and AU-8 Time Stamps with SC-45 System Time Synchronization make the collected records usable across 5,000 machines, and AU-6(3) Correlate Audit Record Repositories turns them into a timeline. NIST SP 800-92 is the dedicated log-management guide; the requirement above stands without it.
Get the record off the box.
questionsV2.recallLine: Local logs vanished when a machine rebooted. What most improves the next investigation?

optionsShort.A: Extend local retention to a year
optionsShort.B: Forward events to a separate repository
optionsShort.C: Written report after every visit
optionsShort.D: Anti-malware writes to the event log

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Treats the age of a record and leaves it where it can still be destroyed.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Gives an administrative account of a visit. Machine evidence is what the stem is missing.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Enriches one source on the same host that loses everything.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9(2) Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4; AU-8 Time Stamps; AU-11 Audit Record Retention; AU-6(3) Correlate Audit Record Repositories; SC-45 System Time Synchronization

questionsV2.question: Analysts confirm unauthorized code on four machines and cannot yet say how it arrived. Management wants the fleet protected today. Which action BEST fits mitigation at this point?

options.A: Reimaging the four machines from the standard build and returning them to service.
options.B: Opening a change request to add allow-listing across the fleet at the next window.
options.C: Isolating the four machines from the management network while the fleet stays monitored.
options.D: Notifying the card brands and the state regulator that a compromise has been confirmed.

questionsV2.explanation:
Isolation (C) is the only option here that stops the incident growing while the question of how it started is still open.
NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 places this in the Respond Function: RS.MI-01 covers containment, RS.MI-02 covers eradication. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 supplies the mechanism in IR-4 Incident Handling, IR-4(2) Dynamic Reconfiguration, and SC-7(20) Boundary Protection | Dynamic Isolation and Segregation. One structural note is worth carrying. Revision 2 of SP 800-61 grouped containment, eradication and recovery into a single phase and was withdrawn on 3 April 2025; Revision 3 puts containment and eradication under Respond, and recovery under Recover.
Contain first.
questionsV2.recallLine: Unauthorized code is confirmed on four machines and the entry point is unknown. What fits mitigation?

optionsShort.A: Reimage and return to service
optionsShort.B: Change request for fleet allow-listing
optionsShort.C: Isolate the four, keep monitoring
optionsShort.D: Notify card brands and regulator

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Jumps to eradication and recovery, erasing the evidence of the entry point.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: The durable fix, on a schedule the stem calls too slow. It comes after isolation.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: A reporting obligation under IR-6. It protects nothing today.

sources: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 | Section 3.2, Respond Function (RS.MI-01, RS.MI-02)
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IR-4 Incident Handling; IR-4(2) Dynamic Reconfiguration; SC-7(20) Dynamic Isolation and Segregation
NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 withdrawn 2025-04-03; the four-phase lifecycle is not restated in Rev 3

questionsV2.question: Three weeks later the incident is closed. Which outcome BEST shows that the lessons-learned step actually worked?

options.A: The software policy, the maintenance contract and the response playbook were each changed.
options.B: A report was circulated describing the timeline and the root cause in full detail.
options.C: The analysts who handled the incident briefed the wider team on what they had seen.
options.D: A follow-up meeting was scheduled once recovery of the four machines was complete.

questionsV2.explanation:
Only one option names artifacts that changed: the software policy, the maintenance contract and the response playbook were each revised (A). That is the test of a lessons-learned step. Something is different afterwards.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IR-4 Incident Handling states the obligation directly. Incorporate lessons learned from ongoing incident handling into response procedures, training and testing, then implement the resulting changes. IR-8 Incident Response Plan requires the plan itself to be reviewed and updated. NIST CSF 2.0 carries the same idea in ID.IM-01 through ID.IM-04: improvements are identified from evaluations, from tests and exercises, and from operational processes, then reflected in the plans. NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 adds a change of emphasis worth knowing. Share a lesson as soon as it is identified, without waiting for recovery to conclude.
Look for the diff.
questionsV2.recallLine: An incident closes. Which outcome shows the lessons-learned step actually worked?

optionsShort.A: Policy, contract and playbook all changed
optionsShort.B: Detailed timeline report circulated
optionsShort.C: Analysts briefed the wider team
optionsShort.D: Follow-up meeting scheduled after recovery

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Documents the incident. Nothing about the response changed.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Moves knowledge between people and stops short of changing a procedure.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Schedules a meeting, which is the habit Revision 3 argues against.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IR-4 Incident Handling; IR-8 Incident Response Plan
NIST CSF 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) | ID.IM-01 to ID.IM-04
NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 | Sections 1 and 3.1, lessons shared as identified

questionsV2.question: The tabletop found the plan readable. The operations director wants the next exercise to confirm that each named person can state their own steps. Which test type BEST fits?

options.A: A walkthrough in which each role reads and talks through its own procedures in sequence.
options.B: A simulation in which the team responds to an injected scenario under time pressure.
options.C: A parallel test bringing the alternate switch up beside production and comparing output.
options.D: A full interruption test failing production over to the alternate site and back.

questionsV2.explanation:
The ladder the exam tests runs read-through and tabletop, then walkthrough, then simulation, then parallel, then full interruption. Each rung adds one thing. A walkthrough is the rung where the plan stops being a document the team has read and becomes procedures individuals can state for their own role (A).
Be careful with the sourcing. This five-type ladder is CISSP-canon vocabulary, and NIST's taxonomy differs: NIST SP 800-84 uses training sessions, tabletop exercises, functional exercises and tests, while NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.5.3 defines a tabletop as discussion-based only, with no equipment deployed. The control obligation is NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing.
Climb one rung at a time.
questionsV2.recallLine: The plan reads well. Which test type confirms each named person can state their own steps?

optionsShort.A: Walkthrough of procedures by role
optionsShort.B: Simulation under time pressure
optionsShort.C: Parallel test beside production
optionsShort.D: Full interruption failover

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: The next rung up. It measures reaction under pressure, when the board asked whether people know the steps.

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Commits real recovery infrastructure to procedures nobody has yet performed.

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Off the table. The board has ruled out an outage of production.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing
NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 | Section 3.5.3 Exercises (tabletop is discussion-based only)
NIST SP 800-84 | Chapters 3 to 6 (NIST taxonomy differs from the CISSP five-type ladder)

questionsV2.question: The walkthrough passed. The director now wants to see whether the team decides correctly when facts arrive out of order and time is short, still without touching production. Which test type BEST fits?

options.A: A tabletop exercise, facilitated by an outside consultant against a new scenario.
options.B: A parallel test, with the alternate switch processing a copy of live traffic.
options.C: A simulation, with the team responding to injected events in a controlled environment.
options.D: A full interruption test, scheduled inside an approved maintenance window.

questionsV2.explanation:
The director wants to measure judgment under incomplete information. That is the rung a simulation occupies (C): the team performs its roles against events fed to it, in a controlled environment, with production never at risk.
NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.5.3 describes the nearest NIST equivalent, the functional exercise, as personnel validating operational readiness by performing their duties in a simulated operational environment. Remember that the five-type ladder is CISSP-canon. SP 800-84's categories are training sessions, tabletop exercises, functional exercises and tests, and only tabletop is common to both vocabularies. The control obligation sits in SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 with CP-4(1) Coordinate with Related Plans.
Match the rung to the question being asked.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which test type measures decision quality under pressure without putting production at risk?

optionsShort.A: Facilitated tabletop, new scenario
optionsShort.B: Parallel test on copied traffic
optionsShort.C: Simulation with injected events
optionsShort.D: Full interruption in a maintenance window

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: A rung already cleared. The team has discussed the plan and the walkthrough has passed.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Proves the alternate switch computes correctly. It says nothing about how well people decide.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: The top rung, and it depends on all the others passing first.

sources: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 | Section 3.5.3 Exercises (functional exercise definition)
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing; CP-4(1) Coordinate with Related Plans
NIST SP 800-84 | exercise taxonomy, distinct from the CISSP five-type ladder

questionsV2.question: The simulation stalls for fifty minutes because the only person who can authorize the failover is on a flight. Which change to the plan MOST directly addresses that?

options.A: Adding a second alternate site so the failover has more than one destination.
options.B: Naming a deputy for every plan role, with the authority each deputy may exercise.
options.C: Recording the exercise so the delay can be reviewed with the recovery team afterwards.
options.D: Moving the call tree from a printed sheet to an automated notification service.

questionsV2.explanation:
Eleven people across three time zones guarantees somebody is unreachable, and a recovery plan that waits on one named human has a single point of failure made of flesh. The fix is delegation recorded in advance: who stands in, and what they may decide (B).
NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 4.2.2 Notification Procedures requires the plan to document how recovery personnel are notified during business and non-business hours, and the plan structure that document specifies carries delegation of authority alongside the team rosters. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-2 Contingency Plan requires roles, responsibilities and contact information for key personnel, with CP-3 Contingency Training behind it.
Name the deputy before the flight.
questionsV2.recallLine: A recovery exercise stalls waiting for the one person who can authorize failover. What fixes it?

optionsShort.A: Add a second alternate site
optionsShort.B: Name deputies and their authority
optionsShort.C: Record the exercise for review
optionsShort.D: Automate the call tree

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Adds destinations for the failover. What failed was authority, not the supply of places to go.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Captures the delay for review afterwards and leaves the cause of it in place.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Makes the notification faster. It still reaches the same absent person.

sources: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 | Section 4.2.2 Notification Procedures; plan structure and delegation of authority
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CP-2 Contingency Plan; CP-3 Contingency Training

questionsV2.question: Both exercises are finished. Which follow-up BEST converts them into an improvement the next real outage would feel?

options.A: Filing the two exercise reports with the evidence pack for the annual examination.
options.B: Repeating the simulation next quarter to see whether the team's timings improve.
options.C: Briefing the board on the fifty-minute delay and the reasons that produced it.
options.D: Revising the plan's authority and notification steps, then retesting those steps.

questionsV2.explanation:
An exercise produced a finding, and a finding that does not change the plan is a cost with no return. Closing the loop means revising the authority and notification steps, then retesting the steps you changed (D).
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing requires the organization to review the contingency plan test results and initiate corrective actions if needed. CP-2 Contingency Plan requires the plan to be revised to address changes and problems encountered during implementation, execution or testing. NIST CSF 2.0 makes the same point from the framework side: ID.IM-02 identifies improvements from security tests and exercises, and ID.IM-04 requires the affected plans to be updated.
Change the plan, then test the change.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two exercises are done. Which follow-up turns them into an improvement the next outage would feel?

optionsShort.A: File reports in the examination pack
optionsShort.B: Repeat the simulation next quarter
optionsShort.C: Brief the board on the delay
optionsShort.D: Revise the plan, retest those steps

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Files evidence for the examiner. The plan reads exactly as it did before.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Retests before anything has been altered, so it measures the same plan twice.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Reports the delay upward and leaves the document as written.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing; CP-2 Contingency Plan
NIST CSF 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) | ID.IM-02, ID.IM-04

questionsV2.question: An analyst investigating a suspected insider at Global ATM Corp needs to establish which technician was physically at the Toledo machine on the night in question. The suspect is the administrator of the badge system, holds the account that exports its records, and has not yet been told that he is under investigation. Which step should the analyst take FIRST?

options.A: Interview the suspect's supervisor about the technician's assignment for that week.
options.B: Query the badge system directly for the day's entries and export them to a report.
options.C: Compare the badge records with the ATM's local event log on the machine itself.
options.D: Preserve the badge records from a source beyond the suspect's reach, then compare.

questionsV2.explanation:
The suspect administers the system that holds the evidence, so custody is the first problem, ahead of every other (D).
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9 Protection of Audit Information requires audit information and tooling to be protected from unauthorized access, modification and deletion. Its enhancements say how: AU-9(2) Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components, and AU-9(4) Access by Subset of Privileged Users, which limits management of audit functionality to a defined subset of privileged users. Those controls exist so that the administrator of a system is never the custodian of the record about them. IR-4(12) Incident Handling | Malicious Code and Forensic Analysis covers the analysis that follows, and NIST SP 800-86 is the guide to forensic technique itself.
Secure the record before you read it.
questionsV2.recallLine: The suspect administers the system holding the evidence. What should the analyst do first?

optionsShort.A: Interview the supervisor
optionsShort.B: Query and export the badge records
optionsShort.C: Compare against the ATM's local log
optionsShort.D: Preserve from a source beyond his reach

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Belongs in the investigation, later. It protects nothing about an alterable record.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Produces an answer from a system the suspect controls, so the answer cannot be defended later.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Correlates before preserving, and touches the live machine to do it.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 Protection of Audit Information; AU-9(2); AU-9(4) Access by Subset of Privileged Users
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IR-4(12) Malicious Code and Forensic Analysis
NIST SP 800-86 named as the dedicated forensic-technique source

questionsV2.question: Global ATM Corp's cash-replenishment crews work alone at night, opening safes at unattended machines in retail car parks. After a crew member was followed and threatened at a site last month, the safety committee has asked for a way for someone under coercion to summon help without the coercer noticing anything unusual. Which measure BEST meets that requirement?

options.A: A distinct code that opens the safe normally and silently raises an alarm at dispatch.
options.B: A panic button in the service vehicle that the crew member presses before approaching.
options.C: A check-in call to dispatch on arrival at each site, logged with the arrival time.
options.D: A requirement that two crew members be present for every replenishment visit.

questionsV2.explanation:
The requirement has two halves, and most controls satisfy one. The signal has to reach help, and the coerced person has to appear to be complying. A duress code does both (A): the safe opens exactly as it would on a normal visit, while dispatch receives an alert nobody at the machine can see.
Sourcing matters here and is worth stating plainly. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 contains no duress control and no travel-security control. The single occurrence of the word duress in the catalog sits in the discussion of AC-2(6) Dynamic Privilege Management, about privileges under emergency conditions, and it is not a control. The nearest catalog neighbors are PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access and IR-6 Incident Reporting. The substantive requirement belongs to physical security and safety of life.
A duress signal has to look like compliance.
questionsV2.recallLine: A lone worker under coercion must summon help without the coercer noticing. What meets that?

optionsShort.A: Duress code opens safe, alerts silently
optionsShort.B: Panic button in the vehicle
optionsShort.C: Logged arrival check-in call
optionsShort.D: Two-person replenishment crews

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Puts the signal in the vehicle. Coercion usually begins at the machine.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Detective when preventive is asked, and a coercer can stand beside the call.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Reduces the chance of an approach. It supplies no signal once one happens.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | verified absence of any duress control; the single 'duress' occurrence is in the AC-2(6) discussion
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access; IR-6 Incident Reporting (nearest neighbors)

questionsV2.question: Which change to the deployment process would MOST reduce the impact of a future patch that conflicts with fleet hardware?

options.A: Schedule fleet deployments for the overnight low-transaction window with support staff on standby.
options.B: Obtain written vendor certification of compatibility for each patch before it is approved.
options.C: Release each patch to a small canary group, then a pilot ring, then the wider fleet.
options.D: Prepare a scripted, tested uninstall routine that can be triggered remotely after deployment.

questionsV2.explanation:
No amount of pre-release checking rules out a conflict with hardware the test lab does not contain. So the winning control limits how many machines a bad patch can reach: a canary group, then a pilot ring, then the fleet (C). Damage caps at the first ring whatever the cause.
Limit exposure first; prediction and rollback are supplements.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which change to Global ATM Corp's patch deployment process would MOST reduce the impact of a future patch that conflicts with dispenser hardware?

optionsShort.A: Deploy overnight with support staff standing by
optionsShort.B: Require written vendor compatibility certification first
optionsShort.C: Canary group, then pilot ring, then fleet
optionsShort.D: Prepare a remotely triggered uninstall script

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Changes the variable of timing. An overnight window changes when 4,000 machines crash.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: The assurance that already failed here. Certification runs against a reference build, not every hardware variant.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Worth having, and it needs a staged deployment to work. A fleet-wide failure saturates the network and blocks it.

questionsV2.question: How should the registry fix be handled given the board's schedule?

options.A: Process it as an emergency change with expedited approval and a full CCB review afterward.
options.B: Hold the fix until the next scheduled CCB meeting so the standard process is followed.
options.C: Let the engineer deploy it immediately, since incident response takes precedence over change control.
options.D: Have the operations director approve it verbally and skip the change record to save time.

questionsV2.explanation:
The emergency-change path reconciles governance with speed (A). An authorized approver acts now, the change still carries documentation and a backout plan, and the full board reviews it retrospectively. Only the timing of accountability moves.
Emergency changes move the timing of review. They never remove it.
questionsV2.recallLine: The change board meets in three days and a registry fix would end the ATM reboot loop now. How should the fix be handled?

optionsShort.A: Emergency change now, full board review afterward
optionsShort.B: Wait for the next scheduled board meeting
optionsShort.C: Let the engineer deploy it immediately
optionsShort.D: Verbal approval, no change record

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Treats the meeting calendar as the point of change control. Days of downtime to honor a schedule inverts its purpose.

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Assumes incident response suspends change governance. An unreviewed fix pushed fleet-wide repeats the failure.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Removes the backout review and the audit trail. Afterward nobody can say what changed or how to reverse it.

questionsV2.question: When the report classifies the security impact of the outage, which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.A: Integrity was the primary impact, because the patch modified system files on every machine.
options.B: Confidentiality was the primary impact, because cardholder data resided on the crashed ATMs.
options.C: Non-repudiation was the primary impact, because interrupted sessions could no longer be attributed.
options.D: Availability was the primary impact, because authorized customers were denied use of the service.

questionsV2.explanation:
Authorized customers were denied a legitimate service. That is the definition of an availability impact, so the correct classification is an availability impact (D). A faulty patch applied through an approved process is not an integrity compromise, however costly the day was. Each property in the set is decided by what actually happened to the data and the service.
Classify impact by what the business lost.
questionsV2.recallLine: The patch outage left 5,000 ATMs unusable for eighteen hours. Which classification of the incident's security impact is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Integrity, because the patch modified system files
optionsShort.B: Confidentiality, because cardholder data resided there
optionsShort.C: Non-repudiation, because interrupted sessions lost attribution
optionsShort.D: Availability, because authorized customers were denied service

A.label: true of a different thing
A.wouldAnswer: Integrity concerns unauthorized or incorrect modification of data, and the investigation confirmed no records were altered.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Confidentiality breaks only on disclosure to unauthorized parties. Data on a crashed machine has not been disclosed.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Non-repudiation concerns a party denying an action they performed. No completed transaction was in dispute.

questionsV2.question: Service was restored eighteen hours in. Which conclusion about recovery performance is MOST accurate?

options.A: The recovery breached the RTO but remained inside the maximum tolerable downtime.
options.B: The recovery met its objectives because service returned before the 24-hour limit.
options.C: The recovery breached the MTD because restoration took longer than four hours.
options.D: The RPO was breached because 18 hours of transaction data was lost in the outage.

questionsV2.explanation:
Two clocks were running. The 4-hour RTO, the committed recovery objective, was missed by 14 hours; the 24-hour MTD, the survival threshold, was never crossed. Only one option states both facts (A).
Keep the recovery metrics distinct. RTO is the promise, MTD is the outer tolerance, RPO is about data.
questionsV2.recallLine: The fleet's RTO is four hours and its MTD twenty-four; service returned after eighteen. Which conclusion about recovery performance is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Breached the RTO, stayed inside the MTD
optionsShort.B: Objectives met; service returned before 24 hours
optionsShort.C: Breached the MTD by exceeding four hours
optionsShort.D: RPO breached; eighteen hours of data lost

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Reads the intact MTD as success. The RTO is the objective, and it was breached by fourteen hours.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Swaps the two terms. Four hours is the RTO, and the 24-hour MTD held.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: RPO measures acceptable data loss. Machines that are down serve nobody while losing no committed data.

questionsV2.question: Which submission should the board accept as a valid backout plan?

options.A: Restore every affected ATM from the previous month's full system backup if problems appear.
options.B: An uninstall script validated in the staging environment, with defined criteria for when to invoke it.
options.C: Keep the firmware vendor's support line on standby to advise the team if the change fails.
options.D: Re-image affected machines on site as technicians can be dispatched to each location.

questionsV2.explanation:
A backout plan is judged on two things: whether it returns systems to a known-good state quickly, and whether that has been demonstrated. Only the validated uninstall script was exercised in staging and defines the conditions that trigger it (B).
Untested recovery is hope.
questionsV2.recallLine: The change board is judging four backout plans filed with a dispenser firmware change. Which submission should it accept as a valid backout plan?

optionsShort.A: Restore from last month's full system backup
optionsShort.B: Staging-validated uninstall script with defined trigger criteria
optionsShort.C: Vendor support line on standby for advice
optionsShort.D: Dispatch technicians to re-image machines on site

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Rolls every machine back past weeks of legitimate changes, on backups never rehearsed at fleet scale.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Offers advice. Nothing in a support line returns the fleet to its prior state.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Concedes the outage. Dispatching technicians to every site is the worst case this incident demonstrated.

questionsV2.question: Which process would BEST bring the inconsistent fleet back under control?

options.A: Monthly vulnerability scans of the fleet, with findings routed to the operations work queue.
options.B: Change control approval requirements for any future technician modification to an ATM.
options.C: Patch management, with security updates deployed automatically across the fleet.
options.D: Configuration management, with an approved baseline and automated detection of drift from it.

questionsV2.explanation:
The audit found no defined desired state. Without one, nobody can even say which machines are wrong. Configuration management supplies the missing piece (D): an approved, documented baseline for the fleet, plus continuous comparison that surfaces any machine drifting from it, whoever caused the drift.
First define correct, then detect departure from it. That is configuration management.
questionsV2.recallLine: A fleet audit found ATMs with mismatched settings and no record of the intended build. Which process would BEST bring them back under control?

optionsShort.A: Monthly vulnerability scans routed to operations
optionsShort.B: Change control approval for future technician modifications
optionsShort.C: Patch management deploying updates automatically fleet-wide
optionsShort.D: Approved baseline with automated drift detection

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Reports known weaknesses. A re-enabled service that carries no CVE passes the scan and still breaks the build.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Governs future modifications, and only the honest ones. Without a baseline there is nothing to approve against.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Treats patch level as the whole of configuration. A fully patched machine running the wrong services is still out of control.

questionsV2.question: Which control principle, applied to the change process, would BEST prevent a recurrence of one person requesting, approving and executing?

options.A: Least privilege, narrowing the engineer's deployment rights down to the test collection.
options.B: Job rotation, assigning a different engineer to handle each month's deployments.
options.C: Defense in depth, layering compensating technical controls around the deployment tooling.
options.D: Separation of duties, so no one person can request, approve, and execute a change.

questionsV2.explanation:
One person held every role in the change, so no independent judgment ever examined the deployment plan before it ran. Separation of duties breaks that structure (D). Requester, approver and executor become different people, and a reckless full-fleet push has to convince someone with no stake in the request.
Concentrated roles call for separation.
questionsV2.recallLine: One engineer wrote, approved and ran his own deployment change request. Which control principle applied to the change process would BEST prevent a recurrence?

optionsShort.A: Least privilege limiting deployment rights to test
optionsShort.B: Job rotation across each month's deployments
optionsShort.C: Defense in depth around deployment tooling
optionsShort.D: Separation of duties across request, approval, execution

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Relocates the concentration. Somebody must hold production deployment rights, so the problem moves to whoever does.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Rotates who holds the conflict and leaves the conflict intact. The engineer can still request, approve and execute.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: An architecture strategy. Layered tooling around an unreviewed decision still deploys the unreviewed decision.

questionsV2.question: A rollback failed because crashing machines saturated the management network. Which safeguard would BEST ensure a rollback can succeed?

options.A: Requiring the CCB to record a named rollback owner for every change it approves.
options.B: A dedicated out-of-band management channel with reserved capacity for recovery commands.
options.C: Compressing rollback packages so they consume less bandwidth on the shared network.
options.D: Scheduling an automatic fleet-wide reboot to clear the check-in storm before rollback.

questionsV2.explanation:
The rollback failed for one reason: the recovery path shared the network the failure had already destroyed. Four thousand machines rebooting and checking in saturated the link. A management channel that is physically or logically separate, with capacity reserved for command traffic, keeps working while the production network drowns (B). That is the condition leadership told the team to plan for.
A recovery mechanism has to survive the failure it exists to fix.
questionsV2.recallLine: The fleet rollback failed because rebooting ATMs saturated the management network. Which safeguard would BEST ensure the next rollback reaches the machines?

optionsShort.A: CCB records a named rollback owner
optionsShort.B: Out-of-band channel with reserved recovery capacity
optionsShort.C: Compress rollback packages to save bandwidth
optionsShort.D: Fleet-wide reboot to clear the check-in storm

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: A governance improvement. A named owner issuing commands into a saturated network fails identically.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Misidentifies the bottleneck. Shaving kilobytes off one command does not clear a saturated link.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Prescribes more of the disease. A simultaneous fleet-wide reboot re-creates the storm that blocked the rollback.

questionsV2.question: Which statement about the recovery test result is MOST accurate?

options.A: The test failed the RTO, because six hours elapsed before the business resumed processing.
options.B: The test exceeded the MTD, because validation doubled the time the systems were unusable.
options.C: The test breached the RPO, because three hours of transactions required reconciliation.
options.D: The test met the RTO, and reconciliation consumed work recovery time inside the MTD.

questionsV2.explanation:
Restoring the system took three hours, inside the 4-hour RTO. The further three hours of validation is work recovery time, and the six-hour total interruption sits within the 8-hour MTD. The test met its RTO, and reconciliation consumed work recovery time inside the MTD (D).
Carry the frame into any BCP question: RTO plus WRT must fit inside the MTD. In this test both did their job.
questionsV2.recallLine: Trentham's switch was working three hours into the test and reconciliation took three more, against a four-hour RTO and eight-hour MTD. Which statement is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Failed the RTO; six hours before processing
optionsShort.B: Exceeded the MTD; validation doubled the outage
optionsShort.C: Breached the RPO; three hours needed reconciliation
optionsShort.D: Met the RTO; work recovery inside MTD

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Folds work recovery time into the RTO. The RTO governs restoring the system; verification that follows is measured separately.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Overstates the damage. The MTD caps total business interruption, and only six of the eight tolerable hours elapsed.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Misreads the RPO, which concerns data lost before recovery. Reconciling restored transactions verifies data that survived.

questionsV2.question: Which data-protection design is MOST appropriate for the fifteen-minute requirement?

options.A: Nightly full backups shipped to the recovery site, with weekly restore verification.
options.B: Synchronous replication in which both sites commit every transaction together.
options.C: Transaction-log shipping to the recovery site every ten minutes.
options.D: Hourly incremental backups retained on site and copied to the recovery site.

questionsV2.explanation:
A 15-minute recovery point objective bounds acceptable data loss at 15 minutes of committed transactions. Shipping transaction logs every ten minutes meets that bound with margin, at modest cost (C).
Match the control to the stated objective. Undershoot the RPO and you lose data the business said it cannot lose; overshoot it and you spend money the business said it will not spend.
questionsV2.recallLine: Trentham's switch database may lose at most fifteen minutes of committed transactions, without overspending. Which data-protection design is MOST appropriate?

optionsShort.A: Nightly full backups shipped off site
optionsShort.B: Synchronous replication committing at both sites
optionsShort.C: Transaction-log shipping every ten minutes
optionsShort.D: Hourly incrementals copied to the recovery site

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Exposes up to a full day of transactions, a recovery point roughly a hundred times looser than the requirement.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Delivers a near-zero RPO nobody asked for, charging dedicated bandwidth and write latency the cost constraint rules out.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Still permits four times the tolerated loss of committed transactions.

questionsV2.question: Which metric is MOST appropriate for comparing the reliability of two hardware models over a year?

options.A: Mean time to repair, showing how quickly technicians restore a failed dispenser.
options.B: Mean time between failures, showing how long each model runs before it fails.
options.C: Recovery time objective, showing the downtime the business tolerates per failure.
options.D: Availability percentage, showing the fraction of time each fleet segment was in service.

questionsV2.explanation:
Reliability is the property of running without failing, and mean time between failures is the metric built to express it. Tracked per dispenser model, it answers directly which hardware fails more often (B).
Pick the metric that isolates the property under comparison.
questionsV2.recallLine: Operations wants to compare two dispenser models' reliability over the coming year. Which metric is MOST appropriate for that comparison?

optionsShort.A: Mean time to repair a failed dispenser
optionsShort.B: Mean time between failures per model
optionsShort.C: Recovery time objective for the fleet
optionsShort.D: Availability percentage per fleet segment

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Measures maintainability, not reliability. A model could fail weekly and still post an excellent MTTR.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: A planning target. The recovery time objective says nothing about how the hardware actually behaves.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Blends failure frequency with repair speed, so a fragile model and a robust one can score the same.

questionsV2.question: A service carries a thirty-minute objective, a near-zero data-loss tolerance and two million dollars an hour offline. Which recovery strategy is MOST appropriate despite its cost?

options.A: A warm site with servers installed, restored from the previous night's backups at activation.
options.B: A cold site with power, cooling, and connectivity, with equipment shipped in after declaration.
options.C: A reciprocal agreement with a partner processor to share capacity during a disaster.
options.D: A hot site running synchronized systems, ready to take over processing within minutes.

questionsV2.explanation:
The BIA numbers dictate the strategy. Only a facility already running, with data already synchronized, resumes processing inside 30 minutes at near-zero data loss (D), and a downtime cost of two million dollars an hour is what justifies paying for it.
The RTO and RPO choose the recovery strategy.
questionsV2.recallLine: A payment service carries a thirty-minute recovery objective, near-zero data-loss tolerance and two million dollars an hour offline. Which recovery strategy is MOST appropriate?

optionsShort.A: Warm site restored from last night's backups
optionsShort.B: Cold site with equipment shipped after declaration
optionsShort.C: Reciprocal agreement sharing a partner's capacity
optionsShort.D: Hot site synchronized and ready within minutes

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Misses both objectives. A warm site takes hours to days, and last night's backups forfeit a day of authorizations.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Weeks-scale recovery. Procuring and building equipment after declaration is the opposite end of the spectrum.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: The partner's spare capacity, software versions and compliance posture are outside the processor's control.

questionsV2.question: What should the security manager advise about the mirror and the backups?

options.A: Keep the mirror and drop the backups, because two synchronized copies cover both risks.
options.B: Adopt the mirror for disk-failure tolerance and keep backups for deletion and corruption.
options.C: Retire the backups once the mirror has run reliably through one full patch cycle.
options.D: Skip the mirror and shorten the backup interval, since backups cover disk failure too.

questionsV2.explanation:
The two failures in the stem have different mechanisms and need different controls. Mirroring keeps the server running through a disk failure; it also copies an operator's deletion to both disks in the same instant, so backups are the only route back to deleted or corrupted history. Keeping the mirror for disk failure and the backups for deletion retains both protections (B).
RAID buys availability; backups buy recoverability. Each covers the loss the other cannot.
questionsV2.recallLine: An administrator proposes mirrored disks and asks whether nightly backups can be retired, though an operator once deleted a week of alert history. What should the manager advise?

optionsShort.A: Keep the mirror, drop the backups
optionsShort.B: Mirror for disk failure, backups for deletion
optionsShort.C: Retire backups after one reliable patch cycle
optionsShort.D: Skip mirroring; shorten the backup interval

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Relies on the mirror alone. Synchronization is exactly why it cannot help: the deletion reaches every copy at once.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Reasons from hardware reliability. Months of flawless mirroring says nothing about deletion, which is human error.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Accepts hours of downtime. Recovering a disk failure by restore leaves the availability failure unsolved.

questionsV2.question: Which configuration BEST meets the single-drive-failure requirement while keeping capacity?

options.A: RAID 5 across the four disks, striping data with distributed parity.
options.B: RAID 1 on one mirrored pair, keeping the other two disks as hot spares.
options.C: RAID 0 across the four disks, striping data for the fastest throughput.
options.D: RAID 10, striping data across two mirrored pairs of disks.

questionsV2.explanation:
With four disks, striping with distributed parity survives any single-drive failure and leaves three disks of usable capacity. That is the best ratio of any fault-tolerant option offered (A).
When two options both satisfy the fault-tolerance requirement, the stem's capacity constraint is the tiebreaker.
questionsV2.recallLine: A log-collection server has four drive bays and must survive any single drive failure with as much usable capacity as possible. Which RAID configuration is BEST?

optionsShort.A: RAID 5 striping with distributed parity
optionsShort.B: RAID 1 pair plus two hot spares
optionsShort.C: RAID 0 striping for maximum throughput
optionsShort.D: RAID 10 across two mirrored pairs

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Yields a single disk of usable space, spending most of the capacity on standby redundancy nobody asked for.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: No redundancy at all. One failed drive destroys the entire set, so it fails the core requirement outright.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: RAID 10 survives a single drive failure too, and returns only two disks of usable space.

questionsV2.question: Which recovery strategy is MOST appropriate for the archived-records system?

options.A: A hot site keeping a synchronized replica of the records system continuously available.
options.B: A warm site with standby servers that can be restored within a day or two.
options.C: A cold site providing space, power, and connectivity, with hardware procured at declaration.
options.D: A mobile recovery trailer contracted for delivery to the site within 48 hours.

questionsV2.explanation:
Two weeks of tolerated downtime, and daily off-site backups already covering the 24-hour RPO. The cheapest strategy that can rebuild the system inside a fortnight wins, and a cold site's procure-and-build timeline fits comfortably inside that window at a fraction of any alternative's cost (C).
Overshooting an RTO takes budget from systems that need it more.
questionsV2.recallLine: An archived-records system used a few times a month carries a two-week recovery objective on a tight budget. Which recovery strategy is MOST appropriate?

optionsShort.A: Hot site with a continuously synchronized replica
optionsShort.B: Warm site restoring standby servers within days
optionsShort.C: Cold site with hardware procured at declaration
optionsShort.D: Mobile recovery trailer delivered within 48 hours

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Buys minutes of recovery for a system the business can live without for fourteen days.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: The same premium at smaller scale. Standby servers recovering in a day answer a requirement nobody set.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Contracts a 48-hour delivery guarantee this system does not need. Mobile facilities suit recovery at your own premises.

questionsV2.question: Each returned machine holds a self-encrypting drive with cardholder data and must go back working. Which sanitization approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Degauss each drive to magnetically scramble the recorded data before the machines ship.
options.B: Shred the drives and fit replacement blanks into every machine before returning them.
options.C: Perform a cryptographic erase, destroying each drive's media encryption keys and verifying the result.
options.D: Run a quick format on each drive so the file system no longer references the stored data.

questionsV2.explanation:
For self-encrypting drives, SP 800-88 recognizes cryptographic erase as a purge technique. Destroying the media encryption keys renders the ciphertext permanently unreadable in seconds, and the drive keeps working, which satisfies both the data risk and the lease at once (C).
Choose the 800-88 method that matches the media type and what happens to the media next.
questionsV2.recallLine: Leased ATMs must be returned in working order, each holding a self-encrypting drive with cardholder data. Which sanitization approach is MOST appropriate?

optionsShort.A: Degauss each drive before the machines ship
optionsShort.B: Shred the drives and fit replacement blanks
optionsShort.C: Cryptographic erase destroying the media encryption keys
optionsShort.D: Quick format the drive's file system

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Degaussing leaves flash-based media readable, and on drives it does affect it destroys the working-order term.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Does sanitize, and it destroys 200 functional drives to solve a problem cryptographic erase solves for nothing.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Clears pointers and leaves the content. Trivial recovery tools read formatted data back.

questionsV2.question: Which restore approach returns the server to its most recent recoverable state with the fewest operations?

options.A: Sunday's full backup followed by Monday's, Tuesday's, and Wednesday's differentials in order.
options.B: Wednesday night's differential alone, since it holds the newest copy of the data.
options.C: Restore Sunday's full backup, then apply Wednesday night's differential on top of it.
options.D: Wednesday's differential first, then Sunday's full backup to fill in the older files.

questionsV2.explanation:
