Option B is wrong because blacklist-style stripping chases an open-ended set of bypasses and can break legitimate input (O'Brien); validation is worthwhile defense in depth, not the cure. Option D is wrong because the application must decrypt data to serve queries, so data stolen through the application arrives in plaintext; encryption at rest answers stolen-media risk, a different problem.

questions.question: Customers of a web forum report that simply viewing a certain product review causes their browsers to send their session cookies to an unknown domain. Investigators find script tags stored in the review text, which the page renders verbatim for every visitor. Which remediation most directly addresses this vulnerability?

options.A: Add anti-forgery tokens to every state-changing form so requests from other sites are rejected
options.B: Move all pages to HTTPS so session cookies are protected from network eavesdropping
options.C: Use parameterized queries so review text cannot alter the structure of database commands
options.D: Encode user-supplied content on output so browsers render it as text and not script

questions.explanation: This is stored cross-site scripting: attacker-supplied markup was saved and later delivered into victims' pages, where the browser executed it. The defect is at the rendering step, so the direct fix is contextual output encoding (D): the stored text is displayed as inert characters, never parsed as script; a Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add depth. Option A is wrong because anti-forgery tokens counter CSRF, where an attacker forges requests using the victim's session; here the attacker injected script, a different mechanism. Option B is wrong because TLS protects cookies in transit; these cookies are being read and exfiltrated by script running inside the page itself, over any transport. Option C is wrong because parameterized queries stop SQL injection; the review was stored through a legitimate write, and the database behaved correctly throughout.

questions.question: A bank customer, while logged in to online banking in one tab, opens an email link in another. A transfer the customer never initiated is immediately sent, and server logs show the request arrived from the customer's own browser carrying a valid session cookie. Which control would most effectively prevent this class of attack?

options.A: Require multi-factor authentication when the customer first signs in to the banking site
options.B: Embed unpredictable per-session tokens in forms and reject requests that lack a valid one
options.C: Encode all user-supplied content the application displays to keep scripts from executing
options.D: Lock accounts after repeated failed logins to defeat automated password guessing

questions.explanation: What happened is cross-site request forgery: the attacker's page made the victim's browser submit a request, and the browser helpfully attached the session cookie, so the server saw an authenticated transfer. An anti-CSRF token (B) defeats it because the forging site cannot read the unpredictable token to include it, so the forged request fails validation; SameSite cookie attributes reinforce the same boundary. A protects the wrong moment: MFA strengthens the login event, and this attack rides a session that is already authenticated. MFA at sign-in is the right answer to stolen credentials, and step-up MFA per transfer would be a separate, additional control. Option C is wrong because output encoding counters XSS; no script was injected into the bank's pages here. Option D is wrong because there were no failed logins; the attacker never touched credentials.

questions.question: A crash dump from a C-based payment service shows that an oversized message-length field in a client packet overwrote the function's return address, after which the service executed attacker-supplied instructions. The team must correct the defect in the code itself. Which change best addresses the root cause?

options.A: Validate length fields and use bounds-checked memory operations for every buffer write
options.B: Enable address space layout randomization so injected code lands at unpredictable locations
options.C: Filter inbound packets at the network firewall to drop traffic from untrusted address ranges
options.D: Raise the service's logging level so malformed packets are recorded for later investigation

questions.explanation: A buffer overflow happens when code writes more data into a buffer than was allocated, corrupting adjacent memory, in this case the saved return address. The root cause is the unchecked write, so the fix is in the code: validate untrusted length fields and use bounds-checked operations so an oversized value can no longer spill past the buffer (A); migrating hot paths to a memory-safe language is the same idea taken further. Option B is wrong as the answer here because ASLR is an exploit mitigation: it makes a successful overflow harder to weaponize but leaves the memory-corruption defect in place; it is the right answer for hardening a platform in depth. C fails because the service must accept client packets to function, and any permitted source can send the malformed field; that is scope, not cause. Option D is wrong because logging is detective; it records the compromise without preventing it. Mitigations raise attacker cost, but only correct code removes the vulnerability.

questions.question: A newly hired application security lead must choose a starting point for developer training and secure-coding standards at a company that has no existing program and a small budget. How should the lead best use the OWASP Top 10 in this effort?

options.A: Adopt it as the complete set of security requirements the finished application must satisfy
options.B: Treat it as a substitute for penetration testing, since it already lists the likely findings
options.C: Use it as an awareness baseline that focuses training on the most common web risk categories
options.D: Apply it as a hardening checklist for the servers that will host the company's applications

questions.explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document: a consensus ranking of the most prevalent categories of web application risk. That makes it an ideal seed for a first training curriculum and coding standard: maximum coverage of common failure classes for minimal budget (C). Option A is wrong because OWASP itself warns the Top 10 is a starting point, not a complete requirements set; when the lead needs verification-grade requirements, the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) is the right artifact. Option B is wrong because a list of risk categories cannot examine an actual implementation; testing finds the specific instances a list can only name. Option D is wrong because the Top 10 addresses application-layer risks; server hardening belongs to configuration baselines such as CIS Benchmarks.

questions.question: A document portal serves files through /download?file=report.pdf. An auditor demonstrates that requesting file=..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd returns the server's password file. The developers must correct the flaw in the application itself. Which fix is most effective?

options.A: Reject any filename containing the ../ character sequence before it reaches the file system call
options.B: Canonicalize each requested path and serve it only if it resolves inside the approved directory
options.C: Run the web server behind a reverse proxy that hides internal directory names from clients
options.D: Require users to authenticate before the download endpoint will serve them any file

questions.explanation: This is a path traversal flaw, and the durable fix is to resolve the requested path to its canonical form and then check it against an allow-list boundary (B): whatever encoding or nesting the attacker uses, the final resolved path either falls inside the approved directory or is refused. Option A is wrong because it is a blacklist: the auditor's own request already used %2F encoding, and variants such as double encoding, ....//, or absolute paths slip past literal matching; filtering one bad pattern treats the symptom while the resolution logic stays broken. Option C is wrong because hiding directory names is obscurity; the operating system still resolves the traversal sequence regardless of what the client can see. Option D is wrong because authentication changes who can exploit the flaw, not whether it exists; any logged-in user could still walk out of the web root. Validate the destination the path resolves to, never the characters it contains.

questions.question: A payment form accepts a destination-account field that feeds several downstream systems. The team maintains an ever-growing filter of known malicious strings, yet bypasses keep appearing after each release. Which validation strategy would most durably reduce this input risk?

options.A: Expand the filter with new attack strings as each bypass technique is discovered in the wild
options.B: Move the existing filter into client-side JavaScript so bad input is caught before submission
options.C: Normalize input to lowercase before matching it against the list of known malicious patterns
options.D: Accept only input matching the defined format for account numbers and reject everything else

questions.explanation: Valid account numbers form a small, precisely definable set, while the space of malicious strings is unbounded, so define the former and reject everything else. Allow-list validation (D) is durable because a brand-new attack technique still fails the format check; nobody has to anticipate it. A merely continues the losing race the stem describes: a blacklist is always one bypass behind, by construction. Option B is wrong because client-side checks improve user experience but provide no security: an attacker posts directly to the server, skipping the JavaScript entirely; validation must be enforced server-side. Option C is wrong because normalization only tightens the matching of a blacklist that remains reactive at its core; it hardens the wrong model.

questions.question: An administrator investigating a server sees connections in firewall logs that no local tool reports; process listings, file searches, and the installed antivirus all show nothing unusual. The team suspects kernel-level malware is concealing its presence. What is the most reliable way to restore trust in this system?

options.A: Rebuild the system from known-good installation media and restore data from clean backups
options.B: Run a full scan with the installed antivirus using its most aggressive detection settings
options.C: Delete the executables owning the suspicious connections and then reboot the server
options.D: Patch the operating system to the current level so the malware can no longer operate

questions.explanation: A rootkit subverts the operating system itself, so every answer that system gives, from process lists to scan results, is suspect; the firewall seeing traffic the host denies is the classic symptom. Once the kernel is untrusted, the only way to re-establish a trusted computing base is to rebuild from media you trust and restore data verified clean (A). Option B is wrong because the antivirus runs on, and asks questions of, the compromised OS; the rootkit filters what it is allowed to see; aggressive settings do not fix a lying oracle. Option B is reasonable when the suspected malware is ordinary user-mode code. Option C is wrong twice over: the hiding means you cannot reliably find the owning executables, and deleting visible components leaves whatever the kernel implant protects. Option D is wrong because patching closes entry vectors for the future; it does not evict malware already resident below the tools that would remove it.

questions.question: A company's antivirus quarantines one variant of a malware family, yet new infections keep appearing; each captured sample has a different hash and byte pattern although its behavior on the host is identical every time. Which detection approach is best suited to this threat?

options.A: Distribute the newest signature databases to every endpoint several times per day
options.B: Block executable email attachments at the gateway so samples cannot reach users
options.C: Deploy behavior-based monitoring that flags the malware's actions and not its code
options.D: Compare file hashes on each host against the list of previously quarantined samples

questions.explanation: Identical behavior with a different hash every generation is the fingerprint of polymorphic malware: it re-encrypts or mutates its code on each infection, so static patterns never stabilize. What it cannot cheaply change is what it does: the files it touches, the persistence it sets, the traffic it sends. That is why behavior-based or heuristic detection (C) catches the family that signatures keep missing. Option A is wrong because faster signature delivery still loses the race: each new variant is born unsigned; frequency does not fix a model keyed to bytes that keep changing. Option B is wrong in scope; it narrows one delivery vector while the family may arrive by web, removable media, or lateral movement, and it still detects nothing. Option D is wrong because hash comparison is the most brittle signature of all: a single changed byte produces a new hash, which is precisely the property the malware exploits. When the code mutates, anchor detection to the behavior that stays constant.

questions.question: A hospital's risk committee is prioritizing defenses after a nearby facility paid attackers to recover encrypted patient records. The committee wants the single control that most reduces the business impact of a successful ransomware attack. Which option should it choose?

options.A: An endpoint protection platform that detects and quarantines known ransomware families
options.B: Offline, regularly tested backups kept isolated from production networks and credentials
options.C: Full-disk encryption on all servers so stolen patient records remain confidential
options.D: A cyber-insurance policy that reimburses ransom payments and recovery expenses

questions.explanation: The discriminator is impact of a successful attack: the committee is asking what limits the damage once prevention has already failed. Ransomware is fundamentally an availability attack, and isolated, tested backups (B) restore availability without paying: offline and credential-separated because modern operators hunt down and encrypt or delete any backup they can reach, and tested because an unrestorable backup is discovered at the worst possible moment. Option A is wrong for this question because detection reduces the likelihood of success, which the stem has already conceded; it is the right answer to lowering the odds of infection. Option C is wrong because your own disk encryption does nothing against the attacker layering their encryption on top; it addresses confidentiality of stolen media, a different threat. Option D is wrong because insurance transfers part of the financial loss while patient care stays down; payment is no guarantee of working decryption and may raise legal issues.

questions.question: During an acrimonious layoff period, a database administrator with commit access inserts code that will delete the payroll tables if his employee ID ever disappears from the HR system. Which safeguard would most likely catch this insertion before it reaches production?

options.A: Antivirus scanning on the database server to detect malicious executable files
options.B: Full-disk encryption of the storage volumes holding the payroll tables
options.C: An annual disaster-recovery exercise proving that payroll can be restored intact from backup tapes
options.D: Mandatory peer review of every code change before it can be merged and deployed

questions.explanation: This is a logic bomb: legitimate-looking code carrying a malicious trigger. Because it is written by an authorized insider and contains no malware signature, the control most likely to catch it is another human reading the change. Mandatory peer review (D) puts a second set of eyes on a deletion routine conditioned on an HR lookup, an obvious red flag, and its mere existence deters the attempt. A fails because the bomb is source code committed through normal channels, not a foreign binary; antivirus is the right answer for commodity malware dropped onto the host. Option B is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality of data at rest, and the bomb will delete data through fully authorized paths that decrypt transparently. Option C is wrong for this question because recovery exercises are corrective; they limit the damage after detonation, which makes them the right answer to reducing impact, not to catching the insertion beforehand. Insider code threats are defeated by process controls on the change pipeline, not by malware tooling.

questions.question: Help-desk tickets reveal that several employees installed a free PDF converter from a download site; the tool works exactly as advertised, but network monitoring shows it also opens a remote-control channel to an external host. Which control would most effectively have prevented these installations?

options.A: Application allow-listing that permits only approved software to execute on endpoints
options.B: A security awareness campaign warning staff about software from unofficial sources
options.C: An intrusion detection sensor tuned to alert on remote-access tool network traffic
options.D: Prompt operating system patching to close the vulnerabilities the malware exploited

questions.explanation: A working program that secretly carries a hostile payload is a Trojan horse, and its defining property is that the user willingly runs it, so the strongest defense is one that does not depend on the user's judgment. Application allow-listing (A) blocks the unapproved binary from executing at all, no matter how convincing it looked or who double-clicked it. Option B is wrong as the most effective choice because awareness is administrative and probabilistic: it lowers the click rate but some installs still happen, as this incident shows; it is the right complement, and the right answer where technical enforcement is infeasible. Option C is wrong because IDS is detective; it raises an alert after the channel opens and not preventing the installation the question asks about. Option D is wrong because no vulnerability was exploited: the user granted execution voluntarily, so patching, the right answer for worm-style exploitation, has nothing here to close.

questions.question: Overnight, malware spreads to hundreds of servers across a flat internal network while no user is logged in anywhere; each infected host scans for neighbors exposing the same vulnerable file-sharing service and infects them directly. Which combination of controls best limits this class of attack in the future?

options.A: Phishing simulations and awareness training so employees stop opening malicious attachments
options.B: Timely patching of exposed network services plus segmentation to contain lateral movement
options.C: Stronger password complexity requirements and lockout thresholds across all accounts
options.D: Full backups of every server retained for ninety days at a separate offsite location

questions.explanation: Self-propagation through a vulnerable network service with zero user involvement is the signature of a worm, and the stem hands you both contributing causes: an unpatched exposed service, and a flat network where every host can reach every other. Patching removes the exploitable flaw; segmentation shrinks the population each infected host can even reach; together (B) they attack propagation at both ends. A guards the human vector, and the defining clue is that no human acted; training is the right answer when malware arrives by phishing or Trojanized downloads. Option C is wrong because the worm exploited a service flaw, not credentials; hardening passwords is the right answer when spread rides password spraying or credential reuse. Option D is wrong for this question because backups are corrective; they rebuild servers after the damage and do nothing to limit the spread itself. Read the propagation mechanism first; it tells you which control family is even in play.

questions.question: An analyst studying an outbreak finds malicious code that appends itself to spreadsheet macro files; it lies dormant until an infected file is opened, and it spreads only when users share those files with each other. Nothing propagates unless a person opens a document. How should the analyst classify this malware?

options.A: A worm, since it eventually reached many machines across the company's network
options.B: A logic bomb, since it stays dormant until a specific condition has been met
options.C: A virus, since it attaches to host files and requires user execution to spread
options.D: A rootkit, since it conceals its code inside legitimate document files

questions.explanation: Two properties decide the classification: the code attaches itself to a host file, and it advances only when a human opens that file. Host-dependence plus required user execution defines a virus, in this case a macro virus (C). Option A is wrong because a worm's defining trait is autonomous spread, exploiting services with no user action; the stem states the opposite, and mere breadth of infection does not make a worm. Option B is wrong because a logic bomb is code planted in a system awaiting a trigger; it does not replicate by attaching to files; the dormancy here is just the wait for an ordinary open, which is the execution vector, not a chosen trigger condition. Option D is wrong because a rootkit's concealment means subverting the operating system so that tools cannot see it; riding inside a document is a carrier, not OS-level hiding.

questions.question: A university network team receives abuse complaints that campus machines are flooding an external website. Investigation shows two hundred workstations making identical periodic connections to one overseas domain, from which they fetch commands. Which control would most reduce the ongoing harm from this compromise?

options.A: Requiring password changes for all users whose workstations were observed beaconing
options.B: Encrypting the hard drives of the affected workstations to protect the stored data
options.C: Scheduling monthly vulnerability scans across the campus workstation address space
options.D: Egress filtering and DNS monitoring to block and expose command-and-control traffic

questions.explanation: Two hundred hosts beaconing to one domain for instructions is a botnet, and a bot's value to its herder depends entirely on the command-and-control channel. Cutting that channel at the network edge (D), by blocking the domain, filtering outbound traffic, and watching DNS, both stops the flooding and enumerates the infected hosts for cleanup; it attacks the one thing every bot must do. A misreads the cause: the workstations are compromised by resident malware, not by stolen passwords; new credentials on an infected host are promptly available to the malware anyway. Option B is wrong because disk encryption protects data confidentiality on lost or stolen media and is irrelevant to a machine actively attacking others while running. Option C is wrong for the timescale asked about: scanning is preventive hygiene that may reduce future infections, but a monthly detective cycle does nothing about the harm in progress.

questions.question: A vendor discloses that attackers are actively exploiting a flaw in its widely deployed VPN appliance and states that no patch will be available for several weeks. An organization depends on this appliance for all remote access. What is the most appropriate immediate course of action?

options.A: Wait for the vendor patch, since interim changes to the appliance would need rework later
options.B: Apply compensating controls, restricting exposure of the device and increasing monitoring
options.C: Run signature-based antivirus scans against the appliance to remove any implanted malware
options.D: Formally accept the risk, documenting that exploitation is unlikely before the patch ships

questions.explanation: Active exploitation with no patch available is the zero-day window, and the playbook for it is compensating controls (B): shrink the attack surface (restrict which addresses can reach the device, disable the vulnerable feature if the advisory allows, add virtual-patch rules where possible) and watch it closely for indicators of compromise while the fix is pending. Option A is wrong because it leaves the sole remote-access path exposed for weeks of known, in-the-wild exploitation; a little rework is a trivial price. Option C is wrong because signature tools recognize known malware, an unknown exploit's payload rarely has one yet, and appliances seldom support host scanners anyway. It is the right reflex for commodity infections, not this one. Option D is wrong because its own premise is false: exploitation is not unlikely, it is happening now; acceptance is legitimate only when the exposure is genuinely tolerable or mitigation costs more than the risk. When no patch exists, reduce exposure and heighten detection; documenting a risk is not the same as treating it.

questions.question: A team is starting a multi-year system that depends on an unproven biometric technology. Management's chief concern is that unexplored technical risks could sink the project, and it wants each round of work to begin with an explicit risk evaluation before more money is committed. Which lifecycle model best fits this need?

options.A: The spiral model, in which each cycle opens with objectives and a fresh risk analysis
options.B: Extreme Programming, in which paired developers and test-first coding control quality
options.C: The waterfall model, in which risks are addressed once during the initial planning phase
options.D: Rapid Application Development, in which quick prototypes surface problems through user feedback

questions.explanation: Management has literally described the spiral model's engine: repeated cycles that each begin by setting objectives, evaluating risks and alternatives, often retiring the worst risk with a prototype, before committing to the next round of investment (A). It was conceived precisely for large projects burdened with unproven technology. Option B is wrong because XP's practices manage code quality within iterations; they provide no project-level gate that weighs risk before funding continues. Option C is wrong because a single up-front risk pass cannot handle risks that only surface mid-build, and with novel technology most of them do; waterfall fits stable, well-understood work. Option D is wrong because RAD's prototypes optimize for speed and requirements discovery through user reaction; user feedback exposes usability gaps, not systematic engineering risk, and RAD imposes no formal risk-evaluation checkpoint.

questions.question: A software firm loses a government bid because it cannot demonstrate the maturity of its development processes; internally, project success still depends on individual heroics and no two teams work alike. Leadership wants a recognized framework for assessing and improving how the organization builds software. Which framework best meets this goal?

options.A: STRIDE, which categorizes design-level threats to a system under development
options.B: CVSS, which scores the severity of published vulnerabilities on a common scale
options.C: The OWASP Top 10, which ranks the most critical web application risk categories
options.D: CMMI, which appraises process maturity in staged levels and guides improvement

questions.explanation: The firm's problem is the process itself: ad hoc, heroics-dependent, inconsistent across teams, which is the textbook description of the lowest maturity level. CMMI (D) is built for exactly this: it appraises how an organization develops software against defined maturity levels, produces the recognized rating acquirers ask for, and lays out the practice areas to institutionalize next. Option A is wrong because STRIDE examines one system's design for threat categories; it says nothing about how consistently the organization works. It is the right answer during a product's design phase. Option B is wrong because CVSS rates individual known vulnerabilities for prioritization; it measures findings, not capability. Option C is wrong because the Top 10 educates developers about common application risks; awareness of risks is not evidence of repeatable process. Distinguish product-level tools (threats, vulnerabilities, risks) from organization-level frameworks that measure and mature the process itself.

questions.question: Following a disappointing CMMI appraisal, an organization launches a process-improvement program using the IDEAL model. The improvement team is eager to begin rewriting development procedures immediately. According to the model, what must happen first?

options.A: Acting on the weakest findings from the appraisal to demonstrate early momentum
options.B: Diagnosing the current state of practice against the desired future state
options.C: Initiating the effort by securing sponsorship, resources, and an improvement infrastructure
options.D: Learning from a pilot project so that later phases can be adjusted with evidence

questions.explanation: IDEAL sequences an improvement program as Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning, and the ordering is the model's whole point. Before anything else, the Initiating phase (C) sets the business context, wins executive sponsorship, and builds the infrastructure (charter, roles, resources) that will carry the effort; improvement programs launched without that foundation stall as soon as the work gets contentious or expensive. Option B is wrong only in its timing: diagnosing comes second, and a diagnosis performed with no sponsor or charter produces findings nobody is bound to act on. Option A is wrong because Acting is the fourth phase; rushing straight to fixes is precisely the trap the eager team in the stem is walking into, changes without diagnosis or plan. Option D is wrong because Learning is the final phase, harvesting lessons to refine the next pass.

questions.question: A billing team discovers that a customer's mailing address differs across three tables in the same database; an update routine changed one copy but missed the others, and refunds are now being mailed to an outdated address. Which database design practice most directly prevents this class of defect?

options.A: Normalization, so each fact is stored once and referenced and not duplicated
options.B: Transparent encryption, so address data is protected from any unauthorized reading
options.C: Nightly integrity jobs that compare the three address copies and report mismatches
options.D: Database activity monitoring that logs every change made to customer records

questions.explanation: Three divergent copies of one fact is an update anomaly, and update anomalies are exactly what normalization exists to eliminate: store the address once, reference it by key everywhere else, and there is no second or third copy to miss (A); the defect becomes structurally impossible. Option C is a detective patch on the symptom: it tolerates the redundancy, lets copies diverge, and then notices, with refunds already misdirected in the meantime; reconciliation jobs are the right answer only for data you cannot restructure, such as feeds from external systems. Option B is wrong because encryption addresses confidentiality; every one of the three copies can be perfectly encrypted and still inconsistent. Option D is wrong because an audit log records who changed what, which serves accountability and forensics but does nothing to keep the copies in step.

questions.question: A clinic's reporting system hides individual diagnoses but permits statistical queries. A clerk runs a count of patients with a rare condition across the ward, then the same count excluding one named patient, and subtracts the results to learn that patient's diagnosis. Neither query exceeded the clerk's permissions. Which term best describes this attack?

options.A: SQL injection, because crafted queries extracted data the interface was built to conceal
options.B: Inference, because a protected fact was deduced from individually authorized results
options.C: Privilege escalation, because the clerk obtained information above their access level
options.D: Aggregation, because a large volume of harmless records was fused into a sensitive whole

questions.explanation: The clerk never broke a rule: each query was authorized and well formed. Yet arithmetic across the answers revealed a fact the system withholds. Deducing protected information from legitimately obtainable results is an inference attack (B), and it is countered by controls on the answers, not the access: minimum query-set sizes, noise or perturbation in statistics, and polyinstantiation in multilevel databases. Option A is wrong because injection means input that subverts the structure of the query itself; these queries ran exactly as designed. Option C is wrong because no permission boundary was crossed or elevated, which is what makes inference so hard to police; escalation would involve gaining rights the clerk was never granted. Option D is the closest wrong answer: aggregation is the sibling threat in which many individually non-sensitive records are combined until the collection itself is sensitive. Here the clerk combined two statistics to derive one specific withheld fact: deduction, not accumulation. Aggregation piles data up; inference reasons a secret out, and access control alone stops neither.

questions.question: A logistics contractor is granted access to several databases, each individually rated non-sensitive: truck maintenance schedules, fuel purchases, and driver duty rosters. By correlating them, the contractor reconstructs the timing and routes of classified weapons shipments. Which security concern does this scenario best illustrate?

options.A: Inference, since the contractor deduced one hidden value from a permitted statistical result
options.B: Collusion, since several parties pooled their separate accesses to reach protected data
options.C: Data remanence, since sensitive residue persisted inside systems rated non-sensitive
options.D: Aggregation, since individually non-sensitive data sets combined into sensitive knowledge

questions.explanation: Every source the contractor touched was legitimately non-sensitive; the classified picture emerged only when the sources were correlated. That is aggregation (D): the combination carries a higher sensitivity than any of its parts, which is why access decisions must consider what a subject can assemble in total: need-to-know evaluated across holdings, not per database. Option A is the closest wrong answer: inference is the sibling concern where someone reasons a specific withheld fact out of permitted answers, as with statistical queries; here nothing was individually withheld or deduced; the sensitivity arose from assembly. Option B is wrong because collusion requires multiple actors combining their separate privileges; this was one contractor acting within one set of grants. Option C is wrong because remanence is data physically surviving on media after deletion or reuse; nothing here was residual; the databases were serving their intended content.

questions.question: During a funds transfer, a database server crashed after debiting the source account but before crediting the destination; on restart, the half-completed change remained in the database and the money was missing from both accounts. Which ACID property did the transaction processing fail to uphold?

options.A: Atomicity, because a transaction's operations must apply entirely or leave no effect at all
options.B: Isolation, because concurrent transactions must remain invisible to one another while running
options.C: Durability, because once a transaction commits its effects must survive crashes and remain permanent
options.D: Consistency, because each transaction must move the database between valid states

questions.explanation: The debit and credit form one logical transaction, and the system let half of it persist. The property that forbids exactly that is atomicity (A): all of a transaction's operations commit together, or recovery rolls every one of them back so the transaction never happened; a correct engine would have undone the debit on restart. Option D is the tempting wrong answer because the books are certainly now inconsistent; but the unbalanced state is the consequence, and consistency between valid states is what atomic all-or-nothing execution exists to preserve. Consistency is the direct culprit when a transaction commits while violating a declared rule or constraint. B does not fit because isolation governs interference between transactions running concurrently, and this failure involved a single transaction and a crash. Option C is wrong because durability protects work that had committed; the problem here is the mirror image: uncommitted, partial work that survived when it should have vanished. Partial effects persisting after recovery point at atomicity; constraint violations at commit point at consistency.

questions.question: A penetration tester on a coffee-shop network captures traffic from a company web portal that uses HTTPS for its login page but plain HTTP for everything afterward. Using a session cookie copied from another patron's traffic, the tester opens that user's account without ever entering credentials. Which change most directly defeats this attack?

options.A: Enforce a stronger password policy, since the portal's accounts were too easily guessed
options.B: Add a CAPTCHA challenge to the login form to block automated credential attacks
options.C: Serve every page over TLS and mark the session cookie with the Secure attribute
options.D: Shorten the password expiration interval so captured credentials age out quickly

questions.explanation: The attacker performed session hijacking: the login was protected, but the session cookie, which is the credential after login, traveled in cleartext on every subsequent request and was simply copied. Extending TLS to the whole session and setting the cookie's Secure attribute (C) keeps the token off the wire in readable form and instructs the browser never to send it over an unencrypted connection; regenerating session IDs and HttpOnly add depth. A, B, and D all defend the authentication step, and the tester never touched it: no password was guessed (A), no automated login attempts occurred (B), and no credential was captured to age out (D); a hijacked session bypasses all three. A would be right against brute-force guessing, B against credential-stuffing bots, D against stale stolen passwords.

questions.question: An application review finds that the session cookie can be read by any script running in the page and is also transmitted when users follow links over unencrypted connections. Which pair of cookie attributes most directly closes these two exposures?

options.A: Domain and Path, which limit the hosts and URL prefixes to which the cookie is sent
options.B: HttpOnly and Secure, which deny script access and restrict the cookie to encrypted transport
options.C: Max-Age and Expires, which bound how long the browser retains the session cookie
options.D: SameSite and Path, which control whether cross-site navigation includes the cookie

questions.explanation: Map each finding to the attribute built for it: script access to the cookie is removed by HttpOnly, which hides the cookie from the page's JavaScript so even a successful XSS payload cannot read it; cleartext transmission is removed by Secure, which forbids the browser from sending the cookie over anything but an encrypted connection (B). Option A is wrong because Domain and Path only scope which requests include the cookie; within that scope, scripts can still read it and HTTP links still carry it. Option D is wrong for the same reason at a different boundary: SameSite governs whether cross-site requests attach the cookie, which is a CSRF defense, and neither finding involves cross-site requests. Option C is wrong because lifetime limits shrink the window of misuse without closing either exposure: a cookie can be stolen by script or sniffed off the wire in its first minute.

questions.question: A monitoring service alerts a bank that a production API key is visible in a public repository, pushed there three days ago by a developer. The security team confirms the key grants administrative access to the transaction backend. What should the team do first?

options.A: Delete the offending file from the repository and rewrite its commit history to purge the key
options.B: Make the repository private so that no additional external parties can view the key
options.C: Revoke the exposed key immediately and issue a replacement through approved channels
options.D: Interview the developer to establish how the key came to be committed and pushed

questions.explanation: Automated bots scrape public repositories for credential patterns within seconds of a push; after three days, the only safe assumption is that the key has already been copied. Nothing that changes who can see the repository going forward alters that, so the first move is to make the stolen value worthless: revoke it and reissue through a proper channel (C), then hunt for fraudulent use during the exposure window. A treats the visible symptom: history rewriting is worth doing afterward for hygiene, but it cannot recall the copies already harvested, and doing it first leaves an active admin credential in attackers' hands meanwhile. B fails the same way: private visibility stops future viewers, not past ones. D matters for the lessons-learned and for fixing the process, but root-cause interviews come after containment, not before it.

questions.question: After a credential leak, a bank decides that commits containing secrets must be blocked before they can ever enter the central code repository, in a way that individual developers cannot bypass from their own machines. Which mechanism best meets this requirement?

options.A: A server-side pre-receive hook that scans incoming pushes and rejects any containing secrets
options.B: A client-side pre-commit hook on every developer workstation that runs local secret scanning
options.C: A nightly scheduled job that scans the repository contents and alerts on any secrets found
options.D: A mandatory code-review checklist item requiring reviewers to look for embedded credentials

questions.explanation: The requirement has two halves, enforcement before the secret enters the shared repository and enforcement developers cannot switch off, and only a control running on the server itself satisfies both. A pre-receive hook (A) evaluates every push at the moment the server is asked to accept it and refuses the whole push if a secret is detected: nothing to install, nothing to bypass. Option B is the closest wrong answer: client-side hooks give excellent fast feedback, but they live on machines the developer controls: they can be skipped with a flag, and a fresh clone simply does not have them; they complement the server hook, they cannot replace it. Option C is wrong on timing: by the nightly run the secret has been in shared history for hours, cloned and mirrored. Option D is wrong because human review is fallible, and in pull-request workflows the code has already been pushed to the server before anyone reviews it. Guarantees of the form 'never enters the repository' can only be enforced where the repository lives.

questions.question: An architecture team is designing a new payment API and wants a structured way to enumerate potential threats (spoofed callers, tampered messages, repudiated transactions, leaked records) before any code has been written. Which technique fits this stage of the lifecycle best?

options.A: Scoring each of the system's known vulnerabilities with CVSS to rank their severity
options.B: Running a dynamic application security test against the deployed staging environment
options.C: Commissioning an external penetration test of the completed payment service
options.D: Threat modeling with STRIDE to categorize design-level threats to each component

questions.explanation: At design time there is no code, no build, and no findings, only architecture. The one technique that operates on architecture alone is threat modeling, and STRIDE (D) is a natural choice here because the team's worry list maps onto its categories one for one: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, plus denial of service and elevation of privilege they have not thought of yet, which is exactly the value of using a structured taxonomy over brainstorming. Option A is wrong because CVSS scores vulnerabilities that have been discovered in something that exists; there is nothing to score yet. Option B is wrong because DAST probes a running application: right technique, later phase, once a staging build exists. Option C is wrong the same way at still a later stage: penetration testing validates the finished, deployed service.

questions.question: A threat-modeling workshop for a trading platform produces forty distinct threats, far more than the team can address this quarter. The security lead needs a repeatable way to rank them so that remediation effort goes to the worst ones first. Which method is designed for this purpose?

options.A: STRIDE, which sorts each threat into one of six categories of malicious behavior
options.B: DREAD, which scores each threat on factors such as damage potential and exploitability
options.C: CVSS, which computes severity scores for vulnerabilities published against shipped software
options.D: CMMI, which appraises the maturity of an organization's development processes

questions.explanation: Ranking forty hypothetical threats needs a rating scheme, and DREAD (B) is exactly that: each threat is scored on Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, and Discoverability, and the totals give a defensible, repeatable priority order for remediation. A cannot rank anything: STRIDE was the enumeration step the workshop just completed; it tells you what kind each threat is, and nothing about which is worse; category membership carries no severity. Option C is the plausible near-miss: CVSS also produces severity numbers, but it is built for disclosed vulnerabilities in released software, scoring concrete flaws with known exploit characteristics; design-stage threats have no CVE, no patch state, and often no implementation yet. It is the right answer when the input is a vulnerability-scan report. Option D is wrong because CMMI evaluates how the organization builds software, an entirely different altitude from ranking one system's threats. STRIDE finds and names threats, DREAD ranks them; CVSS rates real vulnerabilities after release.

questions.question: Weeks after launching a public API, a retailer finds one client has issued millions of requests enumerating sequential customer identifiers, and stolen credential lists are being replayed against the login endpoint at high speed. Which pair of controls most directly counters this abuse?

options.A: Moving the API to an undocumented URL path and randomizing its response formats
options.B: Deploying additional API servers behind a load balancer to absorb the request volume
options.C: Rate limiting per client plus strong authentication with authorization checks on every object
options.D: Requiring API consumers to accept terms of service that prohibit automated scraping

questions.explanation: Both abuse patterns exploit the same two gaps: nothing slows a caller down, and nothing verifies that a caller may access the specific record it names. Per-client rate limiting throttles the millions-of-requests behavior that enumeration and credential replay both depend on, and object-level authorization ensures that even a valid session can only retrieve its own records (C), closing the sequential-ID harvest. Option A is wrong because hidden paths and shuffled formats are security through obscurity; the current abuser already found the API, and any future one will. Option B is wrong because adding capacity treats hostile traffic as a scaling problem; it makes the abuse run more smoothly at higher cost to the retailer. Option D is wrong as a technical counter because a terms-of-service document enforces nothing at request time; it has real value as the legal basis for action against an identified abuser, which makes it a complement, not a control.

questions.question: Stakeholders for a new claims-processing interface cannot articulate what they need; two requirements workshops have produced contradictory documents. The delivery lead wants an approach that lets users react to something concrete before the team commits to full development. Which approach best serves this goal?

options.A: Completing a comprehensive requirements specification and having every stakeholder sign it
options.B: Adopting cleanroom methods so that defects are formally prevented from the earliest phase
options.C: Proceeding directly to full construction so users can react to the finished system itself
options.D: Building a limited working model of the interface for stakeholders to evaluate and refine

questions.explanation: When stakeholders cannot say what they want, showing beats asking: a prototype (D) gives them something concrete to react to, converts vague or contradictory wishes into specific corrections, and costs little enough to throw away and iterate, which is the entire reason prototyping exists as a development approach. A doubles down on the technique that has already failed twice; signatures on an ambiguous document create commitment, not clarity, and the conflicts will resurface as change requests during build. Option B is wrong because cleanroom's formal rigor prevents implementation defects; it verifies the software against its specification, and here the specification itself is the problem: a formally verified wrong product is still wrong. Option C is wrong because it takes the largest possible bet on the least information; feedback arrives only after the full cost is sunk, when rework is most expensive. Prototype when requirements are the risk; formalize when correctness against known requirements is the risk.

questions.question: To hit a marketing deadline, a team adopts rapid application development: time-boxed cycles, heavy prototyping, and minimal up-front design. The CISO is asked to name the greatest security risk this delivery style introduces. Which answer is most accurate?

options.A: Schedule pressure squeezes security requirements and testing out of each compressed cycle
options.B: The extensive documentation the method demands will delay security review sign-offs
options.C: Requirements frozen at project start will block security fixes once the cycles begin
options.D: The absence of user involvement means real-world abuse goes unconsidered until launch

questions.explanation: RAD's defining trade is rigor for speed. When a time-box tightens, whatever is not demanded by the demo gets cut, and security work such as threat modeling and security test cases is the classic casualty; worse, prototypes that were never meant for production get promoted into it under deadline pressure with their shortcuts intact (A). This is the very pattern behind Global Bank's hackathon key. Option B is wrong because it describes the opposite methodology: RAD is documentation-light by design; heavy documentation gates belong to waterfall-style processes. Option C is wrong for the same reason: RAD embraces changing requirements across iterations; frozen baselines are a plan-driven trait. Option D is wrong because RAD is built around continuous user involvement; the subtle truth, worth keeping, is that users exercise intended behavior while abusers exercise unintended behavior. But the option's premise, absent involvement, is simply false. Fast lifecycles do not forbid security work, they starve it. The countermeasure is making security part of each cycle's definition of done.

questions.question: A medical-device maker must build infusion-pump firmware for which regulators demand evidence that defects are prevented during development and not found and patched afterward, and that failure rates be certified statistically. Which software engineering approach best aligns with these demands?

options.A: Extreme Programming, relying on test-driven development and continuous pair review
options.B: Cleanroom engineering, using formal specification, verification, and statistical quality control
options.C: Rapid application development, iterating prototypes quickly until users accept the behavior
options.D: Scrum, delivering the firmware in sprints with a defect backlog groomed by the product owner

questions.explanation: The regulator's two demands are the two pillars of cleanroom software engineering (B): defects are prevented before test through formal specification and mathematically based verification of the code, and quality is then demonstrated through statistical usage testing that supports certified reliability claims, precisely the evidence sought. Option A is the strongest wrong answer: TDD and pair programming are powerful, but they find defects moments after they are written; that is still detect-and-fix, not formal prevention, and XP offers no statistical certification of failure rates. It is the right choice for quality-focused commercial teams without a certification burden. Option C is wrong because RAD optimizes speed and user acceptance; its tolerance for rough prototypes is the opposite of certifiable rigor. Option D is wrong because Scrum is a management wrapper that explicitly routes defects into a backlog for later resolution; it prescribes no engineering rigor at all.

questions.question: An organization adopting Scrum asks its security architect how security work should fit a process that ships a product increment at the end of every two-week sprint. Which arrangement best integrates security with this cadence?

options.A: Hold all security requirements for a hardening phase scheduled after the final sprint
options.B: Have the security team test a copy of the product on its own quarterly timetable
options.C: Put security items in the product backlog and security checks in the definition of done
options.D: Dedicate one sprint per quarter entirely to security fixes while feature work pauses

questions.explanation: In Scrum, work exists only if it is in the product backlog, and quality bars exist only in the definition of done, so that is where security must live (C): threat-driven requirements and abuse cases enter the backlog to be prioritized alongside features, and the definition of done makes passing security checks a condition of calling any increment complete. Every sprint then ships software that has met the bar. Option A is wrong because it recreates the bolt-on waterfall pattern inside an iterative process, and every increment before that final phase ships unexamined. Option B is wrong because out-of-band quarterly testing lags up to six releases behind; findings arrive divorced from the sprint that caused them. Option D is the seductive anti-pattern: a periodic security sprint batches risk, lets unvetted features ship for months between passes, and frames security as a tax that pauses real work. It is defensible only as an occasional remediation push on top of, never instead of, per-sprint integration.

questions.question: A product group plagued by defects reaching production is adopting Extreme Programming. The quality manager asks which XP practices will most directly catch defects at the moment the code is being written. Which pairing should the manager highlight?

options.A: The planning game and small releases, which shorten the feedback loop with customers
options.B: Collective code ownership and coding standards, which keep the code base uniform
options.C: On-site customer and system metaphor, which keep development aligned with business intent
options.D: Pair programming and test-driven development, which review and test code as it is typed

questions.explanation: The discriminator is at the moment the code is being written, and two XP practices operate at exactly that instant (D): in test-driven development the failing test exists before the code, so the first run verifies the new logic immediately; in pair programming a second developer is reviewing each line as it appears, catching slips that the author is blind to. Together they are XP's tightest defect-feedback loop. A operates at the wrong range: the planning game and small releases work at release granularity; they surface wrong priorities and integration surprises in days or weeks, not keystrokes. Option B is wrong because shared ownership and standards improve maintainability and consistency, which prevents some future defects but examines nothing as it is created. Option C is wrong because the on-site customer and metaphor align the product with business intent: they catch building the wrong thing, not building the thing wrong.

questions.question: A regulator requires a bank to demonstrate that no change to its payment module is written and merged by a single unreviewed developer, and expects the review to occur as early in development as possible. Which practice most directly satisfies this requirement?

options.A: Pair programming, in which a second developer reviews each line as it is being written
options.B: Static analysis in the pipeline, which examines every commit for known insecure patterns
options.C: Raising unit-test coverage thresholds so that untested changes cannot be merged
options.D: Annual secure-coding training so that each developer can review their own work reliably before merging

questions.explanation: The requirement names two things: a second person on every change, and review at the earliest possible point. Pair programming (A) delivers both at once: the navigator is a continuous human reviewer sitting beside the author, so no line is ever written unobserved, and the review happens at the moment of creation and not at a later gate. It is two-person integrity applied to code. Option B is wrong because a static analyzer, however valuable, is not a reviewer: it matches known insecure patterns and misses flawed business logic; a bogus transfer-approval rule sails through; it is the right automated complement, not the human control the regulator described. Option C is wrong because coverage measures how much code the author's own tests execute; it neither adds a second person nor evaluates intent. Option D is wrong because training improves the individual, and self-review is precisely what the requirement rules out. When a control demands independent human review, only another human, pairing or a required reviewer, satisfies it; automation assists, it does not substitute.

questions.question: A bank wants its pipeline to catch hardcoded credentials and injection-prone code in its own source before each merge, without waiting for a build to be deployed anywhere. Which testing technology is the most appropriate choice?

options.A: Dynamic application security testing, which probes a running application from the outside
options.B: Static application security testing, which examines source code without executing it
options.C: Software composition analysis, which flags known vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies
options.D: Interactive application security testing, which instruments the app while tests exercise it

questions.explanation: Two constraints in the stem decide this: the flaws live in first-party source (hardcoded secrets, injection-prone patterns), and the check must run before merge, when nothing is deployed. Only static analysis (B) works under both: it reads the code itself, so a credential string or an unsanitized query concatenation is visible directly, and it needs no running instance. Option A is wrong because DAST attacks an application from outside while it runs; it cannot see a hardcoded key that never appears in a response, and there is no running app at merge time. It is the right tool against the deployed build in staging. D fails for the same reason one layer in: IAST observes an instrumented application during test execution, so it also requires a runtime. Option C is wrong on target instead of timing: SCA inventories the third-party libraries you import and matches them against known-vulnerability data; it does not analyze the code your own developers wrote. SAST reads your source, DAST probes your running app, IAST watches from inside it, SCA audits what you imported. Pick by where the flaw lives and what exists when you test.

questions.question: A penetration test of a production banking app uncovers a URL, absent from all design documents, that grants administrative access with no credentials; version control shows a developer added it during testing to save time and never removed it. What is the most accurate name for this finding?

options.A: A logic bomb left in the code awaiting a trigger condition chosen by the developer
options.B: A Trojan horse embedded in the application and disguised as a legitimate feature
options.C: A maintenance hook, an undocumented backdoor that bypasses normal authentication
options.D: A race condition that intermittently allows requests to skip the authentication check

questions.explanation: An undocumented access path that developers created for their own convenience and that sidesteps authentication is the definition of a maintenance hook, a backdoor (C). Intent barely matters: left in production, it grants the same unauthenticated administrative access to whoever finds it, which is why removal must be verified before release. Option A is wrong because a logic bomb carries a malicious payload waiting on a trigger, such as a date or an HR record change; this URL does nothing on its own and harbors no destructive action. Option B is wrong because a Trojan horse is malicious software a victim is deceived into installing because it appears desirable; this is the bank's own application, not a disguised foreign program. Option D is wrong because a race condition is a timing defect, authentication skipped only when operations interleave badly, appearing intermittently; this bypass is deterministic and works on every request. Deliberate shortcut paths are backdoors, and the fix is process: code review and pre-release checks that hunt for them.

questions.question: A mobile team plans to protect the API key shipped inside its Android app by running the code through an obfuscator, arguing that renamed classes and scrambled control flow will keep the key safe. Which assessment of this plan is most accurate?

options.A: Adequate, because obfuscated binaries cannot be decompiled back into readable source
options.B: Adequate, provided the key is also encrypted inside the binary before obfuscation
options.C: Insufficient, because obfuscation degrades performance too severely for production apps
options.D: Insufficient, because obfuscation only delays analysis; the secret should move server-side

questions.explanation: Anything the app can use at runtime, an attacker holding the binary can eventually recover by decompiling, hooking the app, or dumping memory at the moment the key is used. Obfuscation raises the effort and is worth applying as one layer, but it converts none of that into confidentiality; a secret shipped to every customer's device is disclosed by design, so the durable fix is architectural: keep the key server-side and issue short-lived, per-user tokens to the client (D). Option A is wrong on its facts: decompilers process obfuscated code readily; the output is uglier, not unreadable. Option B is wrong because it recurses: the app must carry the decryption key to use the encrypted one, and that key is recoverable the same way. C reaches the right verdict for a wrong reason; modern obfuscation overhead is modest, and rejecting a control on false grounds discredits the review.

questions.question: A web application lets users submit a URL to generate a link preview. An attacker submits http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and the application returns the cloud account's temporary credentials, fetched by the application server itself. Which vulnerability class does this demonstrate?

options.A: Server-side request forgery, since the server was induced to request an internal resource
options.B: Cross-site request forgery, since a forged request was executed without a victim's intent
options.C: XML external entity injection, since a parser was made to retrieve a protected document
options.D: An open redirect, since the application forwarded a browser to an attacker-chosen address

questions.explanation: The decisive detail is who made the request: the application server itself fetched the metadata address on the attacker's behalf. Abusing a server's own network position to reach resources the attacker cannot touch directly, such as internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint that only the instance may query, is server-side request forgery (A); the fix is an allow-list of fetchable destinations with internal and link-local ranges denied. Option B is the classic confusion: in CSRF the forged request is sent by a victim's browser, riding that user's session; here there is no victim user and the server is the one doing the fetching. Option C is wrong because XXE requires an XML parser resolving external entities; a URL form field involves no XML; XXE is better thought of as one specific vector that can produce SSRF-like fetches. Option D is wrong because an open redirect bounces the client's browser to another site; this server retrieved the content itself and handed it back. SSRF forges requests from the server, CSRF forges them from the user; identify the party being tricked.

questions.question: A Java service accepts serialized objects from partner systems over the Internet and rebuilds them in memory; researchers show that a crafted object chain in this stream executes arbitrary commands during reconstruction. Which remediation most effectively addresses the root cause?

options.A: Encrypt the serialized stream in transit so intermediaries are unable to modify the objects
options.B: Add a web application firewall rule that inspects payloads for known gadget-chain signatures
options.C: Replace native object deserialization with a data-only format validated against a strict schema
options.D: Shorten connection timeouts so any single compromised session has a limited useful lifetime

questions.explanation: Insecure deserialization is dangerous because rebuilding a native object graph lets the sender choose which classes get instantiated, and chains of innocent classes can be assembled into code execution. The root-cause fix removes that power from the sender: exchange plain data in a format such as JSON, validate it against a strict schema, and construct objects yourself (C); where native deserialization is unavoidable, a tight class allow-list is the fallback. A protects the wrong layer: encryption authenticates the channel, not the content's safety. The malicious payload comes from a partner system, or from a partner that has itself been compromised, and travels happily through the encrypted pipe. Option B is wrong because signature matching known gadget chains is a reactive race with researchers who keep finding new ones; it earns its keep only as an interim virtual patch. Option D is wrong because the exploit fires during reconstruction of a single message; session lifetime never enters into it. Never let untrusted bytes decide what code runs; deserialize data, not objects.

questions.question: An invoice-upload feature parses customer XML. A tester uploads a file whose DOCTYPE declaration defines an external entity pointing at /etc/passwd, and the parsed output returns that file's contents. Which change best fixes this flaw at its source?

options.A: Validate that uploaded invoices are well-formed XML before passing them to the parser
options.B: Configure the XML parser to disable document type definitions and external entity resolution
options.C: Run the upload service in a container so its file reads are confined to the container image
options.D: Scan uploaded files with antivirus to reject those containing known malicious markup

questions.explanation: XML external entity injection is unusual among injection flaws: the vulnerability is a feature, not a bug. The parser is doing exactly what DTD processing specifies, resolving an entity that happens to point at a local file, so the source-level fix is configuration: turn off DTDs and external entity resolution in the parser (B), and the attack ceases to be expressible. Option A is wrong because the tester's exploit file is perfectly well-formed XML; well-formedness checks syntax, and this attack is syntactically impeccable. Option C is wrong because containment shrinks the blast radius without fixing the flaw: everything inside the container, including its own credentials and configuration secrets, remains readable, and SSRF-style entity fetches still reach the network. It is reasonable defense in depth. Option D is wrong because antivirus recognizes known malware, and a three-line DOCTYPE crafted for this one application matches nothing in a signature set. When a parser's features are the attack surface, hardening its configuration is the fix, a lesson that generalizes to any dangerous default.

questions.question: A logged-in customer of a banking site changes the number in the URL /statements?account=1001 to 1002 and receives another customer's statement. The request was well formed, contained no attack syntax, and the server processed it exactly as designed. Which weakness best explains this behavior?

options.A: An injection flaw, because the customer's input altered how the server-side query executed
options.B: A security misconfiguration, because a hardening option that conceals identifiers was disabled
options.C: A cryptographic failure, because financial records reached a party unauthorized to read them
options.D: Broken access control, because the application never checked object-level authorization

questions.explanation: Everything about this request was legitimate except the outcome: the user was authenticated, the syntax was clean, and the server did what its code says, which is precisely the point. The code never asks whether the requester owns account 1002 before serving it, a missing object-level authorization check known as an insecure direct object reference, the canonical broken access control flaw (D) and the same defect that let Global Bank's leaked key read any customer's records. A does not apply: injection means input that changes the structure or logic of a command; here the query ran exactly as designed with a different, valid parameter; nothing was subverted. Option B is wrong because misconfiguration lives in settings, defaults, and deployment options; this flaw lives in application logic, and no configuration toggle supplies a missing ownership check. Option C is wrong because cryptographic failures concern absent or weak protection of data; the TLS on this site could be flawless and the flaw would remain untouched.

questions.question: A scan of a newly deployed application server finds the vendor's sample applications still installed, an admin console reachable with the documented default password, directory listing enabled, and stack traces returned to clients on error. Under which OWASP risk category do these findings best fit?

options.A: Security misconfiguration, since insecure default settings and features were left in place
options.B: Broken access control, since unauthorized parties could reach administrative functions
options.C: Vulnerable and outdated components, since the server carried unneeded sample software
options.D: Identification and authentication failures, since a default password guarded the console

questions.explanation: Look for the common cause: sample apps present, default credentials unchanged, directory listing on, verbose errors leaking internals: four symptoms of one omission, an unhardened out-of-the-box deployment. That is security misconfiguration (A), and its remedy is a repeatable hardening baseline applied to every build, not four one-off fixes. Option B is wrong because broken access control describes missing or faulty authorization logic in the application; here the checks exist and were simply undermined by a published password. That is a settings problem, not a logic problem. Option C is wrong because the components category targets software that is outdated or known-vulnerable; the samples' sin is being present and unneeded, a deployment choice, whatever their patch level. Option D is the defensible near-miss: the default password in isolation could file under authentication failures, and on a question about that single finding it would be the answer. But it cannot account for directory listings, stack traces, or sample apps, and the question asks where the findings as a set belong.

questions.question: Forensic investigators determine that attackers were active inside a retailer's network for five months. In that time no alerts fired; the web servers kept only seven days of logs, application logins were never recorded, and log review was a manual task performed quarterly. Which improvement should the security program prioritize?

options.A: Deploying stronger encryption for stored data so future intrusions yield nothing readable
options.B: Centralized log collection with longer retention and automated alerting on suspicious activity
options.C: Commissioning an annual external penetration test to uncover exploitable weaknesses
options.D: Adopting a stricter rotation schedule for all privileged administrator account passwords

questions.explanation: Five months of undetected activity is a visibility failure, and the stem lists its three ingredients: logs that expire in a week, security-relevant events never captured, and review too infrequent and manual to notice anything. The remedy attacks all three (B): collect logs centrally where intruders cannot quietly erase them, retain them well beyond realistic dwell times so investigations have evidence, and let automation watch continuously so detection happens in hours, not quarters. Option A is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality against stolen media and eavesdroppers; attackers operating through compromised applications and accounts read data exactly as legitimate users do, and encryption restores no visibility. Option C is a point-in-time probe for ways in; this organization's demonstrated failure is not knowing when someone is already inside. Option D is wrong because nothing ties the intrusion to stale passwords, and rotation would not have surfaced the five-month presence. Fix the control family the incident actually indicts. Long dwell times indict detection, so build logging and monitoring before buying more prevention.

questions.question: In a post-incident review of the Global Bank key leak, the team maps events to STRIDE. One member asks how to categorize the moment the Master_API_Key became readable by anyone browsing the public repository, before any attacker had used it. Which STRIDE category best fits that specific event?

options.A: Spoofing, because the key would later let outsiders authenticate as an administrator
options.B: Tampering, because the repository's contents were changed by the developer's push
options.C: Information disclosure, because a secret became visible to parties never meant to see it
options.D: Elevation of privilege, because possession of the key conferred administrative rights

questions.explanation: Precision about which event is being classified decides this question. The event named in the stem is the exposure itself, a confidential value becoming readable by unauthorized parties, and confidentiality violations are STRIDE's information disclosure category (C), regardless of whether anyone had exploited the exposure yet. A and D fail on phase, not on substance: when attackers later authenticated to the API as an administrator using the stolen key, that was spoofing, and the administrative capability they gained maps to elevation of privilege — each is the right answer to a question about the attack that followed, not about the leak. B fails on definition: tampering is unauthorized modification of data or code, and the developer's push was an authorized, well-intentioned change that happened to be unsafe; nothing was maliciously altered. A real incident spans several STRIDE categories in sequence; classify each event on the timeline separately instead of forcing one label onto the whole story.

questions.question: A bank's platform team runs two hundred microservices that call each other directly. Security requires mutual TLS and per-call authorization between every pair of services, but modifying two hundred codebases has been ruled out as infeasible. Which approach best delivers these controls?

options.A: An API gateway at the network edge that authenticates external clients before they enter
options.B: A perimeter firewall policy limiting which outside networks can reach the service cluster
options.C: A shared library implementing TLS and authorization, to be integrated into each service
options.D: A service mesh whose sidecar proxies supply mutual TLS and policy without code changes

questions.explanation: The requirement is service-to-service (east-west) security at a scale where touching application code is off the table, and that is the problem service meshes were built for (D): a sidecar proxy deployed beside each service intercepts its traffic, so mutual TLS, service identity, and per-call authorization policy are supplied by infrastructure, uniformly and without modifying any of the two hundred codebases. Option A is wrong on direction: a gateway guards north-south traffic where external clients enter; once inside, service-to-service calls never traverse it. It is the right answer for authenticating outside consumers. Option B is wrong on granularity as well as direction: a perimeter policy knows networks and ports, not service identities, and offers nothing between two services inside the cluster. C meets the functional need but fails the stated constraint: it requires integrating and re-releasing every service, and forever ties security upgrades to two hundred deployment schedules.

questions.question: A review of a company's container platform finds application containers running as root, built from unscanned images pulled from public registries, on shared hosts. Which change most reduces the risk of container compromise and escape?

options.A: Installing traditional antivirus agents inside every running application container
options.B: Scanning images for known vulnerabilities and running containers as non-root users
options.C: Moving all images into a private registry while continuing to build them unchanged
options.D: Restarting every container on a nightly schedule so intrusions do not persist
