questions.explanation: The review names the two dominant risks and B answers both: scanning images before deployment catches the known-vulnerable packages that public-registry images routinely carry, the most likely route to compromise, and dropping root strips a compromised container of the privileges that make kernel exploits and host escape practical on a shared node. Option A is wrong because an in-container antivirus agent is a host-era control transplanted badly: it bloats the image, sees only one container's namespace, and does nothing about the vulnerable packages or the root privilege; container defense lives in image hygiene and runtime policy. Option C is wrong because provenance without inspection just relocates the risk: the same unscanned, vulnerable images are served from a private address. It is worthwhile against registry tampering, as a complement to scanning. Option D is wrong because recycling containers evicts an intruder only until the same unpatched flaw readmits them; persistence is not the vulnerability, and treating restarts as cleansing mistakes the symptom for the cause.

questions.question: A development team is migrating a document-processing workload from self-managed virtual machines to a serverless functions platform. The operations lead asks which security responsibilities the team retains after the migration. What is the most accurate answer?

options.A: Securing the function code, its dependencies, its secrets, and its least-privilege IAM roles
options.B: Patching the operating system kernels of the servers on which the functions execute
options.C: Hardening the hypervisor layer that isolates the provider's tenants from one another
options.D: Managing host firewalls and antivirus on the machines running the function runtime

questions.explanation: Serverless shifts the shared-responsibility line sharply toward the provider, but never past the customer's own workload. What remains is everything the team writes or configures (A): the function code and its input handling, the third-party dependencies bundled with it (composition analysis still applies), the secrets it uses, and above all the IAM role it executes under, since over-permissioned functions are the signature serverless failure. B and D are wrong for the same reason: in a functions platform the customer cannot even reach the operating system, hosts, or runtime; the provider owns their patching and protection; both answers describe responsibilities the team held on its old self-managed VMs and would still hold under IaaS. Option C is wrong one layer deeper still: hypervisor isolation between tenants is the provider's responsibility in every cloud service model, and no customer ever hardens it.

questions.question: When a critical flaw is announced in a popular open-source logging library, a bank needs to know within hours which of its four hundred applications embed a vulnerable version, including transitive dependencies pulled in automatically during builds. Which tooling most directly answers this question?

options.A: Static analysis of each application's own source code for insecure logging patterns
options.B: Dynamic scanning of the running applications to probe for exploitable behaviors
options.C: A questionnaire asking each development team to list the libraries their apps use
options.D: Software composition analysis that inventories every dependency against vulnerability data

questions.explanation: The question being asked, which applications contain component X at a vulnerable version, is an inventory question, and software composition analysis (D) is the tooling built to answer it: it resolves each application's full dependency tree, transitive imports included, records exact versions, and matches them against vulnerability advisories, turning a fleet-wide audit into a query. Option A is wrong on target: static analysis examines code your own developers wrote for flaw patterns; it does not catalogue which third-party library versions the build pulled in. The flaw here is in someone else's code. Option B is wrong on speed and coverage: dynamically probing four hundred applications takes far longer than hours, and a vulnerable library that the scanner's inputs never trigger produces no signal while still being present. Option C is wrong because developers reliably know their direct imports and reliably do not know the transitive ones, which is exactly where such libraries hide, and any answers gathered are stale by the next build.

questions.question: Customers of a network-management vendor are breached through a signed, official product update that contained hidden malicious code; investigators find the vendor's build server had been compromised months earlier, and every customer who applied the legitimate update received the implant. Which term best describes this attack?

options.A: A watering-hole attack, since victims were compromised at a resource they habitually trust
options.B: Spear phishing, since the malicious payload reached a specifically chosen set of targets
options.C: A supply chain attack, since the vendor's build pipeline was subverted to reach its customers
options.D: An insider threat, since the compromise originated within the vendor's own build systems

questions.explanation: The attackers never touched the victims directly: they compromised a supplier's build pipeline so that the trusted product itself became the delivery vehicle, arriving with a valid signature through the official update channel, which is the definition of a supply chain attack (C) and the SolarWinds pattern precisely. The signature is what makes it devastating: the victims' verification checks passed, because the code was signed after the implant was inserted. Option A is the closest wrong answer: a watering hole also exploits a trusted habit, but it poisons a website the targets visit and exploits their browsers there; here the poison traveled inside a purchased product's update, not a webpage. Option B is wrong because spear phishing works by deceiving chosen individuals into opening a lure; no human at any customer was deceived; administrators applied a legitimate update correctly. Option D is wrong because an insider threat is an authorized person misusing their own access; the build server was breached by external attackers, and location inside the vendor does not make them insiders. When upstream trust is the vector, defenses shift to vendor assurance, build integrity, and monitoring what updates actually do.

questions.question: After a supply chain compromise, regulators ask a software vendor to state precisely which open-source and commercial components, at which versions, ship inside each of its products. The vendor cannot answer without weeks of archaeology. Which artifact, produced with each release, would have provided the answer immediately?

options.A: A software bill of materials enumerating every component and version in each release
options.B: A penetration test report demonstrating the release resisted realistic attack attempts
options.C: A hardware asset inventory recording every server involved in building the product
options.D: A change log summarizing the features and fixes the release delivered to customers

questions.explanation: The regulators are asking for a parts list, and that is literally what a software bill of materials is (A): a machine-readable inventory, generated at build time, of every component a release contains, direct and transitive, open-source and commercial, with versions and origins. With an SBOM per release, the question 'which products contain component X?' becomes a lookup; without one, it becomes the weeks of archaeology the vendor is now doing. Option B is wrong because a penetration test report attests to behavior under attack at a point in time; it contains no component inventory and cannot say what is inside the product. C inventories the wrong things: the build servers are infrastructure, and listing them says nothing about what went into the shipped artifact. Option D is wrong because change logs describe features and fixes for human readers; they rarely mention dependencies at all, let alone exhaustively with versions.

questions.question: A payments provider must ship a rewritten authentication service to production. The change passed every test, but leadership fears an unforeseen defect could lock out the entire customer base at once. Which deployment strategy best limits the blast radius of such a defect?

options.A: Blue-green deployment, cutting all traffic over to the new version while the old stands ready
options.B: A canary release, sending a small share of live traffic to the new version under monitoring
options.C: A big-bang upgrade during a weekend maintenance window with extended staff on call
options.D: Two additional weeks of soak testing in staging before releasing to every customer at once

questions.explanation: Leadership's fear is a defect that tests did not catch, so the strategy must assume the defect ships and minimize who meets it. A canary release (B) does exactly that: a small fraction of real production traffic exercises the new version while metrics are watched, so a lockout bug strands one percent of customers for minutes as opposed to all of them, and rollback is a routing change. Option A is the strong near-miss: blue-green also offers instant rollback, but its cutover sends one hundred percent of users to the new version, so the entire customer base is exposed during the window before the defect is noticed; it is the right answer when the priority is a fast, clean switch and versions cannot serve traffic side by side. Option C is wrong because timing does not shrink exposure; every customer still hits the new code at once, just on a Sunday. Option D is wrong because the feared defect is precisely the kind staging did not produce; more of the same environment yields more of the same blind spot; only production traffic reveals production behavior. When residual risk is unknown unknowns, expose it to the smallest real audience first.

questions.question: A product manager reports that the redesigned login page is shown to half of all users while the rest see the old page, and argues that because real users are exercising the new page in production, it has effectively been security tested. How should the security team respond to this claim?

options.A: Agree, because production traffic exercises more code paths than scripted security scans
options.B: Agree, provided the experiment runs long enough to reach statistical significance
options.C: Disagree, because A/B testing compares feature performance, not resistance to attack
options.D: Disagree, because only half of the users saw the new page, so coverage was incomplete

questions.explanation: An A/B test is a controlled experiment on user behavior: two variants, live traffic split between them, business metrics compared: completion rates, conversions. Its participants are benign users doing intended things, so it generates no evidence about malicious inputs, session handling under attack, or authentication bypass attempts; security assurance requires deliberately adversarial testing, DAST or penetration testing, before the redesign reaches anyone (C). A measures the wrong dimension, breadth of benign traffic: normal users walk happy paths no matter how many of them there are, while attacks are crafted inputs that ordinary usage never produces. Option B is wrong because statistical significance strengthens the UX conclusion only; a rigorous experiment measuring the wrong property yields a very confident answer to a different question. Option D is the trap for careful readers: it rejects the claim for a wrong reason, since routing every user to the new page would still test nothing adversarial; endorsing that reasoning would imply full exposure equals security testing.

questions.question: To meet a hackathon deadline, Global Bank's developers hardcoded an API key and skipped input validation, filing tickets to redo both properly later. A year on, the tickets remain open, and the estimate to retrofit the fixes has tripled as new features were built on top. Which concept should the security manager use to frame this situation for executives?

options.A: Risk transference, since responsibility now rests with whoever approved the deadline
options.B: Residual risk, since some exposure legitimately remains after controls are applied
options.C: Sunk cost, since money already spent on the shortcuts ought not drive decisions
options.D: Technical debt, since deferred engineering shortcuts compound in cost and risk over time

questions.explanation: The pattern in the stem is the definition of technical debt (D): a deliberate shortcut taken for speed, a promise to fix it later, and a remediation bill that grows as new work is layered on top. The metaphor is what makes it board-ready: the shortcut borrowed time, the tripling estimate is the interest, and this debt's principal is security exposure: a live administrative credential and unvalidated input sitting in production, which is why security debt demands tracking and scheduled repayment like any liability. Option A is wrong because transference means shifting risk to another party, an insurer or contractor, through a formal arrangement; an executive having approved a deadline shifts nothing; the bank still holds every consequence. Option B is wrong because residual risk is what remains after controls are implemented and is often acceptable; these controls were never implemented, so the exposure is untreated, not residual. Option C is wrong because sunk cost is a decision-making principle about ignoring unrecoverable past spending; the manager's problem is the future, costs still growing, not attachment to money already gone. Name deferred security work as debt with compounding interest; executives fund debt repayment far more readily than vague hygiene.

stimuli.title: Global Bank: the pipeline rebuild
stimuli.text: Global Bank is rebuilding the build pipeline for Cardless Cash, its cardless ATM withdrawal service, after a master key committed to source reached a public repository. The new design keeps the same three teams and the same weekly release. Secrets move to a managed vault. Builds run on shared runners any team can queue work on, and the repository is private, but every developer can push to the main branch. Nobody can currently say which build produced the artifact running in production. The bank's examiner has asked for evidence that the pipeline enforces the bank's own rules, not merely that the rules exist somewhere.

profile.organization: Global Bank · Cardless Cash mobile app and API
profile.environment: Private repository · shared build runners · weekly release · managed secret vault
profile.state: Pipeline rebuild after a hardcoded key reached a public repository

stimuli.title: A key in a public repository
stimuli.text: A monitoring service tells Global Bank that a production API key for its Cardless Cash service, the mobile app that lets customers withdraw at an ATM without a card, is sitting in a public repository. A developer pushed it there three days ago while working from home during a hackathon, and scanning bots reach new repositories within seconds. The key grants administrative access to the transaction backend. It is also compiled into the Android and iOS clients already in the app stores. The bank bought a managed secret vault last year and never wired it into anything, and nothing in its process would stop a credential being committed.

profile.organization: Global Bank · Cardless Cash mobile app and API
profile.environment: Hackathon build · public repository · clients already in the app stores
profile.state: Key public for three days, still valid

stimuli.title: Walking a payment API endpoint by endpoint
stimuli.text: Coastal Savings processes card transactions for its own customers and for eight hundred merchants. An administrator credential has been found reaching its backend from outside the company, and the security team is now walking the customer API endpoint by endpoint. Statements are served from a path carrying the account number in the query string. The login endpoint builds its database query by concatenating the values submitted to it. Nothing in the API records which caller owns which record. Forensic work has been slow: the servers keep seven days of logs, application logins were never recorded at all, and log review is a manual quarterly task.

profile.environment: REST API · mobile and web clients · seven-day log retention
profile.state: Administrator credential found reaching the backend from outside

stimuli.title: A penetration test of the customer portal
stimuli.text: Global Bank commissioned a penetration test of its customer web portal, the browser front end customers use for statements and transfers. The testers were given one customer login and nothing else. Every finding sits in a part of the portal that renders or fetches content on a user's behalf: a review board that stores and redisplays what customers type, the funds-transfer form, a document download endpoint that takes a filename, and a link-preview feature that fetches whatever URL a user supplies. The portal runs inside the bank's cloud account, on instances that can reach the cloud provider's own metadata service.

profile.environment: Browser front end for statements and transfers · runs in the bank's cloud account
profile.state: Test complete, four findings reported

stimuli.title: The oldest code in the estate
stimuli.text: Northbridge Clearing settles interbank payments and takes files and messages from card processors and correspondent banks all day. Its partner integration service is the oldest code it runs: a C daemon that parses binary payment messages, a Java component that accepts serialized objects from partner systems over the internet and rebuilds them in memory, and an XML invoice upload used by three suppliers. A destination-account field feeds several downstream systems, and the team maintains an ever-growing filter of known malicious strings against it. None of the service has ever been fuzzed, and a settlement transfer crashed the daemon last week.

profile.environment: C payment daemon · Java object stream · XML invoice upload
profile.state: Never fuzzed; the daemon crashed last week

stimuli.title: How a portal holds a session
stimuli.text: Kestrel Mutual, a general insurer, has commissioned a review of how its policyholder portal handles a session once someone has signed in. The login page is served over HTTPS and every page after it over plain HTTP. The session cookie can be read by any script running in the page, and is transmitted whenever a user follows a link over an unencrypted connection. Version control shows a URL one developer added during testing to save time and never removed. The application server underneath was deployed straight from the vendor's installer and has never been hardened.

profile.environment: HTTPS login, HTTP thereafter · application server from the vendor's installer
profile.state: Review of session handling only

stimuli.title: Global Bank: four programs, four models
stimuli.text: Global Bank's program office is starting four builds in one quarter and must pick a delivery model for each. A regulatory reporting system is fixed by contract: every requirement is agreed up front, formal documentation with approval gates at every stage is mandated, and scope cannot change without a contract modification. A new consumer feature enters a market whose customer needs are poorly understood and expected to shift every few weeks. A multi-year biometric authentication program depends on technology nobody has proved. And a claims-processing interface has produced two contradictory requirements documents from stakeholders who cannot say what they need.

profile.regime: Banking examination · fixed-price supplier contract on one program
profile.environment: Four builds starting in the same quarter
profile.state: Delivery model not yet chosen for any of them

stimuli.title: Two squads, two cadences
stimuli.text: Global Bank's payments squad has moved to two-week sprints and ships a product increment at the end of each one. Defects keep reaching production anyway. The regulator has told the bank that no change to the payment module may be written and merged by a single unreviewed developer, and expects that review to happen as early in development as possible. Marketing has separately put another squad on a hard launch date using time-boxed cycles, heavy prototyping and minimal up-front design, and the CISO has been asked what that approach costs in security terms.

profile.organization: Global Bank · payments and marketing squads
profile.regime: Banking examination · regulator directive on the payment module
profile.environment: Two-week sprints, an increment each sprint · a second squad on a hard launch date
profile.state: Defects still reaching production

stimuli.title: A firm that cannot show how it builds
stimuli.text: Ardent Systems writes software for payment terminals. It lost a government bid because it could not demonstrate the maturity of its development processes: internally, project success still depends on individual heroics and no two teams work alike. An improvement program has been funded and the team wants to start rewriting development procedures immediately. Its terminal firmware is separately certified, and the certifier demands evidence that defects are prevented during development as opposed to found and patched afterwards, with failure rates certified statistically. Two shortcuts taken to hit a deadline a year ago, a hardcoded credential and skipped input validation, still have open tickets and a tripled estimate.

profile.environment: No two teams work alike · terminal firmware certified separately
profile.state: Improvement program funded after a lost bid

stimuli.title: Twenty deploys a day
stimuli.text: Vantage Retail deploys to production twenty times a day through an automated pipeline. Security review is manual, performed by a separate team in the week before each quarterly compliance audit, so findings routinely reach developers months after the code shipped. A rewritten authentication service has passed every test and is ready to ship, but leadership fears an unforeseen defect could lock out the entire customer base at once. The company is in an acrimonious layoff period and a database administrator due to leave still holds commit access. The product manager has begun showing a redesigned login page to half of all users.

profile.environment: Automated pipeline, twenty production deploys a day · manual security review before each audit
profile.state: Rewritten authentication service ready to ship

stimuli.title: A flaw in a library everybody uses
stimuli.text: A critical flaw is announced in a widely used open-source logging library, and exploitation is already being reported. Global Bank runs four hundred applications and cannot say within hours which of them embed a vulnerable version, including the dependencies pulled in automatically during builds. In the same week a network-management vendor discloses that its customers were breached through a signed, official product update: investigators found the vendor's build server had been compromised months before. And the bank's own VPN appliance carries an actively exploited flaw for which the manufacturer says no patch will exist for several weeks.

profile.environment: Open-source logging library in unknown numbers of builds · vendor-supplied VPN appliance
profile.state: Flaw announced, exploitation already reported

stimuli.title: Two hundred services, no shared plumbing
stimuli.text: Trellis Pay is moving its payments backend off self-managed virtual machines. Two hundred microservices call each other directly, and security now requires mutual TLS and per-call authorization between every pair; modifying two hundred codebases has been ruled out as infeasible. A review of the container platform finds application containers running as root, built from unscanned images pulled from public registries, on shared hosts. A document-processing workload is moving to a serverless functions platform. The architects want the new payment API's threats enumerated before code is written, and the API it replaces is already taking millions of requests enumerating sequential customer identifiers, with stolen credential lists replayed against its login.

profile.environment: Two hundred microservices · container platform on shared hosts · serverless functions
profile.state: Moving off self-managed virtual machines

stimuli.title: A first application security lead
stimuli.text: Global Bank has hired its first application security lead into a company with no existing program, a small training budget and no secure-coding standard, and the lead must choose a starting point for developer training. A threat-modeling workshop for the trading platform has just produced forty distinct threats, far more than the team can address this quarter, and the lead needs a repeatable way to decide which ones get remediation effort first. A separate review is examining an episode in which a master API key became readable by anyone browsing a public repository, and is classifying each event in it.

profile.organization: Global Bank · new application security function
profile.environment: No existing program · small training budget · trading platform under review
profile.state: Lead in post four weeks

stimuli.title: Three incidents on the store estate
stimuli.text: Vantage Retail's in-store machines run a fixed, unchanging set of approved applications and staff cannot administer them. The security team is reviewing three incidents from the quarter. On one server, firewall logs show connections that no local tool reports: process listings, file searches and the installed antivirus all show nothing unusual. Antivirus quarantines one variant of a malware family, yet new infections keep appearing, each sample carrying a different hash and byte pattern while behaving identically on the host. And help-desk tickets reveal that several employees installed a free PDF converter which works as advertised and also opens a remote-control channel.

profile.environment: Fixed set of approved applications · staff cannot administer their machines
profile.state: Quarterly incident review

stimuli.title: An overnight spread, and two peer reports
stimuli.text: Overnight, malware spread to hundreds of Halden Logistics servers across a flat internal network while no user was logged in anywhere: each infected host scanned for neighbors exposing the same vulnerable file-sharing service and infected them directly. Through the sector information-sharing group it belongs to, the company received two reports the same week. A university network team traced abuse complaints to two hundred campus workstations making identical periodic connections to one overseas domain from which they fetch commands. A hospital paid attackers to recover encrypted patient records. An analyst is separately classifying code that appends itself to spreadsheet macro files.

profile.environment: Hundreds of servers on one flat segment · two peer reports received the same week
profile.state: Spread contained, committee prioritizing

stimuli.title: Global Bank: the reporting warehouse
stimuli.text: Global Bank's reporting warehouse serves branch operations, fraud analytics and its cash-in-transit contractor from one database. A customer's mailing address differs across three tables: an update routine changed one copy and missed the others, and refunds are being posted to an outdated address. The fraud reporting view hides individual case records but permits statistical queries. The contractor holds access to three datasets each rated non-sensitive on its own: vehicle maintenance schedules, fuel purchases and crew duty rosters. Nobody has reviewed what those three together would tell a reader, because each was approved on its own rating.

profile.environment: One database serving branch operations, fraud analytics and a logistics contractor
profile.state: Data-quality review after misdirected refunds

questionsV2.question: The examiner wants evidence that the pipeline enforces the bank's rules instead of merely documenting them. Which approach BEST produces that evidence?

options.A: A quarterly audit sampling merged changes against the written development standard.
options.B: A checklist each team lead signs before a release is promoted into production.
options.C: Policy expressed as machine-checked pipeline rules that fail the build and record the result.
options.D: A dashboard showing how many findings each team closed in the most recent release.

questionsV2.explanation:
An examiner asking for enforcement wants something that cannot have been skipped, and a rule that runs is the only artifact on this list with that property (C). It also produces its own evidence as a by-product, which is the second half of what was asked.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-50 Software-Enforced Separation and Policy Enforcement is the nearest control in the catalog, and it is new in Revision 5. CM-6 Configuration Settings governs the settings the rules assert, and NIST SP 800-218 PO.3.3 requires the toolchain to be configured to generate artifacts that support the security checks. Be precise about one thing: the phrase software-defined security appears in no NIST document, so SC-50 is a functional match, and it should be presented that way.
Evidence is what the machine produced.
questionsV2.recallLine: An examiner wants proof the pipeline enforces the rules and not documenting them. What produces it?

optionsShort.A: Quarterly audit sampling merges
optionsShort.B: Team lead checklist before promotion
optionsShort.C: Machine-checked rules that fail builds
optionsShort.D: Dashboard of findings closed

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: Detective when preventive is asked, sampling a quarter after the fact.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Captures a person's assertion. The stem asks for an enforced condition.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Measures remediation throughput, not whether any rule was applied.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-50 Software-Enforced Separation and Policy Enforcement (new in Rev 5); CM-6 Configuration Settings
NIST SP 800-218 | PO.3.3 toolchain generates supporting artifacts

questionsV2.question: Any team can queue work on the shared build runners. Which risk does that arrangement MOST directly create for the Cardless Cash release?

options.A: One team's build step can read another team's secrets or artifacts.
options.B: Builds will queue behind each other and the weekly release will slip.
options.C: Teams will adopt different build tools and the artifacts will diverge.
options.D: The runners will fall behind on operating-system patches between releases.

questionsV2.explanation:
A build runner holds every credential its jobs need and every artifact they produce, and a shared runner holds all of them at once. A job is arbitrary code by definition, so the team that queues it inherits whatever the runner can reach (A). The vault the bank has just bought stops helping the moment a job can ask the vault on someone else's behalf.
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 Least Privilege, SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality, and SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources name this class of exposure. Note that SC-2's Revision 4 title was Application Partitioning. NIST SP 800-218 PO.5 requires environments involved in software development to be separated and protected.
Ask what the runner can reach.
questionsV2.recallLine: Any team can queue jobs on shared build runners. Which risk does that most directly create?

optionsShort.A: Cross-team access to secrets and artifacts
optionsShort.B: Queueing delays the weekly release
optionsShort.C: Divergent build tools between teams
optionsShort.D: Runners fall behind on patching

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: A capacity concern. Queueing delays a release and crosses no boundary.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: A consistency issue between teams, and no boundary failure inside one runner.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: A real maintenance gap that shared queueing did not cause.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 Least Privilege; SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality (renamed from Rev 4 Application Partitioning); SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources
NIST SP 800-218 | PO.5 secure development environments

questionsV2.question: The rebuilt API will issue short-lived tokens instead of a master key. Which additional check MOST directly addresses the failure that let attackers read any account?

options.A: Rate limiting each token so bulk enumeration of accounts is slow.
options.B: Verifying on every request that the token's subject owns the record requested.
options.C: Rotating the token signing key on a schedule the managed vault enforces.
options.D: Logging every API call with its token subject and the record it touched.

questionsV2.explanation:
Short-lived tokens fix who is calling. The original failure was different: the API never asked whether the caller was entitled to the object it named, so any authenticated caller could read any account. A token with a fifteen-minute lifetime does that just as thoroughly as a master key did, which is why the fix is an ownership check on every request (B).
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-3 Access Enforcement requires the system to enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information, and AC-6 Least Privilege sizes what those authorizations should be. OWASP Top 10:2025 places object-level authorization failures under A01 Broken Access Control, which in the 2025 edition also absorbs server-side request forgery.
Authentication says who; authorization has to say what. Every request needs both.
questionsV2.recallLine: Short-lived tokens replace a master key. What still has to be checked on every request?

optionsShort.A: Rate limit each token
optionsShort.B: Check the subject owns the record
optionsShort.C: Rotate the signing key
optionsShort.D: Log every call and record touched

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Slows the enumeration and still returns records the caller should never see.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Protects the token's integrity. The decision made after the token is validated is where this breaks.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Detective when preventive is asked. A log records the reads it did not stop.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 Access Enforcement; AC-6 Least Privilege
OWASP Top 10:2025 | A01 Broken Access Control

questionsV2.question: The key is still live and the repository is still public. What should the team do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the offending file from the repository and rewrite its commit history to purge the key
options.B: Make the repository private so that no additional external parties can view the key
options.C: Revoke the exposed key immediately and issue a replacement through approved channels
options.D: Interview the developer to establish how the key came to be committed and pushed

questionsV2.explanation:
Automated bots scrape public repositories for credential patterns within seconds of a push. After three days, the only safe assumption is that the key has already been copied. Nothing that changes who can see the repository going forward alters that, so make the stolen value worthless first: revoke and reissue through a proper channel (C), then hunt for fraudulent use during the exposure window.
Containment comes before cleanup, and before understanding.
questionsV2.recallLine: A production API key with administrative access has sat in a public repository for three days. What should the team do FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Delete the file and rewrite commit history
optionsShort.B: Make the repository private
optionsShort.C: Revoke the key and reissue it
optionsShort.D: Interview the developer about the commit

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Treats the visible symptom. It cannot recall the copies already harvested, and leaves an active credential live meanwhile.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Fails the same way. Private visibility stops future viewers and does nothing about what is already copied.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Matters for the lessons learned and for fixing the process. Root-cause interviews come after containment.

questionsV2.question: Commits containing secrets must be blocked before they reach the central repository, in a way an individual developer cannot bypass from their own machine. Which mechanism BEST meets this?

options.A: A server-side pre-receive hook that scans incoming pushes and rejects any containing secrets
options.B: A client-side pre-commit hook on every developer workstation that runs local secret scanning
options.C: A nightly scheduled job that scans the repository contents and alerts on any secrets found
options.D: A mandatory code-review checklist item requiring reviewers to look for embedded credentials

questionsV2.explanation:
The requirement has two halves: enforcement before the secret enters the shared repository, and enforcement developers cannot switch off. Only a control running on the server satisfies both. A pre-receive hook (A) evaluates every push at the moment the server is asked to accept it and refuses the whole push if a secret is detected. Nothing to install, nothing to bypass.
A guarantee of the form 'never enters the repository' can only be enforced where the repository lives.
questionsV2.recallLine: Commits carrying secrets must be blocked before they reach the bank's central repository, unbypassable from a developer's own machine. Which mechanism BEST meets this?

optionsShort.A: Server-side pre-receive hook rejecting pushes containing secrets
optionsShort.B: Client-side pre-commit hook on each workstation
optionsShort.C: Nightly scan of repository contents, alerting
optionsShort.D: Code-review checklist item for embedded credentials

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: The closest wrong answer. Client hooks live on machines the developer controls: a flag skips them, a fresh clone lacks them.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Too late. By the nightly run the secret has been in shared history for hours, cloned and mirrored.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Relies on human review, and in pull-request workflows the code reaches the server before anyone reviews it.

questionsV2.question: The bank also wants each merge checked for hardcoded credentials and injection-prone code in its own source, without waiting for a build to be deployed anywhere. Which testing technology fits BEST?

options.A: Dynamic application security testing, which probes a running application from the outside
options.B: Static application security testing, which examines source code without executing it
options.C: Software composition analysis, which flags known vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies
options.D: Interactive application security testing, which instruments the app while tests exercise it

questionsV2.explanation:
Two constraints in the stem decide this. The flaws live in first-party source, hardcoded secrets and injection-prone patterns, and the check must run before merge, when nothing is deployed. Static analysis (B) satisfies both: it reads the code itself, so a credential string or an unsanitized query concatenation is visible directly, and it needs no running instance.
SAST reads your source, DAST probes your running app, IAST watches from inside it, SCA audits what you imported. Pick by where the flaw lives and what exists when you test.
questionsV2.recallLine: The bank wants every merge checked for hardcoded credentials and injection-prone patterns in its own source, with nothing deployed. Which testing technology fits BEST?

optionsShort.A: DAST, probing a running application from outside
optionsShort.B: SAST, examining source code without executing it
optionsShort.C: SCA, flagging known flaws in third-party dependencies
optionsShort.D: IAST, instrumenting the app during test execution

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: DAST probes a running application from outside. It cannot see a hardcoded key, and nothing runs at merge time.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: SCA inventories the third-party libraries you import against known-vulnerability data. It never reads your own code.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: IAST observes an instrumented application during test execution, so it too requires a runtime.

questionsV2.question: A request submitting the login value admin' OR '1'='1 returns every row of the customer table, on a fully patched and hardened server. Which type of flaw MOST likely explains this?

options.A: An injection flaw, because untrusted input was interpreted as part of a database command
options.B: A broken access control flaw, because the user viewed rows belonging to other customers
options.C: A security misconfiguration, because the database account held more privileges than needed
options.D: A cross-site scripting flaw, because attacker-supplied text was reflected in the response

questionsV2.explanation:
The tell is the quote and OR '1'='1. The input escaped its role as data and changed the logic of the SQL statement, turning a login check into a query that matches every row. Input interpreted as code is the mechanism that defines injection (A).
Classify a flaw by its mechanism.
questionsV2.recallLine: A login value of admin' OR '1'='1 returns every customer row from a fully patched Coastal Savings server. Which type of flaw MOST likely explains this?

optionsShort.A: Injection: input interpreted as database command
optionsShort.B: Broken access control: other customers' rows exposed
optionsShort.C: Security misconfiguration: over-privileged database account
optionsShort.D: Cross-site scripting: attacker text reflected back

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Describes a well-formed request whose authorization is never checked. This one was malformed and subverted the query.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Contradicts the stem, which follows the hardening guide. Over-privileged accounts amplify injection and never create it.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Puts the victim in the wrong place. Cross-site scripting executes script in other users' browsers.

questionsV2.question: The team must remediate that flaw at its root as opposed to filter attack traffic. Which control should it implement FIRST?

options.A: Deploy a web application firewall with rules that detect and drop known injection patterns
options.B: Sanitize request input by stripping quotes, comments, and SQL keywords before processing
options.C: Rewrite the data-access code to use parameterized queries that bind input as data values
options.D: Encrypt the customer database so records extracted through the flaw stay unreadable

questionsV2.explanation: Injection exists because input and query text are concatenated into one string the database must reinterpret. Parameterized queries remove that root cause (C). The statement's structure is compiled first and input binds strictly as data, so no input value can change what the query does. Filtering the traffic and validating the input are both worthwhile defense in depth, and neither removes the concatenation that makes the flaw possible.
questionsV2.recallLine: Coastal Savings must fix the login endpoint's injection flaw at its root and not filter attack traffic. Which control should it implement FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Deploy a WAF dropping known injection patterns
optionsShort.B: Strip quotes, comments and SQL keywords from input
optionsShort.C: Rewrite data access to bind input as values
optionsShort.D: Encrypt the customer database at rest

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: A compensating control: pattern-based, bypassable through encoding tricks, and it leaves the vulnerable code in place.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Chases an open-ended set of bypasses and breaks legitimate input such as O'Brien.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Answers stolen-media risk. The application decrypts to serve queries, so data stolen through it arrives in plaintext.

questionsV2.question: Investigators establish the attackers were active for five months and no alert ever fired. Which improvement should the security program prioritize?

options.A: Deploying stronger encryption for stored data so future intrusions yield nothing readable
options.B: Centralized log collection with longer retention and automated alerting on suspicious activity
options.C: Commissioning an annual external penetration test to uncover exploitable weaknesses
options.D: Adopting a stricter rotation schedule for all privileged administrator account passwords

questionsV2.explanation:
Five months of undetected activity is a visibility failure, and the stem lists its three ingredients: logs that expire in a week, security-relevant events never captured, and review too infrequent and manual to notice anything. Centralized collection with longer retention and automated alerting attacks all three (B). Collect logs centrally where intruders cannot quietly erase them, retain them well beyond realistic dwell times so investigations have evidence, and let automation watch continuously, so detection happens in hours.
Long dwell times indict detection. Build logging and monitoring before buying more prevention.
questionsV2.recallLine: Attackers worked inside Coastal Savings' payment API for five months and no alert ever fired. Which improvement should the security program prioritize?

optionsShort.A: Stronger encryption for stored data
optionsShort.B: Central logs, longer retention, automated alerting
optionsShort.C: An annual external penetration test
optionsShort.D: Stricter rotation of privileged account passwords

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Protects confidentiality against stolen media. Attackers using compromised accounts read data exactly as users do.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: A point-in-time probe for ways in. The demonstrated failure is not knowing when someone is already inside.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Nothing in the incident ties it to stale passwords, and rotation would not have surfaced a five-month presence.

questionsV2.question: Simply viewing a certain product review causes browsers to send their session cookies to an unknown domain; script tags stored in the review text are rendered verbatim to every visitor. Which remediation MOST directly addresses this?

options.A: Add anti-forgery tokens to every state-changing form so requests from other sites are rejected
options.B: Move all pages to HTTPS so session cookies are protected from network eavesdropping
options.C: Use parameterized queries so review text is treated as data, not command structure
options.D: Encode user-supplied content on output so browsers render it as text as opposed to script

questionsV2.explanation: This is stored cross-site scripting. Attacker-supplied markup was saved and later delivered into victims' pages, where the browser executed it. The defect sits at the rendering step, so the direct fix is contextual output encoding (D): the stored text displays as inert characters and is never parsed as script. A Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add depth.
questionsV2.recallLine: Script tags stored in a product review render verbatim and send every viewer's session cookie to an unknown domain. Which remediation MOST directly addresses this?

optionsShort.A: Anti-forgery tokens on state-changing forms
optionsShort.B: Move all portal pages to HTTPS
optionsShort.C: Parameterized queries for stored review text
optionsShort.D: Encode user content on output as text

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Counters CSRF, where an attacker forges requests using the victim's session. Here the attacker injected script.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Protects cookies in transit. These are read by script running inside the page itself, over any transport.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Stops SQL injection. The review was stored through a legitimate write, and the database behaved correctly.

questionsV2.question: A customer signed in to the portal opens an email link in another tab, and a transfer they never initiated is sent from their own browser with a valid session cookie. Which control BEST prevents this?

options.A: Require multi-factor authentication when the customer first signs in to the banking site
options.B: Embed unpredictable per-session tokens in forms and reject requests that lack a valid one
options.C: Encode all user-supplied content the application displays to keep scripts from executing
options.D: Lock accounts after repeated failed logins to defeat automated password guessing

questionsV2.explanation: What happened is cross-site request forgery. The attacker's page made the victim's browser submit a request, the browser attached the session cookie, and the server saw an authenticated transfer. An anti-CSRF token defeats it (B), because the forging site cannot read the unpredictable token to include it, so the forged request fails validation. SameSite cookie attributes reinforce the same boundary. Step-up authentication per transfer would be a separate, additional control.
questionsV2.recallLine: A signed-in customer opens an emailed link and their own browser sends a transfer they never initiated. Which control BEST prevents this?

optionsShort.A: Multi-factor authentication at customer sign-in
optionsShort.B: Unpredictable per-session tokens required in forms
optionsShort.C: Encode displayed content so scripts cannot run
optionsShort.D: Lock accounts after repeated failed logins

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Protects the wrong moment. MFA strengthens the login event, and this attack rides a session already authenticated.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Counters cross-site scripting, and no script was injected into the bank's pages here.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Responds to failed logins, of which there were none. The attacker never touched credentials.

questionsV2.question: The link-preview feature is given http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and returns the cloud account's temporary credentials, fetched by the application server itself. Which vulnerability class is this?

options.A: Server-side request forgery, since the server was induced to request an internal resource
options.B: Cross-site request forgery, since a forged request was executed without a victim's intent
options.C: XML external entity injection, since a parser was made to retrieve a protected document
options.D: An open redirect, since the application forwarded a browser to an attacker-chosen address

questionsV2.explanation:
The decisive detail is who made the request: the application server itself fetched the metadata address on the attacker's behalf. Abusing a server's own network position to reach resources the attacker cannot touch directly, such as internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint only the instance may query, is server-side request forgery (A). The fix is an allow-list of fetchable destinations with internal and link-local ranges denied.
SSRF forges requests from the server, CSRF forges them from the user. Identify the party being tricked.
questionsV2.recallLine: The link-preview feature fetches http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and hands back the cloud account's temporary credentials. Which vulnerability class is this?

optionsShort.A: Server-side request forgery by the application server
optionsShort.B: Cross-site request forgery without the victim's intent
optionsShort.C: XML external entity injection through a parser
optionsShort.D: An open redirect to an attacker-chosen address

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: In CSRF the forged request comes from a victim's browser, riding that session. Here the server does the fetching.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Requires an XML parser resolving external entities, and a URL form field involves no XML at all.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Bounces the client's browser to another site. This server retrieved the content itself and handed it back.

questionsV2.question: A crash dump shows an oversized message-length field overwriting the C daemon's return address, after which the service executed attacker-supplied instructions. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?

options.A: Validate length fields and use bounds-checked memory operations for every buffer write
options.B: Enable address space layout randomization so injected code lands at unpredictable locations
options.C: Filter inbound packets at the network firewall to drop traffic from untrusted address ranges
options.D: Raise the service's logging level so malformed packets are recorded for later investigation

questionsV2.explanation:
A buffer overflow happens when code writes more data into a buffer than was allocated, corrupting adjacent memory, here the saved return address. The root cause is the unchecked write, so the fix is in the code (A): validate untrusted length fields and use bounds-checked operations so an oversized value can no longer spill past the buffer. Migrating hot paths to a memory-safe language is the same idea taken further.
Mitigations raise attacker cost. Only correct code removes the vulnerability.
questionsV2.recallLine: An oversized message-length field overwrote the C daemon's return address and the service then ran attacker instructions. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?

optionsShort.A: Validate lengths and bounds-check every buffer write
optionsShort.B: Enable ASLR so injected code lands unpredictably
optionsShort.C: Drop untrusted address ranges at the firewall
optionsShort.D: Raise logging so malformed packets are recorded

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: An exploit mitigation. ASLR makes a successful overflow harder to weaponize and leaves the defect in place.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: The service must accept client packets to function, and any permitted source can send the malformed field.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Detective when preventive is asked. Logging records the compromise after it has happened.

questionsV2.question: An uploaded invoice whose DOCTYPE declaration defines an external entity pointing at /etc/passwd returns that file's contents. Which change BEST fixes this flaw at its source?

options.A: Validate that uploaded invoices are well-formed XML before passing them to the parser
options.B: Configure the XML parser to disable document type definitions and external entity resolution
options.C: Run the upload service in a container so its file reads are confined to the container image
options.D: Scan uploaded files with antivirus to reject those containing known malicious markup

questionsV2.explanation:
XML external entity injection is unusual among injection flaws: the vulnerability is a feature. The parser does exactly what DTD processing specifies and resolves an entity that happens to point at a local file. So the source-level fix is configuration (B). Turn off DTDs and external entity resolution, and the attack stops being expressible.
When a parser's features are the attack surface, harden its configuration. The lesson generalizes to any dangerous default.
questionsV2.recallLine: An uploaded invoice whose DOCTYPE points at /etc/passwd returns that file's contents to the supplier. Which change BEST fixes the flaw at its source?

optionsShort.A: Check uploads are well-formed XML first
optionsShort.B: Disable DTDs and entity resolution
optionsShort.C: Run the upload service in a container
optionsShort.D: Antivirus-scan uploads for malicious markup

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Checks syntax, and the exploit file is perfectly well-formed XML. This attack is syntactically impeccable.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Shrinks the blast radius and leaves the flaw. Container secrets stay readable and entity fetches still reach the network.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Recognizes known malware. A three-line DOCTYPE crafted for this one application matches nothing in a signature set.

questionsV2.question: A settlement transfer crashed the daemon after debiting the source account; on restart the half-completed change was still there and the money was in neither account. Which ACID property failed?

options.A: Atomicity, because a transaction's operations must apply together or leave no effect at all
options.B: Isolation, because concurrent transactions must remain invisible to one another while running
options.C: Durability, because once a transaction commits its effects must survive crashes and remain permanent
options.D: Consistency, because each transaction must move the database between valid states

questionsV2.explanation:
The debit and credit form one logical transaction, and the system let half of it persist. Atomicity forbids exactly that (A): all of a transaction's operations commit together, or recovery rolls every one of them back so the transaction never happened. A correct engine would have undone the debit on restart.
Partial effects persisting after recovery point at atomicity. Constraint violations at commit point at consistency.
questionsV2.recallLine: A settlement transfer crashed after the debit had persisted and the matching credit never happened. Which ACID property failed?

optionsShort.A: Atomicity: all operations apply or none
optionsShort.B: Isolation: concurrent transactions stay mutually invisible
optionsShort.C: Durability: committed effects survive a crash
optionsShort.D: Consistency: transactions move between valid states

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Governs interference between transactions running concurrently. This failure involved a single transaction and a crash.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Protects work that had committed. Here uncommitted, partial work survived when it should have vanished.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: The tempting one, because the books are inconsistent now. That unbalanced state is the consequence, not the property broken.

questionsV2.question: Which pair of cookie attributes MOST directly closes the script-access and unencrypted-transport exposures together?

options.A: Domain and Path, which limit the hosts and URL prefixes to which the cookie is sent
options.B: HttpOnly and Secure, which deny script access and restrict the cookie to encrypted transport
options.C: Max-Age and Expires, which bound how long the browser retains the session cookie
options.D: SameSite and Path, which control whether cross-site navigation includes the cookie

questionsV2.explanation: Map each finding to the attribute built for it. HttpOnly hides the cookie from the page's JavaScript, so even a successful XSS payload cannot read it. Secure forbids the browser from sending the cookie over anything but an encrypted connection. HttpOnly and Secure carry both (B).
questionsV2.recallLine: Kestrel Mutual's session cookie is readable by page scripts and travels over plain HTTP. Which pair of cookie attributes MOST directly closes both exposures?

optionsShort.A: Domain and Path, scoping hosts and prefixes
optionsShort.B: HttpOnly and Secure, denying scripts and cleartext
optionsShort.C: Max-Age and Expires, bounding cookie lifetime
optionsShort.D: SameSite and Path, governing cross-site navigation

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Scopes which requests include the cookie. Within that scope, scripts can still read it and HTTP links still carry it.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Shrinks the window of misuse and closes neither exposure. A cookie can be stolen or sniffed in its first minute.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: SameSite governs whether cross-site requests attach the cookie, a CSRF defense. Neither finding is cross-site.

questionsV2.question: That leftover URL is absent from all design documents and grants administrative access with no credentials. What is the MOST accurate name for this finding?

options.A: A logic bomb left in the code awaiting a trigger condition chosen by the developer
options.B: A Trojan horse embedded in the application and disguised as a legitimate feature
options.C: A maintenance hook, an undocumented backdoor that bypasses normal authentication
options.D: A race condition that intermittently allows requests to skip the authentication check

questionsV2.explanation:
An undocumented access path that developers created for their own convenience, sidestepping authentication, is the definition of a maintenance hook (C). Intent barely matters. Left in production, it grants the same unauthenticated administrative access to whoever finds it, which is why removal has to be verified before release.
Deliberate shortcut paths are backdoors, and the fix is process: code review and pre-release checks that hunt for them.
questionsV2.recallLine: A leftover URL absent from every design document grants administrative access with no credentials at all. What is the MOST accurate name for this finding?

optionsShort.A: A logic bomb awaiting a chosen trigger
optionsShort.B: A Trojan horse disguised as a feature
optionsShort.C: A maintenance hook bypassing normal authentication
optionsShort.D: A race condition intermittently skipping authentication

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Carries a malicious payload waiting on a trigger such as a date. This URL does nothing on its own.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Malicious software a victim is deceived into installing because it looks desirable. This is the bank's own application.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: A timing defect that appears intermittently. This bypass is deterministic and works on every request.

questionsV2.question: The scan also finds the vendor's sample applications installed, an admin console on its documented default password, directory listing enabled, and stack traces returned to clients. Which OWASP category fits?

options.A: Security misconfiguration, since insecure default settings and features were left in place
options.B: Broken access control, since unauthorized parties could reach administrative functions
options.C: Vulnerable and outdated components, since the server carried unneeded sample software
options.D: Identification and authentication failures, since a default password guarded the console

questionsV2.explanation: Look for the common cause. Sample apps present, default credentials unchanged, directory listing on, verbose errors leaking internals: four symptoms of one omission, an unhardened out-of-the-box deployment. That is security misconfiguration (A), and its remedy is a repeatable hardening baseline applied to every build. The question asks where the findings as a set belong, so the category has to cover all four.
questionsV2.recallLine: A scan finds vendor sample apps, a default admin password, directory listing enabled and stack traces returned to clients. Which OWASP category fits these findings?

optionsShort.A: Security misconfiguration from insecure defaults left in place
optionsShort.B: Broken access control reaching administrative functions
optionsShort.C: Vulnerable and outdated components, the sample software
optionsShort.D: Identification and authentication failures from the default password

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Describes missing or faulty authorization logic. Here the checks exist and a published password undermined them.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Targets software that is outdated or known-vulnerable. The samples' sin is being present and unneeded.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: The defensible near-miss, and right if the password stood alone. It cannot account for listings, traces or sample apps.

questionsV2.question: Leadership wants working software delivered early and refined continuously from real user feedback. Which approach BEST fits the consumer feature?

options.A: Waterfall, since completing the full design before coding avoids expensive rework later
options.B: Cleanroom, since formally verified increments give the highest confidence in each release
options.C: Agile, since short iterations and continuous customer feedback absorb changing requirements
options.D: The V-model, since pairing every build phase with a matching test phase catches defects early

questionsV2.explanation: Rapidly shifting requirements plus a demand for early, continuously refined releases are the exact conditions iterative Agile methods were created for (C). Each short cycle delivers working software and folds user feedback into the next.
questionsV2.recallLine: Leadership wants the new consumer feature delivered early and refined continuously from real user feedback in a market that shifts every few weeks. Which approach fits BEST?

optionsShort.A: Waterfall, full design completed before coding
optionsShort.B: Cleanroom, formally verified increments each release
optionsShort.C: Agile, short iterations absorbing changing requirements
optionsShort.D: V-model, each build phase paired with testing

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Assumes requirements can be fixed before design begins. Here they cannot, so the design describes the wrong product.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Slow, and it assumes a precise spec exists. Cleanroom's formal verification suits safety-critical software.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Still a sequential, plan-driven shape. Its paired test phases verify a fixed specification and cannot absorb change.

questionsV2.question: Management's chief concern on the biometric program is that unexplored technical risks could sink it, and it wants each round of work to open with an explicit risk evaluation. Which lifecycle model fits?

options.A: The spiral model, in which each cycle opens with objectives and a fresh risk analysis
options.B: Extreme Programming, in which paired developers and test-first coding control quality
options.C: The waterfall model, in which risks are addressed once during the initial planning phase
options.D: Rapid Application Development, in which quick prototypes surface problems through user feedback

questionsV2.explanation: Management has literally described the spiral model's engine (A): repeated cycles that each begin by setting objectives, evaluating risks and alternatives, often retiring the worst risk with a prototype, before committing to the next round of investment. It was conceived for large projects burdened with unproven technology.
questionsV2.recallLine: Management fears unproven technology could sink the biometric program and wants every round of work to open with an explicit risk evaluation. Which lifecycle model fits?

optionsShort.A: Spiral, each cycle opening with fresh risk analysis
optionsShort.B: Extreme Programming, pairing and test-first coding
optionsShort.C: Waterfall, risks addressed once during planning
optionsShort.D: RAD, quick prototypes surfacing problems through feedback

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Manages code quality within iterations. XP has no project-level gate that weighs risk before funding continues.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Does one up-front risk pass, which cannot handle risks that surface mid-build. With novel technology most of them do.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Optimizes for speed and requirements discovery through user reaction. RAD imposes no formal risk-evaluation checkpoint.

questionsV2.question: The delivery lead wants claims-processing stakeholders to react to something concrete before the team commits to full development. Which approach BEST serves this goal?

options.A: Completing a comprehensive requirements specification and having every stakeholder sign it
options.B: Adopting cleanroom methods so that defects are formally prevented from the earliest phase
options.C: Proceeding directly to full construction so users can react to the finished system itself
options.D: Building a limited working model of the interface for stakeholders to evaluate and refine

questionsV2.explanation:
When stakeholders cannot say what they want, showing beats asking. A prototype gives them something concrete to react to (D), converts vague or contradictory wishes into specific corrections, and costs little enough to throw away and iterate. That is the entire reason prototyping exists as a development approach.
Prototype when requirements are the risk. Formalize when correctness against known requirements is the risk.
questionsV2.recallLine: Claims-processing stakeholders have produced two contradictory requirements documents. Which approach BEST gives them something concrete to react to before the team commits?

optionsShort.A: A comprehensive specification, signed by every stakeholder
optionsShort.B: Cleanroom methods preventing defects formally
optionsShort.C: Proceed directly to full construction
optionsShort.D: A limited working model for stakeholders to evaluate

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Doubles down on a technique that has already failed twice. The conflicts resurface as change requests during build.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Prevents implementation defects. Here the specification is the problem, and a formally verified wrong product is wrong.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: The largest possible bet on the least information. Feedback arrives after the full cost is sunk.

questionsV2.question: The security architect is asked how security work should fit a process that ships an increment every two weeks. Which arrangement BEST integrates the two?

options.A: Hold all security requirements for a hardening phase scheduled after the final sprint
options.B: Have the security team test a copy of the product on its own quarterly timetable
options.C: Put security items in the product backlog and security checks in the definition of done
options.D: Dedicate one sprint per quarter to security fixes while feature work pauses

questionsV2.explanation: In Scrum, work exists only if it is in the product backlog, and quality bars exist only in the definition of done. That is where security has to live (C). Threat-driven requirements and abuse cases enter the backlog to be prioritized alongside features, and the definition of done makes passing security checks a condition of calling any increment complete. Every sprint then ships software that has met the bar.
questionsV2.recallLine: Global Bank's payments squad ships a product increment every two weeks. Which arrangement BEST integrates security work into that cadence?

optionsShort.A: A hardening phase after the final sprint
optionsShort.B: Security tests a copy on a quarterly timetable
optionsShort.C: Security items in backlog and definition of done
optionsShort.D: One security-only sprint each quarter

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Recreates the bolt-on waterfall pattern inside an iterative process. Every increment before it ships unexamined.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Lags up to six releases behind, so findings arrive divorced from the sprint that caused them.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: The seductive anti-pattern. A periodic security sprint batches risk and lets unvetted features ship for months.

questionsV2.question: Which pairing of Extreme Programming practices MOST directly catches defects at the moment the code is being written?

options.A: The planning game and small releases, which shorten the feedback loop with customers
options.B: Collective code ownership and coding standards, which keep the code base uniform
options.C: On-site customer and system metaphor, which keep development aligned with business intent
options.D: Pair programming and test-driven development, which review and test code as it is typed

questionsV2.explanation: The discriminator is the moment the code is being written, and two XP practices operate at exactly that instant (D). In test-driven development the failing test exists before the code, so the first run verifies the new logic immediately. In pair programming a second developer reviews each line as it appears, catching slips the author is blind to. Together they are XP's tightest defect-feedback loop.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which pairing of Extreme Programming practices MOST directly catches defects at the moment payment code is being typed?

optionsShort.A: Planning game and small releases
optionsShort.B: Collective ownership and coding standards
optionsShort.C: On-site customer and system metaphor
optionsShort.D: Pair programming and test-driven development

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Operates at release granularity, surfacing wrong priorities and integration surprises in days or weeks.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Improves maintainability and consistency. It examines nothing at the moment the code is created.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Aligns the product with business intent. It catches building the wrong thing, not writing it wrongly.

questionsV2.question: Which answer MOST accurately names the greatest security risk the second squad's compressed delivery style introduces?

options.A: Schedule pressure squeezes security requirements and testing out of each compressed cycle
options.B: The extensive documentation the method demands will delay security review sign-offs
options.C: Requirements frozen at project start will block security fixes once the cycles begin
options.D: The absence of user involvement means real-world abuse goes unconsidered until launch

questionsV2.explanation:
RAD trades rigor for speed. When a time-box tightens, whatever the demo does not demand gets cut, and security work such as threat modeling and security test cases is the classic casualty (A). Worse, prototypes never meant for production get promoted into it under deadline pressure with their shortcuts intact. This is the very pattern behind Global Bank's hackathon key.
Fast lifecycles do not forbid security work. They starve it, and the countermeasure is making security part of each cycle's definition of done.
questionsV2.recallLine: Marketing's squad uses time-boxed cycles, heavy prototyping and minimal up-front design. Which answer MOST accurately names the greatest security risk that style introduces?

optionsShort.A: Schedule pressure squeezes out security requirements and testing
optionsShort.B: Extensive documentation delays security sign-offs
optionsShort.C: Frozen requirements block security fixes mid-project
optionsShort.D: No user involvement leaves abuse unconsidered

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Describes the opposite methodology. RAD is documentation-light by design, and heavy gates belong to waterfall.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: RAD embraces changing requirements across iterations. Frozen baselines are a plan-driven trait.

D.label: true of a different thing
D.wouldAnswer: A false premise. RAD is built around continuous user involvement, though users exercise only intended behavior.

questionsV2.question: The firm wants a recognized framework for assessing and improving how it builds software. Which BEST meets that goal?

options.A: STRIDE, which categorizes design-level threats to a system under development
options.B: CVSS, which scores the severity of published vulnerabilities on a common scale
options.C: The OWASP Top 10, which ranks the most critical web application risk categories
options.D: CMMI, which appraises process maturity in staged levels and guides improvement

questionsV2.explanation:
The firm's problem is the process itself: ad hoc, heroics-dependent, inconsistent across teams, which is the textbook description of the lowest maturity level. CMMI is built for exactly this (D). It appraises how an organization develops software against defined maturity levels, produces the recognized rating acquirers ask for, and lays out the practice areas to institutionalize next.
Distinguish product-level tools, which look at threats, vulnerabilities and risks, from organization-level frameworks that measure and mature the process itself.
questionsV2.recallLine: Ardent Systems lost a bid because it could not show how consistently its teams build software. Which recognized framework BEST meets that goal?

optionsShort.A: STRIDE, categorizing design-level threats
optionsShort.B: CVSS, scoring published vulnerability severity
optionsShort.C: OWASP Top 10, ranking common web risks
optionsShort.D: CMMI, appraising process maturity in staged levels

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Examines one system's design for threat categories. STRIDE says nothing about how consistently the firm works.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Rates individual known vulnerabilities for prioritization. CVSS measures findings, never a process.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: The OWASP Top 10 educates developers about common application risks. Awareness is no evidence of repeatable process.

questionsV2.question: The certifier wants defects prevented during development as opposed to found and patched afterwards, with failure rates certified statistically. Which software engineering approach aligns BEST?

options.A: Extreme Programming, relying on test-driven development and continuous pair review
options.B: Cleanroom engineering, using formal specification, verification, and statistical quality control
options.C: Rapid application development, iterating prototypes quickly until users accept the behavior
options.D: Scrum, delivering the firmware in sprints with a defect backlog groomed by the product owner

questionsV2.explanation: The regulator's two demands are the two pillars of cleanroom software engineering (B). Defects are prevented before test, through formal specification and mathematically based verification of the code. Quality is then demonstrated through statistical usage testing that supports certified reliability claims, which is precisely the evidence sought.
questionsV2.recallLine: The firmware certifier wants defects prevented during development as opposed to patched afterwards, with failure rates certified statistically. Which engineering approach aligns BEST?

optionsShort.A: Extreme Programming, test-driven development and pair review
optionsShort.B: Cleanroom, formal specification, verification, statistical quality control
optionsShort.C: RAD, iterating prototypes until users accept
optionsShort.D: Scrum, sprints with a groomed defect backlog

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: The strongest wrong answer. TDD and pair review find defects after they are written, and certify no failure rate.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Optimizes speed and user acceptance. RAD's tolerance for rough prototypes is the opposite of certifiable rigor.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: A management wrapper that routes defects into a backlog for later, and prescribes no engineering rigor at all.

questionsV2.question: Which concept should the security manager use to frame the two open hackathon tickets for executives?
