options.A: Risk transference, since responsibility now rests with whoever approved the deadline
options.B: Residual risk, since some exposure legitimately remains after controls are applied
options.C: Sunk cost, since money already spent on the shortcuts ought not drive decisions
options.D: Technical debt, since deferred engineering shortcuts compound in cost and risk over time

questionsV2.explanation:
A deliberate shortcut taken for speed, a promise to fix it later, and a remediation bill that grows as new work is layered on top. That is the definition of technical debt (D). The metaphor is what makes it board-ready: the shortcut borrowed time, the tripling estimate is the interest, and this debt's principal is security exposure, a live administrative credential and unvalidated input sitting in production. Security debt earns tracking and scheduled repayment like any liability.
Name deferred security work as debt with compounding interest. Executives fund debt repayment far more readily than vague hygiene.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two hackathon shortcuts taken a year ago still sit in production with open tickets and a tripled estimate. Which concept should the security manager use with executives?

optionsShort.A: Risk transference to whoever approved the deadline
optionsShort.B: Residual risk remaining after controls are applied
optionsShort.C: Sunk cost that should not drive decisions
optionsShort.D: Technical debt compounding in cost and risk

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Transference moves risk to an insurer or contractor by formal arrangement. The bank still holds every consequence.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Describes what remains after controls are implemented. These controls were never implemented, so the exposure is untreated.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: A principle about ignoring unrecoverable past spending. The problem here is the future, and costs still growing.

questionsV2.question: The administrator inserts code that will delete the payroll tables if his employee ID ever disappears from the HR system. Which safeguard would MOST likely catch this insertion before it reaches production?

options.A: Antivirus scanning on the database server to detect malicious executable files
options.B: Full-disk encryption of the storage volumes holding the payroll tables
options.C: An annual disaster-recovery exercise proving that payroll can be restored intact from backup tapes
options.D: Mandatory peer review of every code change before it can be merged and deployed

questionsV2.explanation:
This is a logic bomb: legitimate-looking code carrying a malicious trigger. An authorized insider wrote it and it contains no malware signature, so the control most likely to catch it is another human reading the change. Mandatory peer review (D) puts a second set of eyes on a deletion routine conditioned on an HR lookup, an obvious red flag, and its mere existence deters the attempt.
Insider code threats are defeated by process controls on the change pipeline.
questionsV2.recallLine: A departing administrator inserts code that deletes the payroll tables if his employee ID leaves the HR system. Which safeguard would MOST likely catch it beforehand?

optionsShort.A: Antivirus scanning on the database server
optionsShort.B: Full-disk encryption of the payroll volumes
optionsShort.C: An annual disaster-recovery restore exercise
optionsShort.D: Mandatory peer review of every code change

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Hunts foreign binaries. The bomb is source code committed through normal channels.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Protects confidentiality of data at rest. The bomb deletes through authorized paths that decrypt transparently.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Corrective. Recovery exercises limit the damage after detonation rather than prevent it.

questionsV2.question: Which deployment strategy BEST limits the blast radius of an unforeseen defect in the rewritten authentication service?

options.A: Blue-green deployment, cutting all traffic over to the new version while the old stands ready
options.B: A canary release, sending a small share of live traffic to the new version under monitoring
options.C: A big-bang upgrade during a weekend maintenance window with extended staff on call
options.D: Two additional weeks of soak testing in staging before releasing to every customer at once

questionsV2.explanation:
Leadership fears a defect the tests did not catch, so the strategy has to assume the defect ships and minimize who meets it. A canary release does exactly that (B). A small fraction of real production traffic exercises the new version while metrics are watched, so a lockout bug strands one percent of customers for minutes, and rollback is a routing change.
When residual risk is unknown unknowns, expose it to the smallest real audience first.
questionsV2.recallLine: Leadership fears an unforeseen defect in the rewritten authentication service could lock out every customer at once. Which deployment strategy BEST limits the blast radius?

optionsShort.A: Blue-green cutover with the old version standing by
optionsShort.B: A canary release monitored on a small traffic share
optionsShort.C: A big-bang weekend upgrade with staff on call
optionsShort.D: Two more weeks of soak testing in staging

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: The strong near-miss, with instant rollback. Its cutover still sends every user to the new version at once.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Changes only the timing. Every customer still hits the new code at once, on a Sunday.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: More of the same blind spot. The feared defect is precisely the kind staging did not produce.

questionsV2.question: The product manager argues that because real users are exercising the new login page in production, it has effectively been security tested. How should the security team respond?

options.A: Agree, because production traffic exercises more code paths than scripted security scans
options.B: Agree, provided the experiment runs long enough to reach statistical significance
options.C: Disagree, because A/B testing compares feature performance, not resistance to attack
options.D: Disagree, because half the users saw the old page, so coverage was incomplete

questionsV2.explanation: An A/B test is a controlled experiment on user behavior: two variants, live traffic split between them, business metrics compared, completion rates and conversions. Its participants are benign users doing intended things, so it generates no evidence about malicious inputs, session handling under attack, or authentication bypass attempts. Security assurance requires deliberately adversarial testing, DAST or penetration testing, before the redesign reaches anyone (C).
questionsV2.recallLine: The product manager claims the redesigned login page is effectively security tested because half of all users are exercising it in production. How should the security team respond?

optionsShort.A: Agree: production traffic covers more code paths
optionsShort.B: Agree once the experiment reaches statistical significance
optionsShort.C: Disagree: A/B tests compare features, not attack resistance
optionsShort.D: Disagree: half the users saw the old page

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Measures breadth of benign traffic. Attacks are crafted inputs that ordinary usage never produces.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Strengthens the UX conclusion alone. A rigorous experiment on the wrong property answers a different question.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: The trap for careful readers. Routing every user to the new page would still test nothing adversarial.

questionsV2.question: Which tooling MOST directly answers which of the four hundred applications embed a vulnerable version, transitive dependencies included?

options.A: Static analysis of each application's own source code for insecure logging patterns
options.B: Dynamic scanning of the running applications to probe for exploitable behaviors
options.C: A questionnaire asking each development team to list the libraries their apps use
options.D: Software composition analysis that inventories every dependency against vulnerability data

questionsV2.explanation: Which applications contain component X at a vulnerable version is an inventory question, and software composition analysis is the tooling built to answer it (D). It resolves each application's full dependency tree, transitive imports included, records exact versions, and matches them against vulnerability advisories. A fleet-wide audit becomes a query.
questionsV2.recallLine: Global Bank cannot say which of its four hundred applications embed the vulnerable logging library, transitive imports included. Which tooling MOST directly answers that?

optionsShort.A: Static analysis of each application's own source
optionsShort.B: Dynamic scanning of the running applications
optionsShort.C: A questionnaire asking teams which libraries they use
optionsShort.D: Composition analysis inventorying dependencies against vulnerability data

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Examines code your own developers wrote. It never catalogs which third-party library versions the build pulled in.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Too slow and too partial. A vulnerable library the scanner's inputs never trigger produces no signal while sitting there.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Developers know their direct imports and not the transitive ones, which is exactly where such libraries hide.

questionsV2.question: Every customer who applied the vendor's legitimate update received the implant. Which term BEST describes this attack?

options.A: A watering-hole attack, since victims were compromised at a resource they habitually trust
options.B: Spear phishing, since the malicious payload reached a specifically chosen set of targets
options.C: A supply chain attack, since the vendor's build pipeline was subverted to reach its customers
options.D: An insider threat, since the compromise originated within the vendor's own build systems

questionsV2.explanation:
The attackers never touched the victims directly. They compromised a supplier's build pipeline so the trusted product itself became the delivery vehicle, arriving with a valid signature through the official update channel. That is the definition of a supply chain attack (C), and the SolarWinds pattern precisely. The signature is what makes it devastating: verification passed at every customer, because the code was signed after the implant went in.
When upstream trust is the vector, defenses shift to vendor assurance, build integrity, and monitoring what updates actually do.
questionsV2.recallLine: Every customer that applied a network vendor's signed, official update received an implant planted months earlier on the vendor's build server. Which term BEST describes this?

optionsShort.A: A watering-hole attack on a trusted resource
optionsShort.B: Spear phishing aimed at chosen targets
optionsShort.C: A supply chain attack through the build pipeline
optionsShort.D: An insider threat within the vendor's systems

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: The closest wrong answer. A watering hole poisons a site the targets visit; this poison rode inside a purchased product.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Works by deceiving chosen individuals. No human was deceived; administrators applied a legitimate update correctly.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Requires an authorized person misusing their own access. Breaching the build server does not make attackers insiders.

questionsV2.question: Regulators ask that vendor to state precisely which components, at which versions, ship inside each product, and it cannot answer without weeks of archaeology. Which artifact would have answered immediately?

options.A: A software bill of materials enumerating every component and version in each release
options.B: A penetration test report demonstrating the release resisted realistic attack attempts
options.C: A hardware asset inventory recording every server involved in building the product
options.D: A change log summarizing the features and fixes the release delivered to customers

questionsV2.explanation: The regulators are asking for a parts list, and that is literally what a software bill of materials is (A). A machine-readable inventory, generated at build time, of every component a release contains, direct and transitive, open-source and commercial, with versions and origins. With an SBOM per release, 'which products contain component X?' becomes a lookup. Without one it becomes the weeks of archaeology the vendor is now doing.
questionsV2.recallLine: Regulators want the vendor to state which components, at which versions, ship inside each product release. Which artifact would have answered immediately?

optionsShort.A: A software bill of materials per release
optionsShort.B: A penetration test report for the release
optionsShort.C: A hardware inventory of the build servers
optionsShort.D: A change log of features and fixes

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Attests to behavior under attack at a point in time. The report contains no component inventory.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Inventories infrastructure. Listing the build servers says nothing about what went into the shipped artifact.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Describes features and fixes for human readers. Change logs rarely mention dependencies at all.

questionsV2.question: The bank depends on the VPN appliance for all remote access and no patch is coming. What is the MOST appropriate immediate course of action?

options.A: Wait for the vendor patch, since interim changes to the appliance would need rework later
options.B: Apply compensating controls, restricting exposure of the device and increasing monitoring
options.C: Run signature-based antivirus scans against the appliance to remove any implanted malware
options.D: Formally accept the risk, documenting that exploitation is unlikely before the patch ships

questionsV2.explanation:
Active exploitation with no patch available is the zero-day window, and the playbook for it is compensating controls (B). Shrink the attack surface: restrict which addresses can reach the device, disable the vulnerable feature if the advisory allows, add virtual-patch rules where possible. Then watch it closely for indicators of compromise while the fix is pending.
When no patch exists, reduce exposure and heighten detection. Documenting a risk is not treating it.
questionsV2.recallLine: The bank's VPN appliance carries an actively exploited flaw and the manufacturer says no patch exists for weeks. What is the MOST appropriate immediate course of action?

optionsShort.A: Wait for the vendor patch, avoiding rework
optionsShort.B: Restrict exposure and increase monitoring meanwhile
optionsShort.C: Run signature antivirus scans against the appliance
optionsShort.D: Formally accept the risk until the patch ships

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Leaves the sole remote-access path exposed for weeks of known exploitation. A little rework is a trivial price.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Recognizes known malware, and an unknown exploit's payload rarely has a signature yet. Appliances seldom run scanners.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Rests on a false premise. Exploitation is happening now, so the exposure is not the tolerable kind.

questionsV2.question: Which approach BEST delivers mutual TLS and per-call authorization across the two hundred services without changing their code?

options.A: An API gateway at the network edge that authenticates external clients before they enter
options.B: A perimeter firewall policy limiting which outside networks can reach the service cluster
options.C: A shared library implementing TLS and authorization, to be integrated into each service
options.D: A service mesh whose sidecar proxies supply mutual TLS and policy without code changes

questionsV2.explanation: The requirement is service-to-service, east-west security at a scale where touching application code is off the table. Service meshes were built for that problem (D). A sidecar proxy deployed beside each service intercepts its traffic, so mutual TLS, service identity and per-call authorization policy come from infrastructure, uniformly, and none of the two hundred codebases changes.
questionsV2.recallLine: Trellis Pay needs mutual TLS and per-call authorization between two hundred microservices, and rewriting their code has been ruled out. Which approach BEST delivers that?

optionsShort.A: An API gateway authenticating external clients at the edge
optionsShort.B: A perimeter firewall policy for outside networks
optionsShort.C: A shared library integrated into every service
optionsShort.D: Sidecar proxies supplying mutual TLS and policy

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Guards north-south traffic where external clients enter. Once inside, service-to-service calls never traverse it.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Misses on granularity and direction. A perimeter policy knows networks and ports, not two services inside a cluster.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Meets the functional need and fails the stated constraint. It ties security upgrades to two hundred release schedules.

questionsV2.question: Which change MOST reduces the risk of container compromise and escape on the platform as reviewed?

options.A: Installing traditional antivirus agents inside every running application container
options.B: Scanning images for known vulnerabilities and running containers as non-root users
options.C: Moving all images into a private registry while continuing to build them unchanged
options.D: Restarting every container on a nightly schedule so intrusions do not persist

questionsV2.explanation:
The review names the two dominant risks, and one option answers both (B). Scanning images before deployment catches the known-vulnerable packages that public-registry images routinely carry, which is the most likely route to compromise. Dropping root strips a compromised container of the privileges that make kernel exploits and host escape practical on a shared node.
Container defense lives in image hygiene and runtime policy.
questionsV2.recallLine: Trellis Pay's containers run as root, built from unscanned public images, on shared hosts. Which change MOST reduces the risk of compromise and escape?

optionsShort.A: Antivirus agents inside every running container
optionsShort.B: Scan images and run containers as non-root
optionsShort.C: Move the same images to a private registry
optionsShort.D: Restart every container on a nightly schedule

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: A host-era control transplanted badly. It sees one container's namespace and touches neither the packages nor the privilege.

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Relocates the risk. The same unscanned, vulnerable images get served from a private address.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Evicts an intruder until the same unpatched flaw readmits them. Persistence is not the vulnerability.

questionsV2.question: Which security responsibilities does the team retain once the document-processing workload runs serverless?

options.A: Securing the function code, its dependencies, its secrets, and its least-privilege IAM roles
options.B: Patching the operating system kernels of the servers on which the functions execute
options.C: Hardening the hypervisor layer that isolates the provider's tenants from one another
options.D: Managing host firewalls and antivirus on the machines running the function runtime

questionsV2.explanation: Serverless shifts the shared-responsibility line sharply toward the provider, and never past the customer's own workload. What remains is everything the team writes or configures (A): the function code and its input handling, the third-party dependencies bundled with it, where composition analysis still applies, the secrets it uses, and above all the IAM role it executes under. Over-permissioned functions are the signature serverless failure.
questionsV2.recallLine: The document-processing workload now runs on a serverless functions platform. Which security responsibilities does the Trellis Pay team retain?

optionsShort.A: Function code, dependencies, secrets and IAM roles
optionsShort.B: Patching the kernels of the executing servers
optionsShort.C: Hardening the tenant-isolating hypervisor layer
optionsShort.D: Host firewalls and antivirus on runtime machines

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: In a functions platform the customer cannot reach the operating system, and the provider owns its patching.

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: One layer deeper still. Hypervisor isolation between tenants is the provider's duty in every cloud service model.

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: A responsibility the team held on its old self-managed machines, and would still hold under IaaS.

questionsV2.question: How should the lead BEST use the OWASP Top 10 in building the program?

options.A: Adopt it as the complete set of security requirements the finished application must satisfy
options.B: Treat it as a substitute for penetration testing, since it already lists the likely findings
options.C: Use it as an awareness baseline that focuses training on the most common web risk categories
options.D: Apply it as a hardening checklist for the servers that will host the company's applications

questionsV2.explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document, a consensus ranking of the most prevalent categories of web application risk. That makes it an ideal seed for a first training curriculum and coding standard (C): maximum coverage of common failure classes for minimal budget.
questionsV2.recallLine: The new application security lead has a small training budget and no secure-coding standard. How should the lead BEST use the OWASP Top 10?

optionsShort.A: The complete set of requirements the application must satisfy
optionsShort.B: A substitute for penetration testing
optionsShort.C: An awareness baseline focusing training on common risks
optionsShort.D: A hardening checklist for the hosting servers

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Overstates it. OWASP warns the Top 10 is a starting point; ASVS carries the verification-grade requirements.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Asks a list of risk categories to examine an implementation. Testing finds the specific instances a list can only name.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Reaches the wrong layer. Server hardening belongs to configuration baselines such as the CIS Benchmarks.

questionsV2.question: Which method is designed for ranking the forty threats so that remediation effort goes to the worst ones first?

options.A: STRIDE, which sorts each threat into one of six categories of malicious behavior
options.B: DREAD, which scores each threat on factors such as damage potential and exploitability
options.C: CVSS, which computes severity scores for vulnerabilities published against shipped software
options.D: CMMI, which appraises the maturity of an organization's development processes

questionsV2.explanation:
Ranking forty hypothetical threats needs a rating scheme, and DREAD is one (B). Each threat is scored on Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users and Discoverability, and the totals give a defensible, repeatable priority order for remediation.
STRIDE finds and names threats, DREAD ranks them, CVSS rates real vulnerabilities after release.
questionsV2.recallLine: A workshop produced forty distinct threats to the trading platform, more than the team can address. Which method is designed for ranking them?

optionsShort.A: STRIDE, sorting threats into six behavior categories
optionsShort.B: DREAD, scoring damage potential and exploitability
optionsShort.C: CVSS, rating published flaws in shipped software
optionsShort.D: CMMI, appraising development process maturity

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: The enumeration step the workshop has just completed. Category membership carries no severity.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: The plausible near-miss, built for disclosed vulnerabilities. Design-stage threats have no CVE and no patch state.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: CMMI evaluates how the organization builds software, a different altitude from ranking one system's threats.

questionsV2.question: Which STRIDE category BEST fits the moment the key became readable by anyone browsing the repository, before any attacker had used it?

options.A: Spoofing, because the key would later let outsiders authenticate as an administrator
options.B: Tampering, because the repository's contents were changed by the developer's push
options.C: Information disclosure, because a secret became visible to parties outside its intended audience
options.D: Elevation of privilege, because possession of the key conferred administrative rights

questionsV2.explanation:
Precision about which event is being classified decides this question. The stem names the exposure itself: a confidential value becoming readable by unauthorized parties. Confidentiality violations are STRIDE's information disclosure category (C), whether or not anyone had exploited the exposure yet.
Real incidents span several STRIDE categories in sequence. Classify each event on the timeline separately.
questionsV2.recallLine: At the moment the master API key became readable in the public repository, before anyone had used it, which STRIDE category BEST fits?

optionsShort.A: Spoofing, since outsiders could later authenticate as administrator
optionsShort.B: Tampering, since the push changed the repository
optionsShort.C: Information disclosure, a secret visible to unauthorized parties
optionsShort.D: Elevation of privilege, since the key conferred admin rights

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Spoofing is what followed, when attackers authenticated to the API as an administrator with the stolen key.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Tampering is unauthorized modification of data or code. The developer's push was authorized and well-intentioned.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Elevation of privilege describes the administrative capability gained once the key was being used.

questionsV2.question: The team suspects kernel-level malware is concealing its presence on that server. What is the MOST reliable way to restore trust in the system?

options.A: Rebuild the system from known-good installation media and restore data from clean backups
options.B: Run a full scan with the installed antivirus using its most aggressive detection settings
options.C: Delete the executables owning the suspicious connections and then reboot the server
options.D: Patch the operating system to the current level so the malware can no longer operate

questionsV2.explanation: A rootkit subverts the operating system itself, so every answer that system gives, from process lists to scan results, is suspect. The firewall seeing traffic the host denies is the classic symptom. Once the kernel is untrusted, the only way to re-establish a trusted computing base is to rebuild from media you trust and restore data verified clean (A).
questionsV2.recallLine: Firewall logs show connections that no tool on the server reports, and kernel-level malware is suspected. What is the MOST reliable way to restore trust?

optionsShort.A: Rebuild from known-good media, restore clean backups
optionsShort.B: Full antivirus scan at aggressive detection settings
optionsShort.C: Delete the suspicious executables and reboot
optionsShort.D: Patch the operating system to current level

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Runs on, and asks questions of, the compromised OS. Aggressive settings do not fix a lying oracle.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: The hiding means the owning executables cannot be found reliably, and deleting what is visible leaves the implant.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Closes entry vectors for the future. Patching evicts nothing already resident below the tools that would remove it.

questionsV2.question: Which detection approach is BEST suited to the malware family whose samples differ in code but not in behavior?

options.A: Distribute the newest signature databases to every endpoint several times per day
options.B: Block executable email attachments at the gateway to keep samples from users
options.C: Deploy behavior-based monitoring that flags the malware's actions as opposed to its code
options.D: Compare file hashes on each host against the list of previously quarantined samples

questionsV2.explanation:
Identical behavior with a different hash every generation is the fingerprint of polymorphic malware. It re-encrypts or mutates its code on each infection, so static patterns never stabilize. What it cannot cheaply change is what it does: the files it touches, the persistence it sets, the traffic it sends. Behavior-based or heuristic detection catches the family that signatures keep missing (C).
When the code mutates, anchor detection to the behavior that stays constant.
questionsV2.recallLine: New infections keep appearing with a different hash and byte pattern each time but identical actions on the host. Which detection approach suits this family BEST?

optionsShort.A: Distribute new signature databases several times daily
optionsShort.B: Block executable email attachments at the gateway
optionsShort.C: Behavior-based monitoring flagging what malware does
optionsShort.D: Compare host file hashes against quarantined samples

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Still loses the race. Each new variant is born unsigned, and frequency cannot fix a model keyed to changing bytes.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Narrows one delivery vector while the family may arrive by web, removable media or lateral movement.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: The most brittle signature of all. A single changed byte produces a new hash, which is what this family does.

questionsV2.question: The converter does what it advertises and staff installed it themselves on machines they cannot administer. Which control would MOST effectively have prevented these installations?

options.A: Application allow-listing that permits approved software to execute and blocks the rest
options.B: A security awareness campaign warning staff about software from unofficial sources
options.C: An intrusion detection sensor tuned to alert on remote-access tool network traffic
options.D: Prompt operating system patching to close the vulnerabilities the malware exploited

questionsV2.explanation: A working program that secretly carries a hostile payload is a Trojan horse, and its defining property is that the user willingly runs it. So the strongest defense does not depend on the user's judgment. Application allow-listing blocks the unapproved binary from executing at all (A), however convincing it looked and whoever double-clicked it.
questionsV2.recallLine: Staff installed a free PDF converter that works as advertised and also opens a remote-control channel. Which control would MOST effectively have prevented these installations?

optionsShort.A: Allow-listing: approved software runs, the rest blocked
optionsShort.B: An awareness campaign about unofficial software sources
optionsShort.C: IDS alerting on remote-access tool traffic
optionsShort.D: Prompt patching of operating system vulnerabilities

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Administrative and probabilistic. Awareness lowers the click rate, and some installs still happen, as this incident shows.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Detective. An alert arrives after the channel opens, and the question asks about preventing the installation.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Has nothing here to close. No vulnerability was exploited; the user granted execution voluntarily.

questionsV2.question: Each infected server infected its neighbors directly, with no user action anywhere. Which combination of controls BEST limits this class of attack in future?

options.A: Phishing simulations and awareness training so employees stop opening malicious attachments
options.B: Timely patching of exposed network services plus segmentation to contain lateral movement
options.C: Stronger password complexity requirements and lockout thresholds across all accounts
options.D: Full backups of every server retained for ninety days at a separate offsite location

questionsV2.explanation:
Self-propagation through a vulnerable network service with zero user involvement is the signature of a worm, and the stem hands you both contributing causes: an unpatched exposed service, and a flat network where every host can reach every other. Patching removes the exploitable flaw. Segmentation shrinks the population each infected host can even reach. Together (B) they attack propagation at both ends.
Read the propagation mechanism first. It tells you which control family is even in play.
questionsV2.recallLine: Malware spread overnight across Halden Logistics' flat network with nobody logged in, each host infecting neighbors through the same service. Which controls BEST limit this?

optionsShort.A: Phishing simulations and awareness training
optionsShort.B: Timely patching plus network segmentation
optionsShort.C: Stronger password complexity and lockout thresholds
optionsShort.D: Offsite full backups retained ninety days

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Guards the human vector, and the defining clue is that no human acted anywhere in this outbreak.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Hardens credentials, and the worm exploited a service flaw rather than an account.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Corrective. Backups rebuild the servers after the damage has been done.

questionsV2.question: Which control would MOST reduce the ongoing harm from the compromised campus workstations fetching commands?

options.A: Requiring password changes for all users whose workstations were observed beaconing
options.B: Encrypting the hard drives of the affected workstations to protect the stored data
options.C: Scheduling monthly vulnerability scans across the campus workstation address space
options.D: Egress filtering and DNS monitoring to block and expose command-and-control traffic

questionsV2.explanation: Two hundred hosts beaconing to one domain for instructions is a botnet, and a bot's value to its herder depends entirely on the command-and-control channel. Cut that channel at the network edge (D), by blocking the domain, filtering outbound traffic and watching DNS. It stops the flooding and enumerates the infected hosts for cleanup, and it attacks the one thing every bot must do.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two hundred campus workstations make identical periodic connections to one overseas domain and fetch commands from it. Which control MOST reduces the ongoing harm?

optionsShort.A: Password changes for users of beaconing workstations
optionsShort.B: Encrypting the affected workstations' hard drives
optionsShort.C: Monthly vulnerability scans of the workstation range
optionsShort.D: Egress filtering and DNS monitoring of outbound traffic

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Misreads the cause. New credentials on an infected host are promptly available to the resident malware anyway.

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Protects data confidentiality on lost or stolen media. It is irrelevant to a machine attacking others while running.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Preventive hygiene that may reduce future infections. A monthly detective cycle does nothing about harm in progress.

questionsV2.question: The macro code lies dormant until an infected file is opened and spreads only when users share those files. How should the analyst classify it?

options.A: A worm, since it eventually reached many machines across the company's network
options.B: A logic bomb, since it stays dormant until a specific condition has been met
options.C: A virus, since it attaches to host files and requires user execution to spread
options.D: A rootkit, since it conceals its code inside legitimate document files

questionsV2.explanation: Two properties decide the classification. The code attaches itself to a host file, and it advances only when a human opens that file. Host-dependence plus required user execution defines a virus, here a macro virus (C).
questionsV2.recallLine: Macro code copies itself into spreadsheet files, lies dormant until one is opened, and travels only when users share them. How should the analyst classify it?

optionsShort.A: A worm, since it reached many machines
optionsShort.B: A logic bomb, dormant until a condition
optionsShort.C: A virus, attaching to files and needing user execution
optionsShort.D: A rootkit, concealing code inside documents

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Describes autonomous spread with no user action. Breadth of infection alone does not make a worm.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Code planted in a system awaiting a trigger, and it does not replicate by attaching itself to files.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Hides by subverting the operating system so tools cannot see it. Riding inside a document is a carrier.

questionsV2.question: The bank's risk committee wants the single control that MOST reduces the business impact of a successful ransomware attack. Which should it choose?

options.A: An endpoint protection platform that detects and quarantines known ransomware families
options.B: Offline, regularly tested backups kept isolated from production networks and credentials
options.C: Full-disk encryption on all servers so stolen patient records remain confidential
options.D: A cyber-insurance policy that reimburses ransom payments and recovery expenses

questionsV2.explanation: The discriminator is impact once prevention has already failed, which the committee has conceded. Ransomware is fundamentally an availability attack, and isolated, tested backups restore availability without paying (B). Offline and credential-separated, because modern operators hunt down and encrypt or delete any backup they can reach. Tested, because an unrestorable backup is discovered at the worst possible moment.
questionsV2.recallLine: The risk committee wants the single control that MOST reduces the business impact of a ransomware attack that has already succeeded. Which should it choose?

optionsShort.A: Endpoint protection detecting known ransomware families
optionsShort.B: Offline, tested backups isolated from production credentials
optionsShort.C: Full-disk encryption so stolen records stay confidential
optionsShort.D: Cyber-insurance reimbursing ransom and recovery costs

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Reduces the likelihood of success. The committee has already conceded that prevention fails.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Does nothing against an attacker layering their encryption on top of yours. It addresses stolen media.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Transfers part of the financial loss while patient care stays down. Payment guarantees no working decryption.

questionsV2.question: Which database design practice MOST directly prevents the class of defect behind the mismatched addresses?

options.A: Normalization, so each fact is stored once and referenced as opposed to duplicated
options.B: Transparent encryption, so address data is protected from any unauthorized reading
options.C: Nightly integrity jobs that compare the three address copies and report mismatches
options.D: Database activity monitoring that logs every change made to customer records

questionsV2.explanation: Three divergent copies of one fact is an update anomaly, and update anomalies are what normalization exists to eliminate. Store the address once, reference it by key everywhere else (A), and there is no second or third copy to miss. The defect becomes structurally impossible.
questionsV2.recallLine: A customer's mailing address differs across three warehouse tables because an update routine changed one copy and missed the rest. Which database design practice MOST directly prevents this?

optionsShort.A: Normalization, storing each fact once and referencing it
optionsShort.B: Transparent encryption of the address data
optionsShort.C: Nightly jobs comparing the copies for mismatches
optionsShort.D: Activity monitoring logging every record change

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Addresses confidentiality. All three copies can be perfectly encrypted and still inconsistent with each other.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: A detective patch on the symptom. It tolerates the redundancy, lets copies diverge, then notices.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Records who changed what, which serves accountability and forensics. It does nothing to keep the copies in step.

questionsV2.question: A clerk counts customers in a rare fraud category, repeats the count excluding one named customer, and subtracts to learn that customer's flag. Neither query exceeded the clerk's permissions. Which term BEST describes this?

options.A: SQL injection, because crafted queries extracted data the interface was built to conceal
options.B: Inference, because a protected fact was deduced from individually authorized results
options.C: Privilege escalation, because the clerk obtained information above their access level
options.D: Aggregation, because a large volume of harmless records was fused into a sensitive whole

questionsV2.explanation:
The clerk never broke a rule. Each query was authorized and well formed, and arithmetic across the answers revealed a fact the system withholds. Deducing protected information from legitimately obtainable results is an inference attack (B). It is countered by controls on the answers: minimum query-set sizes, noise or perturbation in statistics, and polyinstantiation in multilevel databases.
Aggregation piles data up; inference reasons a secret out. Access control alone stops neither.
questionsV2.recallLine: A clerk subtracts two permitted counts of a rare fraud category to learn one named customer's flag. Which term BEST describes this?

optionsShort.A: SQL injection extracting concealed data
optionsShort.B: Inference deducing a fact from authorized results
optionsShort.C: Privilege escalation above the clerk's access level
optionsShort.D: Aggregation fusing harmless records into a sensitive whole

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Means input that subverts the structure of the query itself. These queries ran exactly as designed.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Requires a permission boundary crossed or elevated, and none was. That is what makes inference so hard to police.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: The closest wrong answer, and the sibling threat. Here two statistics were combined to derive one withheld fact.

questionsV2.question: By correlating the three datasets the contractor reconstructs the timing and routes of cash-in-transit runs. Which security concern does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: Inference, since the contractor deduced one hidden value from a permitted statistical result
options.B: Collusion, since several parties pooled their separate accesses to reach protected data
options.C: Data remanence, since sensitive residue persisted inside systems rated non-sensitive
options.D: Aggregation, since individually non-sensitive data sets combined into sensitive knowledge

questionsV2.explanation: Every source the contractor touched was legitimately non-sensitive. The classified picture emerged when the sources were correlated. That is aggregation (D): the combination carries a higher sensitivity than any of its parts, which is why access decisions have to consider what a subject can assemble in total, with need-to-know evaluated across holdings.
questionsV2.recallLine: The cash-in-transit contractor correlates maintenance schedules, fuel purchases and duty rosters to reconstruct run timings and routes. Which security concern does this BEST illustrate?

optionsShort.A: Inference, deducing a hidden value from statistics
optionsShort.B: Collusion, parties pooling their separate accesses
optionsShort.C: Data remanence, residue persisting in non-sensitive systems
optionsShort.D: Aggregation, non-sensitive sets combining into sensitive knowledge

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: The closest wrong answer, and the sibling concern. Here nothing was withheld; the sensitivity arose from assembly.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Requires multiple actors combining their separate privileges. This was one contractor inside one set of grants.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Data physically surviving on media after deletion or reuse. The databases were serving their intended content.

questionsV2.question: Harlow Grid Metering collects telemetry from 60,000 field meters through a gateway daemon written in C that parses a proprietary binary frame format. Three of the last four critical advisories against the daemon were memory-corruption defects in that parser, each found after release, and one was exploited to run code on a substation gateway. The architecture board is approving a standard for the rewrite and has budget to rebuild that component from scratch. Which decision MOST durably removes that class of defect from the rewritten code?

options.A: Compile the rewritten parser with stack canaries, address space layout randomization and non-executable memory enabled.
options.B: Mandate a restricted, automatically enforced subset of C for the parser, with conformance checked on every commit.
options.C: Reimplement the parsing layer in a memory-safe language whose runtime bounds-checks each buffer access.
options.D: Require two-engineer review and a fuzzing campaign against the parser before each release of the daemon.

questionsV2.explanation:
Memory corruption is a property of a language that lets a program address storage it does not own. Move the work to a language whose runtime checks each access (C) and the whole class stops being expressible in the new code.
When a defect class keeps recurring, ask what would stop it being writable before asking what would catch it sooner.
questionsV2.recallLine: A metering gateway's C parser keeps producing memory-corruption advisories. Which standard for the rewrite MOST durably removes that defect class?

optionsShort.A: Compile with canaries, ASLR and non-executable memory
optionsShort.B: Enforce a restricted subset of C
optionsShort.C: Reimplement in a memory-safe language
optionsShort.D: Two-engineer review plus a fuzzing campaign

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Hardens exploitation. Canaries, randomized layout and non-executable memory leave the defect itself in place.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: The closest competitor, and durability is the tiebreaker. It holds only while every engineer and tool keeps enforcing it.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Discovers defects that already exist. Worth doing, and a different thing from making them impossible to write.

sources: ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 8.2.1 Programming languages
NIST SP 800-218 SSDF v1.1 | PW.5 Create Source Code by Adhering to Secure Coding Practices
CISA, NSA and partners | The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps (December 2023)

questionsV2.question: Halyard Mutual's policy rating engine depends on an open-source numerical library that one volunteer maintains. The last release was fourteen months ago, an unpatched advisory against it has been open for five, and the maintainer has not answered two issues Halyard filed. The library is embedded in nine internal applications. Halyard's architecture group is now writing the admission criteria that every open-source component must satisfy before a team may take a new dependency on it. Which criterion MOST directly prevents a repeat of the position Halyard is in?

options.A: Documented evidence of an active maintainer group and a published process for handling reported vulnerabilities.
options.B: Broad industry adoption and a high download count, on the reasoning that widely used code is widely reviewed.
options.C: A license compatible with Halyard's distribution model and reviewed by counsel before the dependency is taken.
options.D: A clean software composition analysis scan of the component and its transitive dependencies at adoption.

questionsV2.explanation:
What went wrong at Halyard is a maintenance failure. The library works, and nobody is going to fix it. An admission criterion helps only if it predicts whether someone will respond to the next advisory, and evidence of a maintainer group with a stated vulnerability-handling process measures precisely that (A).
Taking an open-source dependency moves the vendor's patching obligation onto you, unless somebody upstream has agreed to carry it.
questionsV2.recallLine: An insurer is setting admission criteria for new open-source dependencies after one went unmaintained. Which criterion MOST directly prevents that recurring?

optionsShort.A: Active maintainers with a vulnerability process
optionsShort.B: Wide adoption and high download counts
optionsShort.C: License reviewed by counsel before adoption
optionsShort.D: Clean composition analysis scan at adoption

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Tests popularity. Heavily used projects with a single maintainer are common, and eyes review features first.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: A real gate, and a legal one. Permissive licenses say nothing about whether the project is alive in two years.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: A point-in-time measurement. A clean scan cannot say what happens when the first advisory lands.

sources: ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 8.4.2 Open source
NIST SP 800-218 SSDF v1.1 | PW.4 Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible
NIST SP 800-161r1 | Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations

questionsV2.question: Brightmoor Health Partners has moved payroll and general ledger onto an enterprise application that the supplier hosts and administers on Brightmoor's behalf. Four of the supplier's operations engineers hold standing administrative accounts inside Brightmoor's instance so they can apply configuration changes and run month-end jobs. Brightmoor's own staff cannot see what those accounts do, and the contract is silent on the subject. The finance director wants the renewal to close this exposure. Which contractual requirement would MOST improve Brightmoor's control over that administrative access?

options.A: An annual SOC 2 Type II report covering the supplier's hosting operations, delivered to Brightmoor's audit committee.
options.B: No standing supplier accounts: each session is requested, approved by Brightmoor and recorded for later review.
options.C: Background screening and annual security training for every supplier engineer who touches the hosted application.
options.D: Notification within seventy-two hours of any incident affecting Brightmoor's instance, with defined liability for costs.

questionsV2.explanation:
Standing access is the exposure. The requirement that removes it makes each supplier session an event Brightmoor grants and can replay afterwards (B).
When a third party administers a system for you, write into the contract whether their access is yours to grant.
questionsV2.recallLine: A supplier's engineers hold standing administrative accounts inside a hosted payroll system. Which contract requirement MOST improves the customer's control over that access?

optionsShort.A: Annual SOC 2 Type II report
optionsShort.B: Just-in-time sessions, approved and recorded
optionsShort.C: Background screening and training for supplier staff
optionsShort.D: Breach notification within seventy-two hours

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Assurance about the supplier's control environment as a whole, once a year, over a scope the supplier chose.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: A hiring control. It does nothing about the four accounts still sitting there when one of those engineers is phished.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Governs what happens after harm. A notification clause with liability attached prevents nothing at all.

sources: ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 8.4.4 Managed services
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2(7) Account Management: Privileged User Accounts
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-9 External System Services

questionsV2.question: Thurlow University's research office uses a software-as-a-service collaboration platform under a signed enterprise agreement. The provider publishes a current SOC 2 Type II report, encrypts customer data at rest and in transit, and runs a documented vulnerability program. A researcher nonetheless exposed forty thousand participant records by leaving a folder shared with anyone holding the link, a setting the provider offers and the university never restricted. The information security officer is deciding where to place assurance effort this year. Which activity MOST directly addresses the risk that remains Thurlow's under this arrangement?

options.A: Reviewing the provider's SOC 2 Type II report and its exception list each year at renewal.
options.B: Continuously assessing and enforcing the tenant's sharing and access settings against a documented university baseline.
options.C: Requiring the provider to hold university data encrypted with keys the university generates.
options.D: Producing a quarterly report of externally shared folders for research data owners to review.

questionsV2.explanation:
Everything the provider is responsible for was already in place, and none of it failed. The university's own user shared the folder, through a setting the university's own administrators control, so assurance effort has to follow the responsibility line (B).
Provider assurance and tenant configuration are two different jobs, and buying the first does not do the second.
questionsV2.recallLine: A university's SaaS tenant leaked records through an over-permissive sharing setting. Which assurance activity MOST directly covers the risk the customer retains?

optionsShort.A: Annual review of the provider's SOC 2
optionsShort.B: Continuously enforce tenant settings against a baseline
optionsShort.C: Customer-generated encryption keys held by the provider
optionsShort.D: Quarterly report of externally shared folders

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Measures the provider's half of that line, competently, once a year. It would have reported no exception.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Moves key custody, which matters against the provider itself. An authorized user publishing a link is untouched.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Inspects the same settings after the fact, four times a year, naming folders that were already public all quarter.

sources: ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 8.4.5 Cloud services
NIST SP 800-145 | The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (service model responsibilities)
Cloud Security Alliance | Cloud Controls Matrix v4, shared responsibility model

questionsV2.question: Tallow Creek Systems builds dispatch software for ambulance services on eight-week release trains. Security review happens once, in the last week before each release, and is done by a central team that sees the design for the first time then. The last three releases shipped with findings marked accept-for-now, because reworking the architecture would have slipped the date, and two of those findings later became customer-reported defects. The engineering vice-president will change how security work is organized, not how much of it is bought. Which arrangement BEST addresses why findings keep arriving too late to act on?

options.A: Move the central team's review two weeks earlier and give it authority to block a release.
options.B: Add an architecture review board that examines every proposed design at its monthly meeting.
options.C: Place a security engineer inside the product team, accountable with it for the release outcome.
options.D: Have the central team run automated scans each night and file defects into the product backlog.

questionsV2.explanation:
Findings arrive too late because the person who could have changed the design was not in the room when it was made. Move a security engineer inside the team (C) and the security position becomes an input to the design. Shared accountability for the release also removes the incentive to trade a finding for the date.
An integrated product team works because the discipline is a member of it.
questionsV2.recallLine: Security review of a dispatch product happens once, late, by an outside team. Which organizational arrangement BEST stops findings arriving too late to act on?

optionsShort.A: Earlier central review with authority to block
optionsShort.B: A monthly architecture review board
optionsShort.C: Embed a security engineer in the team
optionsShort.D: Nightly automated scans filed to the backlog

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Keeps the same handoff and adds a veto, which converts a late finding into a late release.

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: A governance body meeting on its own calendar. Each team still waits on an outside opinion.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Produces more findings, sooner, about code. The last three failures were architectural, which no scanner reports.

sources: ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 8.1.5 Integrated Product Team
NIST SP 800-218 SSDF v1.1 | PO.2 Implement Roles and Responsibilities
NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev 1 | Integrating security into the systems engineering effort

questionsV2.question: Pellham Analytics publishes forty internal Python packages to a private index and lets each build resolve dependencies from both that index and the public registry, taking whichever source offers the highest version number. A researcher demonstrated the consequence: she registered one of Pellham's internal package names on the public registry at version 99.0.0, and the next build of the billing service installed and executed her code. Nothing in the build was misconfigured by Pellham's own written standards. Which change MOST directly removes the mechanism the researcher used?

options.A: Run software composition analysis on every build and fail it on any package with known advisories.
options.B: Commit a lockfile pinning every dependency to an exact version and reviewed hash.
options.C: Register Pellham's internal package names on the public registry so nobody else can claim them.
options.D: Resolve internal package names from the private index alone, with no fallback to the public registry.

questionsV2.explanation:
The mechanism is name resolution across two sources, with a version comparison deciding the winner. So the fix belongs at resolution (D). Let internal names come from the private index and nowhere else, and a public package wearing that name is never consulted. The version number stops mattering.
Work out where the decision is made before choosing what to inspect.
questionsV2.recallLine: A public package registered under a company's internal name was installed by the next build. Which change MOST directly removes that substitution mechanism?

optionsShort.A: Composition analysis failing builds on known advisories
optionsShort.B: Lockfile pinning exact versions and hashes
optionsShort.C: Defensively register internal names publicly
optionsShort.D: Resolve internal names from the private index

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Finds packages carrying published advisories, and a package uploaded an hour ago has none.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Narrows the window. The substitution reappears the moment someone adds or upgrades a dependency legitimately.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: The widely recommended companion, and a race. It protects the names registered today, not the forty-first.

questionsV2.question: Marlowe Freight's two hundred developers install extensions into their integrated development environments freely from a public marketplace. An extension runs with the developer's own privileges: it can read every file in the workspace, the local credential store, and the environment variables the debugger uses. A popular formatting extension changed hands last quarter, and its new owner shipped an update that transmitted workspace contents to an external host. Marlowe learned this from a researcher's blog post. The head of engineering wants a control at the development environment itself. Which measure BEST addresses this exposure?

options.A: Restrict extension installation in the development environments to an internally curated and reviewed registry.
options.B: Deploy endpoint detection on developer laptops and alert on outbound connections from editor processes.
options.C: Require static application security testing to pass before any branch may be merged.
options.D: Publish a policy naming approved extensions and confirm compliance at the annual access review.

questionsV2.explanation:
An extension is third-party code executing inside the tool that holds the source and the credentials, so the control has to sit where that code is admitted (A). A curated registry makes admission a decision somebody reviews, and the change of ownership that turned a formatting tool into an exfiltration tool becomes a change requiring re-approval.
Developer tooling is part of the software supply chain, and admission control belongs at install time.
questionsV2.recallLine: Developers install IDE extensions freely, and one hijacked extension exfiltrated workspace files. Which control at the development environment BEST addresses that exposure?

optionsShort.A: Install extensions only from a curated registry
optionsShort.B: EDR alerting on outbound connections from editors
optionsShort.C: Static analysis must pass before any merge
optionsShort.D: Approved-extension policy checked at annual review

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: Would probably have caught this one afterwards. Detection on the laptop reports what has already left.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Tests Marlowe's own source for defects. A merge gate never sees a component running beside the editor.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Writes the rule down and checks it once a year, leaving eleven and a half months of unreviewed installs.

questionsV2.question: Quarrymount Distribution runs a vendor-supplied Java warehouse-management application that its contract forbids it to modify. A deserialization flaw in the application's message handler is public, proof-of-concept code is circulating, and the vendor has committed to a fix in ninety days. The application runs today as a privileged account on a container image that can write anywhere on its filesystem and reach any host on the internal network. Quarrymount controls the runtime even though it cannot touch the code. Which runtime measure MOST reduces the damage an attacker could do before the fix arrives?

options.A: Run the application unprivileged, with an immutable filesystem and egress limited to its database.
options.B: Place a web application firewall in front of it with signatures for the published payload.
options.C: Increase logging on the message handler and alert on deserialization of unexpected classes.
options.D: Schedule an authenticated dynamic scan of the application nightly until the vendor's fix ships.

questionsV2.explanation:
The question is about reach, and reach is decided by the privileges and the network position the process is given. Strip the account, freeze the filesystem, cut egress (A). The flaw stays exploitable, and the attacker holds a process that cannot install anything, cannot persist and cannot call out.
When you cannot fix the code, shrink what the code is permitted to do.
questionsV2.recallLine: A vendor application with a public deserialization flaw cannot be modified for ninety days. Which runtime measure MOST reduces the damage from exploitation?

optionsShort.A: Unprivileged account, immutable filesystem, restricted egress
optionsShort.B: WAF signatures for the published payload
optionsShort.C: Alert on deserialization of unexpected classes
optionsShort.D: Nightly authenticated dynamic scans until patched

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: The standard virtual patch. Deserialization payloads are trivially re-encoded, and one request through lands on root.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Tells Quarrymount that it happened, and leaves the attacker's reach exactly as it was.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Looks for flaws Quarrymount already knows about, in software it cannot change. That produces a report.

questionsV2.question: Verity Payments runs one continuous integration pipeline for its checkout service. Any pull request, including one opened from an outside contributor's fork, triggers a build job, and every job in the pipeline receives the same environment. Among its variables is a long-lived cloud credential with permission to deploy to production, because the deploy job later in the pipeline needs it. Nothing has gone wrong yet. Verity's platform team can make one change this sprint. Which change MOST directly removes the exposure a fork's pull request currently has?

options.A: Move the credential into the CI platform's encrypted secret store and mask it in job logs.
options.B: Require a maintainer to approve each fork's workflow run before the pipeline executes it.
options.C: Issue each job a short-lived identity scoped to its own task, leaving build jobs without deploy rights.
options.D: Rotate the deployment credential every thirty days and alert on use from an unexpected address.

questionsV2.explanation:
A build job able to read a production deploy credential has production access, whoever opened the pull request. The exposure is the credential's presence in that job's environment, so stop issuing it there (C).
Scope the identity before hardening the secret.
questionsV2.recallLine: A fork's pull request triggers a build job holding a production deploy credential. Which pipeline change MOST directly removes that exposure?

optionsShort.A: Encrypted secret store with masked job logs
optionsShort.B: Maintainer approval before a fork's workflow runs
optionsShort.C: Short-lived per-job identities without deploy rights
optionsShort.D: Rotate the credential and alert on anomalies

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Protects the credential at rest and in the log, then hands the same plaintext value to a job running a stranger's code.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: The documented mitigation, and a human reading a diff indefinitely. A build script need not look malicious.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Shortens the life of a credential that is exposed continuously. It changes the size of the window.

questionsV2.question: Coldbrook Instruments builds firmware for laboratory analyzers. Every change is reviewed by two engineers and merged to a protected main branch; the release engineer then creates a tag, and the build system compiles whatever that tag points at. During an audit Coldbrook found that a tag can be deleted and recreated pointing at a different commit, that four engineers are able to do this, and that the repository keeps no record of who moved a tag. The shipped firmware and the reviewed code are therefore not provably the same. Which repository control BEST closes that gap?

options.A: Require three reviewers instead of two on every pull request into the protected branch.
options.B: Reduce the number of engineers holding the maintainer role from four to two.
options.C: Record every reference update in the repository's audit log and review it weekly.
options.D: Protect release tags against deletion and movement, and have builds reference the commit digest.

questionsV2.explanation:
The name the build trusts is mutable, so an artifact's provenance runs back to a label instead of to content. Freeze the label and build from the immutable commit digest (D), and the chain from review to binary becomes verifiable.
Release integrity depends on what the build refers to.
questionsV2.recallLine: Release tags in a firmware repository can be moved to a different commit without record. Which repository control BEST restores provable provenance?

optionsShort.A: Three reviewers per pull request
optionsShort.B: Fewer engineers holding the maintainer role
optionsShort.C: Audit log of reference updates, reviewed weekly
optionsShort.D: Immutable tags; build by commit digest

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Improves the quality of review and leaves the tag mutable afterwards. The code was reviewed twice already.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Lowers how many people can move a tag without removing the capability. Verifiable provenance should not rest on trust.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Would say after the fact who moved what. A log entry does not establish that firmware and reviewed code match.

questionsV2.question: Fennimore Retail's checkout application is covered by two security tools. A static analyzer reports nine hundred findings per release, most of them on code paths the application never reaches, and developers have stopped triaging them. A dynamic scanner run against the staging site reports a handful of genuine defects but cannot say which line of code produced them, so each one takes a day to locate. Fennimore's automated functional tests already exercise every checkout flow nightly. Which testing approach BEST gives findings that are both exploitable and traceable to a line of code?

options.A: Tune the static analyzer's rule set and suppress the categories the team judges to be noise.
options.B: Instrument the running application during the functional tests so findings carry runtime context and code location.
options.C: Add software composition analysis so third-party components are assessed alongside Fennimore's own code.
options.D: Commission a manual penetration test of the checkout application before each quarterly release.

questionsV2.explanation:
Each tool's weakness in the stem names the property the other one lacks. The static analyzer has the code location and no evidence the path is reachable. The dynamic scanner has the evidence and no location. Instrumenting the application while the existing functional tests drive it produces both at once (B), which is what interactive testing is for, and the nightly run already exists, so no new test window is needed.
Match the technique to the property of the finding you need.
questionsV2.recallLine: A static analyzer reports unreachable findings and a dynamic scanner reports findings without code locations. Which testing approach BEST supplies both properties?

optionsShort.A: Tune and suppress static analyzer rules
optionsShort.B: Instrument the app during functional tests
optionsShort.C: Add software composition analysis
optionsShort.D: Quarterly manual penetration test

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Worth doing, and it cannot manufacture reachability evidence. Suppressing categories buries genuine findings too.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Covers a different population, the third-party components. The question is about Fennimore's own checkout logic.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Produces exploitable findings by hand, four times a year, at a cost per finding nine hundred of them cannot bear.

questionsV2.question: Sable Point Utilities restored service on a Saturday by having a developer apply a fix directly to the production billing servers, bypassing the pipeline. On Monday nobody could say which files changed, who changed them, or whether the same fix reached all four servers; the developer's shell history is the only record, and it lives on a host the developer administers. The billing platform sits in regulatory scope and the audit is in six weeks. Which improvement MOST directly restores the ability to answer those questions after a future emergency change?

options.A: Require an emergency change ticket to be raised retrospectively within one business day.
options.B: Deploy file integrity monitoring on the billing servers and alert on unexpected file changes.
options.C: Prohibit direct production access and route every emergency fix through the normal pipeline.
options.D: Forward change and session records to a write-once store outside the developers' control.

questionsV2.explanation:
Each question the utility could not answer is an evidence question, and evidence counts only if the person who made the change could not have edited the record of it. Ship change and session records off the host into a write-once store (D) and Sable Point has that record for the next emergency, whether or not the next emergency follows the process.
Logs are evidence only when the subject of the log cannot rewrite them.
questionsV2.recallLine: An emergency fix applied straight to production left no reliable record of what changed or who changed it. Which improvement MOST directly restores that evidence?

optionsShort.A: Retrospective emergency change ticket within a day
optionsShort.B: File integrity monitoring with change alerts
optionsShort.C: Ban direct production access; use the pipeline
optionsShort.D: Write-once change records outside developer control

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Creates a document written from memory by the person being audited, after the fact. That is a governance artifact.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Detects that a file differs from a known state. It cannot attribute the change to a person or to an authorization.

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: The control the auditor will also want. A rule forbidding bypasses produces an unrecorded change the moment one happens.

questionsV2.question: Merrivale Health System is choosing between two commercial off-the-shelf clinical scheduling products. Neither vendor will permit a customer penetration test or release source code, both return completed security questionnaires, and both offer a demonstration tenant. The chief information security officer must give the procurement committee an opinion on the security of the products themselves, and not on the vendors' corporate practices, before a contract is signed. Which form of evidence BEST supports a statement about the security functions built into the product?

options.A: The vendor's SOC 2 Type II report covering its development and hosting operations.
options.B: The vendor's completed security questionnaire, countersigned by an authorized officer of the company.
options.C: An independent evaluation of the product against a published protection profile and assurance level.
options.D: A vulnerability scan of the demonstration tenant conducted by Merrivale's own testers.

questionsV2.explanation:
The committee is asking about the product, and three of these instruments describe the company that sells it or the instance it happens to be running in. A laboratory evaluation against a published protection profile is the only one whose subject is the software's security functions (C), tested against a specification the buyer can read, with the depth of testing declared.
Ask what a piece of evidence is evidence about before asking how strong it is.
questionsV2.recallLine: A hospital must judge the security of two COTS scheduling products, not of their vendors. Which form of evidence BEST supports that judgment?

optionsShort.A: Vendor SOC 2 Type II report
optionsShort.B: Countersigned vendor security questionnaire
optionsShort.C: Independent evaluation against a protection profile
optionsShort.D: Scan of the demonstration tenant

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: A strong report about the vendor's control environment. A well-run vendor can still ship weak authorization logic.

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: Self-attestation. A signature makes it contractually useful and never makes it tested.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Findings about one demonstration tenant's configuration and patch level, which Merrivale will not have to live with.

questionsV2.question: Pellamar Logistics supports three programming languages. Its dependency scanner, secret-detection hook, hardened cryptography wrapper and linter rules exist for those three and nothing else. A delivery team has built a new customer-facing shipment tracker in a fourth language because it suited the web framework they preferred, and the tracker is due in production in five weeks. None of the four controls covers it, and no one has reviewed the language's package ecosystem. Which course should the security architect press for FIRST?

options.A: Let the tracker ship on schedule and add its language to the security toolchain roadmap for next year.
options.B: Hold the tracker out of production until its language has equivalent scanning, secret detection and cryptography support.
options.C: Commission a manual code review and a penetration test of the tracker, leaving the toolchain gap open.
options.D: Publish a standard listing the three supported languages and requiring an architecture exception for anything outside them.

questionsV2.explanation:
Security capability follows language support. A dependency scanner, a secret hook, a vetted cryptography wrapper and a linter are what make defects visible, and not one of them can see this service. Until they can, the tracker would run in production with no continuous assurance at all, so the release gate comes before the paperwork (B).
Ask what tooling exists for a language before a team commits to it.
questionsV2.recallLine: A team is shipping a production service in a language the firm's scanners, secret hook and crypto wrapper do not support. What should security require FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Ship now, add tooling next year
optionsShort.B: Hold release until the tooling covers it
optionsShort.C: One-off code review and penetration test
optionsShort.D: Publish a supported-language standard with exceptions

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Ships the risk and defers the fix to a roadmap the tracker will outlive. The exposure starts on launch day.

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Buys one snapshot. A review and a test leave every later change unexamined, and the service will change weekly.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: The durable governance answer, and it should follow. A standard does not alter what the tracker lacks at go-live.
