questionsV2.question: Kestrel Yards writes flight-planning software for regional airlines. Developers install the compiler, build plugins and code generators from whichever public source their onboarding page happens to name, and the build server pulls a code-generation plugin at build time from an author's personal hosting. Rebuilding last month's release on two machines produced two different binaries, and nobody could say which one the airlines received. The security manager wants the toolchain itself brought under control. Which measure would BEST achieve that?

options.A: Run software composition analysis over the application's declared dependencies on every merge and block known vulnerabilities.
options.B: Serve compilers and plugins from an internal mirror, pinned by version and checked against publisher signatures, on workstations and build servers.
options.C: Require developers to upgrade the compiler and every plugin to the newest published release at each sprint start.
options.D: Compare the binaries the release produces on two machines and investigate any difference before the release is signed.

questionsV2.explanation:
The toolchain produces the artifact, so its integrity bounds every other control. A tampered code generator writes a backdoor into a binary whose source is clean, and a plugin fetched from personal hosting is an unowned dependency of every release. Pin versions, verify publisher signatures, serve one mirror to workstations and build servers alike (B), and the two-machine mismatch becomes diagnosable.
Treat build tooling as production software with an owner, a pinned version and a source of record.
questionsV2.recallLine: Developers and the build server fetch compilers and plugins from assorted public sources, and two rebuilds differ. Which measure BEST brings the toolchain under control?

optionsShort.A: Scan application dependencies on every merge
optionsShort.B: Internal mirror, pinned and signature-verified toolchain
optionsShort.C: Upgrade compiler and plugins every sprint
optionsShort.D: Diff the two binaries before signing

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Watches the application's own declared dependencies, and says nothing about the compiler that consumed them.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Confuses currency with provenance. The newest plugin from an unverified source is still unverified.

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Checks the outcome. It says that something changed after the fact and leaves the team to guess what.

sources: NIST SP 800-218 v1.1 | PO.3.1 Specify which tools must be included in each toolchain
NIST SP 800-161r1 | Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices

questionsV2.question: Ambergate Utilities keeps application configuration in the same repository as its source code. A single database service account is used by development, test and production; its password sits in a properties file in that repository and was last changed four years ago. Nineteen contractors hold read access to the repository, the deployment job copies the properties file unchanged into each environment, and the account can write to the customer billing tables. Which change would MOST reduce the exposure this arrangement creates?

options.A: Encrypt the properties file in the repository and keep the decryption key in the deployment job that reads it.
options.B: Scan the whole repository history for committed secrets and rotate every credential the scan reports finding.
options.C: Issue a distinct credential per environment from a managed secret store, injected at deployment and rotated on schedule.
options.D: Withdraw the contractors' read access to the repository and review the remaining permissions each quarter.

questionsV2.explanation:
One credential shared by every environment has the whole estate as its blast radius. A contractor reading a test configuration holds production write access to the billing tables, and rotating it means coordinating three environments at once, which is why it has not been rotated in four years. Environment-scoped secrets issued at deploy time break that link and make rotation routine (C).
Ask who can read a secret and what it opens.
questionsV2.recallLine: One database account serves development, test and production, with its password in the source repository for four years. Which change MOST reduces the exposure?

optionsShort.A: Encrypt the file, key in the pipeline
optionsShort.B: Scan history and rotate what leaked
optionsShort.C: Per-environment secrets from a managed store
optionsShort.D: Remove contractor read access, review quarterly

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Moves the secret. Whatever decrypts the file is itself a secret in the same pipeline, and one account still spans three.

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: Worth doing once the credential model changes. Scanning history finds what has leaked and stops no future copy.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Shrinks the audience for the file, and one password still opens production.

NIST SP 800-218 v1.1 | PO.5.1 Separate and protect each environment involved in software development

questionsV2.question: Northwater Insurance embedded an open-source rules engine in its claims platform six years ago and patched the engine locally to add behavior the project declined to accept upstream. The local copy is now eleven minor versions behind. Upstream has published a fix for an authentication bypass, and its maintainers state that the fix depends on a refactor made in a version Northwater skipped; the platform team estimates six weeks to port it by hand. Which practice would BEST keep the firm's other open-source components out of this position?

options.A: Take local changes upstream, or hold them as a thin patch set rebased onto each release, staying close to upstream.
options.B: Pin each open-source component at the version in use today and lift the pin in an annual planned window.
options.C: Run software composition analysis on every build so the team learns quickly when a component carries a published flaw.
options.D: Replace the engine with a commercially supported product whose vendor accepts contractual responsibility for security fixes.

questionsV2.explanation:
Distance from upstream is the cost that compounds. Every local patch the project will not take makes the next upgrade harder, until a security fix arrives that the fork structurally cannot absorb and a six-week port becomes the exposure window. Keeping the delta small, upstreamed where possible and rebased where not (A), is what keeps a supported fix applicable on the day it ships.
Judge an open-source component by how easily you can take its next security release.
questionsV2.recallLine: A locally patched open-source engine has drifted so far from upstream that a security fix cannot be applied. Which practice BEST prevents this?

optionsShort.A: Stay close to upstream, rebase thin patches
optionsShort.B: Pin versions, upgrade in an annual window
optionsShort.C: Composition analysis on every build
optionsShort.D: Buy a commercially supported replacement

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Formalizes the trap. An annual window still leaves eleven versions to cross, and freezing is how Northwater arrived here.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Tells the firm sooner that it holds a vulnerable component. The team already knows and still cannot apply the fix.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Swaps one dependency for another and buys a contract. Portability is the engineering problem underneath.

sources: NIST SP 800-218 v1.1 | PW.4 Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software
NIST SP 800-161r1 | Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices

questionsV2.question: Bexley Mutual is contracting an outside development house to build its member portal, which will hold policy and payment data for 240,000 members. The draft statement of work says the supplier will "follow industry best practice for application security" and that Bexley may review the work on request. Payment falls due on delivery of a working system by a fixed date, and there is no description of what "secure" means for this system. Which addition should the security lead insist on BEFORE Bexley signs?

options.A: A requirement that the supplier hold ISO/IEC 27001 certification covering its development offices for the contract term.
options.B: A right for Bexley to commission an annual penetration test of the portal once it runs in production.
options.C: A requirement that supplier developers complete accredited secure coding training before they join the project.
options.D: Named, testable security requirements with acceptance criteria Bexley verifies before acceptance, and final payment tied to verification.

questionsV2.explanation:
A contract that promises 'industry best practice' transfers no obligation anyone can test, and a review on request is a right Bexley will exercise once the code is written and the invoice is due. Requirements written as acceptance criteria change both facts (D). They tell the supplier what to build, and they give Bexley something to verify while it still holds the money.
Write security into the deliverable and into the payment terms.
questionsV2.recallLine: A statement of work promises "industry best practice" for a member portal and a review on request. Which addition should security insist on BEFORE signature?

optionsShort.A: Supplier ISO 27001 certification for the term
optionsShort.B: Right to an annual production penetration test
optionsShort.C: Accredited secure coding training for developers
optionsShort.D: Testable requirements with acceptance criteria and payment

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Certifies the supplier's own management system, which describes how it runs its offices. The authorization model is not that.

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Arrives after go-live, when defects cost the most and the invoice is paid. A sensible right, a poor substitute for acceptance.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Improves the people writing the code and creates no obligation about the code they produce.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-4 Acquisition Process
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | A.8.30 Outsourced development

questionsV2.question: Harnwell Foods runs its enterprise resource planning suite as a managed service: the supplier hosts it, patches it, and provides an annual independent assurance report over the base product. Harnwell's own analysts write scripts in the platform's customization layer, one of which publishes a web endpoint on the supplier's infrastructure so a haulage partner can post invoices. The supplier's terms state that customer-written extensions are the customer's responsibility. Which control should Harnwell treat as PRIMARY for those extensions?

options.A: Harnwell's own development lifecycle applied to the customization layer: requirements, peer review, testing and change approval.
options.B: A request that the supplier review and approve each customization before it reaches the hosted production tenant.
options.C: The web application firewall the supplier operates in front of the hosted platform for all of its tenants.
options.D: The supplier's annual assurance report, checked each year to confirm that its scope covers the hosted platform.

questionsV2.explanation:
Responsibility follows authorship. The supplier's patching and assurance report cover the base product. The invoice endpoint was written by Harnwell's analysts, runs Harnwell's logic and exposes Harnwell's data, so the assurance it needs is Harnwell's own (A): requirements, review, test, and an approval before promotion.
Ask who wrote the code before asking who runs the servers.
questionsV2.recallLine: A managed enterprise application lets the customer's own analysts write extensions the supplier will not support. Which control is PRIMARY for those extensions?

optionsShort.A: The customer's own development lifecycle
optionsShort.B: Supplier review of each customization
optionsShort.C: The supplier's shared web application firewall
optionsShort.D: The supplier's annual assurance report

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: Asks the supplier to accept work its terms exclude, and it carries no liability when it misses a flaw.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: A perimeter control tuned to the base product's traffic, and blind to authorization logic an analyst wrote last week.

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Confirms the supplier is doing what it promised. It covers precisely the part of the system that is not in question.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-9 External System Services
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | A.8.25 Secure development life cycle

questionsV2.question: Calder Trust, a hospital charity, licenses a low-code platform bundled with its cloud productivity suite. Any member of staff with a license can build an application, connect it through a stored connection to the patient-transport database, and share it by link. An inventory finds forty-one such applications; IT knows the owner of nine, two authenticate nobody, and one copies donor records into an external mailing tool each night. Which measure should the security manager put in place FIRST?

options.A: Withdraw the low-code licenses until a development standard for the platform is written and approved.
options.B: Deliver secure development training to every member of staff who has built an application on the platform.
options.C: Bring platform applications under the approval and inventory required of other software before they may reach production data.
options.D: Run static analysis across the applications the platform generated and remediate the injection defects reported.

questionsV2.explanation:
An application that reads the patient-transport database is a production system whichever tool built it. The failure here is not code quality. Forty-one systems entered service with no owner, no approval and no record of what they connect to. Governance over the connectors is the lever (C), because the connector turns a personal spreadsheet replacement into a clinical data processor.
Ask what an application is allowed to connect to before asking how it was written.
questionsV2.recallLine: Staff have built forty-one low-code applications that reach a patient database, most with no known owner. Which measure should the security manager take FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Withdraw licenses until a standard exists
optionsShort.B: Train the staff who built applications
optionsShort.C: Approval and inventory before production data
optionsShort.D: Static analysis of the generated applications

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Stops the bleeding and stops the service with it. The unowned forty-one stay live while a standard is drafted.

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Raises awareness among people who can still publish tomorrow. The nightly donor export was no ignorance defect.

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Reads for injection flaws in generated artifacts the platform does not expose, and says nothing about ownership.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-8 System Component Inventory
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-9 External System Services

questionsV2.question: Marchpoint Health codified its security standards as pipeline policy checks: unencrypted storage, public network exposure and missing authentication each fail the build. To keep deliveries moving, the platform team added a repository label that skips the checks and needs no approval. Ninety of the company's 260 services now carry the label, six of them applied during an incident eighteen months ago and never removed. An auditor has asked what the checks actually enforce. Which change would BEST restore their value?

options.A: Remove the label from all ninety services this quarter and let the failing builds block those teams.
options.B: Report to engineering leadership each month on the number of services still carrying the label.
options.C: Add further policy checks to the pipeline so the codified standard covers more classes of defect.
options.D: Make each skip an approved exception with a named owner and an expiry date, so it lapses unless renewed.

questionsV2.explanation:
A control with an unapproved, permanent bypass is a suggestion with a build step attached. The six labels left over from an incident eighteen months ago show what an exception without an expiry becomes. Require a named owner and a lapse date (D) and the label turns into a recorded, time-bounded risk decision, which is also the artifact the auditor is asking for.
Codified controls are worth no more than the process that governs their exceptions.
questionsV2.recallLine: A pipeline's security policy checks can be skipped with an unapproved repository label that ninety services now carry. Which change BEST restores their value?

optionsShort.A: Strip the label from all ninety services
optionsShort.B: Report the label count monthly
optionsShort.C: Add more policy checks
optionsShort.D: Approved exceptions with owners and expiry dates

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Treats all ninety alike, including teams with a legitimate reason. A quarter of blocked delivery reverses the policy.

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: Measures the problem monthly and changes nobody's behavior. A count with no owner attached is a chart.

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Widens a net that ninety services already step around, adding rules for the population that still passes.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-5 Plan of Action and Milestones
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 Configuration Change Control

questionsV2.question: Westhaven Bank requires a threat model for every new service. In practice one of its two application security engineers writes the model after code complete, working from the design document, and files it with the release record. Developers rarely read it. The last three models missed abuse paths the delivery teams already knew about, one of which caused a four-hour outage in March, and the engineers are now eleven services behind. The security director wants the activity to justify its cost. Which change should she make FIRST?

options.A: Engage an external consultancy to threat model the firm's ten highest-value services once each quarter.
options.B: Have delivery teams model their own designs at design time, with security facilitating and findings entering the backlog.
options.C: Replace the threat model with a penetration test booked two weeks before each planned release.
options.D: Publish a catalog of common threats for the two engineers to work through more consistently.

questionsV2.explanation:
Timing and authorship are both wrong here, and they are the same defect. A model written after the code is finished can only describe what was built, by someone who was not in the design conversation and cannot see the abuse paths the builders discuss among themselves. Move the activity into design, with the people making the design decisions holding the pen (B), and it becomes a design input. Two engineers scale as facilitators.
Model where the design decisions are made, by the people making them.
questionsV2.recallLine: Threat models are written after code complete by two central engineers, and teams ignore them. Which change should the security director make FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Quarterly external models of top services
optionsShort.B: Teams model their own designs, security facilitates
optionsShort.C: Penetration test instead, before each release
optionsShort.D: Threat catalog for the two engineers

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Buys expert models for the largest ten services, quarterly. The other services and the timing problem stay put.

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Swaps analysis of a design for a test of an implementation, and arrives too late to change either.

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Makes the existing bottleneck more consistent without widening it or moving it earlier.

sources: NIST SP 800-218 v1.1 | PW.1.1 Use forms of risk modeling to assess the security risk for the software
NIST SP 800-154 | Guide to Data-Centric System Threat Modeling

questionsV2.question: Ridgeline Software releases its billing platform about forty times a week through an automated pipeline that runs unit and integration tests, a dependency scan and a policy check, records the merge approver and the artifact digest, and can roll back in two minutes. The change advisory board meets on Tuesdays and expects a form for each change; the team files them in a batch on Wednesday, describing changes already live. An auditor has reported the platform as operating outside change control. Which response is MOST defensible?

options.A: Classify pipeline releases as pre-approved standard changes, with the pipeline's gates and records serving as evidence of control.
options.B: Require the advisory board to approve each of the forty weekly releases before the pipeline may deploy them.
options.C: Suspend automated release until the board can review changes at the rate the team produces them.
options.D: Extend the pipeline to raise a change form automatically for each release once it has completed.

questionsV2.explanation:
Change control is a property of the process. The pipeline already records who approved what, what was built, which tests it passed and how to reverse it, which is more evidence than a form filled in the following day. Name those releases as standard changes, with written criteria for what falls outside the pattern (A), and the board gets an exception queue it can genuinely review.
Ask what a control achieves before defending how it is recorded.
questionsV2.recallLine: An automated pipeline releases forty times a week while a weekly board expects a form per change. Which response to the audit finding is MOST defensible?

optionsShort.A: Pre-approved standard changes evidenced by the pipeline
optionsShort.B: Board approval for every release
optionsShort.C: Suspend automation until the board copes
optionsShort.D: Auto-file a change form after release

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Puts a weekly meeting in front of forty releases. It becomes a rubber stamp, or a reason to batch changes.

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Removes the fastest rollback the platform has and calls the loss a control improvement.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Automates the artifact the auditor complained about and keeps the timing that made it meaningless.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 Configuration Change Control
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 | A.8.32 Change management

questionsV2.question: Aldermere Systems has assessed its eleven development teams against a software assurance maturity model. Practice scores range from level 1 to level 3; secure design scores lowest in the two teams that build the card payment services and highest in the internal tooling team. The chief executive wants to put "assessed at level 3" into a customer proposal, and to set level 3 as a target for every team by December. The security director must advise. Which use of the assessment would deliver the GREATEST risk reduction?

options.A: Set the same maturity target for all eleven teams and track them monthly against the December date.
options.B: Quote the assessment in the proposal as evidence that the delivered software meets the customer's security requirements.
options.C: Direct improvement effort where a low practice score meets high business risk, starting with secure design in payments.
options.D: Repeat the assessment each quarter so that the trend across the eleven teams becomes visible to leadership.

questionsV2.explanation:
A maturity model measures how an organization builds software, and its value lies entirely in where it points the next investment. This assessment already says where risk concentrates: the weakest secure-design practice sits in the teams handling card payments, which is where an improvement pound buys the most (C).
Use a maturity score to choose the next improvement.
questionsV2.recallLine: A maturity assessment scores eleven development teams from level 1 to 3. Which use of that result would deliver the GREATEST risk reduction?

optionsShort.A: Same target for every team by December
optionsShort.B: Quote the level in a customer proposal
optionsShort.C: Improve where low scores meet high risk
optionsShort.D: Reassess quarterly to show the trend

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Spends the same effort everywhere. The internal tooling team reaches the target on schedule and payments does not.

B.label: true of a different thing
B.wouldAnswer: Claims product assurance from a process measurement. A level 3 organization can still ship an authorization flaw.

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Keeps measuring at four times the cost and changes nothing between measurements. Cadence is not action.

sources: OWASP SAMM v2 | Assessment, roadmap and business-risk driven prioritization
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 8.1.2 Maturity models

questionsV2.question: Calverton Rail accepted a supplier's crew-scheduling application after the supplier demonstrated each item on the security requirements list: the login page prompted for a second factor, the audit log showed entries for privileged actions, and idle sessions expired. Two months into service, a tester found that the second factor could be skipped by calling the authentication API directly, and that any administrator could clear the audit log. Which weakness in Calverton's acceptance testing MOST explains both findings?

options.A: Tests were run by the supplier's own staff and not by an independent tester engaged by Calverton.
options.B: The requirements list was too short to cover the application's full range of functions.
options.C: Testing happened at acceptance as opposed to continuing at intervals after the application entered service.
options.D: Tests confirmed each control was present, without attempting to defeat it or use the paths around it.

questionsV2.explanation:
Both findings share one root: the tests asked whether the control existed and stopped there. A prompt on a login page proves a second factor is present on one path and says nothing about the API behind the page. A log that shows entries is not a log that resists deletion. Acceptance criteria have to be written as claims someone tries to break (D). Call the API without the factor, clear the log as an administrator, and see whether the attempt is refused and recorded.
Test the requirement, not the feature that claims to satisfy it.
questionsV2.recallLine: Acceptance testing demonstrated that each security control was present, yet a bypass and a log-clearing flaw survived. Which testing weakness MOST explains both?

optionsShort.A: Supplier staff ran the tests
optionsShort.B: Requirements list too short
optionsShort.C: No retesting after go-live
optionsShort.D: Controls checked for presence, not challenged

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: The closest rival, and worth fixing. A demonstration of presence would have passed both controls whoever ran it.

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Misreads the problem. The two requirements were on the list and were tested, badly.

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: A real gap in ongoing assurance that would have caught these flaws two months later at best.

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-2 Control Assessments
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-11 Developer Testing and Evaluation

questionsV2.question: Selbridge Water must open a new customer billing portal on 1 April, the date its regulator set for a tariff change; the date does not move. The internal delivery team works in two-week iterations, and eight weeks out its burn-down shows about a quarter more scope than it can finish. When this happened on the last program, the team dropped the work nobody was asking for, which turned out to be the authorization test suite and the audit-logging story. Which practice would BEST protect the security of what ships?

options.A: Add contractors to the team for the remaining eight weeks so that the full scope can be delivered.
options.B: Write the security requirements into each story's definition of done, so scope cuts remove features and not controls.
options.C: Ask the regulator for a four-week extension so that the outstanding security work can be completed.
options.D: Book a penetration test for the week after launch and fix what it finds in the next iteration.

questionsV2.explanation:
In an iteration-based method the date and the team are fixed and scope is the variable, so the question is what gets dropped. Security work goes first by default, because no user is asking for it, and the last program shows exactly that pattern. Put the security criteria inside the definition of done (B) and they leave the negotiable pile: a story either meets them or is not finished, and the cut falls on whole features.
Decide what done means before the schedule decides it for you.
questionsV2.recallLine: A fixed regulatory launch date leaves a quarter more scope than the team can finish. Which practice BEST protects the security of what ships?

optionsShort.A: Add contractors to deliver the full scope
optionsShort.B: Security criteria inside the definition of done
optionsShort.C: Ask the regulator to move the date
optionsShort.D: Penetration test the week after launch

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Adds people to a late project, which usually slows it. Contractors joining with eight weeks left have the least context.

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Asks a regulator to move a date the stem says will not move, and spends the team's credibility on the answer.

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Accepts the flaws into production and schedules their discovery. A test after launch says what was shipped.

sources: NIST SP 800-218 v1.1 | PO.1 Define Security Requirements for Software Development
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 8.1.1 Development methodologies
